## 1. Divāseyyavinicchayakathā

In those mātikā terms, "divāseyyā" means sleeping during the day. Regarding the decision on sleeping during the day: Based on the statement (from the Parājika Pāḷi), "Bhikkhus, I allow a bhikkhu who is resting during the day to rest after closing the door," a bhikkhu who sleeps during the day must sleep after closing the door. Here, although it is not directly stated in the Pāḷi text that "this specific offense is incurred," the Aṭṭhakathā states that a dukkhaṭa offense is incurred by one who sleeps without closing [the door], because permission was given to sleep after closing the door when a case arose involving a fault from sleeping with the door open. The Elders, such as the Venerable Upāli, established this Aṭṭhakathā, having known the intention of the Blessed One. This point is also evident from the statement (in the Parivāra Pāḷi), "Certain offenses are incurred during the day, but not at night."

What kind of door must be closed, and what kind of door can be left unclosed? Only a revolving door (parivattakadvāra)—made by using any material such as wooden planks, bamboo slats, mats, or leaves to form a door-leaf, and inserting it into a lower socket and an upper ring—must be closed. Other types, such as a door with a wooden bolt or a thorn door as in cattle pens, a door with wheels like a village gate, a sliding door made by attaching two or three wheels to planks or screens (kiṭikā), a trapdoor/shutter as in shops, a bamboo-arm door made in leaf-roofed huts by weaving bamboo strips in two or three places, or a cloth-curtain door—such doors do not need to be closed. For a bhikkhu holding an alms-bowl, only the cloth-curtain door does not cause an offense when opening it; opening the remaining types of doors results in an offense. However, for a bhikkhu wishing to sleep during the day, an offense is incurred only if the revolving door (parivattakadvāra) is not closed. For the remaining types of doors, there is no offense whether one sleeps with them closed or unclosed. Nevertheless, sleeping with them closed is the duty (vatta) to be performed.

To what extent is a revolving door considered closed? It is called closed if the small or large bolts are fastened. Furthermore, it is acceptable if only the small bolt is fastened, or only the large bolt is fastened, or if it is just placed to touch the doorpost. Even if it does not quite touch, it is acceptable. At the very least, by way of arrangement, it is acceptable if it is left unclosed only to the extent that a head cannot enter. If it is a place used by many people, one may sleep after telling a bhikkhu or a sāmaṇera, "Friend, please watch the door."

Furthermore, if bhikkhus are sitting while sewing robes or doing some other work, one may sleep with the thought, "These bhikkhus will watch the door." In the Kurundī Aṭṭhakathā, it is said that one may also sleep with the thought of a lay follower (upāsaka), thinking, "This upāsaka will watch." It is stated that it is not proper to sleep while only a bhikkhunī or a woman is present. This statement is very appropriate. Thus, in all Aṭṭhakathā traditions, the Theravāda and the Aṭṭhakathā tradition should be taken as the standard as stated later.

If the lower socket or the upper ring of the door is broken, or if one is unable to close it, it is not necessary to close it. Or, if one is unable to close it because piles of bricks, earth, etc., for new construction are placed inside the doorway, or because scaffolding has been erected—if such obstacles exist, it is proper to sleep without closing [the door].
3:
It is also permissible to lie down with the intention, "These monks will guard the door." In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is stated: "It is permissible to lie down after either asking a lay devotee (upāsaka) or intending, 'This lay devotee will guard it'; but it is not permissible to lie down after asking a bhikkhunī or a woman (mātugāma)." This statement is very appropriate. Thus, in all cases, whatever Theravāda opinion or Commentarial opinion (Aṭṭhakathāvāda) is mentioned later should be taken as the standard.

Furthermore, if the lower socket or the upper pivot of the door is broken or removed, so that it cannot be closed; or if for the purpose of new work, a pile of bricks or a heap of mud etc. is placed inside the doorway; or if scaffolding is erected such that it cannot be closed—in the presence of such obstacles, it is permissible to lie down even without closing the door. If there is no door leaf at all, it is simply a permissible opportunity. One sleeping on an upper floor should lie down after pulling up the ladder. If there is a hatch at the top of the ladder, one should lie down after closing it. One sleeping in a chamber should lie down after closing either the chamber door or the porch door, whichever is applicable. If in a house with a single wall, doors are made on both sides for use, both doors must be closed. Even in a three-storied palace (pāsāda), the door must certainly be closed. If many monks returning from the alms round enter a palace like the Lohapāsāda for the daytime rest, the Elder of the Saṅgha should enter and lie down either after telling the gatekeeper, "Guard the door," or after intending, "Guarding the door is the duty of this gatekeeper." Monks down to the most junior (saṅghanavaka) should do the same. For those entering first, it is also permissible to intend, "Guarding the door is the duty of those who enter later." There is an offense for those who lie down inside a chamber or outside with an unclosed door without asking or without such intention. Even when lying down in a chamber or outside, it is certainly permissible to lie down after intending, "Guarding the door is the duty of the gatekeeper at the main gate." Thus, even one lying down in an open space in places like the Lohapāsāda must certainly close the door.

The summary here is: this daytime rest is spoken of regarding a place enclosed by some sort of fence and having a door. Therefore, a monk lying down in any place with a door—whether in the open, at the foot of a tree, or in a pavilion—must lie down only after closing the door. If it is a large courtyard like the precinct of the Mahābodhi or the Lohapāsāda, which is a place where many people frequent, and where the door does not remain closed even if shut, or where people climb over the wall because they cannot get through the door, then there is no duty of closing the door. A monk who lies down at night having opened the door and gets up when the dawn rises commits no offense. If one wakes up and sleeps again, there is an offense. If a monk lies down at night without closing the door, intending only "I will get up when the dawn rises," if he gets up as intended, (there is no offense).
4:
If one sleeps again after waking up, there is an offense. If a monk, having determined, "I will get up when the dawn rises," lies down at night without closing the door, even if he gets up exactly at the determined time, there is an offense for that monk. However, in the Mahāpaccari, it is stated: "One who sleeps in this manner is not exempt even from the dukkaṭa offense of disrespect (anādariya)."

If a monk, having stayed awake for much of the night or having traveled a long distance, being exhausted during the day, sits on a couch and falls into a deep sleep without lifting his feet from the ground, there is no offense for him. If, while falling asleep, he unknowingly places his feet upon the couch, there is indeed an offense. For a monk who sleeps while sitting without leaning back, there is no offense. Also, if a monk, while walking [in meditation] to dispel sleepiness, falls down and gets up immediately, there is no offense for him. However, if he falls down and sleeps right there without getting up, there is an offense for him.

Who is exempt and who is not? In the Mahāpaccari, it is first stated: "Only one who sleeps lying on one side is exempt. One who sleeps having lifted his feet from the ground, or one possessed by a yakkha, or one who is unconscious, is not exempt." In the Kurundaṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: "Only one who is made to lie down after being bound is exempt." In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is said: "If a monk, while walking [in meditation], faints and falls, and sleeps right there, no offense is apparent because it is beyond his control. However, the teachers do not say so; therefore, there is indeed an offense," said the Elder Mahāpaduma. Only these two persons are truly exempt from the offense: one who is possessed by a yakkha and one who is made to lie down after being bound.

## In the Palimuttakavinayavinicchayasangaha,
## The Discussion on the Decision regarding Sleeping during the Day is finished.
## 2. Discussion on the Decision regarding Requisites
Requisites (parikkhāra) means the requisites of a recluse. Therein, this is the decision regarding allowable and unallowable requisites: Some people make palm-leaf umbrellas, sewing them either inside or outside with five-colored thread to make the color smooth and beautiful; doing so is not allowable. If sewn with thread of a single color, such as blue or yellow, or any unspecified single color, either inside or outside
5:
It is allowable to sew (an umbrella) and to bind the tip of the umbrella handle to make it firm. Such binding is allowable only for the purpose of making it firm, not for the sake of beauty. It is not allowable to carve patterns such as crocodile teeth (makara-dantaka) or half-moons on the leaves of the umbrella. On the umbrella handle, ornaments such as a pot-shape (ghaṭaka) or a beast-figure (vāḷarūpaka), like those on house pillars, are not allowable. Even if incised lines are made with a lathe tool along the entire handle, those lines are not allowable. A pot-shape or a beast-figure must be broken off before use. Incised lines must also be removed by grinding, or the handle must be wrapped with thread. However, it is allowable to make a mushroom-shape at the knob of the handle (the base). To prevent the umbrella from moving due to the wind, they hold the center of the umbrella with small cords and tie them to the handle; at that point of tying, they carve an incised line like a bracelet, and that line is allowable.

For the purpose of decorating the robe, they sew with threads of various colors to resemble a centipede and place an additional border (āgantukapaṭṭa); they also perform other various fancy needlework. All such things, such as making patterns of barley-corn, chain-links, or mallets at the corners or along the edges of the robe, are not allowable; only ordinary needlework (plain sewing) is allowable. They make the ends of the button-fastener (gaṇṭhikapaṭṭaka) and the loop-fastener (pāsakapaṭṭaka) eight-sided or sixteen-sided. On those fasteners, they display shapes of shrines (agghiya), stakes, mallets, etc., or carve crab-eye patterns (kakkaṭakkhī); all these are not allowable; only a four-sided shape is allowable. Small beads of thread sewn at the corners of the robe are allowable if they are difficult to discern once the robe is dyed.

It is not allowable to put the robe into sour gruel (kañjika), flour-paste, etc. However, it is allowable for the purpose of washing away hand-dirt or needle-dirt after the robe is sewn, and for washing when the robe is soiled. It is not allowable to put perfumes for fragrance, lac-resin for redness, or oil for durability into the dye.

Regarding dyes: excluding turmeric (haliddī), all root-dyes are allowable. Excluding jackfruit-wood (kaṇṭakarucckha) and madder (mañjiṭṭhā), all trunk-dyes are allowable. Tungahāra is a type of thorny tree, and the dye from its trunk is the color of yellow orpiment (haritāla-vaṇṇa). Excluding lodh-bark (lodda) and kaṇḍula-bark, all bark-dyes are allowable. Excluding henna-leaves (allipatta) and indigo-leaves (nīlipatta), all leaf-dyes are allowable. However, it is allowable to dye a cloth previously used by laypeople once with indigo-leaves for the sake of durability. Excluding flame-of-the-forest flowers (kiṃsuka) and safflower (kusumbha), all flower-dyes are allowable. Regarding fruit-dyes, there is no fruit-dye that is not allowable (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 344).

After dyeing the robe, it should not be rubbed for a sheen with a conch-shell, a gem, or anything else. One should not kneel on the ground, hold it with the hands, and scrub it even in the dye-trough. Placing it in the dye-trough or on a plank, having someone hold the ends, and striking it with the hand...
6:
...is allowable for the purpose of striking it with the hand; however, this striking should not be done with a clenched fist. The ancient Elders did not even place it in the dye-trough. One person stands holding the robe while another places it on his hands and strikes it with his hand. The corner-thread (kaṇṇasuttaka) of the robe is not allowable; it must be cut off after dyeing. However, as for the corner-thread allowed by the Blessed One saying, 'Bhikkhus, I allow a corner-thread' (Mahāvagga 344), that should be made into a loop at the edge of the border and tied for the purpose of hanging it on a rack during the time of dyeing. On the button-fastener (gaṇṭhika), incised lines or small beads for the sake of beauty are not allowable; they must be removed before use.

Making incised lines with a lathe tool on the inside or outside of an alms bowl or a bowl-vessel is not allowable. Placing the bowl on a lathe, polishing it, and firing it with the intention, 'I will make it the color of a gem (emerald),' is not allowable; however, the color of oil is allowable. Decorative figures of beasts, etc., on the base-rim of the bowl are not allowable, but crocodile-tooth patterns (makara-dantaka) are allowable.

Incised lines on the top, bottom, or the body of a water filter (dhamakaraṇa) are not allowable; however, a circular incised line on the rim of the filter's opening is allowable.

For the sake of decorating the waistband (kāyabandhana), plaiting with double-threads in various places or making crab-eye patterns (kakkaṭakkhī) appear is not allowable. However, plaiting with double-threads at both ends to make the base of the fringes firm is allowable. On the fringes, it is not allowable to make any fancy figures such as a pot-shape, a crocodile-mouth, or a water-snake's head. A waistband plaited with patterns of elephant-eye-rings or flower-garlands in various places is also not allowable. It is allowable to plait it straight, making patterns of fish-bones (macchakaṇṭaka), date-palm leaves (khajjūripattaka), or smooth strips (maṭṭhakapaṭṭika). A single fringe for the waistband is allowable; two, three, or even four are allowable; beyond that, they are not allowable. A single-cord waistband is allowable. A waistband in the shape of a necklace (pāmanga) is not allowable even if it is a single cord. However, fringes are allowable even if they are in the shape of a necklace. If many cords are gathered together and wrapped continuously with a single cord so that there are no gaps, it should not be called a 'multi-cord' waistband, and it is allowable.

On the waistband-buckle (vidha), any fancy figures such as the eight auspicious symbols (aṭṭhamaṅgala) are not allowable; only a simple boundary line is allowable. They make a pot-shape at both ends of the buckle for the sake of firmness; this too is allowable.

On a collyrium tube (añjanī), fancy figures such as the shapes of women, men, quadrupeds, or birds, or various patterns such as flower-work, vine-work, crocodile-teeth, cow-urine-line patterns, or half-moons are not allowable. By grinding or...
7: Alternatively, it may be used by breaking it or by wrapping it with thread so that its [original] form is not apparent. A collyrium pot (añjanī) is allowable if it is straight and has four, eight, or sixteen sides. Two or three circular lines at the bottom of that collyrium pot are allowable; a single circular line at the neck for the purpose of tying the lid is also allowable. Decorative work (vaṇṇamaṭṭhakamma) on a collyrium rod (añjanīsalākā) is not allowable. Decorative work made with threads of various colors on a collyrium pot bag is also not allowable. The same rule applies to a key-case (kuñcikakosaka). Decorative work on a key (kuñcikā) or on a razor-sheath (sipāṭikā) is not allowable. However, sewing anything with thread of a single color is allowable. On small knives such as an awl (ārakaṇṭaka), large beads or other decorative work are not allowable; however, a demarcating line at the neck is allowable. On a razor or a small lancet (pipphalika), it is not allowable to raise anything like a bead or a boil-like protrusion; however, a demarcating line on the handle is allowable. They make nail-cutters curved (valitaka); therefore, such a curved nail-cutter is allowable. On a fire-drill (uttarāraṇi), a drill-press (araṇidhanuka), or an upper pressing-stick (upari-pellanadaṇḍaka), decorative work such as floral designs (mālākamma) is not allowable. There is a hub in the middle of the pressing-stick; only a line demarcating that hub is allowable. They make needle-pliers (sūcisaṇḍāsa) to hold and rub needles; decorative work such as a Makara-mouth (makaramukha) is not allowable on them. There should only be an opening for the purpose of gripping the needle; that opening is allowable. On a small billhook for cutting tooth-sticks (dantakaṭṭhacchedanavāsi), decorative work is not allowable; it is allowable to bind it with allowable metal on both sides to make it four-sided or eight-sided. On a walking staff (kattaradaṇḍa), decorative work is not allowable; one or two circular lines at the bottom and a mushroom-bud shape at the top are allowable. In oil containers made of horn, bamboo, gourd, or castor-seed kernel, all decorative work is allowable, except for figures of women and men. On couches (mañca), stools (pīṭha), mattresses (bhisi), pillows (bimbohana), floor coverings, foot-wiping rugs, walkway mats, brooms, waste baskets, dyeing vats, water ladles, water pots, foot-scrubbers (pādakathalikā), wooden stools, circular bowl-supports, rod-supports, bowl-lids, palm-leaf fans, and bamboo fans—on all these items, all decorative work such as floral designs is allowable. In a dwelling (senāsana), decorative work made even with various jewels is allowable on door-panels, window-shutters, and so on. In a dwelling, there is nothing prohibited except for a 'conflicting dwelling' (viruddhasenāsana).
8:
Conflicting lodgings (viruddhasenāsana). A conflicting lodging refers to a dwelling built by monks who are favorites of the king (shameless ones) within the boundary (sīmā) of other monks. Therefore, those who build such a dwelling should be told: "Do not build a dwelling within our boundary." If they continue to build, disregarding the advice, they should be told again: "Do not do this; do not create an obstacle to our Uposatha and Pavāraṇā; do not break our unity; even if your dwelling is built, it will not remain in the place where it is built."

If they continue to build by force, when the virtuous (lajjī) followers of those boundary-owners become numerous and a righteous decision can be obtained, then they should be ordered: "Take away your dwelling." If they take it away after being ordered up to three times, it is well. If they do not take it away, except for the Bodhi tree and the shrine (cetiya), the remaining buildings should be dismantled. However, this should not be done in a way that makes them useless; rather, the roofing, rafters, bricks, etc., should be removed in order, and they should be ordered: "Take away your building materials."

If they take them away, it is well. If they do not take them away, and those building materials rot due to frost, rain, wind, or sun, or are stolen by thieves, or are burnt by fire, the monks who are the owners of the boundary are not at fault. It is not permissible to accuse them, saying, "You have destroyed our materials," or "They are of great value to you." The dismantling done by the monks who own the boundary is indeed well done.

If a monk who is learned and expert in the Vinaya sees another monk traveling with an unallowable requisite and causes it to be cut or destroyed, he is not at fault. That monk who destroys it should neither be accused nor reminded of the fault. It is not permissible to say to that monk, "This requisite of mine has been destroyed by you; give it to me."

## Thus in the Palimuttakavinayavinicchayasangaha,
## The Discussion on the Decision regarding Requisites is finished.
## 3. Discussion on the Decision regarding Medical Treatment, etc.
Among medical treatment, chanting paritta, and social hospitality, this decision regarding medical treatment should first be noted. One should not provide medical treatment to any outsider who comes; if one does, one incurs a dukkaṭa offense. However, medical treatment may be provided to the five fellow practitioners: monks, bhikkhunīs, sikkhamānās, sāmaṇeras, and sāmaṇerīs...
9:
## 3. Bhesajjādikaraṇavinicchayakathā
The discussion regarding the decision on requisites in the Vinayasaṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā, which is a compendium of Vinaya decisions not found in the Pāḷi Canon, is finished here.

## 3. Bhesajjādikaraṇavinicchayakathā
Regarding medicine, the chanting of protective verses (paritta), and applications, this decision concerning medical treatment should be noted first. One should not provide medical treatment to any stranger who happens to come; if one does, one commits an offense of dukkhaṭa. Those who should be given medicine are the five co-religionists (sahadhammika): monks, nuns, sikkhamānās, sāmaṇeras, and sāmaṇerīs. Indeed, it is not proper to refrain from treating them, as they possess equal virtue (sīla), faith (saddhā), and wisdom (paññā), and are engaged in the three trainings (sikkhā). A monk who provides treatment should use their own medicine if they have it. If they do not, he should use his own. If he does not have any himself, he should seek it through the duties of the alms-round or from relatives and those who have invited him (pavārita). If it cannot be found, he should bring it even through an improper intimation (viññatti) for the sake of the sick person and treat them.

16. It is also proper to treat five others: mother, father, those who attend to the mother and father, one's own attendant (veyyāvaccakara), and the candidate for ordination (paṇḍupalāsa). A paṇḍupalāsa is one who, aspiring for ordination, resides in the monastery as long as his bowl and robes are being prepared. Among them, if the mother and father are self-sufficient and do not desire help, one may refrain from acting. However, even if they are in the position of royalty but still desire help, one must not refrain. If they desire medicine, it should be given; if they do not know how to prepare it, it should be prepared and given. For all of them, medicine should be sought in the same manner as mentioned for the five co-religionists. If the mother is brought to the monastery and cared for, all services must be performed without touching her body; food and snacks should be given with one's own hand. As for the father, he should be attended to by bathing and massaging with one's own hand, just as one would care for a sāmaṇera. The same should be done for those who attend to and care for one's mother and father. A veyyāvaccakara is one who takes wages to cut wood in the forest or performs any other work; if a disease arises in him, he should be treated until his relatives arrive. For one who relies on a monk and performs all tasks (bhikkhunissitaka), he must certainly be treated. In the case of a paṇḍupalāsa, one should act as one would toward a sāmaṇera.

17. It is also proper to treat ten other persons: elder brother, younger brother, elder sister, younger sister, younger stepmother, elder stepmother, younger stepfather, elder stepfather, paternal aunt, and maternal uncle. In treating them, one should only take their own medicine and prepare it for them. However, if they do not have enough and request, "Venerable sir, please give us your property, we will repay you," it should be given as a temporary loan (tāvakālika). Even if they do not request it, one may give it by saying, "We have medicine, take it as a temporary loan," or by thinking...
10:
...or by thinking, "When they have property, they will give it back." If they return it, it should be accepted. If they do not return it, it should not be demanded. Except for these ten relatives, one should not do so for others.

For the descendants of these ten relatives up to the seventh generation, for a monk who brings the four requisites [for them], it does not constitute improper intimation (viññatti); for a monk who treats them, it does not constitute medical practice (vejjakamma) or the offense of corrupting families (kuladūsaka). If a brother's wife, a younger brother's wife, an elder sister's husband, or a younger sister's husband is ill, it is proper to treat them if they are relatives. If they are not relatives, one should give by intending it for the brother, younger brother, elder sister, or younger sister, saying, "Give this for your care." Alternatively, one should give by intending it for their children, saying, "Give this to your parents." In this manner, the decision should be understood in all cases.

When wishing to have medicine brought from the forest by sāmaṇeras for their sake, it should be brought by sāmaṇeras who are relatives. If using sāmaṇeras who are not relatives, one should have it brought by saying it is for oneself, and then give it. Those sāmaṇeras should also bring it as a duty, saying, "We are bringing this for the preceptor (upajjhāya)." If the preceptor's parents come to the monastery while ill, and the preceptor has gone to another direction, the resident pupil (saddhivihārika) should give the preceptor's medicine. If the preceptor's medicine is not available, he should give his own medicine, dedicating it to the preceptor. If he does not have any himself, he should seek it as mentioned before and give it, making it the preceptor's property. The preceptor should also act in the same way toward the parents of the saddhivihārika. This same method applies to the teacher (ācariya) and the pupil (antevāsika). Furthermore, if any other person—whether a guest, a thief, a defeated king, a poor person abandoned by relatives, or a traveler—enters the monastery while ill, they should all be treated without expecting any gain.

If there is a faithful family that supports the Saṅgha of monks with the four requisites and is like a mother or father, and someone there is ill, and they say out of intimacy, "Venerable sir, please prepare and give medicine," it should not be given or done. However, knowing the allowable (kappiya) way, if they ask, "Venerable sir, what medicine is used for such and such a disease?", it is proper to say, "They take this and that to make it." But if they ask, "Venerable sir, my mother is ill, please tell me the medicine first," it should not be told directly. However, through mutual conversation...
11:
“Friends, what medicine did they use for this illness of the monk named so-and-so?” Thus, they should ask one another. “Venerable sir, they used this and that medicine,” (should be the reply). Having heard that, if another person (a layman) provides medical treatment for his mother, it is allowable. It is said that when an illness arose in the queen of King Vasabha, Mahāpaduma Thera, being asked by a certain woman who came to him, did not say “I do not know,” but spoke in this manner with the monks. Having heard that, those women provided medical treatment for the queen. When the illness was cured, they filled a medicine basket along with three robes and three hundred kahāpaṇas, brought it, placed it at the feet of the Elder, and said, “Venerable sir, please perform a flower offering.” The Elder, saying “This is the portion for the teachers,” had it accepted in an allowable way and performed the flower offering. This is how one should conduct oneself regarding medical matters.

19. Regarding the chanting of Paritta, however, if it is said, “Venerable sir, please make a Paritta for the sick person,” it should not be done. But if it is said, “Please chant the Paritta,” then it should be chanted. If one thinks, “People do not know (the monks' practice); if it is not done, they will become remorseful,” then it should be done. If they say, “Please make and give Paritta water and Paritta thread,” one should only stir their water with the hand and rub the thread before giving it. If one gives water from the monastery or one's own thread, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If people bring water and thread, place them in front, sit down, and say, “Please chant the Paritta,” it should be chanted. If they do not know (how to do this), they should be told. If they pour water on the feet of the sitting monks, place the thread, and leave saying, “Make the Paritta, chant the Paritta,” the feet should not be moved. This is because people tend to become remorseful.

Even in the village, if they send word to the monastery for a sick person, saying “Please chant the Paritta,” one should go and chant. In the village, at the royal palace and so on, if an illness or a calamity arises and they invite and ask for a chant, the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta and others should be chanted. Even if they send word saying, “Please come and give the precepts to the sick person, preach the Dhamma,” or “Please come to the royal palace or the minister's house and give the precepts, preach the Dhamma,” one should go and give the precepts and preach the Dhamma.

If they invite saying, “Please come to be an entourage for the dead,” one should not go. It is allowable to go for the purpose of meditation, thinking, “By seeing the cemetery and seeing the corpse, I will gain mindfulness of death (maraṇassati).” Even though it is said, “There is no offense if there is no intention to kill even if death occurs when striking,” one should not strike a person possessed by a non-human being (amanussa) just with that much...
12: ...(the precepts) are given. One should tie either a palm leaf or a Paritta thread to the hand or the foot. Paritta suttas such as the Ratana Sutta should be chanted. A Dhamma talk should be given, saying, “Do not harm a virtuous monk.” Or the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta should be chanted. Here, the preliminary procedure for the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta should be known. Indeed, the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should not be chanted first. The Metta Sutta, Dhajagga Sutta, and Ratana Sutta—these suttas should be chanted for seven days. If (the spirit) releases, it is good. If it does not release, the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should be chanted. The monk chanting that sutta should not eat flour-based food or meat, and should not stay in a cemetery. Why? Because non-human beings (amanussa) find an opportunity. The place for chanting Paritta should be smeared with fresh cow dung, and a clean seat should be prepared there for sitting. When the monk who will chant the Paritta is brought from the monastery to the house, he should be escorted by those carrying wooden weapons. He should not sit and chant in the open air; he should sit with the doors and windows closed, surrounded by those holding weapons, and chant with a mind of loving-kindness (metta) foremost. First, the precepts should be administered, and the Paritta should be performed for the person established in virtue (sīla). If it is still not possible to release (the spirit) in this way, the person should be taken to the monastery, made to lie down on the pagoda courtyard, offerings of seats should be made, lamps should be lit, the pagoda courtyard should be swept, and a discourse on blessings (mangala) should be given. An announcement should be made for all monks to assemble. There is usually a large tree in the grove near the monastery; word should be sent there, saying, “The Saṅgha of monks awaits your arrival.” No one can fail to come to the place where all assemble. Then, the person possessed by the non-human being should be asked, “What is your name?” When the name is told, he should be addressed by that name: “So-and-so spirit, the merit from these flowers, scents, seat offerings, and alms-food is shared with you. The Saṅgha of monks has preached the Mahāmangala discourse as a gift to you; out of respect for the Saṅgha, release this person.” Thus he should be asked to release. If he does not release, the deities (devas) should be informed: “May you deities know, this non-human being does not obey our words; we shall exercise the authority of the Buddha.” Then the Paritta should be chanted. This is the preliminary procedure for laypeople. If, however, a monk is possessed by a non-human being, the seats should be washed, and an announcement should be made for all the Saṅgha to assemble...
13:
After sharing the merit of offerings such as scents and flowers, the Paritta should be recited; this is the preparatory duty (parikamma) of the monks. In this way, the practice regarding Paritta should be understood.
Regarding hospitality (paṭisanthāra), this is the decision (from the Pārājika-aṭṭhakathā, Vol. 2, pp. 185-187): To whom should untouched (anāmaṭṭha) alms-food be given, and to whom should it not be given? First, it should be given to parents. Even if that alms-food is worth ten thousand kahāpaṇas, it does not constitute the destruction of a gift given out of faith. It should also be given to those who attend to one's parents, to those who perform services for oneself, and to a candidate for novicehood (paṇḍupalāsa). Among them, it is allowable to give to the candidate for novicehood by placing it in the bowl. Except for that candidate for novicehood, it is not allowable to give it in the bowl even to one's own parents who are laypeople. This is because the requisites of those who have gone forth are to be held in high esteem like a shrine (cetiya) by laypeople. Furthermore, untouched alms-food should be given to a thief who aspires to kingship or to a king who has come to one. Why? Because if it is not given, they may become resentful, saying 'They do not give,' and if it is given after being touched (partially eaten), they may become angry, saying 'They give us leftovers.' When angry, they might even take one's life or cause harm to the Dispensation (sāsana). Here, the story of Coranāga, who wandered about aspiring to kingship, should be told. In this way, the practice regarding untouched alms-food should be understood.
To whom should hospitality (paṭisanthāra) be shown, and to whom should it not be shown? Hospitality should indeed be shown to anyone who has arrived at the monastery, whether a guest, a poor person, a thief, or a ruler. How? Seeing a guest who has arrived at the monastery with exhausted provisions, water should be given, saying, 'Please drink water,' and oil for massaging the feet should be given. To one who arrives at the proper time, rice gruel or a meal should be given; to one who arrives at the improper time (after noon), if there is raw rice, raw rice should be given. Even to one who arrives at an unseasonable time, one should not say, 'Go away'; a place to sleep should be given. All this should be done without any expectation of return. One should not harbor the thought: 'People are donors of the four requisites; if treated with such kindness, they will be repeatedly inspired and return the favor.' To thieves, even property belonging to the Saṅgha should be given. To illustrate the benefits of hospitality, many stories such as the story of Coranāga, the story of King Mahānāga who went to Jambudīpa with his younger brother, the story of the four ministers in the kingdom of King Pitu, and the story of Abhaya the thief are told in detail in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā.
Among those stories, this is the illustration of one story: It is said that in the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka), a thief named Abhaya, with a retinue of five hundred, established a camp in a certain place and lived there, terrorizing the surrounding area of three yojanas. The people of Anurādhapura did not dare to cross the Kadamba River. On the road to Cetiya Mountain, the travel of people...
14:
(The bandit) lived causing terror. The residents of Anurādhapura did not dare to cross the Kadamba River, and the movement of people on the road to Cetiyagiri was cut off. Then one day, the bandit went with the intention, "I will loot Cetiyagiri." The monastery attendants, seeing him, reported it to the Elder Abhaya, the reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya (Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya Thera). The Elder asked, "Is there ghee, molasses, and so forth?" "There is, venerable sir," they replied. "Give them to the bandits." "Is there rice?" he asked again. "Venerable sir, there is rice brought for the Sangha, as well as cooked vegetables and dairy products (gorasa)," they replied. "Prepare the meal completely and give it to the bandits," he instructed. The monastery attendants did accordingly. After the bandits had eaten the meal, they asked, "Who performed this hospitality?" "It was performed by our master, the Elder Abhaya," they said. The bandits went to the Elder, paid homage, and said, "We came with the intention, 'We will loot and take the property of the Sangha and the shrine,' but because of this hospitality of yours, we are inspired. From this day forth, let the righteous protection of the monastery be our responsibility; let the townspeople come and give alms, and let them worship the shrine." From then on, when the townspeople came to give alms, the bandits met and protected them right at the riverbank and escorted them to the monastery; they also remained protecting those giving alms at the monastery. They (the townspeople) also gave the leftovers of the monks to the bandits. When it was time to leave, those bandits escorted them back to the riverbank before returning.

Then one day, a critical discussion arose among the community of monks: "The Elder, by his own authority, gave the property of the Sangha to bandits." The Elder caused an assembly of the Sangha to be held and said, "The bandits came saying, 'We will loot and take the regular provisions of the Sangha and the property of the shrine.' At that time, I thought, 'They shall not take these properties,' and performed this much hospitality. Let all that was given be gathered together and valued. For that reason, let the property that remained unlooted also be gathered together and valued." Then, even when everything given by the Elder was summed up, it did not equal the value of a single excellent embroidered rug in the shrine room. Thereupon they said, "The hospitality performed by the Elder was well done; it is not proper to accuse or remind him of it. There is no obligation for replacement nor is there any act of theft." Thus, realizing that hospitality is of great benefit, it should be performed by a wise monk.

## Thus ends the Discussion on the Decision regarding Medicines and so forth

15:
## 4. Viññatti-vinicchaya-kathā

Viññatti means requesting. Regarding this requesting, there is this decision (from the Pārājikakaṇḍa Commentary): It is not allowable to ask for a man for permanent acquisition (as a slave); it is allowable to ask, "Please give a man for the purpose of companionship or for the purpose of performing work." It is certainly allowable to ask for the manual labor (hatthakamma) to be performed by a man, which is described as the work done by a man.

Manual labor is not a material object; therefore, with the exception of that manual labor, all other work of hunters, fishermen, and so forth, which remains from their own trade, is permissible (kappiya). Whether asked, "Venerable sirs, why have you come? What work is there?" or not asked, it is allowable to request; there is no fault due to the reason of requesting (viññatti). However, hunters and the like should not be asked for their own trade, nor should they be asked without specifying, such as "Please give manual labor." For if requested in this way, they might say, "Very well, venerable sir," and after sending the monks away, they might kill animals and bring them. However, one should request by specifying, "There is something to be done at the monastery; please give manual labor for that monastery work." It is certainly allowable to ask for manual labor from a farmer or anyone else who is occupied with their own business, such as one taking tools like plowshares and plow-poles to plow, sow, or reap. If a certain person who eats leftovers or anyone else remains idle, talking useless talk or sleeping, it is allowable to employ them as desired, even without requesting, saying, "Hey man, come here, do this or do that."

To demonstrate the complete permissibility of manual labor, they state this method: If a monk wishes to have a palace-style dwelling (pāsāda) built, he should go to the houses of stone-masons for the sake of pillars and say, "Lay devotees, it is allowable to obtain manual labor." If they ask, "Venerable sir, what should be done?" he should say, "Stone pillars should be extracted from the ground and given." If they extract and give them, or if they give their own pillars that have already been extracted and laid down, it is allowable. Furthermore, if they say, "Venerable sir, we have no time to perform manual labor; please have someone else extract them, and we will give the wages for that person," it is allowable to have them extracted and then say, "Give the wages to the people who extracted the stone pillars." By this same method, for the sake of timber for the palace-style dwelling, one should go to carpenters; for bricks, to brick-makers; for roofing, to roofers; for painting work, to painters; for whatever purpose one has, one should go to those respective craftsmen and it is allowable to ask for manual labor. By means of requesting manual labor, it is allowable to accept everything obtained, whether through permanent acquisition or by providing food and wages. And when having things brought from the forest, one should only have those things brought that are ownerless.
16:
It is not only for one wishing to have a palace-style dwelling built; a monk wishing to have a couch, a stool, a bowl, a water-filter, a water-strainer (dhamakaraṇa), robes, and so forth made, should, upon obtaining wood, metal, thread, etc., approach those respective craftsmen and request manual labor in the same manner as already stated. By means of requesting manual labor, everything obtained, whether through permanent acquisition or by providing food and wages, should be accepted. However, if they do not wish to do it and expect food and wages, one should not give unallowable money (kahāpaṇa) and the like, but it is proper to seek rice and so forth through the duty of alms-round and offer them.

After having a bowl made by means of manual labor and having it fired in the same way, when entering the village for the sake of oil to coat the newly-fired bowl, if people bring gruel or rice, assuming "He has come for alms," the bowl should be covered with the hand. If a laywoman asks, "Venerable sir, what is the matter?" one should say, "The bowl is newly fired; there is a need for oil to coat it." If that laywoman says, "Venerable sir, please give it," and takes the bowl, coats it with oil, and then fills it with gruel or rice and offers it, this is not called requesting (viññatti); it is proper to accept it.

When monks go to the alms hall (āsanasālā) after wandering for alms early in the morning and stand because they do not see a seat, if the lay devotees see the monks standing and bring seats of their own accord, the monks should ask for permission (āpucchā) before leaving after sitting. Even if they go without asking for permission, there is no liability for loss (gīvā) if items are lost, but going after asking for permission is the proper practice. If the seats were brought because the monks said, "Bring seats," they must go only after asking for permission. For those who go without asking for permission, there is a breach of duty and liability for loss (gīvā) if items are lost. This same method applies to floor coverings, rugs, and so forth.

If there are many flies, one should say, "Bring a fly-whisk." If they bring neem branches and the like, they should be made allowable and then accepted. If the water vessel in the alms hall is empty, one should not say, "Take the water-strainer (dhamakaraṇa)." For if one puts a water-strainer into an empty vessel, it might break. However, it is proper to say, "Go to the river or the pond and bring water." One should not say, "Bring it from the house," nor should one use water brought from a house. In the alms hall or in the forest, if monks performing the meal-service have someone who is doing some work bring any leaves or fruits that are grown there, are ownerless, and are suitable as side dishes, it is proper to have them brought by means of manual labor and then consume them. However, shameless (alajjī) monks or novices should not be made to perform manual labor. This is the method regarding manual labor performed by a man.
17:
It is not allowable to have an ox brought from the place of those who are unrelated and have not given an invitation; for a monk who has it brought, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Even from the place of those who are related or have given an invitation, it is not allowable to ask for it permanently (by cutting off the root of ownership); however, it is allowable in all places on a temporary basis. An ox brought in this manner must be protected and cared for, and then returned to the owners. If the ox's leg or horn is broken, or if it is lost, and the owners accept the situation with forbearance, that is good and blameless. If they do not accept it, it becomes a debt. If they say, "We give it only to you (venerable sirs)," it should not be accepted. But if they say, "We give it to the monastery," one should say, "Tell the monastery attendants to look after it."

It is also not allowable to ask unrelated and uninvited persons, saying, "Give me a cart"; it is merely an intimation (viññatti) and one falls into an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). However, it is allowable from the place of those who are related or have given an invitation; it is allowable for temporary use, but after the work is done, it must be returned. If the rim (of the wheel) or such parts are broken, it must be repaired to its original state before returning; if it is lost, it becomes a debt. If they say, "We give it only to you (venerable sirs)," it is allowable to accept it as it is considered wooden property (dārubhaṇḍa). This same principle applies to billhooks, axes, hoes, and spades possessed by others, as well as to creepers and such. Intimation (viññatti) occurs only regarding creepers and such that are large enough to be considered heavy articles (garubhaṇḍa), but not for those smaller than that.

However, it is allowable to have any creeper or such brought that is not possessed by an owner. This is because intimation (viññatti) is said to occur only in places that are protected and guarded. Such intimation is entirely unallowable regarding the two requisites (robes and almsfood). Regarding the requisites for lodgings (senāsana), mere intimation such as "Bring this" or "Give this" is not allowable, but indirect talk (parikathā), hinting (obhāsa), and sign-making (nimittakamma) are allowable. In that context, for a monk who desires an Uposatha hall, a refectory, or any other lodging, speaking in this manner: "Indeed, in this place, it would be allowable to build such a lodging," or "It is suitable," or "It is appropriate," is called indirect talk (parikathā). Asking, "Lay followers, where do you live?" and when they reply, "Venerable sir, we live in a mansion (pāsāda)," saying, "Lay followers, is a mansion not allowable for monks?"—such speech is called hinting (obhāsa). Seeing people and stretching a rope or driving in stakes, and when asked, "Venerable sir, what is this work?" replying, "We will build a dwelling here"—performing such an act is called sign-making (nimittakamma). Regarding requisites for the sick (gilāna-paccaya), even intimation (viññatti) is allowable, let alone indirect talk and the others (which are certainly allowable).

## Thus ends the Discussion on the Decision regarding Intimation (Viññatti-vinicchaya-kathā)
## in the Pālimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-sangaha.
18:
## 5. Kulasangaha-vinicchaya-kathā

Kulasangaha means favoring lay supporters with flowers, fruits, and so on. Regarding this kulasangaha, there is this decision (Samantapāsādikā, Vol. 2, p. 431): For the sake of favoring lay supporters, it is not allowable to personally plant or cause to be planted small flower plants and such, to personally water them or cause them to be watered, to personally pluck flowers or cause them to be plucked, or to personally string them or cause them to be strung. In performing these acts, these five should be understood: inappropriate expression (akappiya-vohāra), appropriate expression (kappiya-vohāra), roundabout talk (pariyāya), hinting (obhāsa), and sign-making (nimittakamma).

Among these five, inappropriate expression (akappiya-vohāra) means: crushing or causing to be crushed green grass and plants; personally digging or causing a pit to be dug; personally planting or causing a flower plant to be planted; personally constructing or causing a dyke to be constructed; personally pouring or causing water to be poured; directing a water channel; pouring allowable water (free of insects); and pouring water used for washing hands, feet, face, or for bathing. Appropriate expression (kappiya-vohāra) means words such as: "Look after this tree," "Look after this pit," "Look after this flower plant," "Look after the water here," and straightening a dry channel that has no water. Roundabout talk (pariyāya) means words such as: "If a wise person has flower plants and such planted, they will soon be of benefit." Hinting (obhāsa) means standing while holding a hoe, spade, or flower plants. When novices and others see one standing thus, they think, "The Elder wishes to have this done," and they go and do it. Sign-making (nimittakamma) means bringing a hoe, spade, billhook, axe, water pot, etc., and placing them nearby.

All these five are unallowable in planting or causing to be planted for the sake of favoring lay supporters. However, for the sake of consuming the fruit, only the two—inappropriate expression and appropriate expression—are unallowable; the other three are allowable. In the Mahāpaccari, however, it is stated: "Appropriate expression is also allowable; and the fruit that is allowable for one's own consumption is also allowable for the sake of another person, the Saṅgha, or a Cetiya." For the sake of a monastery garden, a forest, or for shade, only inappropriate expression is unallowable; the rest are allowable. Not only are the rest allowable, but it is also allowable to straighten any channel, to pour allowable water, to bathe by making a bathing enclosure, and to discard water used for washing hands, feet, and face in that place. In the Mahāpaccari and the Kurundī, it is stated: "It is even allowable to personally plant in allowable soil." It is also allowable to consume the fruit of a tree planted or caused to be planted for the sake of a monastery garden and such.
19:
This is the detailed decision on offenses starting from the beginning. For a monk who plants a small flower plant in unallowable ground for the purpose of corrupting families (kula-dūsana), there is a Pācittiya offense and a Dukkaṭa offense. Likewise, if he has it planted using unallowable terminology, there is a Pācittiya and a Dukkaṭa. If he plants it or has it planted in allowable ground, there is only a Dukkaṭa offense. In both types of ground, if many plants are planted with a single command, there is only one Pācittiya with a Dukkaṭa, or one Dukkaṭa alone. There is no offense in having them planted with allowable terminology in either allowable or unallowable ground for the purpose of personal use. For a monk who plants by himself in unallowable ground for the purpose of a park, etc., or who has them planted with unallowable speech, there is a Pācittiya offense. This method is not well-analyzed in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, but it is analyzed in the Mahāpaccariya.

In the case of watering or having them watered, if it is done with unallowable (containing living beings) water, there is a Pācittiya offense in all instances. If watered with unallowable water for the purpose of corrupting families or personal use, there is also a Dukkaṭa. If watered with allowable water for those two purposes (kula-dūsana and personal use), there is a Dukkaṭa. Here, if he has them watered with allowable terminology for the purpose of personal use, there is no offense. In cases where an offense is incurred, the multiplicity of offenses should be understood according to the interruption of the stream of water and the multiplicity of efforts.

In picking flowers for the purpose of favoring families, there are Dukkaṭa and Pācittiya offenses according to the number of flowers; in other cases, there are only Pācittiya offenses. A monk who picks many flowers with a single effort should be made to undergo the offense according to the effort. In having them picked, if a person commanded once for the purpose of corrupting families picks many flowers, there is only one Pācittiya with a Dukkaṭa; in other cases, there is only a Pācittiya.

Regarding stringing flowers or having them strung, all six types of flower arrangements should be understood: Ganthima, Gopphima, Vedhima, Veṭhima, Pūrima, and Vāyima. Among these six, Ganthima (knotted) is to be understood in the case of blue lotuses, red lotuses, etc., which have stalks, or other flowers with long stems. A flower garland made by rubbing stalk against stalk or stem against stem is called Ganthima. It is not allowable for a monk or a bhikkhunī to make it themselves or to have it made with unallowable speech. However, it is allowable to have it made with allowable speech such as, "Know thus; if done this way, it would be beautiful; do it in such a way that these flowers do not fall off."

Gopphima (braided) refers to stringing flowers like jasmine, etc., using thread or fiber, in the manner of a single-sided or double-sided garland. Making fiber or rope double-ply and inserting stemless flowers like Kadamba (Nīpa) flowers in between and binding them in order is also called Gopphima. All Gopphima is unallowable according to the aforementioned method.
20:
Vedhima (piercing and stringing) refers to piercing and stringing flowers with stems like jasmine, etc., at the stem, or stemless flowers like Bakula, etc., through their own holes using needles, palm-leaf ribs, etc. This Vedhima is unallowable according to the previous method. Some people insert thorns or palm-leaf ribs into a banana trunk and place flowers by piercing them onto those thorns or ribs. Some do so on thorny branches. Some, for the purpose of making flower-umbrellas or flower-pinnacles, place flowers by piercing them onto thorns inserted into umbrellas and walls. Some do so on thorns fixed to the canopy above a Dhamma-seat. Some pierce flowers like Kaṇikāra with bamboo splints and make them like tiered umbrellas; all such actions are very coarse. For the purpose of piercing flowers, it is not allowable to fix thorns to the canopy of a Dhamma-seat, nor to pierce even a single flower with thorns, etc., nor to insert a flower into another flower.

However, there is no fault in inserting flowers into the holes of lattice canopies, turned pillars, wall-pegs (nāgadantaka), flower-receptacles, palm-leaf or palmyra-leaf balls, etc., or between clusters of Asoka flowers. This is because such insertion is not called Vedhima. The same method should be understood for the rope wound around a Dhamma-seat, etc.

Veṭhima (wrapping and stringing) is to be understood in flower-festoons and flower-handfuls. Some, when making a head-garland, wrap it with flowers to show a pot-like shape at the bottom. Some bind eight or ten lotuses, etc., with thread or fiber onto sticks to make lotus-handfuls (uppala-hatthaka) or paduma-lotus-handfuls; all these are unallowable according to the previous method. It is not allowable for novices to bind lotuses, etc., which have been pulled up and placed on the ground, into a bundle using a robe. However, it is allowable to bind those same flowers with fiber or a stick, or to make an aṃsabhaṇḍika (shoulder-bundle). An aṃsabhaṇḍika means taking both ends of the robe placed on the shoulder, making it into a bag-like bundle, and putting flowers into it; this is called an aṃsabhaṇḍika, and it is allowable to do so. When piercing a lotus leaf with skewers and wrapping lotuses with the leaf to take them, it is allowable to bind only the lotus leaf above the flowers; binding a stick below is not allowable.

Pūrima (overlapping the previous place) is to be understood in flower-garlands and flower-cloths. A monk who, when encircling a cetiya, a Bodhi tree, or a turned pillar with a flower-garland, brings it back and overlaps the previous place; by this much, it is called Pūrima. What then can be said of one who encircles it many times? When inserting through the gaps of wall-pegs (nāgadantaka) and carrying it, if he lets it hang and encircles the wall-peg again, that is also called Pūrima.
21:
## 
In a wall-peg (nagadantaka), it is allowable to insert a flower ring. When making a flower cloth (pupphapaṭa) with garlands, it is allowable to take a garland only once. If it is taken back again, it remains as it was before. All that is not allowable according to the previous method. However, if a flower string (pupphadāma) made of many garlands is obtained, it is allowable to bind it at the top of a seat and so on. For a very long garland, it is allowable to take it once, wrap it around, and then give it to another monk; it is allowable for that monk to do the same.

What is called 'vāyima' (woven/knitted) should be understood in the context of flower nets, flower cloths, and flower figures. For a monk making a flower net for a cetiya, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each mesh hole. The same rule applies to walls, umbrellas, Bodhi trees, pillars, and so on. As for a flower cloth, even if it is filled by others, it is not permitted to weave it. Figures such as elephants and horses are made with strung flowers; these also fall under the category of vāyima. According to the previous method, all these are not allowable. However, a monk who places flowers within a boundary set by others is allowed to make even elephant or horse figures. In the Mahāpaccari, eight types of flower arrangements are mentioned, including kalarambaka and aḍḍhacandaka.

Therein, kalarambaka refers to a flower string suspended like a water pot (ghaṭika) between half-moon shapes. Aḍḍhacandaka refers to a flower string wrapped in the shape of a half-moon. Both of these are included in the previous category. In the Kurundī, it is said: "Making a flower string by joining two or three garlands together is also vāyima." This also falls under the previous category here. Not only flower strings, but also strings made of flour and ball-shaped flower strings are mentioned in the Kurundī. A string made of kharapatta (rough-leaf) is also not to be made or caused to be made by monks or nuns because it is common to the training rule; however, it is allowable to speak words of allowance for the purpose of offerings in all places. Actions with the purpose of indirect suggestion are indeed allowable.

If a monk, either by himself or by having another bring it, or by calling or having another call, gives any flower belonging to himself to families for the sake of gaining their favor (kulasangaha), he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If he gives flowers belonging to others, it is also a dukkaṭa. If he gives with a mind of theft, the offense should be determined according to the value of the goods. This method also applies to flowers belonging to the Saṅgha. However, there is this distinction: for a monk who gives flowers designated for the lodgings (senāsana) as if he were the owner, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).

To whom is it allowable to give flowers, and to whom is it not? To mother and father, it is allowable to give, whether by bringing them oneself, having them brought, calling them, or having them called...
22:
...it is allowable; for other relatives, only by having them called. Even then, it is given for the purpose of worshipping the Triple Gem; it is not allowable to give to anyone for the purpose of decoration or for the purpose of worshipping the Sivalinga (Vishnu deity) and so on. If one has flowers brought for mother and father, they should be brought only by novice relatives. If others wish to bring them of their own accord, it is allowable.

A monk appointed by the Saṅgha as a flower-distributor is allowed to give a half-share (from the monks' portion) to novices who arrive at the time of distribution. In the Kurundī, it says, "a half-share to laypeople who have arrived"; in the Mahāpaccari, it says, "it is allowable to give a small amount (one-fourth)." If he is not appointed, he should give after asking permission from the Saṅgha.

Novices who have respect for their teachers and preceptors bring many flowers and arrange them in heaps; the elders, in the early morning, give to arriving co-residents (saddhivihārika) and so on, or to lay followers (upāsaka) and so on, saying, "You take this, you take this." This is not considered "giving flowers" (in the sense of social obligation). Monks who take flowers saying, "We will worship the cetiya," or those who are worshipping, give to those who arrive at various places for the purpose of worshipping the cetiya; this also is not considered "giving flowers."

Seeing lay followers worshipping with Calotropis (akka) flowers and so on, it is allowable to say, "Lay followers, there are Kaṇikāra flowers and so on at the monastery; take those flowers and worship." Monks, having performed flower offerings, enter the village for alms later in the day; when asked, "Venerable sirs, why have you entered so late?" they say, "There were many flowers at the monastery, and we were making offerings." People, learning that "there are many flowers at the monastery," take many kinds of food and snacks the next day, go to the monastery, perform flower offerings, and give gifts; this is allowable.

People request a "flower turn," saying, "Venerable sirs, we will make offerings on such-and-such a day," and arrive on the permitted day. The novices have already plucked and placed the flowers before they arrive. Those people, not seeing flowers on the trees, ask, "Venerable sirs, where are the flowers?" (The monks might say,) "The novices have plucked and placed them; you worship and then go, the Saṅgha will worship on another day." They worship, give gifts, and leave; this is allowable.

In the Mahāpaccari and Kurundī, it is said: "Elders are not permitted to have novices give them; if they themselves give those flowers to them, it is allowable. The elders should only say, 'The novices have plucked and placed them.'" If, having requested a flower turn, people arrive with gruel and food before the flowers are plucked and say to the novices, "Pluck and give them to us," it is allowable only for novice relatives to pluck and give. For non-relatives, the novices may lift them up and place them on a tree branch; they should not climb down and run away (while the people are plucking), but to pluck and give...
23:
It is allowable. If a certain Dhamma preacher (Dhammakathika) says, "Lay devotees, there are many flowers in the monastery; take gruel, rice, and so on, and perform a flower offering," it is stated in the Mahāpaccari and Kurundī commentaries that it is unallowable only for that specific Dhamma preacher. However, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated without distinction (for all monks) that "this is unallowable and should not be done."

It is allowable to give one's own fruit to parents and other relatives in the manner already mentioned. However, for a monk who gives for the sake of favoring families (kula-saṅgaha), it should be understood that offenses such as Dukkhaṭa are incurred regarding one's own fruit, others' fruit, Sangha-owned fruit, and fruit designated for lodgings, as per the manner already mentioned. It is allowable to give only one's own fruit to sick people, visiting officials, or those whose provisions are exhausted; this is not considered [the prohibited] "giving of fruit" (phaladāna). Even a monk appointed as a fruit distributor (phalabhājaka) is allowed to give half a portion [of a monk's share] to people who arrive during the distribution of fruit to the Sangha. If he is not appointed, he must give it after asking permission from the Sangha. In the Sangha's monastery (ārāma), an agreement (katikā) should be made either by the number of fruits or by the number of trees, such as: "From this monastery, four or five fruits should be given to sick people or others who request fruit as per the designation, or trees should be pointed out, saying 'It is permitted to take from here.'" However, one should not say, "The fruits on this tree are good, take from here." If one gives one's own siris-powder or any other astringent powder (kasāva) for the sake of favoring families, a Dukkhaṭa offense is committed. The decision regarding others' property and so on should be understood in the same manner as already mentioned. This is the distinction: tree bark protected and guarded by the Sangha is also heavy property (garubhaṇḍa). Regarding clay, tooth-sticks, bamboo, and leaves, knowing what constitutes heavy property, the decision should be understood in the same manner as mentioned for the powder.

Acting as a messenger for laypeople, which is the work of carrying news, is called "jaṅghapesaniya"; this should not be done. For a monk who carries a message for laypeople, a Dukkhaṭa offense is incurred for every step. For one who eats food obtained by depending on that work, a Dukkhaṭa offense is incurred for every swallow. Even if he did not take the message initially, but later thinks, "Now this is the village [mentioned by that person], I will now convey the message," and turns off the path to enter the village, a Dukkhaṭa offense is incurred for every step. For one who eats food obtained after conveying the message, a Dukkhaṭa offense is incurred in the same manner as before. However, if a monk who came without carrying a message is asked, "Venerable sir, what is the news of such-and-such a person in that village?" it is allowable to tell him; there is no fault in answering the question asked. For the five co-religionists (sahadhammikas), parents, a paṇḍupalāsa, and one's own...
24:
It is allowable to carry a message for a servant (veyyāvaccakara). It is also allowable to carry allowable messages for laypeople. Therefore, one should not have hesitation in carrying such messages as: "By my word, pay homage to the feet of the Blessed One," or "Pay homage to the Cetiya, the Buddha image, the Bodhi tree, or the Elder of the Saṅgha," or "Perform a fragrance offering at the Cetiya," or "Perform a flower offering," or "Invite the monks to assemble; we will give alms, we will have the Dhamma preached." This is because these messages are allowable and are not related to the worldly affairs of laypeople.

However, requisites arising from these eight acts of corrupting families (kuladūsaka-kamma) are not allowable for the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika). These requisites are similar to those arising from falsely claiming superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) or trading with gold and silver.

A monk who has been subjected to the act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma) for corrupting families in a certain village or market town is neither permitted to wander for alms in that village or market town, nor is he permitted to reside in that monastery. Even after that act has been revoked, he must not accept requisites arising from the families he previously corrupted. Even if he has attained the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya) and become an Arahant, he must not accept them; they remain unallowable. If asked, "Why do you not accept?" and he replies, "Because of what was done in the past," and if the donors then say, "We are not giving because of that reason, but we give now because of your virtue (sīla)," then he may accept. If the act of corrupting families was done at a place where alms are normally given, he is allowed to accept only the normal alms. Requisites that are increased and given [due to the corruption] are not allowable. Since there is no fault in answering a question asked, if another monk entering a house in the morning or evening is asked by someone, "Venerable sir, why are you wandering?" he may explain the purpose of his wandering. When asked, "Have you received anything or not?" if he has not yet received anything, he may say, "I have not yet received," and it is allowable to accept what that person gives.

"Monks, one should not live in the forest with a longing [for fame]; for him who does so, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Monks, one should not wander for alms with a longing... Monks, one should not walk up and down with a longing... Monks, one should not stand with a longing... Monks, one should not sit with a longing... Monks, one should not lie down with a longing; for him who does so, there is an offense of wrongdoing." Because this was said, one should not live in the forest with such a longing as: "People will respect me as an Arahant or as a trainee (sekha) because I live in the forest in this way; then I will be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped in the world." For a monk who goes with such a longing, thinking "I will live in the forest,"
25:
an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred for every step. Likewise, in all activities such as building a hut in the forest, walking up and down, sitting, dressing the inner robe, and donning the outer robe, an offense of wrongdoing is incurred for every effort made. Therefore, one should not live in the forest longing for the praise of the multitude. A monk living with such a longing for praise, whether he receives praise or not, certainly incurs an offense of wrongdoing.

If a monk has undertaken ascetic practices (dhuṭaṅga) and thinks, "I will protect the ascetic practices," or thinks, "My mind is distracted while living in a monastery near a village; the forest is suitable for me," or reflects, "By living in the forest, I shall surely attain one of the three kinds of seclusion (viveka)," or "Having entered the forest, I will not leave until I reach Arahantship," or "Living in the forest is praised by the Blessed One; if I live in the forest, many fellow practitioners will leave the village and become forest-dwellers"—if he wishes to live with such a blameless dwelling, only then should he live there.

For a monk wandering for alms, if he thinks, "I will wander for alms after properly establishing my manner of proceeding forward and so on [for the sake of praise]," then from the act of dressing and donning the robes until the end of the meal, an offense of wrongdoing is incurred for every effort made; whether he receives praise or not, it is a wrongdoing. However, for a monk who enters for alms with an inspiring manner of proceeding forward and backward, either to fulfill the duties of the Khandhakas and the Sekhiyas or so that fellow practitioners may follow his example, he is not to be blamed by the wise. The same principle applies to walking up and down and other activities.

## Thus ends the Discussion on the Decision regarding the Corrupting of Families

## 6. Discussion on the Decision regarding Fish and Meat

Among fish and meat, by the term "fish," all aquatic animals are meant. Among those aquatic animals, there is none that is unallowable. Among meats, however, ten kinds of meat are unallowable: human, elephant, horse, dog, snake, lion, tiger, leopard, bear, and hyena. Among these, if one eats human flesh, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya); for the remaining nine, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Thus, the meat, bone, blood, skin, and hair of these ten kinds, starting with humans, are all unallowable. Among fats (vasā), only human fat is unallowable. Among milk and so on, there is nothing unallowable. Regarding these unallowable meats or bones and so on, an offense is incurred whether one eats them knowingly or unknowingly. When one realizes it, the offense must be confessed. For one who takes it thinking, "I will eat without asking," an offense of wrongdoing is incurred even at the moment of receiving. For one who thinks, "I will eat after asking,"
26:
There is no offense for a monk who takes meat with the intention of eating after inquiring. However, an offense is incurred only by a monk who eats meat knowing it was specifically prepared for him (uddissakata). A monk who finds out later should not be penalized with an offense.

Among those types of fish and meat, "specifically prepared" (uddissakata) refers to fish or meat that has been killed and prepared for the sake of monks. In truth, such specifically prepared meat is not allowable. However, even that specifically prepared meat is allowable if it is unseen, unheard, and unsuspected. Indeed, the Blessed One has allowed fish and meat that is pure in three aspects (tikoṭiparisuddha): unseen, unheard, and unsuspected. In this context, "unseen" (adiṭṭha) means not having seen the animals being killed and taken for the sake of monks. "Unheard" (asuta) means not having heard that the animals were killed and taken for the sake of monks. "Unsuspected" (aparisaṅkita) should be understood by knowing its opposite, which includes suspicion through seeing (diṭṭhaparisaṅkita), suspicion through hearing (sutaparisaṅkita), and suspicion arising from both (tadubhayavinimuttaparisaṅkita).

How so? In this world, if monks see people leaving a village or wandering in the forest carrying nets, snares, and so on. On the following day, when those monks enter that village for alms, the people bring alms-food together with fish or meat. Because of that seeing, the monks suspect: "Was this meat prepared for the sake of monks?" This is called "suspicion through seeing" (diṭṭhaparisaṅkita); it is not allowable to accept this fish or meat. Fish or meat that is not suspected in this way is allowable. However, if those people ask, "Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?" and upon hearing the reason, they say, "Venerable sirs, this meat was not prepared for the sake of monks; we prepared it for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and so on," then it is allowable.

If monks do not see but hear: "It is said that people are leaving the village or wandering in the forest carrying nets, snares, and so on." On the following day, when those monks enter that village for alms, the people bring alms-food together with fish or meat. Because of that hearing, the monks suspect: "Was this meat prepared for the sake of monks?" This is called "suspicion through hearing" (sutaparisaṅkita); it is not allowable to accept this fish or meat. Fish or meat that is not suspected in this way is allowable. However, if those people ask, "Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?" and upon hearing the reason, they say, "Venerable sirs, this meat was not prepared for the sake of monks; we prepared it for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and so on," then it is allowable.

If monks neither see nor hear, but the people take the bowls of those monks who have entered the village for alms, specially prepare alms-food with fish and meat, and bring it forward. The monks suspect: "Was this meat prepared for the sake of monks?" This is called "suspicion arising from both [neither seeing nor hearing]" (tadubhayavinimuttaparisaṅkita); it is also not allowable to accept this fish or meat. Fish or meat that is not suspected in this way is allowable. If those people ask, "Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?"...
27:
...and upon inquiring and hearing the reason, they say, "Venerable sirs, this was not done for the sake of monks; we prepared it for ourselves or for royal officials and so on; we only obtained meat that was already available (pavattamaṃsa) and prepared it for the monks," then it is allowable. The same method applies to meat prepared for funeral rites for the deceased or for auspicious ceremonies and so on. Whatever meat is not prepared specifically for the sake of monks and where there is no doubt, all such meat is allowable.

If, however, meat is specifically prepared for monks in a certain monastery, and those monks for whom it was intended do not know it was prepared for them, but other monks know. For those who know, it is not allowable; for the others, it is allowable. If others do not know but only those intended monks know, it is not allowable only for those who know, but allowable for others. If those intended monks know, "It was prepared for us," and others also know, "It was prepared for them," then it is not allowable for all of them. If none of them know, it is allowable for all. This is because if meat is specifically prepared for any one of the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika), it is not allowable for all of them.

If, however, someone kills a living being specifically for one monk, fills that monk's bowl, and offers it, and that monk, even though he knows it was prepared for him, accepts it and gives it to another monk, and that other monk consumes it out of faith in the donor monk, who incurs an offense? There is no offense for either of them. This is because for the intended monk, there is no offense as he did not consume it, and for the other monk, there is no offense as he did not know. There is no offense in accepting allowable meat (kappiyamaṃsa), and if one consumes specifically prepared meat without knowing and finds out later, there is no requirement to confess an offense. However, if one consumes unallowable meat (akappiyamaṃsa) without knowing and finds out later, an offense must be confessed. An offense is incurred only by one who consumes specifically prepared meat while knowing it; however, for unallowable meat, an offense is incurred even if one consumes it without knowing. Therefore, a monk who is scrupulous about offenses, even if he observes the appearance of the meat, should accept meat only after inquiring. At the time of consumption, he should either think, "I will consume it after inquiring," or accept it and consume it only after inquiring. Why? Because it is difficult to distinguish. Bear meat can resemble pork, and leopard meat and so on can resemble venison and so on. Therefore, the teachers say that accepting only after inquiring is the proper practice.

## Thus, in the Pālimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha,
## the Discussion on the Decision regarding Fish and Meat is finished.
