## 7. Discussion on the Decision Regarding Non-touchable Objects

'Anāmāsa' means that which should not be touched. Regarding this 'anāmāsa', there is this decision (Pārājika-aṭṭhakathā, Vol. 2, 281): Since any woman—be she a mother, a daughter, or a sister—is an obstacle to the holy life and is thus non-touchable, it is stated that even for a monk who touches her with worldly affection, thinking, "This is my mother, this is my daughter, this is my sister," it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa).

A monk who remembers this command of the Blessed One, if he sees his mother being carried away by a river current, must not touch her with his hands. A wise monk should instead offer a boat, a plank, a banana trunk, or a log. If such things as a boat are not available, he should offer his own robe and place it in front of his mother; however, he should not say, "Grab here." If she grabs it, he should proceed while pulling it, thinking, "I am pulling my requisites." If she is frightened, he should go ahead of her and encourage her, saying, "Do not be afraid."

If the frightened mother suddenly climbs onto the monk-son's shoulder or grabs his hand, he should not shake her off, saying, "Go away, old woman," but should bring her safely to dry land. The same method applies to a mother stuck in mud or one who has fallen into a well. In such cases, he should throw a rope or a cloth to her, and only after knowing she has grasped it with her hand should he pull her up; he himself must not touch her. 

It is not only the body of a woman that is non-touchable; her undergarments, cloaks, ornaments, and even a grass ring or a palm-leaf ring are also non-touchable objects. These clothes and ornaments are only those intended for wearing or decoration. However, if she exchanges an undergarment or a cloak and places it at his feet for the purpose of making a robe, it is allowable to touch it. Among ornaments, if allowable items such as hair-ornaments, cloth-wraps, or ivory needles are offered, saying, "Venerable sir, we give this to you; please accept it," they may be accepted for use as needle cases, styluses, and the like. Ornaments made of gold, silver, pearls, etc., are strictly non-touchable objects and should not be accepted even if offered.

Furthermore, it is not only things connected to their bodies that are non-touchable; images made in the form of a woman—whether made of wood, ivory, iron, bronze, tin, clay, various jewels, or even an image made of flour—are also non-touchable. If such an image is received for use with the words, "May this be for you," one should set aside those made of various jewels and break the rest to destroy the female form. Then, it is allowable to use what is suitable for construction in construction, and what is suitable for utensils as utensils.

Just as a female image is non-touchable, the seven kinds of grain (dhanya) are also non-touchable. Therefore, a monk walking through a field should not go along touching the ears of grain growing in that field. At the door of a house or on a path...
29:
Just as with the female image, the seven kinds of grain (dhanya) are also non-touchable (anāmāsa) objects. Therefore, a monk walking through a field should not go along touching the fruit of the grain growing there. If grain is spread out at the entrance of a house or on a path, and there is a path to the side, he should go without treading on it. If there is no other path, he should resolve that grain-field as a path in his mind and proceed. If a seat is prepared and offered on top of grain inside a house, it is allowable to sit. Some pour grain inside a rest house; if it is possible to have it moved, one should have it moved. If not, one should set up a stool in one area without treading on the grain and sit. If there is no space and people prepare a seat right in the middle of the grain, it is allowable to sit. Beans such as mung beans and black grams, or fruits such as palm fruits and bel fruits growing in that place, should not be touched playfully. The same method should be understood for piles of beans and fruits gathered by people. However, fruits that have fallen from trees in the forest may be taken with the intention, "I will give these to laypeople or novices."

42. Among these ten jewels—pearl, ruby, lapis lazuli, conch, crystal, coral, silver, gold, red ruby, and masāragalla—teachers say that a pearl that is unwashed and unpierced in its natural state is allowable to touch, while other pearls are non-touchable (anāmāsa); however, that statement should not be accepted. In the Mahāpaccariya, it is said: "A pearl, whether washed or unwashed, is a non-touchable anāmāsa; it should not be accepted even for the price of requisites such as a bowl, but it is allowable to accept it for the purpose of medicine for leprosy." This statement is appropriate. All rubies, from those the color of nutmeg to those of various colors like blue or yellow, if they are washed, pierced, and rounded, are non-touchable anāmāsa. Although teachers say that a raw ruby from a mine may be accepted for the price of requisites like a bowl, that statement is also rejected in the Mahāpaccariya. It is said that only artificial glass gems (kāca-maṇi) made by firing are allowable to touch. Regarding lapis lazuli, the decision should be understood exactly as stated for rubies.

Regarding conchs: a blowing-conch that is washed and pierced or encrusted with jewels is a non-touchable anāmāsa. A drinking-conch, whether washed or unwashed, is touchable (āmāsa). Other conchs may be accepted for the purpose of eye-medicine or for the price of requisites. Crystal is a non-touchable anāmāsa only if it is washed, pierced, set with jewels, and has the color of mung beans. Other crystals may be taken for the purpose of whetstones and the like. Here, teachers say that "set with jewels" means made by firing and mixing with gold. Coral is a non-touchable anāmāsa if it is washed and pierced. Although some say that other coral is touchable and may be accepted for the price of requisites, that statement should not be accepted...
30:
That statement should not be accepted. However, in the Mahāpaccariya Commentary, it is stated: "Whether polished or unpolished, everything is anāmāsa (not to be handled) and should not be accepted." This statement is very appropriate.

Neither silver nor gold, whether in the form of finished articles or unfinished material, should be handled or accepted, starting from the raw ore (gold-stone or silver-stone). It is heard that Prince Uttara had a golden stupa made and sent it to the Elder Mahāpaduma. The Elder refused, saying, "It is not allowable for me." In a stupa-house, there may be golden lotuses, golden stars, and so on; these also are anāmāsa. However, it is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā that for the monks who guard the stupa-house, who stand in the position of those who have relinquished gold and silver, it is allowable to move these items from here to there (for cleaning). But in the Kurundī Commentary, even such an act is forbidden; it is allowed only to remove the rubbish in the golden stupa-house. In all commentaries, it is stated that brass and copper are also anāmāsa, just like gold.

In the case of monastery requisites, however, everything is indeed allowable. Therefore, all monastery requisites made of gold and silver are anāmāsa (allowable to be handled). Monks may set up crystal pillars and decorate them with jewel-garlands in a jewel-pavilion where the Dhamma is preached; it is allowable for monks to maintain and clean all the equipment in such a place. It is stated that if red rubies or blue sapphires are polished or engraved, they are anāmāsa (not to be handled); other types are allowable to be handled, and it is also allowable to accept them for the sake of the value of the goods. However, in the Mahāpaccariya Commentary, it is forbidden, stating: "Whether polished or unpolished, they are anāmāsa in every way and should not be accepted."

All kinds of weapons are anāmāsa; they should not be accepted even if given for the sake of the value of the goods. Trading in weapons is not allowable. Plain bow-staves, bowstrings, goads, forks, hooks, and even billhooks and axes made in the form of weapons are anāmāsa. If someone leaves a spear or a fork in the monastery, the monk guarding the monastery should tell the owners, "Please take them away." If they do not take them, the monastery should be cleaned without moving those weapons. If one sees a sword, spear, or fork left on a battlefield, it is allowable to break the sword with a stone or something else and take it for the purpose of making a small knife. Other weapons may also be dismantled from their original form and taken, some for the purpose of a small knife, some for a walking stick, and so on. If someone offers them saying, "Please take this," it is allowable to accept them all with the intention, "I will destroy them and make allowable requisites."
31:
Fishing nets, bird nets, and the like, as well as wooden lattices and arrow-deflecting shields, are all anāmāsa objects (objects not to be handled). However, when they are obtained for use, it is permissible to take a net with the intention: "I will bind it above a seat or a cetiya, or I will wrap it around a parasol." It is also permissible to accept all arrow-deflecting shields (or nets) for the sake of the value of goods such as alms-bowls. For this is an object that prevents harm from others, not one that causes harm. It is also permissible to take a wooden board with the intention: "I will make a container for tooth-sticks."

Harps, drums, and the like, covered with leather, are anāmāsa objects. In the Kurundī Commentary, it is stated: "Drums covered with leather, harps, empty drum-shells, harp-shells, leather fixed on the rim, and harp-rods are all anāmāsa objects." One should not cover them oneself, have others cover them, play them oneself, or have others play them. Even if they are seen discarded by people at a cetiya courtyard after an offering, one should sweep between them without moving them. However, at the time of discarding rubbish, it is permissible to take them away as rubbish and put them aside; so it is stated in the Mahāpaccari. It is also permissible to accept them for the sake of the value of goods. When obtained for use, it is permissible to take a harp-trough or a drum-shell with the intention: "I will make a container for tooth-sticks," or leather with the intention: "I will make a sheath for a small knife," and to use them for various requisites accordingly.

## Thus, in the Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha,
## The Discussion on the Decision regarding Anāmāsa is finished.
## 8. Discussion on the Decision regarding Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna) and Assignment (Vikappana)

Regarding determination and assignment: "I allow, monks, the triple robe to be determined, not to be assigned; the rainy season robe to be determined for the four months of the rainy season, and after that to be assigned; the sitting cloth to be determined, not to be assigned; the floor covering to be determined, not to be assigned; the itch-covering cloth to be determined as long as the affliction lasts, and after that to be assigned; the face-wiping cloth to be determined, not to be assigned; the requisite cloth to be determined, not to be assigned." (Mahāvagga 358). Therefore, a monk who wishes to use the triple robe, etc., according to the regulations by determining them, should determine them by stating the name, such as "I determine this saṅghāṭi (outer robe)." A monk who performs assignment, however, should do so without taking the name, saying "I assign this robe to you."
32:
## 8. Discussion on the Determination and Assignment (Adhiṭṭhāna-vikappana-vinicchaya)

One should make an assignment by saying, "I make an assignment" (Vikappanemi). In that regard (Pārājika Commentary 2, 469), a monk who wishes to determine the triple robe (ticīvara) should determine only those that are dyed, marked with a smudge point (kappabindu), and of the proper size. Regarding the size of those robes, at the maximum limit, a size slightly smaller than the Buddha’s robe (sugata-cīvara) is allowable. At the minimum limit, the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) and the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) are allowable if they are 5 fists in length and 3 fists in width. The inner robe (antaravāsaka) is allowable if it is 5 fists in length and 2 cubits in width. This is because the navel can be covered even by wearing the outer robe. A robe that is larger or smaller than the aforementioned sizes should be determined as an "accessory cloth" (parikkhāracola).

In this matter, since it is taught that "there are two ways to determine a robe: determination by body or determination by word" (Parivāra 322), one should relinquish the old outer robe by saying, "I relinquish this saṅghāṭi" (Imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paccuddharāmi). Then, holding the new robe with the hand, one should determine it by body, making a mental resolution, "I determine this saṅghāṭi" (Imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmi), while performing a bodily movement. This is determination by body. Such determination by body is not valid for a monk who does not touch the robe with at least some part of his body. In determination by word, one should determine by word through vocal utterance. There are two types of determination by word: if the robe is within reach (hatthapāsa), one should utter the words, "I determine this saṅghāṭi." If it is inside a room, upstairs, or in a nearby monastery, one should note the place where it is kept and utter the words, "I determine that saṅghāṭi" (Etaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmi). This same method applies to the upper robe and the inner robe; the only difference is the name. Therefore, all robes should be determined by their own names as saṅghāṭi, uttarāsaṅga, or antaravāsaka. If one makes an outer robe or similar items from cloths that have already been determined, they must be relinquished by saying, "I relinquish this [name]," and determined again once the dyeing and marking with the smudge point are completed. If one sews a larger second layer or a piece together with a robe that has already been determined, it must be determined again. However, if the piece joined is of equal or smaller size, there is no need for re-determination.

Is it allowable to determine the triple robe as an accessory cloth (parikkhāracola) or not? It is said that the Elder Mahāpaduma stated: "The triple robe should be determined only as the triple robe (as saṅghāṭi, etc.). If determination as an accessory cloth were permitted, the protection in the Udositasikkhāpada would become useless." When this was said, the remaining monks reportedly said: "Since the Blessed One himself taught that an accessory cloth should also be determined, it is allowable." In the Mahāpaccari, it is also stated: "This so-called accessory cloth is a means for separate storage. It is allowable to use the triple robe by determining it as an 'accessory cloth'; however, in the Udositasikkhāpada, having determined the triple robe..."
33:
"...the protection for the monk who carries [the robes] is taught," so it is stated (in the Mahāpaccari). The Elder Mahātissa, a resident of Puṇṇavālikavihāra and a reciter of both Vibhaṅgas, also said: "In the past, we heard the words of the Great Elders: 'Forest-dwelling monks leave their robes in tree hollows and the like and go to strive in their meditation. When those monks have gone to a nearby monastery to listen to the Dhamma and the sun has risen, novices or junior monks take their bowls and robes and follow them. Therefore, for the sake of convenient use, it is allowable to determine the triple robe as an accessory cloth (parikkhāracola).'" In the Mahāpaccari, it is also stated: "In the past, forest-dwelling monks, finding it difficult to carry the triple robe in an unbound boundary (abaddhasīmā), used the triple robe by determining it only as an accessory cloth."

A rain-robe (vassikasāṭikā), if it does not exceed the proper size, should be determined by that very name for the four months of the rainy season in the manner already described. After that, it should be relinquished and assigned (vikappana). It is allowable even if it is dyed only enough to change its color, but having two [determined at once] is not allowable. A sitting cloth (nisīdana) must be determined in the manner described; it must be only one cloth of proper size, two are not allowable. A bedspread (paccattharaṇa) must also be determined; it is allowable even if it is large, and one or many are allowable. It is allowable in all forms, whether blue, yellow, with a fringe, or with a floral fringe. An itch-cloth (kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi) should be determined according to the proper size for as long as the illness exists. When the illness is cured, it should be relinquished and assigned; only one is allowable. A face-towel (mukhapuñchanacola) must also be determined. Since one might be needed for use while another is being washed, two are allowable. Other Elders, however, say: "This face-towel is a means for storage, so many are allowable." There is no numerical limit for accessory cloths (parikkhāracola); as many as one desires may be determined.

A bag or a water-filter should also be determined as an "accessory cloth" if it is at least the size of the smallest robe suitable for assignment (vikappana). The size of such an accessory cloth is two spans in length and one span in width. In terms of a carpenter's cubit, that size is one cubit in length and half a cubit (one span) in width. In this regard, the Pāḷi text says: "Bhikkhus, I allow you to assign a minimum robe (pacchima-cīvara) that is eight fingers long and four fingers wide by the Sugata-finger measurement" (Mahāvagga 358). It is also allowable to determine many cloths together by saying, "I determine these robes as accessory cloths." There is no offense even if one does not determine robes kept for the sake of medicine, new construction, or for one's parents and the like. In the case of stuffing for a couch, stuffing for a chair, a pillow, a rug, or a carpet, and in the case of a bedspread given as a monastery requisite (senāsanaparikkhāra), there is no requirement for determination.
34:
If a monk obtains thread from a relative or an invited person and has a robe woven by that relative weaver or by another person by paying a fee, there is no offense due to the weaving. However, a monk wishing to guard against the offense caused by exceeding ten days should make a determination (adhiṭṭhāna) while the robe is still on the loom, once an amount sufficient for assignment (vikappanā) has been woven. This is because a robe completed after exceeding ten days would become an object to be forfeited (nissaggiya). The same rule applies if relatives or others set up the loom and offer it, saying, 'Venerable sir, please accept this robe.'

If a weaver, whether commissioned in this way or wishing to donate personally, says, 'Venerable sir, I will weave and keep your robe on such-and-such a day,' and the monk allows ten days to pass from that specified day, he incurs a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense. If the weaver says, 'I will weave the robe and send word,' and does so, but the monk sent by him does not inform the [owner] monk, and another person sees or hears and says, 'Venerable sir, the robe is finished,' this announcement is not authoritative. Only when the person actually sent by the weaver informs him, and the monk allows ten days to pass from the day he hears that word, does he incur a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense.

If the weaver says, 'I will weave the robe and send it through a certain monk,' and does so, but the monk who took the robe keeps it in his own dwelling (pariveṇa) and does not inform the [owner] monk, and another person says, 'Venerable sir, the robe just brought is beautiful,' and he asks, 'Friend, where is the robe?' and is told, 'It is in the hands of such-and-such a monk,' even then that person's word is not authoritative. Only when that monk gives the robe, and the monk allows ten days to pass from the day of receipt, does he incur a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense. If the weaving fee has not yet been paid, even if only a small amount (kākaṇika) remains, he is protected [from offense].

How does the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) of a determined robe lapse for a monk who uses it? It lapses due to these nine reasons: giving it to another, it being snatched away, taking it on trust (vissāsaggāha), returning to the lower life (disrobing), renouncing the training, death, change of sex, withdrawal (paccuddharaṇa), and becoming holed (chiddabhāva). Among these nine, for the first eight reasons, the determination of all robes lapses. Specifically, regarding the three robes (ticīvara), all commentaries state that determination lapses due to becoming holed. In saying determination lapses due to a hole, it means a hole the size of a fingernail. That fingernail size should be understood as the size of the fingernail of the little finger. A hole means a hole that goes all the way through. If even a single thread or hair remains unbroken within the hole, the determination is not yet broken. Furthermore, in the case of such a hole, for the double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) and the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), only a hole within one span from the long edge and within eight finger-breadths from the short edge breaks the determination. A hole outside that area does not break the determination.
35:
Due to the eight reasons, the determination of all robes lapses. However, in all commentaries, the lapse of determination for the three robes (ticīvara) is specifically mentioned as being due to the state of having a hole. Such a hole must be the size of a fingernail. This fingernail size should be understood as the fingernail of the little finger. The hole must also be a hole that passes through. If even a single thread remains unbroken within the hole, it still preserves the determination.

Regarding the hole that breaks the determination: for the double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) and the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), if a hole occurs within one span from the long edge and within eight finger-breadths from the short edge, the determination is broken. For the inner robe (antaravāsaka), if a hole occurs within one span from the long edge and within four finger-breadths from the short edge, the determination is broken. If it occurs beyond those limits, the determination is not broken. Therefore, when a hole occurs, that set of three robes becomes extra robes (atirekacīvara). Only after sewing it with a needle should it be determined again.

If a monk first applies a patch (aggaḷa) to a weak spot and then cuts away and removes the weak part, the determination is not broken. The same principle applies to changing a circle (maṇډalaparivattana). If a hole occurs or a tear happens in one layer of a double-layered robe, the determination is not broken. Making a small robe large or a large robe small does not break the determination. If a monk wishing to sew the two ends in the middle first cuts and then joins them, the determination is broken. If he joins them first and then cuts, it is not broken. Even if one has it washed and whitened by laundrymen, the determination remains as determination. This is the decision regarding determination.

In making an assignment (vikappanā), there are two types: assignment in the presence (sammukhā-vikappanā) and assignment in the absence (parammukhā-vikappanā). How is assignment in the presence done? Knowing whether the robes are single or many, and whether they are present or not present, one should say, 'I assign this robe to you,' or 'I assign these robes to you,' or 'I assign that robe to you,' or 'I assign those robes to you.' This is one type of assignment in the presence. With this much, it is allowable to store them. However, it is not allowable to use them, give them away, or determine them. But if it is said, 'Use my property, or give it away, or do as you see fit,' this is called withdrawal (paccuddharaṇa). From then on, use and so forth are allowable.

Another method: In the same way, knowing whether the robes are single or many, and whether they are present or not present, in the presence of that monk, one says, 'I assign this robe...' or 'I assign these robes...' or 'I assign that robe...' or 'I assign those robes...' and then, taking the name of any one of the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika) whom one prefers, one says, 'I assign it to the monk named Tissa,' or 'to the bhikkhunī named Tissā, to the female trainee (sikkhamānā) named Tissā, to the novice (sāmaṇera) named Tissa, to the female novice (sāmaṇerī) named Tissā...'
36:
"I assign [this] to the novice nun (sāmaṇerī)" should also be said; this is another form of assignment in the presence (sammukhā-vikappanā). By saying this much, it is allowable to store [the robe], but not a single act such as using it is yet allowable. Only when that [recipient] monk says, "Use the property of the monk Tissa... the property of the novice nun Tissā, or dispose of it, or do as you see fit," does it become formal relinquishment (paccuddhāra); from then on, using it and so forth are also allowable.

How is assignment in the absence (parammukhā-vikappanā) performed? Having known whether the robes are single or many, and whether they are present or not, one should say, "This robe" or "These robes" or "That robe" or "Those robes," and then say, "I give [this] to you for the purpose of vikappanā." That [recipient] monk should ask, "Who is your friend or acquaintance?" Then, in the same manner as before, one should say, "The monk Tissa" ... "The novice nun Tissā." Again, that monk should say, "I give [it] to the monk Tissa" ... "I give [it] to the novice nun Tissā"; this is assignment in the absence. By this much, it is allowable to store [the robe], but not a single act such as using it is yet allowable. Only when that monk says, in the same manner as mentioned in the second assignment in the presence, "Use the property of such-and-named person, or dispose of it, or do as you see fit," does it become formal relinquishment; from then on, using it and so forth are also allowable.

What is the difference between the two types of vikappanā? In assignment in the presence, one performs the vikappanā oneself and has the other person perform the relinquishment. In assignment in the absence, one has the other person perform the vikappanā and also has the other person perform the relinquishment; this is the difference here. If the person for whom the vikappanā is performed is not skilled in the Vinaya regulations and does not know how to perform relinquishment, one should take that robe, go to another skilled monk, perform vikappanā again, and have the other person perform relinquishment. This is called vikappita-vikappanā and is allowable. Thus far, the method of determination (adhiṭṭhāna) and assignment (vikappanā) regarding robes should be understood.

Regarding the alms-bowl (patta), this is the method: A monk who determines a bowl should determine only one of the bowls—superior (ukkaṭṭha), medium (majjhima), or inferior (omaka)—that is of the proper measure. The measure of that bowl is stated in the Pāli text by the method beginning with "It holds half an āḷhaka of cooked rice." Herein is the decision: Taking two Magadhan measures (nāḷis) of unbroken, three-year-old, well-pounded, pure hill-paddy rice, and cooking those grains into rice that is free of uncooked grains, not overcooked, not lumpy, very clear, resembling a heap of jasmine buds, and without scum...
37:
Having put all that rice (cooked from two Magadhan measures of rice) into the bowl without remainder, one should add mung bean soup (muggasūpa) prepared with all ingredients, which is one-fourth the amount of that rice, neither too thick nor too thin, and of a consistency that can be taken by hand. Then, one should add curries such as fish or meat, suitable for each mouthful and sufficient until the last mouthful. Ghee, oil, buttermilk, vinegar, and so forth are not included in the measurement [of the superior bowl, etc.]. These follow the nature of the rice and are unable to decrease or increase the [bowl's] capacity. If all these added items stand level with the lower line below the rim of the bowl, or if, when cutting across with a thread or a fiber, they touch the lower edge of the thread or fiber, this bowl is called superior (ukkaṭṭha). If it exceeds that line and stands heaped up, this bowl is called ukkaṭṭhomaka (inferior to the superior). If it does not reach that line and remains within, this bowl is called ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭha (exceeding the superior).

A bowl half the size of the superior bowl is called medium (majjhima). A bowl half the size of the medium bowl is called inferior (omaka). Therefore, if all the added items, such as rice cooked from one Magadhan measure, stand level with the lower line in the manner mentioned, this bowl is called majjhima. If it exceeds that line and is heaped up, it is called majjhimomaka. If it does not reach that line and remains within, it is called majjhimukkaṭṭha. If all the added items, such as rice cooked from half a Magadhan measure, stand level with the lower line, this bowl is called omaka. If it exceeds that line and is heaped up, it is called omakomaka. If it does not reach that line and remains within, it is called omakukkaṭṭha. Thus, there are nine [types of] bowls. Among those nine, two—the ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭha and the omakomaka—are not true bowls. Therefore, those two should be used only as ordinary vessels; they are not suitable for determination (adhiṭṭhāna) or assignment (vikappanā). The remaining seven, however, should be used after either determining or assigning them.

The suitability of these seven bowls of proper measure for determination and assignment should be understood thus: An iron bowl is fit for determination after being fired five times, and a clay bowl after being fired twice. For both, they are fit for determination only when the price to be paid has been given. If even one firing is lacking, or if the price, even as much as a kākaṇika, has not been given, it does not reach the state of being fit for determination. Even if the owner of the bowl says, "Give the price when you have it; for now, determine and use it," it cannot reach the state of being fit for determination. This is because, due to the lack of firing, it does not reach the designation of a "bowl," and because the price, in whole or in part, has not been given, it has not become one's own property.
38:
Because a portion of the price of the bowl has not yet been paid, the bowl does not yet become one's own property and remains the property of another. Therefore, only after both the firing and the payment are fully completed does it become a bowl suitable for determination (adhiṭṭhāna). Whatever bowl is suitable for determination is also suitable for assignment (vikappanā). Whether that bowl has reached one's hand or not, determination or assignment should be performed.

If the bowl-maker, having received the price and wishing to give it himself, says, "Venerable sir, I will make your bowl, fire it on such-and-such a day, and keep it," and if the monk allows ten days to pass from that specified day, it is an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya. If the bowl-maker says, "I will make and fire your bowl and then send word," and does so, but the monk he sent does not inform the owner-monk, and another monk who saw or heard of it says, "Venerable sir, your bowl is finished," such a statement is not authoritative (not a valid notice). Only when the person sent by the bowl-maker himself informs him, and the monk allows ten days to pass from the day he heard that word, does he incur an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya.

If the bowl-maker says, "I will make and fire your bowl and place it in the hand of a certain monk," and does so, but the monk who brought the bowl keeps it within his own precinct and does not yet inform the owner-monk, and some other monk says, "Venerable sir, is the bowl just brought now good?" and when asked, "Friend, where is the bowl?" he replies, "The bowl sent for you is in the hand of such-and-such a monk," this statement is also not authoritative. Only when that monk actually hands over the bowl, and the monk allows ten days to pass from the day of receipt, does he incur an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya. Therefore, one should perform determination or assignment without letting ten days pass.

In that determination, there are two ways to determine a bowl: one determines it by body or one determines it by speech. A monk wishing to determine by these two ways should say, "I relinquish this bowl," or "I relinquish that bowl," and after relinquishing the old bowl that is present or absent, or after giving it to another, he should touch the new bowl located anywhere with his hand, and with the mental intention, "I determine this bowl," he should perform it by bodily gesture or by breaking into speech (verbally). In such determination, there are two types: if it is within a reach (hatthapāsa), one should say, "This bowl..."
39:
...one should break into speech saying, "I determine this bowl." If the bowl is inside a room, or on the upper floor of a mansion, or in a nearby monastery, one should note the place where it is kept and break into speech saying, "I determine that bowl." A monk performing determination may do so alone, or he may do so in the presence of another. The benefit of determining in the presence of another is that if the monk has a doubt, "Did I determine it or not?" the other person can remind him and resolve the doubt.

If a certain monk receives ten bowls and wishes to use them all himself, he should not determine all of them. He should determine one bowl, and on the next day, after relinquishing (paccuddharaṇa) it, determine another. In this way, one can maintain ten bowls even for a hundred years.

Can there be a loss of determination for one who is not negligent? Yes, there can be. If one gives the bowl to another, or disrobes, or renounces the training, or dies, or if one's sex changes, or if one relinquishes it, or if a hole appears in the bowl, the determination is lost. It is also said:

"By giving, disrobing, renouncing the training, and by death,
By change of sex, relinquishing, and by a hole, it becomes the seventh."

It is also lost by theft or by taking through trust (vissāsaggāha). By how large a hole is the determination broken? It is broken by a hole through which a grain of millet rice can both exit and enter. This millet rice is the least of the seven kinds of grain. If that hole is repaired with iron powder or an iron peg, it should be determined again within ten days. This is the decision regarding determination.

In assignment (vikappanā), there are two types: assignment in the presence (sammukhā-vikappanā) and assignment in the absence (parammukhā-vikappanā). How is assignment in the presence performed? Knowing whether the bowls are single or many, and whether they are present or absent, one should say, "This bowl," or "These bowls," or "That bowl," or "Those bowls," and then say, "I assign it to you." This is one type of assignment in the presence. By this much, it is proper to store it, but it is not yet proper to use it, or to give it away, or to determine it. However, if it is said, "Use my property, or give it away, or do as you wish," this is called relinquishing (paccuddharaṇa); from then on, use and so forth are proper.

Another method: Similarly, knowing whether the bowls are single or many, and whether they are present or absent, in the presence of that monk, one says, "This bowl," or "These bowls," or "That bowl," or "Those bowls," and among the five groups of fellow practitioners...
40:
Among the five co-religionists, one should take the name of any person one likes and say, "I assign [this] to the monk Tissa," or "I assign [this] to the nun Tissā, the female trainee (sikkhamānā), the novice (sāmaṇera), or the female novice Tissā." This is another form of Sammukhā-vikappanā (assignment in the presence). With this much, it is allowable to store [the item]. However, it is not yet allowable for use or other purposes. Only when that monk says, "Use the property of the monk Tissa (or the female novice Tissā), or give it away, or do as you please with it," does it become Paccuddhāra (withdrawal). From then on, use and other actions are allowable.

How does Parammukhā-vikappanā (assignment in the absence) occur? Knowing whether the bowls are single or many, and whether they are present or not, one should say, "I give this bowl" or "these bowls" or "that bowl" or "those bowls" for the purpose of assignment to you. That monk should ask, "Who is your friend or acquaintance?" Then, as in the previous method, one should say, "The monk Tissa" or "The female novice Tissā," etc. Again, that monk should say, "I give [it] to the monk Tissa" or "I give [it] to the female novice Tissā." This is Parammukhā-vikappanā. With this much, it is allowable to store [the item], but not yet allowable for use. Only when that monk says, as mentioned in the second Sammukhā-vikappanā, "Use the property of the person named so-and-so, or give it away, or do as you please with it," does it become Paccuddhāra. From then on, use and other actions are allowable. This is the method of assignment (Vikappanā).

What should be done if a bowl breaks while being used by a monk who has determined (adhiṭṭhāna) or assigned (vikappanā) it? If there is no crack (rāji) measuring two finger-breadths below the rim of the bowl, nothing needs to be done. If there is even one such crack in a monk's bowl, he should pierce it with a bowl-piercer at the lower edge of that crack, bake it, and bind it with cotton thread, fiber thread, or lead wire. To prevent food from sticking to the binding, it should be covered with a lead plate or some kind of resin. That bowl should then be determined and used. Or, a small hole should be made and bound. It is not allowable to bind it with pure beeswax, lac, or tree resin. It is allowable to bind it with stone powder mixed with boiled syrup. If pierced with a bowl-piercer near the rim, the bowl may break because the shard is thick. Therefore, it should be pierced only at the lower edge of the crack. If a bowl has two cracks of two finger-breadths each, or one crack of four finger-breadths, two bindings are given. If a bowl has three cracks of two finger-breadths each, or one crack of six finger-breadths, three bindings are given. If a bowl has four cracks of two finger-breadths each, or one crack of eight finger-breadths, four bindings are given.
41:
(If pierced near the rim,) the bowl may break because the shard is thick; therefore, it should be pierced only at the lower edge of the crack. If a bowl has two cracks of two finger-breadths each, or one crack of four finger-breadths, two bindings are given. If a bowl has three cracks, or one crack of six finger-breadths, three bindings are given. If a bowl has four cracks, or one crack of eight finger-breadths, four bindings are given. If a bowl has five cracks, or one crack of ten finger-breadths, whether it has five bindings or not, it is no longer considered a bowl; another bowl should be requested. This is the decision regarding clay bowls.

In the case of an iron bowl, even if there are five or more holes, if those holes are bound with iron powder, a needle, or a circular iron plate and are smooth, that bowl itself should be used; another bowl should not be requested. However, if even a single hole is large, and even if bound with a circular iron plate it is not smooth and food sticks to the bowl, it is unsuitable and is no longer considered a bowl; another bowl should be requested. When requesting, in a place where an invitation (pavāraṇā) has been made by the power of the Sangha, another bowl should be requested only with a bowl that has five bindings. In a place where an invitation has been made by the power of an individual, it may be requested even with a bowl having fewer than five bindings. A monk who receives and uses a bowl should not use it for unallowable purposes such as boiling gruel or boiling dye. However, if an illness occurs during a journey and no other vessel is available, it is allowable to coat it with fine clay and boil gruel or heat water. It should not be placed in unsuitable places such as on a couch, a chair, an umbrella, or a wall-peg. The place for putting a bowl has already been mentioned in the Khandhaka in the manner of "Monks, I allow a bowl-stand," etc.

## Thus, in the Pālimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-saṅgaha,
## The Discussion on the Decision regarding Determination and Assignment is finished.
## 9. Discussion on the Decision regarding Separation from Robes

"Separation from robes" (cīvarena-vināvāsa) means being separated from any one of the three robes that have been determined as the triple robes (ticīvara-adhiṭṭhāna). It is not allowable to stay separated from even one of these three determined robes. For a monk who so stays, as soon as the dawn rises, the robe...
42:
(If one stays separated from the robe), it becomes Nissaggiya. Therefore, at the time of dawn, the robe should be kept and one should stay within a hatthapāsa (hand-reach) of two and a half cubits. However, there is this distinction regarding a village, house, hall, market, palace, boat, cart, field, threshing floor, park, monastery, foot of a tree, or open space. If a village belongs to a single king or a village headman and is enclosed by a wall, fence, or moat, it is permissible to leave the robe in such a village and let dawn rise anywhere one wishes within the village. But if it is not enclosed, in such a village, one should stay in the house where the robe is kept, or within two and a half cubits around that house. Even if a monk with psychic powers lets dawn rise in the sky beyond that limit, the robe still becomes Nissaggiya.

If it is a village belonging to various kings or headmen, like Vesālī or Kusinārā, and it is enclosed, one should stay in the house where the robe is kept. If one cannot stay in that house due to noise or overcrowding, one should stay in a hall or near the city gate. If one still cannot stay there, one may stay in any comfortable place and, before dawn, come and stay within a hand-reach of that hall or city gate. It is then no longer necessary to stay in the house where the robe is kept or within a hand-reach of the robe itself.

If, instead of keeping it in a house, one intends to "keep it in a hall" and, while going to the hall, leaves the robe at a shop within a hand-reach for convenience, saying "Please keep this robe," then, as in the previous method, one should stay in the hall, near the gate, or within a hand-reach of them.

If there are many gates and many halls in a city, one does not have the right to stay in all of them. One should only stay within a hand-reach of the hall or gate that is opposite the street where the robe is kept. Only by staying thus can the condition of the robe be known. If a monk going to a hall leaves the robe in the hands of a shopkeeper, and if that shopkeeper moves the robe into a house, the hand-reach of the street can no longer protect it, so [one must stay within] the hand-reach of that house...
43:
...one should stay within a hand-reach. If the house is large and spans two streets, one should let dawn rise within a hand-reach of either the front or the back of the house. If the robe is left in a public hall, one should let dawn rise in that hall, or near the city gate opposite that hall, or within a hand-reach of those places. If the village is unenclosed, one should stay in the house where the robe is kept, or within a hand-reach of that house.

If a residence belongs to a single family and is enclosed, having various chambers and rooms, one should keep the robe inside the residence and stay within the residence. If it is unenclosed, one should stay in the chamber where the robe is kept, or within a hand-reach of that chamber. If a residence belongs to various families and is enclosed, having various chambers and rooms, one should stay in the chamber where the robe is kept, or near the house gate common to all, or within a hand-reach of the chamber or the house gate. If it is unenclosed, one should stay in the chamber where the robe is kept, or within a hand-reach of that chamber. In the case of a udositā (storehouse hall), aḍḍhamāḷa (watchtower), pāsāda (palace), and hammiya (flat-roofed mansion), the decision should be understood in the same manner as stated for the house.

If it is a boat belonging to a single family, one should keep the robe inside the boat and stay within the boat. If it is a boat belonging to various families and has various chambers and rooms, one should stay in the room where the robe is kept, or within a hand-reach of that room.

If it is a caravan belonging to a single family, one should keep the robe in that caravan and must not abandon it by more than seven abbhantaras from the front or back, nor by more than one abbhantara from the sides. One abbhantara is twenty-eight cubits in length. If it is a caravan belonging to various families, one should keep the robe in the caravan and stay within a hand-reach of the robe. If a caravan, while traveling, stops near a village or a river, and if it is connected with the carts entering inside and spans from this side to that side, it receives the protection of the caravan. If it is included within the village or the river, it receives the protection of the village and the protection of the river. If it stands beyond the boundary of a monastery and the robe is within the sīmā (boundary), in the monastery...
44:
One should go and stay. If the robe is outside the monastery boundary (sīmā), one must stay only near the caravan. If the traveling caravan is interrupted in between due to a broken cart or a lost ox, one must stay in that section of the caravan where the robe was placed.

If it is a field belonging to a single family and it is fenced, one should place the robe inside the field and stay within the field itself. If it is not fenced, one must stay within the hatthapāsa (arm's reach) of the robe. If it is a field belonging to many families and it is fenced, one should place the robe inside the field and stay either at the gate or within the hatthapāsa of the gate. If it is not fenced, one must stay within the hatthapāsa of the robe.

If it is a threshing floor belonging to a single family and it is fenced, one should place the robe inside the threshing floor and stay within the threshing floor itself. If it is not fenced, one must stay within the hatthapāsa of the robe. If it is a threshing floor belonging to many families and it is fenced, one should place the robe inside the threshing floor and stay either at the gate or within the hatthapāsa of the gate. If it is not fenced, one must stay within the hatthapāsa of the robe. In the case of flower gardens and fruit gardens, the decision should be understood in the same manner as stated for the field.

If it is a monastery belonging to a single family and it is fenced, one should place the robe inside the monastery and stay within the monastery itself. If it is not fenced, one must stay in that monastery where the robe was placed, or within the hatthapāsa of that monastery.

If it is the foot of a tree belonging to a single family, one should place the robe within the shade where the shade spreads all around at noon and stay within that shade. However, a robe placed in a sunlit spot of a tree with sparse branches becomes nissaggiya (subject to forfeiture). Therefore, it must be placed in the shade of the branches or the shade of the trunk of such a tree. If one wishes to place it on a branch or a fork of the tree, it must be placed only in a spot touched by the shade of another branch above. The shade of a leaning tree reaches far; it is permissible to place it where the shade reaches. If it is the foot of a tree belonging to many families, one must stay within the hatthapāsa of the robe.

In an open space or a forest where there is no village, one should place the robe and stay within seven abbhantaras around that robe. A forest without a village is found in places such as the great Vinjhāṭavī forest or on small islands in the middle of the ocean where fishermen cannot reach. In such a forest...
45:
The measurement of seven abbhantaras around a monk standing in the middle is fourteen abbhantaras in diameter. A monk sitting in the middle guards the robe placed at the edge, whether in the eastern or western direction. However, if at the time of dawn he moves even as much as the tip of a hair towards the east, the robe in the west becomes nissaggiya. This same principle applies to other directions. A monk who uses a nissaggiya robe without forfeiting it commits an offense of dukkaṭa (wrongdoing).

If a monk practicing meditation exerts himself in meditation all night and, at dawn, thinking "I will bathe," places his three robes on the bank and enters the river, and while he is bathing, dawn rises, what should be done? If he comes up to the land and wears the robes, he commits a dukkaṭa offense for using nissaggiya robes without forfeiting them. If he goes back naked, does he not also commit a dukkaṭa offense? No, he does not. This is because as long as he has not yet met another monk to perform the Vinaya-kamma (legal act), those robes are not yet fit for use and he is in the position of a monk who has lost his robes. For a monk who has lost his robes, there is no such thing as an unallowable robe. Therefore, he should wear one, hold two in his hands, go to the monastery, and perform the Vinaya-kamma. If the monastery is far and people are traveling on the road, he should wear one, wrap one around him, place one on his shoulder, and go. If he does not find a fellow monk (sabhāga) at the monastery because they have gone for alms, he should leave the saṅghāṭi (outer robe) outside the village, go to the refectory wearing the antaravāsaka (inner robe) and uttarāsaṅga (upper robe), and perform the Vinaya-kamma. If there is danger from thieves outside the village, he should wrap it and go. If the refectory is cramped and crowded with people such that he cannot set aside the robe in one place to perform the Vinaya-kamma, he should take another monk, go outside the village, perform the Vinaya-kamma, and then use the robes.

If elder monks give their bowls and robes into the hands of junior monks and, while traveling, wish to sleep during the last watch of the night, they must sleep only after keeping their robes within hatthapāsa. If dawn rises while they are traveling before the junior monks arrive, the robe becomes nissaggiya, but the nissaya (dependence) is not severed. The same principle applies when junior monks are traveling ahead and dawn rises before the elders arrive. The same principle applies when they lose their way in the forest and cannot see each other. However, if the junior monks say, "Venerable sirs, we will sleep for a moment and catch up with you at such-and-such a place," and they sleep until dawn rises, the robe becomes nissaggiya and the nissaya is also severed. The same principle applies when the junior monks are sent ahead and the elders sleep while dawn rises. Seeing a fork in the road, if the elders say "This is the way" and the juniors say "This is the way," and they go without listening to each other and dawn rises, the robes become nissaggiya and the nissaya is severed. If the junior monks turn off the path and go down to the village road saying, "We will return before dawn," and enter the village for medicine, but dawn rises before they reach the elders, the robes become nissaggiya, but the nissaya is not severed. If it is due to danger from cattle or danger from dogs...
46: ...It is the path," (the elders said). The junior monks also said, "This is the path," and without listening to each other's words, they went on. As soon as the dawn rose, the robes became Nissaggiya (subject to forfeiture), and the Nissaya (dependence) was terminated. If the junior monks, saying, "We will return before dawn," left the path and entered a village for medicine, and the dawn rose before they reached the elders, the robes become Nissaggiya, but the Nissaya is not terminated. If they stop for a moment due to fear of a cow or a dog, or if they go while standing or sitting, and the dawn rises in the middle of the journey, the robes become Nissaggiya and the Nissaya is terminated. If monks enter a village within the boundary (sīmā) saying, "We will return before dawn," and the dawn rises during the journey, the robes do not become Nissaggiya, nor is the Nissaya terminated. If they sit down saying, "Let it become light first," when the dawn rises, the robes do not become Nissaggiya, but the Nissaya is terminated. If they go eagerly to a nearby monastery to listen to the Dhamma, saying, "We will return before dawn," and the dawn rises while they are on the way, the robes become Nissaggiya, but the Nissaya is not terminated. If, out of respect for the Dhamma, they sit down saying, "We will go only after listening until the end," as soon as the dawn rises, the robes become Nissaggiya and the Nissaya is terminated. When an elder sends a junior monk to a small village to wash a robe, he must give his own robe only after revoking its assignment (paccuddharaṇa), and he must also have the junior monk's robe revoked before leaving it. If he goes without mindfulness, he should revoke the assignment of his own robe and take the junior monk's robe out of trust (vissāsa) and keep it. If the elder does not remember but the junior monk does, the junior monk should revoke the assignment of his own robe, take the elder's robe out of trust, and upon arriving, say, "Venerable Sir, please formally determine (adhiṭṭhāna) and use your robe." He must also formally determine his own robe. In this way, by the mindfulness of even one person, there is liberation from the offense. ## Thus in the Pālimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-saṅgaha, ## The Discussion on the Decision Regarding Being Separated from Robes is finished.
47:
## 10. Bhaṇḍapāṭisāmanavinicchayakathā
Bhaṇḍassa pāṭisāmana means the guarding of others' property. Whether it is a permissible (kappiya) object or an impermissible (akappiya) object of others—even as little as a layperson's property like a mother's palm-leaf ear-ornament—a monk who stores it in the capacity of a storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika) commits a pācittiya offense. If it is the property of one's parents and must definitely be stored, and if it is a permissible object, it should be taken and stored for one's own benefit. If they say, "Please store this for us," one should refuse, saying, "It is not allowable." If they leave it and go, saying "Keep it," it becomes a concern (responsibility), and it is allowable to store it. If carpenters and others working in the monastery, or those close to the king, say, "Please store our tools or bedding," one must not store them out of affection or fear. However, it is allowable to show them a secure place. If they leave it by force and go, it is allowable to store it.

If a monk is asked by the owner for property that was placed in his hands for safekeeping, and not wanting to give it back, he says, "I did not take it," he commits a dukkaṭa offense both because of deliberate lying and because it is an effort (payoga) toward taking what is not given (adinnādāna). A monk who says things like, "What are you talking about? This is not suitable for me, nor for you," also commits only a dukkaṭa offense. If the owner develops a doubt, thinking, "I placed this in this monk's hand in private; no one else knows. Will he give it back to me or not?" the monk commits a thullaccaya offense. Seeing the monk's harsh behavior, if the owner gives up hope (dhura-nikkhepa), thinking, "He will not give it to me," at that point, if the monk still intends to give it, thinking "I will give it to him after making him weary," he is still free from the [grave] offense. Even if the monk has no intention of giving it, but the owner is still striving to get it back, the monk is still free [from the grave offense]. If the monk has no intention of giving it and the owner gives up hope, thinking "He will not give it to me," then because of this double giving up of hope, the monk commits a pārājika offense. Even if he says with his mouth, "I will give it," but in his heart he does not want to give it, and while he is in that state the owner gives up hope, he commits a pārājika offense. There is no offense for a monk who, for the sake of guarding it, moves property placed in his hands by others from an insecure place to a secure place. Even if he moves it from its place with the intention to steal, it does not constitute theft (avahāra). Why? Because it was already placed in his own hands. However, he is liable for the property (bhaṇḍadeyya). The same principle applies to one who uses it with the intention to steal.
48:
It is proper to look after any requisite belonging to the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika). If a visiting monk (āgantuka), while the resident monks are performing the work of sewing robes, places his bowl and robes near them and goes to bathe or elsewhere, thinking, 'These [monks] will look after them,' if the resident monks do look after them, it is well. If they do not look after them and they are lost, there is no offense (no liability to compensate). If that visiting monk says, 'Venerable sirs, please keep these bowl and robes,' and goes, but the resident monks do not know because they are busy with their own work, the same rule applies. Furthermore, if they are told, 'Venerable sirs, please keep these bowl and robes,' and they refuse, saying, 'We are busy,' yet the other monk goes anyway, disregarding their words and thinking, 'They will surely look after them,' the same rule applies. However, if they say, whether requested by that monk or not, 'We will keep them, you may go,' then they must be looked after securely. If they are not looked after securely and are lost, they must be compensated. Why? Because they were accepted.

If a monk who is a storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika), even at dawn, brings down the monks' bowls and robes to the ground floor of the mansion (pāsāda), closes the door, and goes for alms in a distant place without informing those monks, and thieves take them, the liability to compensate lies with that storekeeper alone. If a monk is told by other monks, 'Venerable sir, it is time for the drawing of lots (salāka), please bring down the bowls and robes,' and that storekeeper asks, 'Have you all assembled?' and when told, 'Yes, we have assembled,' he brings out and places the bowls and robes, locks the storehouse door, and says, 'Take your bowls and robes, look after the door of the lower mansion, and then go,' and then he leaves. Among those monks, if a lazy monk, after the others have gone, gets up wiping his eyes and goes to the water-place to wash his face, and thieves, seeing that moment, steal the bowl and robes, it is a 'well-stolen' case; the storekeeper has no liability to compensate.

If any monk leaves his requisites in the storehouse without informing the storekeeper, even if those requisites are lost, the storekeeper has no liability to compensate. However, if the storekeeper sees those requisites and, thinking 'They are placed in an improper spot,' takes and stores them, if they are lost, the liability to compensate lies with that storekeeper alone. If the monk who placed the requisites says, 'Venerable sir, I have left such-and-such a requisite, please look after it,' and the storekeeper accepts, saying 'Very well,' or if he thinks it is placed in a bad spot and moves it to another place, if it is lost, the liability to compensate lies with that storekeeper alone. For a storekeeper who refuses, saying 'I do not know [about it],' there is no liability to compensate. Also, if a monk leaves it while the storekeeper is watching but does not make the storekeeper accept it, its loss is simply a loss (no liability). However, if the storekeeper moves that requisite to another place and it is lost, [he must compensate].
49:
...liability to compensate (gīvā). If the storehouse is well-secured and all the requisites of the Saṅgha and the Cetiya are kept there, but the storekeeper is foolish and unskilled and leaves the door open to go somewhere to listen to a Dhamma talk or to do something else, and thieves steal as much as they can seeing that opportunity, the liability for all of that lies with that storekeeper. Whether he is walking up and down outside after leaving the storehouse, or opening the door to let his body take the breeze, or sitting right there devoted to monkly duties (samaṇadhamma), or sitting there busy with some work, or even if pressed by the need to defecate or urinate, while he is still within the precincts (upacāra) but goes outside, or is negligent in any other way, and thieves steal as much as they can because of his negligence—whether by opening the door, entering through an open door, or breaking through a joint—the liability for all of that lies with him alone. 'However, in hot weather, it is proper to sleep with the window open,' they say. For a monk pressed by the need to defecate, if there is no place to relieve himself within the precincts and he goes elsewhere, it is beyond his control as he is in the category of the sick; therefore, there is no liability to compensate.

If a person, feeling hot inside, secures the door well and goes outside, and thieves catch him and say, 'Open the door,' he should not open it even up to the third time. But if those thieves say, 'If you do not open it, we will kill you and also break the door to take the requisites,' and they raise axes and so on, he may open it, considering, 'There is no benefit in my death and the destruction of the Saṅgha's lodgings.' In such a case, they say: 'There is no liability to compensate because it was beyond his control.' If any visitor (āgantuka) gives the key or opens the door and thieves steal as much as they can, the liability for all of that lies with that visitor alone. If the Saṅgha has provided a bolt (suciyantaka) and a key-ring (kuñcikamuddikā) for the security of the storehouse, but the storekeeper sleeps having only put the latch (ghaṭika), and thieves open it and take the requisites, the liability lies with him alone. If he is sleeping having used the bolt and the key-ring, and thieves come and say, 'Open the door,' he should act according to the previous method. If he is sleeping having secured it well in this way, but they take things by breaking the wall or the roof, or by entering through a tunnel, he has no liability to compensate.

If other elders also live in the storehouse and they take their own requisites and leave while the door is open, and the storekeeper does not look after the door after they have gone, if anything is stolen there, the liability to compensate lies with the storekeeper alone because he is the one in charge. However, the elders should also be helpful (as companions). This is the proper conduct (sāmīcī). If the storekeeper says, 'You stay outside and [take] your requisites...'
50:
If the storekeeper says, "Take your requisites and do not enter," yet a frivolous senior monk among them enters the storehouse with novices and attendants, and sits or lies down there, whatever property is lost or damaged, all that loss is the responsibility (gīvā) of that senior monk alone. The storekeeper, however, should remain with the remaining senior monks and companions. If the storekeeper himself takes frivolous novices and attendants and sits or lies down in the storehouse, whatever is lost, all that is the responsibility of that storekeeper alone. Therefore, only the storekeeper should reside in that storehouse; others should reside only at the foot of trees and not in the storehouse.

If they place their requisites in the living quarters of their compatible (sabhāga) monks, and if the requisites are lost, it is the responsibility of those compatible monks who kept them. The other companion monks should also assist in resolving the matter. If the Sangha provides gruel and meals to the storekeeper within the monastery, but that storekeeper goes to the village for alms, if anything is lost, it is the responsibility of that storekeeper alone. For monks entering for alms, if a monastery guard appointed to protect extra robes also goes for alms despite receiving gruel or provisions, whatever is lost in that monastery is his responsibility alone. Not only this, but like the storekeeper, whatever is lost due to his negligence is entirely his responsibility.

If the monastery is large, and while he goes to guard one area, property kept in another area is stolen, he is not liable (gīvā) because it is beyond his scope. In such a monastery, requisites should be kept in a central location where everyone congregates, or two or three monastery guards should be appointed. If those guards, being diligent, protect here and there, yet something is lost, they are not liable. Whether it is property taken after binding the monastery guards, or property taken by another route while they have gone to the path of the thieves, the guards are not responsible. If there is no gruel or provisions provided to the monastery guards in the monastery, it is proper to set aside two or three extra gruel-tickets and sufficient meal-tickets for them from the gains received by those monks. However, these should not be set aside permanently. This is because laypeople might become dissatisfied, thinking, "Only the monastery guards are eating our food"; therefore, they should be assigned on a rotating basis. If their compatible monks bring and give them the meal-tickets etc., it is well.
51:
It is well. If they do not give, they should be made to take their turn and bring it out. If a monastery guard, while receiving two or three gruel-tickets and four or five meal-tickets, goes to the village for alms, just as with a storekeeper, he is responsible for everything lost (he must compensate). If the Sangha has no meals or provisions to be given to the monastery guards, and the monks take turns for monastery duty and have their own pupils guard the monastery, one is not allowed to refuse the turn when it arrives. One must act just as other monks do. However, the monks should not assign a turn to a monk who has no companion or second person, or to such a monk who has no compatible monk to bring and give him food.

A monk who lives by taking and utilizing rice etc. kept in the monastery for the purpose of cooking should also stand in the rotation. A monk who does not live by depending on that cooking should not be made to take a turn. Monks are also placed in the monastery for the sake of various fruits; they guard and protect them, and eat them by dividing them according to the fruit-turns. A monk who eats those fruits should stand in the rotation; one who does not live by depending on them should not be made to take a turn. They are also placed for the purpose of protecting lodgings, beds, chairs, benches, and floor coverings; a monk residing in the dwelling should stand in the rotation, but a monk who practices the dhutaṅga of living in the open air or at the foot of a tree should not be made to take a turn. If there is a junior monk who is very learned and teaches the Dhamma to many, gives interrogations, explains the Pali, preaches the Dhamma, and carries the burdens of the Sangha, this monk should not be made to take a turn even if he enjoys the gains or resides in the dwelling. It is said, "A distinguished person should be recognized."

For one who guards the Uposatha hall or the Image house, double gruel-meals, a daily measure of rice, three robes annually, and allowable requisites worth ten or twenty (kahāpaṇas) should be given. If, while receiving these, something is lost there due to his negligence, he must compensate for everything. If it is snatched away by force after being bound, he is not liable. In that case, it is proper to have the Cetiya's property protected by the property of the Cetiya or the Sangha; it is not proper to have the Sangha's property protected by the property of the Cetiya. If the Sangha's property is placed together with the Cetiya's property, it is proper to consider that by protecting the Cetiya's property, it is already protected. Even for one who guards the Uposatha hall etc. on a fortnightly rotation, if something is lost due to negligence, he is certainly liable.

## Thus ends the Discussion on the Decision regarding the Storage of Goods

## 11. Discussion on the Determination of Engaging in Buying and Selling

Kayavikkaya-samāpatti means engaging in buying and selling. According to the method stated in the Pārājika-aṭṭhakathā (Vol. 2, p. 595), such as saying "Give this for that," a monk who takes another's allowable item (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) engages in buying, and a monk who gives his own allowable item engages in selling. This kind of buying and selling is not allowable with anyone except the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika); it is not allowable even with laypeople, other ascetics, or even one's own parents.

In this matter, the determination is as follows: whether it be cloth for cloth, or food for food, if one says of any allowable item, "Give this for that," one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). If, after saying so, one gives one's own item even to one's mother, one incurs a dukkaṭa. Alternatively, if one is told by another, "Give this for that," or if one says, "Give this, I will give this to you," and then takes the item from one's mother, one incurs a dukkaṭa. When one's own item reaches the hand of another and the other's item reaches one's own hand, an offense of forfeiture and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya) is incurred.

However, for a monk who says to his mother or father, "Give this," it does not constitute an improper intimation (viññatti). For the parent who gives, saying "Take this," it does not constitute the wasting of a faith-offering (saddhādeyya-vinipātana). For a monk who says "Give this" to a non-relative (aññātaka), it is an improper intimation. For the non-relative who gives, saying "Take this," it is a wasting of a faith-offering. For a monk who engages in buying and selling by saying "Give this for that," a nissaggiya pācittiya offense is incurred. Therefore, when exchanging allowable items, a monk should exchange in a way that is free from these three offenses (viññatti-dukkaṭa, saddhādeyya-vinipātana-dukkaṭa, and nissaggiya pācittiya), whether with parents or with non-relatives.

The procedure for such an exchange is as follows: A monk has rice for his journey. On the way, he sees a man with cooked rice in his hand and says, "We have rice, but we have no need for this; we only have a need for cooked rice." If the man takes the rice and gives the cooked rice, it is allowable. None of the three offenses are incurred, and it does not even amount to making a sign (nimitta-kamma). Why? Because the original item (the rice), which is the value for the cooked rice, exists. If a monk does not act in this way but exchanges by saying, "Give this cooked rice for this rice," he incurs an offense according to the object.

If, seeing a person who eats leftovers, one says, "Eat this rice and bring dye-bark or firewood," one incurs nissaggiya pācittiya offenses according to the number of pieces of dye-bark or firewood. If one says, "Eat this rice and do such-and-such a task," and has requisites such as a water-strainer made by craftsmen like ivory-carvers, or has clothes washed by laundrymen, one incurs an offense according to the object. If one has one's hair cut by a barber...
53:
...or has new construction work done by laborers, one incurs an offense according to the object. However, if one does not say, "Eat this rice and do this task," but instead says, "Eat this rice," and then after they have eaten, or while they are about to eat, one says, "Do such-and-such a task," it is allowable. In this matter, although there is no item belonging to another that has come into one's hands and must be forfeited in tasks such as washing clothes, cutting hair, or new construction like clearing the ground, this cannot be rejected because it is firmly stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. Therefore, just as one confesses a pācittiya offense when a nissaggiya object is consumed or lost, here too, a pācittiya offense should be confessed.

It is allowable to ask the price of any allowable item that one wishes to obtain. Therefore, if one asks, "How much is this bowl of yours worth?" and the owner says, "It is worth such-and-such," and if the monk's own allowable item is of higher value, he should reply, "Lay follower, this item of mine is of great value; give your bowl to someone else." Hearing this, if the lay follower says, "I will give another small vessel as well," it is allowable to take it. If that bowl is of great value and the monk's item is of little value, and the owner of the bowl does not know it is of little value, the bowl should not be taken; the monk must explain, "My item is of little value." A monk who takes it by deception, knowing it is of great value, also falls into the category of having to have the item valued for settlement. If the owner of the bowl says, "Let it be, Bhante, the remaining value will be for my merit," and gives it, it is allowable.

One should tell an attendant (kappiyakāraka), "Take this item and give me this bowl." Therefore, excluding the owner from whom one wishes to take the item, one should appoint another person—at the very least even the owner's son or brother—as an attendant and say, "Take this item and give me such-and-such an item." If that attendant is clever and obtains it after repeatedly bargaining and haggling, the monk should remain silent. If the attendant is not clever and does not know how to obtain it, and the merchant is deceiving him, the monk should say, "Do not take it."

If one says, "We have this oil or ghee that has been formally accepted (pari-ggahita), but we need other oil or ghee that has not been formally accepted," and if the person takes the accepted one and gives another, one should not have one's own oil measured first. Why? Because there may be oil remnants in the measuring vessel, which would spoil the unaccepted oil of the person who measures it later. This term 'buying and selling' (kayavikkaya) is spoken of in terms of allowable items. For a monk who exchanges an allowable item for an allowable item, a nissaggiya offense is stated by the Kayavikkaya training rule. However, if one exchanges an unallowable item for an unallowable item, or an allowable item for an unallowable item, or an unallowable item for an allowable item...
54:
For the monk who exchanges, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred according to the training rule on trading with money (Rūpiyasaṃvohāra). Therefore, if there is an unallowable object in both or even in one of the items, it is called trading with money.

To illustrate the gravity of the offense of trading with money, these four types of bowls (pattacatukka) should be understood. Suppose a monk accepts gold or silver himself and uses that gold or silver to acquire iron ore; he has that iron smelted and has a bowl made from that iron. This bowl is called 'greatly unallowable' (mahā-akappiya). It cannot be made allowable by any means. Even if that bowl is destroyed and made into a small cup, that cup is also unallowable. If it is made into an axe, the tooth-stick cut with that axe is also unallowable. If it is made into a fish-hook, the fish killed with that hook are also unallowable. If the axe is heated in fire to heat water or milk, that heated substance is also unallowable.

Suppose a monk accepts gold or silver himself and buys a bowl with that gold or silver; this bowl is also unallowable. In the Mahāpaccariya, it is stated, 'It is not allowable even for the five classes of fellow practitioners.' However, it can be made allowable. After the price is returned to the owners of the price, and the bowl is returned to the owners of the bowl, it is allowable to take and use it after giving an allowable item in exchange.

Suppose a monk has someone else accept gold or silver and goes to a blacksmith's house with a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka); upon seeing a bowl, he says, 'I like this one.' The lay attendant then gives that gold or silver to inform the blacksmith. Although this bowl is acquired through allowable terminology, it is just like the second bowl. It is unallowable because the money was accepted. Why is it not allowable for others? Because the money has not yet been relinquished.

Suppose a monk does not accept gold or silver himself but goes to a blacksmith's house with a lay attendant who was sent with the instruction, 'Buy a bowl and give it to the Elder.' Upon seeing a bowl, he says, 'Take these coins and give me this bowl,' thus causing the coins to be given and taking the bowl. This bowl is unallowable for that monk alone because it was improperly managed. For others, however, it is allowable because he did not accept the money himself. There was once an Elder named Anuruddha, who was the preceptor of Elder Mahāsuma. That Elder filled such a bowl with ghee and relinquished it to the Saṅgha. The co-residents (saddhivihārika) of Elder Tipitaka Cūḷanāga also had such a bowl. The Elder also had them fill that bowl with ghee and relinquish it to the Saṅgha. This is the fourfold set of unallowable bowls (akappiyapattacatukka).
55:
If, without accepting gold or silver oneself, one goes to a smithy with a kappiyakāraka who has been sent with the instruction "Buy a bowl for the elder and offer it," and upon seeing a bowl, says "I like this bowl" or "I will take this," and the kappiyakāraka gives that gold or silver and makes the smith understand (buys it), then that bowl is entirely allowable and is fit for use even by the Buddhas. However, a monk engaging in this transaction with gold or silver should not even tell the kappiyakāraka, "Buy this bowl with this gold or silver and give it to me."

## Thus, in the Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha,
## The Discussion on the Decision regarding what constitutes Buying and Selling is finished.
## 12. Discussion on the Decision regarding the Acceptance of Gold, Silver, etc.

Rūpiyādipatiggaha means the acceptance of gold, silver, and so on. In that acceptance of gold and silver, there are four types of nissaggiya objects: gold (jātarūpa), silver (rajata), a gold coin (jātarūpa-māsaka), and a silver coin (rajata-māsaka). A coin made of copper, brass, etc., is called a loha-māsaka. A coin made by cutting a figure from heartwood, or from a bamboo strip, or even from a palmyra leaf, is called a dāru-māsaka. A coin made by forming a figure from lacquer or resin is called a jatu-māsaka. Whatever coin is used for trade in whatever region at whatever time—whether it be made of bone, skin, or the seeds of fruits, whether it has a figure or not—all such coins are included under the term rajata-māsaka (silver coin). Pearls, gems, cat's eyes, conch shells, crystal, coral, red rubies, emeralds (masāragalla), the seven kinds of grain, bondwomen, bondmen, fields, lands, flower gardens, fruit gardens, etc.—these are called dukkaṭa objects (objects involving an offense of wrongdoing). Among those objects, it is not permissible to accept nissaggiya objects for oneself, or for the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, or a cetiya.
