For a monk who accepts them for himself, there is a nissaggiya pācittiya offense; if he accepts them for the Saṅgha, etc., there is a dukkaṭa offense. As for dukkaṭa objects, for a monk who accepts them for anyone, there is only a dukkaṭa offense.

Regarding those objects, there is this decision: If someone brings gold or silver and says, "I offer this gold and silver to the Saṅgha; please build a monastery, or a cetiya, or one of the dining halls, etc.," it is not permissible to accept this gold or silver. If, however, it is refused with the words "This gold and silver is not permissible for monks to accept," and [the donor says] "In the hands of the carpenters or the workers..."
56:
If a donor says, "It will be [in the hands of the carpenter or the worker]; you, venerable sirs, should only know what is well-done or poorly-done," and having given it into their hands, he departs, it is allowable. Furthermore, if he says, "It will be in the hands of my people, or it will be in my own hands; you, venerable sirs, may command for the benefit of whoever should be given [the requisites]," this is also allowable.

If, without naming (or touching) the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual, they say, "We give this gold and silver for the Cetiya, we give it for the Vihāra, we give it for new construction (navakamma)," it is not allowable to reject it. One should inform the kappiya-kārakas (attendants), "These people are saying this." However, if it is said, "Venerable sirs, you take and keep it for the Cetiya and so on," it must be rejected, saying, "It is not allowable for us to take it."

If someone brings much gold and silver and says, "I give this to the Saṅgha; please use the four requisites," and if the Saṅgha accepts it, there is an offense in both the acceptance and the use. If one monk therein rejects it, saying, "This is not allowable," and the lay follower (upāsaka) says, "If it is not allowable, let it be my own property," and takes that gold and silver and leaves, no one should say anything to that [rejecting] monk, such as "You have caused an obstacle to the Saṅgha's gain." He who censures or accuses that monk is the one who incurs an offense. That one monk has made many monks free from offense. If, when the monks have rejected it saying "It is not allowable," the donor says, "It will be in the hands of the kappiya-kārakas, or it will be in the hands of my people, or in my own hands; you, venerable sirs, just use the four requisites," it is allowable.

Gold and silver given for the sake of the four requisites should be applied to whatever requisite is needed. That which is given for the sake of robes should be applied only to robes. If there is no such need for robes, but the Saṅgha is weary for lack of alms-food and so on, it may be applied for the sake of alms-food after informing and obtaining the consent of the Saṅgha. This same method applies to gold given for the sake of alms-food and medicinal requisites. However, that which is given for the sake of lodgings (senāsana) must be applied only to lodgings because lodgings are heavy property (garubhaṇḍa). But if the monks have abandoned the lodgings and left, and it is a time when the lodgings would perish, it is permitted for the monks to use them even by disposing of the lodgings; therefore, they should be used just enough for maintenance without exhausting the capital for the upkeep of the lodgings.

If someone says, "I have a great reservoir capable of producing three crops; I give it to the Saṅgha," and if the Saṅgha accepts it, there is an offense in both the acceptance and the use. No one should say anything to the monk who rejects that gift, just as in the previous method. He who censures that monk is the one who incurs an offense. Even though he is but one monk, he makes many monks free from offense. If the donor says, "The Saṅgha has a reservoir of such a name and a reservoir of such a name; why are those allowable for the Saṅgha?" he should be told, "They must have been given after being made allowable (kappiya)." When asked, "How is it given so that it is allowable?" [the answer is] "For the sake of the four requisites..."
57:
[The previous explanation] occurs. That single monk who rejects it effectively makes many monks free from offense. If a donor says, "I give just such a reservoir," and when rejected by the monks saying "It is not allowable," he says, "There are reservoirs belonging to the Saṅgha named such-and-such; why are they allowable?" That donor should be told, "They must have been given after being made allowable (kappiya)." If he asks, "How is it given so that it is allowable?" [the answer is] "It is allowable when given by saying, 'Please use the four requisites.'" If that donor gives it saying, "Excellent, venerable sirs, please use the four requisites," it is allowable.

Furthermore, if he says, "Please accept the reservoir," and it is rejected as "not allowable," and he asks, "Is there a kappiya-kāraka?" and is told "No," and then he says, "So-and-so will manage this reservoir, or it will be in his hand or in my hand; let the Saṅgha use only the allowable items (kappiya-bhaṇḍa)," then it is allowable. Even if it is rejected as "not allowable," and he says, "[The Saṅgha] will use the water, wash clothes, and the wild animals and birds will drink," it is allowable because of such a statement. Again, if it is rejected as "not allowable," and he says, "Please accept it in an allowable manner," [the monks should say] "Excellent, lay follower, the Saṅgha will drink the water, wash clothes, and the wild animals and birds will drink," and having said so, it is allowable to use it. Furthermore, if it is said, "I give my reservoir or pond to the Saṅgha," it is certainly allowable to use it after saying, "Excellent, lay follower, the Saṅgha will drink the water," and so on.

If the monks, having requested labor and having themselves dug allowable ground, have a reservoir made for the purpose of using water, and if people, depending on that reservoir, produce crops and give allowable items to the monastery, it is allowable. Furthermore, if the people themselves, for the sake of benefiting the Saṅgha, dig on Saṅgha land and give allowable items from the crops produced depending on that reservoir, this is also allowable. If it is said, "Please appoint one kappiya-kāraka for us," it is also permitted to appoint one. Furthermore, if those people depart to another place due to being oppressed by royal taxes, and others take over but do not give anything to the monks, it is permitted to block the water. However, such blocking is permitted only during the time of plowing/sowing, not during the time when crops are growing. If those people say, "Venerable sirs, did not people in the past also grow crops depending on this reservoir?" then they should be told, "Those people used to perform such-and-such benefits for the Saṅgha, and gave such-and-such allowable items." If they say, "We too will give," then it is allowable.

If an unskilled monk accepts or causes a reservoir to be made using unallowable terminology, it should not be used by the monks; even the allowable items obtained depending on that reservoir are also unallowable.
58:
It is indeed unallowable. If, knowing that the monks have relinquished it, the owner, or his children, or anyone else born in that lineage gives it again using allowable terminology (kappiya-vohāra), it is allowable. If the family lineage is broken, and the ruler of that district, having seized it, gives it again using allowable terminology—just as the Chief Queen of King Aḷanāga gave back the water channel dug by monks at Cittalapabbata—it is also allowable. In a tank accepted through allowable terminology or by way of water, it is allowable for monks with pure intentions to perform tasks such as digging earth or building embankments. However, seeing those who cultivate crops depending on that tank, it is not allowable to appoint a kappiya-kāraka [for that purpose]. If they themselves offer allowable goods, they should be accepted. If they do not offer, one should not ask. In a tank accepted by way of requisites, it is allowable to appoint a kappiya-kāraka, but it is not allowable to order tasks such as digging earth or building embankments. If the kappiya-kārakas do it of their own accord, it is allowable. If an unskilled but conscientious (lajjī) monk orders such tasks, although the acceptance might be allowable, because of the mixture arising from the monk's effort, it becomes difficult to use—like alms-food mixed with poison or food mixed with the juice of unallowable meat—and is unallowable for all monks.

If there is a place for water and the embankment is firm, it is allowable to manage only the water, saying, 'Do it so that it holds much water; make sure there is water near the bank.' Without placing fire in the hearth, it is allowable to say, 'Lay devotees, let the water-work be successful,' but it is not allowable to say, 'Cultivate crops and bring them.' If, seeing excessive water in the tank, one causes a channel to be drawn out from the side or the back, or causes the forest to be cleared to establish paddy fields, or takes more than the usual portion from old fields, or demands money for new crops that have not been partitioned, saying, 'Give this many kahāpaṇas,' it is unallowable for all monks.

If a monk, without saying 'Plough' or 'Sow,' designates the land saying, 'In this much land, there is this much portion,' or when farmers say, 'We have cultivated crops on this much land; please take this much portion,' he measures with a rope or a stick to know the extent of the land, or stands and guards at the threshing floor, or causes [grain] to be removed from the threshing floor, or causes it to be stored in a granary, that grain is unallowable for that monk alone. If farmers bring money and say, 'We have brought these kahāpaṇas for the Sangha,' and another monk, thinking 'The Sangha does not consume money,' says, 'With this many kahāpaṇas, bring robes...'
59:
...'bring [robes], or with this much, prepare gruel and so on,' if they bring it, it is unallowable for all monks. Why? Because the money (kahāpaṇas) was directed. If they bring paddy and say, 'This is brought for the Sangha,' and another monk says in the same manner as before, 'With this much paddy, bring this and that,' what they bring is unallowable for that monk alone. Why? Because the paddy was directed. If they bring rice or beans and say, 'This is brought for the Sangha,' and another monk says in the same manner as before, 'With this much rice, bring this and that,' what they bring is allowable for all monks. Why? Because allowable items like rice were directed. Even in buying and selling, there is no offense because it was told to a kappiya-kāraka.

In the past, at Cittalapabbata, a monk at the door of the assembly hall (catu-sālā) drew a circle on the ground to give a sign to the monastery attendants (ārāmika), thinking, 'Oh, it would be good if they cooked this many cakes for the Sangha tomorrow.' Seeing that circle, a clever attendant did exactly that, and on the second day when the drum was beaten and the Sangha assembled, he took the cakes and said to the Elder of the Sangha: 'Venerable Sir, before today, we have never heard of such a thing from our fathers or grandfathers. A certain monk made a sign for cakes at the door of the assembly hall. From now on, let the venerable ones speak according to their wishes; it will be for our comfort as well.' The Great Elder turned back from that very spot, and not a single monk accepted the cakes. Thus, in the past, they did not consume what arose in such a way. Therefore:

A monk who does not abandon the practice of effacement (sallekha) and is diligent,
Should not show greed for the sake of material gain, even in allowable things. (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.538-9)

This method mentioned regarding tanks also applies to ponds, small water channels, and so on.

Even if one says 'I give' regarding a field or a garden where cereals, beans, sugarcane, or various fruits grow, it should be rejected saying 'It is not allowable.' It should only be accepted when said using allowable terminology, as in the method for tanks: 'I give for the purpose of using the four requisites.' However, if one says 'I give the forest' or 'I give the wilderness,' it is allowable. If people, without being ordered by monks, clear trees there and plant beans and so on, and then give a portion to the monks, it is allowable. If they do not give, it should not be requested. If they depart due to some danger and others come to cultivate, if they do not give anything to the monks, they should not be prevented. If they say, 'Venerable Sir, did people not cultivate crops here before?' then it should be said, 'Those people donated such allowable goods (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) to the Sangha.'
60:
If people [voluntarily clear trees and] produce crops and give a share to the monks, it is allowable. If they do not give, they should not be asked. If, due to some danger, those people move elsewhere and others cultivate the land but do not give anything to the monks, they should be prevented. If they say, "Venerable sirs, did not people formerly cultivate crops here?", then it should be said, "They used to offer such and such allowable items to the Saṅgha." If they say, "We too will offer," then it is allowable.

If, referring to a plot of land where crops are produced, they say, "We offer this as a sīmā," it is allowable. However, for the purpose of demarcating the sīmā, one should not personally set up pillars or stones. This is because land is priceless; even by a small amount of land, one may fall into a Pārājika offense. But to the monastery attendants (ārāmikas), it should be said, "Our sīmā goes by this place." Even if they take more than intended, there is no offense because it was spoken in a roundabout way. If kings, royal ministers, and so on, personally have the pillars set up and offer, saying, "Please make use of the four requisites," it is indeed allowable.

If someone digs a pond within the sīmā, or channels a watercourse through the middle of the monastery, or if the cetiya courtyard, the Bodhi tree courtyard, etc., are damaged, that person should be prevented. If the Saṅgha, having received some material gain (āmisa), does not prevent it because of regarding that gain highly, but a single monk prevents it, that monk alone is the authority. If a single monk does not prevent it but says, "You may proceed," he becomes a partisan of those people. If the Saṅgha prevents it, the Saṅgha alone is the authority. For in matters pertaining to the Saṅgha (saṅghika), he who performs the act in accordance with the Dhamma is the authority. If they continue to do it even while being prevented, the earth taken from below should be put back below, and the earth taken from above should be put back above to fill it up.

If someone, wishing to offer sugar cane, beans, or vine-fruits such as gourds and pumpkins that have already grown, says, "I offer this entire sugar cane field, bean field, or vine-fruit pit," Mahāsumma Thera said it is not allowable because it is touched together with the ground (vatthu). However, Mahāpaduma Thera said, "This is merely a manner of speaking; since that portion of land belongs only to the owners, it is allowable." If one says, "I offer a slave (dāsa)," it is not allowable. If one says, "I offer an ārāmika, I offer a service-provider (veyyāvaccakara), I offer a kappiyakāraka," it is allowable. If an ārāmika performs the work of the Saṅgha both in the morning and in the evening, all medical care and nursing should be provided to him as if to a sāmaṇera. If he performs the work of the Saṅgha only in the morning and does his own work in the evening, the evening ration should not be given. Those who...
61:
...are offered as ārāmikas and perform the work of the Saṅgha on a five-day rotation or a half-month rotation, and do their own work at other times, the meal and ration should be given to them only during the period they are working. If there is no work for the Saṅgha and they live by doing only their own work, if they bring and offer the wages of their manual labor, it should be accepted. If they do not offer, nothing should be said. It is allowable to accept even a laundry-slave or a weaver-slave under the name of 'ārāmika'.

If they say, "We offer cattle," they should be refused. If they ask, "Why are these cattle not allowable?", and it is said by the wise, "They are offered for the purpose of enjoying the five products of the cow (pañcagorasa)," and they then say, "We too offer them for the purpose of enjoying the five products of the cow," then they are allowable. The same method applies to goats and so on. If they say, "We offer elephants, horses, buffaloes, chickens, or pigs," it is not allowable to accept them. If some people say, "Venerable sirs, please be unconcerned; we will take these animals and offer allowable goods (kappiyabhaṇḍa) to you," and they take them, it is allowable. Regarding chickens and pigs, it is allowable to have them released in the forest with the thought, "May they live happily."

When it is said, "We offer this pond, this field, this land to the monastery," it is not permitted to refuse. If someone, referring to a monk, sends the price of a robe such as gold or silver via a messenger, saying, "Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund, clothe the monk named so-and-so with the robe," and that messenger approaches that monk and says, "Venerable sir, this robe-fund has been brought referring to the venerable one; may the venerable one accept the robe-fund," then that monk should say to that messenger, "Friend, we do not accept a robe-fund; we only accept an allowable robe at the proper time." If that messenger says to that monk, "Does the venerable one have any service-provider (veyyāvaccakara)?", the monk who needs the robe should point out an ārāmika or a lay follower (upāsaka), saying, "Friend, this person is the service-provider for the monks." He should not say, "Give it to him," or "He will keep it," or "He will exchange it," or "He will purchase it." After that messenger has informed the veyyāvaccakara and approaches that monk, saying, "Venerable sir, I have instructed the veyyāvaccakara whom the venerable one pointed out; may the venerable one approach him at the proper time, and he will clothe you with a robe," then that monk who needs the robe, having approached the veyyāvaccakara, should prompt him two or three times...
62:
"Friend, I have need of a robe"—this is how one should remind. One should not say, "Give me a robe," "Bring me a robe," "Exchange a robe for me," or "Purchase a robe for me." If, after urging or reminding two or three times, that robe is produced, that is good. If it is not produced, one should go to where the steward is and stand silently, intending for the robe, four, five, or at most six times. One should not sit on a seat, one should not accept food, and one should not preach the Dhamma. If asked, "Why have you come?", one should only say, "You know, friend."

If one sits on a seat, accepts food, or preaches the Dhamma, one breaks the protocol of standing. If one urges four times, one should stand four times. If one urges five times, one should stand twice. If one urges six times, one should not stand at all. This is because one instance of urging destroys two instances of standing. Just as one should not stand after urging six times, one should not urge after standing twelve times. Therefore, if one only urges and does not stand, one is allowed six urgings. If one only stands and does not urge, one is allowed twelve standings. If one both urges and stands, for every one urging, two standings must be reduced. Among those monks who urge or stand, if a monk goes repeatedly on the same day and urges six times, or if he goes once and says "Friend, I have need of a robe" six times, or if he goes repeatedly on the same day and stands twelve times, or if he goes once and stands in various places—he also destroys all urgings and all standings. How much more so if this is done on different days! If he strives beyond that and produces the robe, there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort, and it becomes an offence of forfeiture (nissaggiya) upon acquisition.

If he cannot obtain the robe, he should go himself or send a messenger to the person from whom the robe-fund was brought for that monk—whether it be a king or a royal minister—and say: "Sirs, you sent a robe-fund intended for a certain monk; that robe-fund is of no use to that monk. May the venerable ones attend to your own property, let not your property be lost." This is the proper procedure in that case. If a monk neither goes himself nor sends a messenger, he incurs an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the breach of duty.

If it is asked whether one should act this way towards all attendants (kappiyakāraka), the answer is: one should not. These attendants are briefly of two kinds: specified (niddiṭṭha) and unspecified (aniddiṭṭha). Among them, the specified are of two kinds: those specified by the monk and those specified by the messenger. The unspecified are also of two kinds: those who speak in one's presence and those who are absent. Among those specified, those specified by the monk himself are of four types according to presence or absence. Those specified by the messenger are likewise of four types. How? In this Dispensation, some donor might send an unallowable object for a robe to a monk. The messenger who is sent approaches the monk and says, "Venerable sir, this object has been sent by a donor named so-and-so for your robe."
63:
There are two kinds: the steward who is present and vocal, and the steward who is absent. Among these, the steward designated by the monk is of four types according to presence or absence; likewise, the steward designated by the messenger is also of four types.

How so? In this Dispensation, some donor sends an unallowable object (akappiyavatthu) for a monk's robe by a messenger. That messenger approaches the monk and says, "Venerable sir, this object has been sent by a donor named so-and-so for your robe; please accept it." The monk refuses, saying, "This object is not allowable for us." The messenger asks, "Venerable sir, do you have a steward (veyyāvaccakara)?" At that time, there may be stewards who have been instructed by lay followers seeking merit, saying, "Perform services for the monks," or there may be those who are acquaintances or regular attendants of the monks. If one of them is sitting near the monk at that moment, the monk designates him, saying, "This person is the monks' steward." The messenger gives the unallowable object into that person's hand, says, "Purchase a robe for the elder and offer it," and departs. This person is a steward designated by the monk in his presence.

If [the steward] is not sitting near the monk, the monk designates him, saying, "In such-and-such a village, a person named so-and-so is the monks' steward." That messenger goes and gives the unallowable object into that person's hand, saying, "Purchase a robe for the elder and give it," then returns to the monk, informs him that he has given it, and departs. This person is the first steward designated by the monk in his absence.

If that messenger does not return to inform him personally but sends another person to say, "Venerable sir, I have given the robe-fund into the hand of the person you designated; please accept the robe," this person is the second steward designated by the monk in his absence.

If he does not send another person but, just before departing, says to the monk, "I will give the robe-fund into that person's hand; please accept the robe," and then departs, this person is the third steward designated by the monk in his absence. Thus, there is one designated in the presence and three designated in the absence, making four who are called stewards designated by the monk. Regarding these persons, one should act as previously stated.

Alternatively, when the monk is asked by the messenger as in the previous method, he says, "We have no steward," either because he truly has none or because he does not wish to investigate. At that moment, some person arrives. The messenger gives the unallowable object into that person's hand and says, "Please accept the robe from this person's hand," and departs. This person is a steward designated by the messenger in his presence. Thus, there is one designated in the presence.
64:
Another messenger, having entered the village, gives the unallowable object into the hand of someone he likes, and returns to report as in the previous method, or sends another person. He departs after saying, "I have given the robe-fund into the hand of such-and-such a person; you should receive the robe." This is the third person pointed out by the messenger in [the monk's] absence. Thus, these four—one pointed out in [the monk's] presence and three pointed out in [the monk's] absence—are called stewards (veyyāvaccakara) pointed out by a messenger. Regarding them, one should proceed according to the method taught in the Meṇḍaka training rule.

Has it not been taught thus: "Bhikkhus, there are people who have faith and confidence. They deposit gold and silver in the hands of stewards, saying, 'With this, give the venerable one whatever is allowable.' Bhikkhus, I allow you to accept what is allowable resulting from that. However, bhikkhus, I do not say that gold and silver should be accepted or sought after by any means."

In this matter, there is no limit to the number of times for prompting (codanā). For a monk who does not accept the original value (gold and silver), it is allowable to accept the allowable object even through prompting or standing [at the steward's place] a thousand times. If [the steward] does not give it, the monk should have it brought even by appointing another steward. If he wishes, he should also inform the original owners of the money. If he does not wish to, he should not inform them.

When another monk is asked by a messenger as in the previous method, he says, "We have no steward." Someone else standing nearby, having heard this, says, "Sir, bring it; I will purchase and offer a robe to the venerable one." The messenger says, "Sir, here, please take and offer it," and having given it into that person's hand, he departs without informing the monk. This person is called a spontaneous (mukhavēvaṭika) steward. Another messenger gives the unallowable object into the hand of the monk's attendant or someone else, says, "Please offer a robe to the elder," and departs from that place. This person is called an absentee (parammukhā) steward. These two are called stewards not pointed out [by the monk]. Regarding them, one should proceed as one would with those who are not relatives or have not invited [the monk]. If they bring the robe and offer it of their own accord, it should be accepted. If they do not offer it, nothing should be said. Just as the decision was stated regarding an unallowable object sent in the hand of a messenger for the sake of a robe, so should the decision be understood when it is sent for the sake of alms-food and so forth, or when [the donor] comes and offers it personally.
65:
Regarding the acceptance of what is deposited (upanikkhittasādiyana), this is the decision: When someone places an unallowable object at one's feet and says, "May this be for the venerable one," if one accepts it with the mind or desires to take it, but rejects it by body or speech saying, "This is not allowable," there is no offense. Even if one does not reject it by body or speech, if one has a pure mind and does not accept it, thinking, "This is not allowable for us," there is no offense. For among the three doors, that which is rejected by any one door is indeed rejected. However, if one does not reject it by body or speech but accepts it with the mind, an offense arises in the body-door and speech-door, which have the origin of non-action (akiriyasamuṭṭhāna), because of the failure to perform the rejection that should be done by body and speech. In the mind-door, however, there is no such thing as an offense.

A donor places a hundred or a thousand [units of] gold or silver at the feet [of a monk] and says, "May this be for you." The monk rejects it, saying, "This is not allowable." The lay follower says, "I have renounced it for you," and departs. If another lay follower comes there and asks, "Venerable sir, what is this?" the monk should tell him what was said by that person and by himself. If that person says, "Venerable sir, I will guard it; please show me a secure place," the monk should point it out, even if it means climbing to a seven-storied palace, saying, "This is a secure place." However, he should not say, "Deposit it here." By this much, it remains dependent on both the allowable and the unallowable. One should live there, closing the door and guarding it. If someone comes bringing a bowl or a robe that is for sale and says, "Venerable sir, please take this," the monk should say, "Lay follower, we have a need for this object, and such a thing as this gold and silver exists, but there is no steward." If that lay follower says, "I will be the steward; please open the door," the monk should open the door and say only, "It is placed in this spot." He should not say, "Take this." In this way also, it remains dependent on both the allowable and the unallowable. If that lay follower takes that [money] and gives the allowable object to the monk, it is proper. If he takes more than what is needed, the monk should say, "We will not take your object; depart."

What should be done by a monk who has accepted the four kinds of objects involving forfeiture (nissaggiya), such as gold and silver? It must be forfeited in the midst of the Sangha. How is it forfeited? That monk should approach the Sangha, arrange his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the senior monks, sit in a squatting position (ukkuṭika), and with joined palms (añjali), he should speak thus: "Venerable sirs, I..."
66:
“I have accepted gold and silver; this gold and silver of mine is to be forfeited; I forfeit this gold and silver.” Having forfeited it, the offense should be confessed. A monk who is skilled in the Vinaya rules and capable of reciting with correct articulation should receive the confession. If a monastery attendant (ārāmika) or a lay devotee (upāsaka) arrives there, he should be told, “Friend, take note of this object.” If he asks, “What shall I bring with this?”, he should not be told, “Bring this or that.” Only allowable items such as ghee, oil, honey, or molasses should be mentioned. Even when mentioning them, the monk should not say, “Bring ghee, oil, honey, or molasses with this [money].” He should only say, “Such and such an item is allowable for the Saṅgha.” If that person brings allowable items in exchange for that object, all the monks except the one who accepted the gold and silver should share and consume them. The monk who accepted the gold and silver must not take a share.

It is not proper to receive and consume a share that belongs to other monks or monastery attendants. Even if it is taken from the place of distribution by monkeys and left in the forest, or dropped from their hands—even if it is handled by animals or found as refuse-rag (paṃsukūla)—it is simply not allowable. It is not proper to fumigate a dwelling with molasses brought from that source. It is not proper to sleep by the light of a lamp, perform the preliminary work for a kasina, or read a palm-leaf manuscript using a lamp made from that ghee or oil. It is also not proper to smear wounds on the body with that oil, honey, or molasses. If one takes beds, stools, etc., with that object, or builds an uposatha hall or a dining hall, it is not proper to use them. Even the shadow of a building constructed with that object is not allowable as long as it remains within the boundary of the building; it is allowable only if it is an “incoming” shadow that exceeds the boundary. It is not proper to travel by means of a road, bridge, boat, or raft made by disposing of that object. It is not proper to drink or use water from a pond dug with that object. If there is no water originating from within the pond, but external water or rainwater enters it, that “incoming” water is allowable. If a pond is purchased with that object, the water already in it at the time of purchase is not allowable, even if it was “incoming” water. If the Saṅgha uses requisites while keeping that object as a deposit (upanikkhepa), those requisites are also not allowable for the monk who forfeited it. If a monastery (ārāma) is acquired, that monastery is also not proper to use. If both the land and the seeds are unallowable, it is not proper to use either the land or the fruit. If only the land was bought and other seeds were planted, the fruit is allowable. If seeds were bought and planted in allowable land, the fruit is not allowable, but it is allowable to sit or lie down on the land.
67:
If the kappiyakāraka (attendant) who arrives there does not know how to exchange that gold and silver to bring allowable items like ghee or oil for the Saṅgha, he should be told, “Friend, discard this gold and silver.” If he discards it, that is good. If he does not discard it, a monk endowed with five qualities should be appointed as a “money-discarder” (rūpiya-chaḍḍaka). That monk must be one who does not follow the wrong path of favoritism, the wrong path of hatred, the wrong path of delusion, or the wrong path of fear, and he must know whether it has been discarded or not.

He should be appointed in this way: First, the monk should be requested. After requesting him, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha with this motion (ñatti): “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint monk so-and-so as the money-discarder. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. The Saṅgha appoints monk so-and-so as the money-discarder. If the appointment of monk so-and-so as the money-discarder is pleasing to any venerable one, let him be silent. If it is not pleasing, he should speak. Monk so-and-so has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the money-discarder. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus I record it.”

The appointed monk, without making a sign, with eyes closed, should discard it into a river, a cliff, or a forest thicket, without concern, as if it were excrement, and without paying attention to where it falls. If he drops it after making a sign, he commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Even regarding such loathsome gold and silver, the Blessed One explained the usage for monks by a certain means. However, for the one who accepted the gold and silver, it is not proper to use the requisites arising from it by any means whatsoever. Just as it is not proper for him, requisites obtained through claiming non-existent qualities (asanta-sambhāvanā), through corrupting families (kula-dūsaka), or through trickery (kuhanā), etc., are not proper for him or for any other monk. Even requisites obtained righteously are not proper to use without reflection.

For there are four types of usage (paribhoga): usage as theft (theyya-paribhoga), usage as debt (iṇa-paribhoga), usage as inheritance (dāyajja-paribhoga), and usage as ownership (sāmi-paribhoga). Among these, the usage by an immoral monk who sits and consumes in the midst of the Saṅgha is called “usage as theft.” The usage without reflection by a virtuous person is called “usage as debt.” Therefore, one should reflect upon the robe every time it is used, and upon the almsfood at every morsel.
68:
A monk who is unable to reflect on alms-food at every mouthful should reflect during the morning, the evening, the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night. If dawn breaks while he has not reflected, he remains in the state of "usage as a debtor" (iṇaparibhoga). Lodgings and bedding should also be reflected upon at every use. Regarding medicine, mindfulness in reflection is appropriate both at the time of receiving and at the time of use. Even so, an offense is incurred only by a monk who is mindful when receiving but fails to be mindful when using. If he fails to be mindful when receiving but is mindful and reflects when using, no offense is incurred. There are four kinds of purity (suddhi): purity through confession (desanāsuddhi), purity through restraint (saṃvarasuddhi), purity through seeking (pariyeṭṭhisuddhi), and purity through reflection (paccavekkhaṇasuddhi).

Among these four, "purity through confession" refers to the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla). It is called "purity through confession" because it is purified by confession. "Purity through restraint" refers to the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara-sīla). It is called "purity through restraint" because it is purified by the mental resolve and restraint of "I shall not do this again." "Purity through seeking" refers to the virtue of purity of livelihood (ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla). It is called "purity through seeking" because of the purity of the search, having abandoned improper seeking (anesanā) and obtaining requisites righteously and fairly. "Purity through reflection" refers to the virtue connected with the use of the four requisites. It is called "purity through reflection" because it is purified by reflection in the manner taught as "Reflecting wisely, I use the robe..." and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "If he fails to be mindful when receiving but is mindful and reflects when using, no offense is incurred."

The use of requisites by the seven types of noble learners (sekhas) is called "usage as an heir" (dāyajja-paribhoga). Since they are the sons of the Blessed One, they use the requisites as heirs to their father's property. Do they use the Blessed One's requisites or the laity's requisites? Although they are items donated by the laity, they become the Blessed One's property because they are authorized by Him. Thus, it should be understood that they use the Blessed One's requisites. The Dhammadāyāda Sutta is the evidence here. The use of requisites by those whose taints are destroyed (arahants) is called "usage as a master" (sāmi-paribhoga). Since they have transcended the slavery of craving, they use them as masters. Thus, among these types of usage, "usage as a master" and "usage as an heir" are appropriate for all (who possess virtue). "Usage as a debtor" is not appropriate. As for "usage as a thief" (theyya-paribhoga), there is no need even to speak of it.

There are also four other types of usage: usage by the modest (lajji-paribhoga), usage by the shameless (alajji-paribhoga), righteous usage (dhammiya-paribhoga), and unrighteous usage (adhammiya-paribhoga). Among these, for a shameless person with a modest person...
69:
Usage by a shameless person together with a modest person is appropriate; it should not be made into an offense. For a modest person, usage together with a shameless person is appropriate as long as he does not yet know the other's shameless nature. Since there is no such thing as being shameless from the very beginning, when he comes to know the other's shameless nature, he should say: "Venerable sirs, you are committing transgressions through the doors of body and speech; such behavior is improper; do not do this." If the other continues to transgress without heed, the monk who continues to use requisites with him also becomes shameless. Using requisites with a shameless person who is one's own burden (dependent) is also forbidden. If he does not stop, this person also becomes shameless. In this way, one shameless person can create a hundred shameless ones. However, there is no offense in shameless persons using requisites together. Usage among modest persons together is like two princes eating from a golden dish. 

Righteous (dhammiya) and unrighteous (adhammiya) usage should be understood by the nature of the requisites. Therein, if the person is shameless and the alms-food is unrighteous, both are loathsome. If the person is shameless but the alms-food is righteous, the food should not be accepted out of loathing for the person. However, in the Mahāpaccari, it is stated: "If an immoral monk receives food designated for the Saṅgha (uddesa-bhatta) and the like from the Saṅgha and gives it back to the Saṅgha, these are allowable because they are taken according to the gift." If the person is modest but the alms-food is unrighteous, the food should not be accepted because it is loathsome. If the person is modest and the alms-food is also righteous, it is appropriate.

There are two other kinds of support (paggaha) and two kinds of usage (paribhoga): support of the modest, support of the shameless, usage of Dhamma, and usage of material things (āmisa). Therein, it is appropriate for a shameless person to support a modest one; it should not be made into an offense for that modest person. However, if a modest person supports a shameless one, inviting him to give a formal appreciation (anumodanā), inviting him to give a Dhamma talk, or supporting him among lay devotees, and the other shameless one also praises that modest person in the assembly saying, "Our teacher is endowed with such and such qualities," then this modest monk should be known as one who causes the Dispensation (Sāsana) to decline and disappear. Between the usage of Dhamma and the usage of material things, wherever the usage of material things is allowable, the usage of Dhamma is also allowable. However, if a certain text exists only with one person and would be lost upon his death, it is said that it is allowable to learn it from him for the sake of supporting the Dhamma.

In this regard, there is this story: It is said that during a time of great peril (Mahābhaya), the Mahaniddesa text was mastered by only a single monk. Then, the Mahātipiṭaka Thera, who was the preceptor (upajjhāya) of Catu-nikāyika Tissa Thera...
70:
The Elder Mahātipiṭaka said to the Elder Mahārakkhita, "Friend Mahārakkhita, learn the Mahāniddesa in the presence of this monk." He replied, "Venerable sir, I hear that this monk is wicked; therefore, I will not learn from him." The Elder said, "Friend, do learn; I will sit near you." He consented, saying, "Very well, venerable sir, if you sit there, I will learn." He began his studies, learning continuously day and night. On the final day, seeing a woman under the couch, he said, "Venerable sir, previously I had only heard of this; had I known it to be so, I would not have learned the Dhamma in the presence of such a monk." However, many other great elders also learned from that monk and established the Mahāniddesa.

## Thus ends the discussion on the decision regarding the acceptance of money, etc.,
## in the Palimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-sangaha.
## 13. Discussion on the Decision regarding the Characteristics of Giving, etc.

In this summary verse, "The transfer of gain through giving and trust," first, "giving" (dāna) refers to the giving of one's own property, such as robes and other requisites, to any recipient monk, such as a co-resident (saddhivihārika). In that giving, the characteristic of giving is this: if one says, "I give this robe to you," "I donate it," "I sacrifice it," or "I give it to so-and-so... I sacrifice it," it is considered given whether in the person's presence or absence. If it is said, "Take this for yourself," and the other says, "I take it for myself," it is well-given and well-received. If it is said, "Make it your property," "Let it be your property," or "It is your property," and the other says, "I make it my property," "Let it be my property," or "I will make it my property," it is poorly given and poorly received. Neither the giver knows how to give effectively, nor the other knows how to receive effectively.

However, if it is said, "Make it your property," and the other says, "Very well, venerable sir, I take it for myself," and then takes it, it is called well-received. If one person says, "Take this robe," and the other says, "I will not take it," and the first says again, "It has been given by me to you, take it," but the other says, "I have no need of this robe," and then the first person, thinking "I have given it," lets ten days pass, and the latter person, thinking "I have rejected it," also lets ten days pass—who incurs an offence? No one incurs an offence. Whichever monk likes it may formally resolve (adhiṭṭhāna) and use it.

A robe given with the instruction "Give this to so-and-so" remains the property of the sender as long as it has not reached the other person's hand. But a robe given with the words "I give this to so-and-so" belongs to the person to whom it is relinquished. Therefore, a monk sends a robe into the hand of another monk, saying, "Give this robe to so-and-so." While on the way, that monk...
71: ...saying, "Give this robe to so-and-so." If that person, while on the way, takes it out of intimacy (vissāsa) with the sender, it is well-taken. If he takes it out of intimacy with the intended recipient, it is poorly taken.A monk sends a robe by the hand of another monk, saying, "Give this robe to so-and-so." That monk, while on the way, hears, "The sender has passed away," and if he determines it as the robe of the deceased (matakacīvara), it is well-determined. If he takes it out of intimacy with the intended recipient, it is poorly taken. A monk sends a robe by the hand of another monk, saying, "Give this robe to so-and-so." That monk, while on the way, hears, "The intended recipient has passed away," and if he determines it as the robe of the deceased, it is poorly determined. If he takes it out of intimacy with the sender, it is well-taken. A monk sends a robe by the hand of another monk, saying, "Give this robe to so-and-so." That monk, while on the way, hears, "Both have passed away," and if he determines it as the robe of the deceased of the sender, it is well-determined. If he determines it as the robe of the deceased of the intended recipient, it is poorly determined. A monk sends a robe by the hand of another monk, saying, "I give this robe to so-and-so." That monk, while on the way, takes it out of intimacy with the sender, it is poorly taken. If he takes it out of intimacy with the intended recipient, it is well-taken. A monk sends a robe by the hand of another monk, saying, "I give this robe to so-and-so." That monk, while on the way, hears, "The sender has passed away," and if he determines it as the robe of the deceased, it is poorly determined. If he takes it out of intimacy with the intended recipient, it is well-taken. A monk sends a robe by the hand of another monk, saying, "I give this robe to so-and-so." That monk, while on the way, hears, "The intended recipient has passed away," and if he determines it as the robe of the deceased, it is well-determined. If he takes it out of intimacy with the sender, it is poorly taken. A monk sends a robe by the hand of another monk, saying, "I give this robe to so-and-so." That monk, while on the way, hears, "Both have passed away." If he determines it as the robe of the deceased of the sender, it is poorly determined. If he determines it as the robe of the deceased of the intended recipient, it is well-determined.Once a gift has been given by relinquishing it, one should not take it back out of anger for some reason later. Even if it is a robe given by oneself, if a monk snatches it back thinking it is his own property, he incurs a Nissaggiya offense. If he snatches back other requisites, even as little as a needle, he incurs a Dukkaṭa offense. If, "Venerable Sir, ..."
72:
If one gives of one's own accord, saying, "This robe is suitable for you," it is proper to accept it. Otherwise, if it is said, "Friend, we gave the robe [intending], 'He will perform the major and minor duties, he will take a preceptor in our presence, he will learn the Dhamma'; now you do not perform the duties, nor take a preceptor, nor learn the Dhamma," and being thus addressed, he gives it, saying, "Venerable sirs, I suppose you speak for the sake of the robe; here is your robe," it is also proper to accept it. Or, if one says to a young monk who is departing for another direction, "Turn back," and he does not turn back, but one says, "Take the robe and keep it," and if he turns back in this way, it is good. If he gives it, saying, "I suppose you speak for the sake of the bowl and robe; take them," it is also proper to accept it. Or, seeing one who is about to disrobe, if one says, "We gave the bowl and robe thinking you would perform the duties; now you are going to disrobe and leave," and the other gives it, saying, "Take your bowl and robe," it is also proper to accept it. However, it is not proper to give [on the condition], "I give only to one who takes a preceptor in my presence, I do not give to one who takes elsewhere; I give only to one who performs the duties, I do not give to one who does not; I give only to one who learns the Dhamma, I do not give to one who does not; I give only to one who does not disrobe, I do not give to one who disrobes." For the one who gives thus, there is a dukkata offense. However, it is proper to ask for it back. One who takes by force what has been given and relinquished should be dealt with according to the value of the bowl and robe. This is the decision regarding giving.

The characteristic of taking on trust (vissāsaggāha) should be known by this scripture: "Monks, I allow you to take on trust [the property] of one who is possessed of five factors: he is an acquaintance, he is an intimate friend, he has spoken [permission], he is alive, and he is pleased when it is taken." (Mahāvagga, 356).

In that scripture, 'sandiṭṭha' means a friend who is merely seen. 'Sambhatta' means a firm friend. 'Ālapita' means a friend who has said, "Whatever of mine you desire, you may take; there is no need to ask before taking." 'Jīvati' means that even if he is lying on a bed from which he cannot rise, he is called 'alive' as long as the life faculty (jīvitindriya) is not cut off. 'Gahite ca attamano' means having a pleased mind when it is taken. One who knows, "If I take the property of such a person, he will be pleased with me," may take it. Although these five factors are stated for the sake of taking without remainder, taking on trust is accomplished by three factors: (1) being an acquaintance, being alive, and being pleased when taken; (2) being an intimate friend, being alive, and being pleased when taken; (3) being one who has spoken [permission], being alive, and being pleased when taken. If that person is not alive, not...
73:
...and is not pleased when it is taken, then even if his property was taken on trust, it must be returned. When giving it back, if it is the property of a deceased person, it should first be given to those who are the owners of that property, whether they be householders or monastics. The property of one who is not pleased should be returned to that person alone. If a monk, having first expressed delight either by speech or by a mere thought, saying, "You have done well by taking my property," later becomes angry for some reason, he cannot demand it back. Even if a person does not wish to give but endures it mentally and says nothing, he also cannot demand it back. However, if when told, "Your property has been taken or used by me," he says, "Whether it is taken or used, let it be; but I had placed that object for a certain purpose, and it should be restored to its original state," then this person has the right to demand it back. This is the decision regarding taking on trust (vissāsaggāha).

Regarding the phrase "lābhassa pariṇāmana" (diversion of gains), this is said with reference to diverting a gain that has been intended for others to oneself or to another. The decision therein is: If a monk, knowing that a gain intended for the Sangha—whether it be the property of fellow practitioners, or of laypeople, or even at the least the property of his mother—has been intended for the Sangha, diverts it to himself saying, "Give this to me," and takes it, he incurs a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense. If he diverts it to another, saying, "Give this to this monk," he incurs a Suddhika Pācittiya offense. Therefore, even in his mother's house during the time for rainy-season robes, if he knows a rainy-season robe is intended for the Sangha and diverts it to himself, he incurs a Nissaggiya Pācittiya; if he diverts it to another, he incurs a Suddhika Pācittiya. If people bring ghee, oil, etc., intending to provide a meal for the Sangha, and a monk, even if he is ill, asks for something knowing it is intended for the Sangha, he incurs only a Nissaggiya Pācittiya. However, if that monk asks, "Do you have any ghee, etc., that you have brought?" and when told, "Yes, we have," he says, "Give some to me as well," it is proper. Or, if the lay devotees say to that monk who is feeling remorse, "Venerable sir, the Sangha also receives only what is given by us; please accept it," it is also proper when said in this way.

If one diverts a gain intended for the Sangha in one monastery by pointing to another monastery and saying, "Give it to the Sangha in such-and-such a monastery," or if one diverts it to a Cetiya, saying, "What is the use of giving to the Sangha? Perform an offering to the Cetiya," he incurs a dukkata offense. If one diverts property intended for a Cetiya to another Cetiya, or to the Sangha, or to a group, or to an individual, he incurs only a dukkata offense. It is not proper to take even a flower from a flower plant specifically planted for one Cetiya and offer it to another Cetiya. However, there are cases where it is proper to offer to another Cetiya what was intended for one Cetiya: for example, a parasol for a Cetiya...
74:
It is not proper to offer flowers to another cetiya from a flower plant that has been specifically planted for the purpose of a particular cetiya. However, if one sees that a parasol or a banner has already been offered to one cetiya, it is proper to have the remainder given to another cetiya. Even in the case of a dog, if something has been dedicated to it, and one diverts it to another person, saying, 'Do not give to this dog, give to that one,' a dukkaṭa offense is committed. If donors say, 'We wish to offer a meal to the Saṅgha, we wish to perform a cetiya-pūjā, we wish to offer requisites to a monk; we will give according to your preference, please tell us where we should give,' then that monk should say, 'Give wherever you wish.' If they merely ask, 'Where should we give?', it is proper to say, 'Give in a place where your gift may be used, or where it may be repaired, or where it may last long, or where your heart is inspired.'

## Thus, in the Pāḷimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-saṅgaha,
## the discussion on the characteristics of giving, etc., is concluded.
## 14. Decision on Digging the Earth
Earth is of two kinds: natural earth (jātā pathavī) and non-natural earth (ajātā pathavī). Among them, natural earth refers to pure soil, pure clay, earth with few stones, few pebbles, few potsherds, few gravels, or few grains of sand—mostly consisting of soil and clay. Unburnt earth is also called 'natural earth.' A pile of soil or a pile of clay that has been wet by rain for more than four months is also called 'natural earth.' Non-natural earth refers to pure stone, pure pebbles, pure potsherds, pure gravel, or pure sand—with little soil or clay—mostly consisting of stone, pebbles, potsherds, gravel, or sand. Burnt earth is also called 'non-natural earth.' A pile of soil or a pile of clay that has been wet by rain for less than four months is also called 'non-natural earth.'

Between these two types of earth, a monk who digs or causes another to dig natural earth commits a pācittiya offense. The decision in this matter is: if he digs it himself, he commits a pācittiya for every stroke.
75:
If he commands another, and the person commanded digs for the whole day, there is only one pācittiya for the monk who gave the command. But if the person is lazy and must be commanded repeatedly, a pācittiya is incurred for every word spoken by the monk who causes him to dig. If he says, 'Dig a pond,' it is allowable. Indeed, it is only after it is dug that it is called a 'pond.' Therefore, this is an allowable expression (kappiya-vohāra). This same method applies to such words as 'Dig a pool, a tank, or a pit.' However, it is not allowable to say, 'Dig this place,' or 'Dig a pond in this place.' It is allowable to say, 'Dig a tuber,' or 'Dig a root,' without specifying the location. It is not allowable to say, 'Dig this vine,' or 'Dig a tuber or a root in this place.'

For those cleaning a pond, it is allowable to remove thin mud that can be scooped out and poured away with pots; it is not allowable to remove thick mud. Mud that has dried due to the heat of the sun and cracked—only that mud which is detached and not connected to the ground below is allowable to be removed. In places where water flows, there is a layer of silt (udakapappaṭaka) that rests on top and moves when the wind blows; it is allowable to remove that silt. If the bank of a pond or similar place collapses and falls near the water's edge, if it is earth wet by rain for less than four months, it is allowable to cut or break it; if it has been wet for more than four months, it is not allowable. If it falls directly into the water, it is allowable to remove it even if the rain has fallen for more than four months, because the rain fell only upon the water.

If they dig a rock-cistern in a rock surface, and fine dust first falls into that rock-cistern and becomes wet by rain, after four months it is reckoned as natural earth (which is unallowable). Monks cleaning the rock-cistern when the water has dried up must not destroy that earth. If it was first filled with water and then dust fell into it, it is allowable to remove that dust. This is because even when it rains, the rain falls only upon the water. If there is fine dust on a rock surface and it becomes stuck due to a drizzle, it is also not allowable to destroy that dust after four months. If a termite mound grows in an unused cave, it is allowable to destroy it as one pleases. If it grows in the open, it is allowable to destroy it only if it has been wet by rain for less than four months. The same method applies to termite mud that has climbed up trees and so on. The same method also applies to worm casts, mouse-dirt, dog tracks, cow tracks, and so on. 'Gokaṇṭaka' refers to mud cut by the hooves of cows. If it is connected to the natural earth below, it is not allowable to remove it even if it has been wet by rain for only one day. The same method applies to a monk who takes a clod of earth cut by a plough in a ploughed field.
76:
An old bedding-place (monastery/dwelling), whether it is unroofed or roofed but with a damaged roof, if it has been wet by rain for more than four months, it is reckoned as natural earth (jātapathavī). It is allowable to take the remaining roofing bricks or building materials such as rafters, with the perception: "I am taking a brick, I am taking a rafter, I am taking a floor-plank at the base of the wall, I am taking a pillar of the multi-storied building." If earth-clods fall along with those bricks, rafters, etc., there is no offense; however, for a monk who takes the wall-earth, there is an offense. If any particular earth is not wet, there is no offense in taking that earth. If there is a heap of earth inside a house (monastery) and the monastery is roofed after that heap has been wet by rain for only one day, [it is allowable]. If it is entirely wet, it becomes natural earth only after the lapse of four months. If only the upper part of that heap is wet and the interior is not wet, it is allowable to have the wet portion removed by lay attendants (kappiya-karaka) using allowable terminology (kappiya-vohāra), and then use the remaining earth as one pleases. This is because it was moistened by water. Only when it is continuous [with the ground] does it become natural earth; other earth is not natural earth. If there is an earth wall in the open and it has been wet by rain for more than four months, it is reckoned as natural earth; however, it is allowable to touch and take the dust clinging to that wall with a wet hand. If it is a brick wall, it is allowable to dismantle it as one pleases, because it mostly stands on ground containing potsherds. It is not allowable to take a mandapa pillar standing in the open by shaking it here and there and thereby damaging the earth; it is only allowable to pull it straight up. The same method applies to a monk taking other dry trees or dry stumps.

For the sake of new construction work (navakamma), monks move a pillar, a stone, or a tree by lifting it with poles and rolling it; in such rolling, the natural earth is broken. If they roll it with a pure mind, there is no offense. However, if they have the intention to break the earth under that pretext, there is an offense. The same method applies to monks dragging branches and the like, or splitting firewood on the ground. It is not allowable to strike or drive anything such as bones, needles, or thorns into the earth. It is also not allowable to pass urine with the thought, "I will break the earth with the force of the stream of urine." If the earth is broken by one who does so, there is an offense. It is not allowable to scrub with a broom with the thought, "I will make the uneven ground even." It should be swept only for the sake of performing the duty (vatta). Some people poke the ground with a staff or scratch it with the big toe; some walk back and forth repeatedly breaking the ground with the thought, "I will show the place for the walking meditation path (caṅkama)"; all such actions are not allowable. However, for the sake of exerting energy while performing the recluses' duties (samaṇadhamma), with a pure mind...
77:
It is allowable to walk on a walking path. Rubbing hands on the ground with the intention 'I will wash my hands' is not allowable; however, it is allowable to take dust by placing wet hands on the ground without rubbing. For monks who have illnesses such as scabies, rubbing their limbs against riverbanks, cliffs, and such places is not allowable. Lighting a fire on natural soil (jātapathavī) or causing another to light it results in a Pācittiya offence. Even for a monk firing an alms-bowl, for as many places as he lights or causes to be lit, that many Pācittiya offences are incurred. Therefore, a monk firing a bowl should only fire it in a place where it has been fired before. It is not allowable to place fire on unburnt ground, but it is allowable to place fire on top of the bowl-firing kiln. If fire is placed on wood and that fire, burning the wood, goes on to burn the ground, it is not allowable. The same applies to brick kilns and the like. In those cases, it is only allowable to place fire on top of the bricks. Why? Because those bricks are not fuel (anupādāna). Indeed, those bricks do not count as fuel for the fire. It is not allowable to give fire to dry stumps, dry trees, and the like. However, if one gives fire thinking 'I will extinguish it before it reaches the ground' and later cannot extinguish it because it is beyond one's power, there is no offence. A monk carrying a grass torch whose hand is being burnt and drops it on the ground, there is no offence. It is allowable to make a fire by providing fuel only at the place where it fell. On ground already burnt, it is allowable to break up the entire area where the heat has reached. If a monk who is ignorant of the training rules produces fire with a fire-drill and, holding it in his hand, asks 'What should I do?', he should be told 'Light it.' If he says 'My hand is burning,' he should be told 'Do it in a way that it does not burn.' He should not be told 'Drop it on the ground.' If he drops it because his hand is burning, there is no offence because it was not dropped with the intention 'I will burn the ground.' It is allowable to make a fire at the place where it fell. It is allowable to command something using allowable terminology (kappiya-vohāra) such as: 'Know the hole for this pillar,' 'Know the great clay,' 'Know the husk-clay,' 'Give the great clay,' 'Give the husk-clay,' 'Bring the clay,' 'Bring the dust,' 'There is a need for clay,' 'There is a need for dust,' 'Make the hole for this pillar allowable,' 'Make this clay allowable,' 'Make this dust allowable.' If a monk, with his mind elsewhere while talking to someone, stands scratching the ground with his big toe or a staff, there is no offence for one who scratches or breaks the ground without mindfulness.

## Thus, in the Pālimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha,
## The Discussion on the Decision regarding Digging the Earth is finished.
78:
## 15. Bhūtagāma-vinicchaya-kathā

Bhūtagāma is a collective term for trees, creepers, and the like that grow from five kinds of seeds. In this context of bhūtagāma, the five kinds of seeds are: root-seed (mūla-bīja), stem-seed (khandha-bīja), joint-seed (phaḷu-bīja), bud-seed (agga-bīja), and grain-seed (bīja-bīja).

Among these, root-seed (mūla-bīja) refers to turmeric (haliddī), ginger (siṅgivera), orris root (vacā), white orris (vacattaṃ), ativisa, kaṭukarohiṇī, vetiver (usīra), and nut grass (bhaddamuttaka). Furthermore, any other seeds that are produced in the root or clearly arise from the root are also called root-seeds. Stem-seed (khandha-bīja) refers to the Bodhi tree (assattha), the banyan (nigrodha), pilakkha, udumbara, kacchaka, and kapitthana. Furthermore, any other seeds that are produced in the stem or clearly arise from the stem are also called stem-seeds. Joint-seed (phaḷu-bīja) refers to sugarcane (ucchu), bamboo (veḷu), and reeds (naḷa). Furthermore, any other seeds that are produced in the joint or clearly arise from the joint are also called joint-seeds. Bud-seed (agga-bīja) refers to basil (ajjuka), phaṇijjaka, and hirivera. Furthermore, any other seeds that are produced in the bud or clearly arise from the bud are also called bud-seeds. Grain-seed (bīja-bīja) refers to the seven kinds of grain (pubbaṇṇa) and various pulses (aparaṇṇa). Furthermore, any other seeds that are produced in the seed or clearly arise from the seed are also called grain-seeds.

Regarding this bhūtagāma, if one perceives it as bhūtagāma and personally cuts it, causes another to cut it, personally breaks it, causes another to break it, personally cooks it, or causes another to cook it, one commits a Pācittiya offense. For a monk who destroys bhūtagāma, there is a Pācittiya offense. However, if one destroys the five kinds of bījagāma that are separated from bhūtagāma, one commits a Dukkaṭa offense.

These bījagāma and bhūtagāma may be water-based or land-based. Among them, water-based bhūtagāma refers to all types of algae (sevala), with or without leaves, including small varieties like those the size of mustard seeds or sesame seeds. At the minimum, even water-moss (udaka-pappaṭaka) should be known as bhūtagāma. Water-moss is hard and rough on the upper surface, and soft and green (or dark) on the lower surface. Among these algae, if the root of the algae descends and is established in the earth, its place is the earth. If the algae floats and moves in the water, its place is the water. If one destroys algae established in the earth at any place, or uproots it and moves it to another place, one commits a Pācittiya offense. If one destroys algae floating in the water, one also commits a Pācittiya offense. However, it is allowable to move it aside with the hands here and there to bathe. Since the entire body of water is its place, it cannot be said that its place has been changed by merely moving it aside. From the water, however, one should not intentionally lift it out without water; but lifting it out together with water and putting it back into the water is allowable. If one uproots water-vines, grasses, or stems growing in water, such as blue lotuses (uppala) or red lotuses (paduma), or destroys them right there in the water, one commits a Pācittiya offense. If one destroys those already uprooted by others, one commits a Dukkaṭa offense. This is because those plants are categorized under bījagāma...
79:
...they fall into the category of bījagāma. Even small algae the size of sesame or mustard seeds, when uprooted from water and withered, fall into the category of bud-seeds (agga-bīja). In commentaries such as the Mahāpaccarī, it is stated: "Small algae the size of mustard seeds, sesame seeds, water-moss, etc., are grounds for Dukkaṭa." In that statement, the underlying reason is not seen. In the Andhaka Commentary, it is stated: "Because it is not a bhūtagāma complete with shoots and roots, a Dukkaṭa offense is committed." This statement also does not harmonize [with the rules]. This is because it is stated that there is a Pācittiya for bhūtagāma and a Dukkaṭa for bījagāma. A third category called 'incomplete bhūtagāma' (lacking shoots and roots) does not appear in the Pali or the Commentaries. Even if it does not appear, if one says that such a thing would fall into the category of bījagāma, that is also not appropriate. This is because such a bījagāma is not the cause/origin of a bhūtagāma. Alternatively, this point—"Between grave and light offenses, one should stand by the grave one"—is a characteristic of the Vinaya.

The remaining part of trees cut down on land is called a green stump (harita-khāṇu). Among those stumps, the stumps of trees such as kakudha, karañja, piyaṅgu, and jackfruit (panasa) grow and increase upwards. Such a stump is included in the category of bhūtagāma. The stumps of palmyra palms, coconut trees, etc., do not grow upwards. Such a stump is included in the category of bījagāma. However, the stump of a banana tree that has not yet fruited is included in bhūtagāma, while the stump of one that has fruited is included in bījagāma. Even a banana tree that has fruited, as long as it has green leaves, is included only in bhūtagāma. Likewise, a bamboo tree that has fruited is the same. When it starts to dry up from the tip, then it falls into the category of bījagāma. To which type of bījagāma? It falls into the category of joint-seed (phaḷu-bīja). What is produced from that fruited bamboo? Nothing at all. If something were produced, it would fall into the category of bhūtagāma. Trees such as the indasāla are cut and piled up. Even if branches the size of a cubit emerge from those piled-up logs, they still fall only into the category of bījagāma. If they are planted in the ground for the purpose of a pavilion, a fence, or for supporting creepers, they return to the classification of bhūtagāma only when both roots and leaves have emerged. If only roots or only leaves have emerged, they are still included only in bījagāma.

Regarding any seeds placed in the earth, or kept by sprinkling with water, or placed in potsherds etc. containing moist soil: all these are still only bīja (seeds) even if only roots or only leaves have emerged. Even if both roots and the shoot above have emerged, as long as the shoot is not green, they are still only bīja. However, in the case of beans (mugga) etc., when leaves have arisen, or in the case of rice (vīhi) etc., when the shoot has become green or dark blue, they fall into the category of bhūtagāma. In palmyra seeds, first a root like a boar's tusk emerges. Even when it has emerged, as long as the leaf-bud above has not emerged, it is still called only bījagāma. In a coconut, after piercing the shell, a shoot like an ivory pin emerges. Even when it has emerged...
80:
As long as the green leaf-curls, which resemble deer horns, have not yet appeared, it is still just a seed-group (bījagāma). Even if the roots have not yet emerged, if such leaf-curls have grown, it is included within the rootless plant-group (bhūtagāma).

Mango seeds and the like are to be judged in the same manner as rice and the like. If a parasitic plant (vandāka) or any other creeper (such as an orchid) grows on a tree and covers it, the tree is the base for that parasite. For a monk who destroys that supporting tree or who pulls the parasite from that tree, there is an offense of pācittiya. There is a type of rootless creeper (such as Cuscuta) that winds around the bark of a tree like a ring; the same judgment applies to this creeper. On the front of a house, on walls, walkways, or stupas, green algae (sevāla) may grow. As long as two or three leaves have not yet appeared, it is included in the category of bud-seeds (aggabīja). When leaves have grown, it becomes a basis for a pācittiya offense. Therefore, it is not proper to apply a plaster of lime in such places. However, it is proper to apply oil over lime that has been applied by a layperson or a novice. If dry algae remains during the summer, it is proper to scrape and remove it with a broom or similar tool. Algae on the outside of water pots and the like is a basis for a dukkaṭa offense. Algae inside the pot is negligible (abbhohārika). Mold that grows on tooth-sticks, cakes, and the like is also negligible. It has been said (in the Mahāvagga): "If a wall finished with red chalk becomes moldy, one should moisten a coarse cloth, wring it out, and wipe it."

Stone-based growths such as stone-moss, stone-algae, and lichens (selayya) are bases for dukkaṭa offenses because they lack green color and leaves. A mushroom bud is a basis for a dukkaṭa offense as long as it remains a bud. From the time it blooms, it is negligible (abbhohārika). However, one who takes a mushroom from a live tree damages the bark of the tree; therefore, in that case, a pācittiya offense is incurred. The same rule applies to the scabs (pappaṭikā) of a tree. However, if the bark of trees like the Indasāla or Kudha has become detached from the tree and remains there, there is no offense for one who takes it. It is also proper to take resin (niyyāsa) that has detached from a tree or is stuck to a dry tree. It is not proper to take it from a live tree. The same rule applies to lac (lākhā). For a monk who shakes a tree to make dry leaves or mature flowers (such as the Kanikāra) fall, there is a pācittiya offense. The same rule applies to a monk who, out of restlessness of the hands, carves letters into the soft trunks of trees like the Indasāla or Nuhī, or into palm leaves and the like growing on those trees. While novices are picking flowers, it is proper to bend the branch down for them. However, one should not scent drinking water with those flowers; one who desires to scent water should lift the novice and have him pick them. Regarding a branch with fruit...
81:
A monk who wishes to eat [the fruit] himself should not bend [the branch]; he should lift a novice to have him take the fruit. It is not proper to hold and pull a stick or a vine together with novices who are uprooting it. However, to inspire effort in those novices, it is proper to hold the tip as if showing the manner of pulling, even if one does not pull it oneself. Regarding trees whose branches grow back, if a branch is taken for the purpose of a fly-whisk or the like after having it made allowable (kappiya), a monk who scratches even a basket, the bark, or a leaf, even with a fingernail, incurs a dukkaṭa offense. The same rule applies to fresh ginger and the like. If, after being made allowable, roots grow on ginger or the like kept in a cool place, it is proper to cut the upper part. If sprouts grow, it is proper to cut the lower part. If both roots and sprouts have grown, it is no longer proper to cut it.

It is not proper for a monk to cut grass himself or have another cut it while sweeping the ground with the intention, 'I will cut the grass even with the broom-splints.' While walking on a walkway, it is not proper to intentionally step on grass, vines, and the like, cutting them oneself or having another cut them with the intention, 'Let what should be cut be cut, let what should be broken be broken, I will show the path of the walkway.' Even if a grass or vine breaks while one is making a knot, it is not proper even to make the knot. It is not proper for monks to hammer in 'wooden monkeys' (steps) or bind thorns to palm trees and the like to prevent thieves from climbing. If the wooden monkey is merely leaning against the tree and does not press against it, it is proper. It is proper to speak without specification, saying, 'Cut the tree,' 'Cut the vine,' or 'Uproot the tuber or the root.' However, it is not proper to speak with specification, saying, 'Cut this tree.' Even mentioning the name, such as 'Cut, break, or uproot the mango tree, the square-stemmed vine, the potato tuber, the Muñja grass, or the bark of such-and-law tree,' is still considered unspecified. Only saying 'this mango tree' and the like is called specifying; that is not proper. A monk who wishes to bake his bowl should not intentionally make a fire on top of grass and the like, baking it himself or having another bake it. It is proper to speak without specification, saying, 'Cook the mung beans,' or 'Cook the black grams'; it is not proper to say, 'Cook these mung beans.' However, it is proper to say, 'Know this medicinal root,' 'Give this root or leaf,' 'Bring this tree or vine,' 'There is a need for this flower or fruit,' or 'Make this tree, vine, or fruit allowable (kappiya).' By speaking in this way, one is released from destroying vegetation (bhūtagāma).
82: A monk who wishes to consume [fruit or seeds] should have them made allowable (kappiya) again to be free from [the offense regarding] vegetation (bījagāma). In this matter, the making of allowability (kappiyakaraṇa) should be understood according to the sequence in this Sutta: "Monks, I allow you to consume fruit that has been made allowable by five means: made allowable by fire, made allowable by a weapon, made allowable by a fingernail, being seedless, and the fifth is where the seed has been removed" (Cullavagga 250). Among those five, 'aggiparijita' means made allowable by fire, overcome, burnt, or touched by fire. 'Satthaparijita' means made allowable by a weapon, overcome, cut, or pierced by a weapon. The same principle applies to being made allowable by a fingernail. Fruits that are seedless or those from which seeds have been removed are naturally allowable. One who makes it allowable by fire should do so using any kind of fire, such as a wood fire or a cow-dung fire, or even at the very least with a glowing hot iron rod. In doing so, it should be done while touching a part of it and saying, "Kappiyaṃ" (It is allowable). One who makes it allowable by a weapon should do so using any kind of iron weapon, even at the very least with the tip or edge of a needle, a stylus, or a nail-cutter, by showing a cut or a pierce while saying, "Kappiyaṃ". One who makes it allowable by a fingernail should not do so with a rotten nail. The fingernails of humans, lions, tigers, leopards, monkeys, and birds are sharp; it should be done with those. The hooves of horses, buffaloes, pigs, deer, cows, and the like are very blunt; it should not be done with those, and even if done, it is as if not done. The nails of elephants, however, are not hooves; it is allowable to use them.
