Among the nails that are allowable to use, whether they are still attached to the hands or feet or have been removed, it should be done by showing a cut or a pierce while saying, "Kappiyaṃ". In this making of allowability, if there is a mountain-sized pile of seeds, or if a thousand trees have been cut and made into a single mass, or if sugarcane stalks are tied into a large bundle, if allowability is made on a single seed, a single branch, or a single stalk of sugarcane, the whole lot is considered made allowable. When sugarcane and firewood are tied together, if one pierces the firewood while saying, "I will make the sugarcane allowable," it is indeed allowable. However, if one pierces the rope or vine with which they are tied, it is not allowable. When baskets are filled with pieces of sugarcane and brought, if one piece is made allowable, the whole lot is indeed made allowable. When a meal is brought mixed with ripe chilies and the like, if one is told, "Kappiyaṃ karohi" (Make it allowable), it is allowable even if one pierces a grain of rice. The same principle applies to sesame, rice, and the like. However, those [chili or sesame seeds] added to gruel...
83: ...do not remain as a single connected mass; therefore, in that gruel, each individual chili or sesame seed must be pierced to make it allowable. If the pulp inside a wood-apple (kapittha) or similar fruit has detached from the shell and moves around (is ripe), one should have it broken to make it allowable. If it is still attached to the shell, it is allowable to make it allowable on just one part of the shell. ## Thus ends the Discussion on the Determination of Vegetation (Bhūtagāmavinicchayakathā) in the Compendium of Vinaya Determinations Transcending the Pali (Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha). ## 16. Discussion on the Determination of Sleeping Together (Sahaseyyavinicchayakathā) Sleeping together (sahaseyya) is of two kinds. It is said with reference to these two Sahaseyya training rules: "If a monk should sleep together with an unordained person for more than two or three nights, it is an offense of Pācittiya" (Pācittiya 49). "If a monk should sleep together with a woman (mātugāma), it is an offense of Pācittiya" (Pācittiya 56). In this regard, the determination is as follows: A monk who sleeps with an unordained person beyond three nights, when the sun has set on the fourth day, in a lodging (senāsana) that is fully covered and fully enclosed, or mostly covered and mostly enclosed, whether sleeping before or after [the other person] or at the same moment, incurs a Pācittiya offense. In that lodging, even if it does not touch the roof, a place enclosed by anything such as a wall at least one and a half cubits high should be understood as 'fully enclosed'. A lodging that is entirely covered above by the five types of roofing or any other means is called a 'fully covered' lodging. In the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), however, adopting common usage and for the sake of easy recitation, it is said, "A fully covered lodging is one covered by the five types of roofing." Although it is so stated, in reality, one cannot avoid an offense even when sleeping in a cloth-roofed hut; therefore, in this context, anything capable of covering or enclosing should be understood as 'covered' and 'enclosed'. If only the five types of roofing were taken, there would be no offense for sleeping together in a plank-roofed lodging; therefore, a lodging that is enclosed from the ground up to the roof by a wall or anything else, even at the very least by a cloth, is called a 'fully enclosed' lodging. Even if it does not touch the roof, a lodging enclosed by a wall or the like at least one and a half cubits high is also 'fully enclosed'. If a lodging has more area covered above than uncovered, or more area enclosed around than unenclosed, such a lodging is called 'mostly covered' and 'mostly enclosed'.
84:
A monastery endowed with these characteristics, even if it is a seven-storied palace, is considered to have a single precinct (if it shares a common entrance). Even if it is a building with a hundred rooms or a four-hall monastery, it is reckoned as a single dwelling. In such a dwelling, it is stated that a pācittiya offense is incurred by a monk who lies down at sunset on the fourth day with an unordained person (anupasampanna). If there are many novices (sāmaṇeras) and only one monk, pācittiya offenses are incurred according to the number of novices. If those novices repeatedly get up and lie down, the monk incurs an offense for every such act of the novices. However, if the monk himself repeatedly gets up and lies down, the monk incurs an offense only by his own act. If there are many monks and only one novice, that single novice causes an offense to all the monks. Even by that novice repeatedly getting up and lying down, the monks incur offenses. The same rule applies when both groups are numerous.

Furthermore, in this training rule, the fourfold classification beginning with 'residing in a single dwelling' (ekāvāsa) should also be noted. For a monk who shares a bed for three nights with a single unordained person in a single dwelling, an offense occurs daily starting from the fourth day. For a monk who shares a bed for three nights with various unordained persons in a single dwelling, it is the same (an offense occurs daily from the fourth day). For a monk who shares a bed for three nights with a single unordained person in various dwellings, it is also the same (an offense is incurred). For a monk who shares a bed for three nights with various unordained persons in various dwellings, even after traveling a hundred leagues (yojanas), an offense occurs daily starting from the fourth day.

This offense of sharing a bed (sahaseyya), according to the statement 'Except for a monk, the rest are called unordained,' occurs even by sleeping with an animal, which is at the very least a basis for a pārājika offense [if sexual]. Therefore, if any animal such as a monitor lizard, a cat, or a mongoose enters and sleeps in a place within the same precinct of the dwelling where a monk resides, it is indeed a sahaseyya offense. If [an animal] enters through a hollow at the end of a beam located above the wall of an upper palace—which has walls not connected to the upper floor of a palace built on pillars—and sleeps inside the beam and then exits through that same hollow, there is no offense for the monk sleeping in the lower palace. If there is a hole in the roof, and [an animal] enters through that hole, stays inside the roof, and leaves through that same hole, an offense is incurred by a monk sleeping inside the roof of the upper floor which has a separate precinct from the lower floor; however, there is no offense for the monk sleeping on the lower floor. If they ascend from within the palace and use all the floors, they have a single precinct. In such cases, an offense of the sahaseyya type is incurred by a monk for sleeping in any unspecified place. For a monk sleeping in a monastery that is half-covered, if animals such as pigeons enter and sleep on beams, rafters, etc., an offense is indeed incurred. If they sleep on the eaves outside the enclosure, there is no offense. In a monastery with a continuous roof, whether circular or square, even if it is a dwelling with a hundred rooms, if there is a single common door and one can enter all rooms without the room precincts being separated by walls, then if an unordained person lies down in even one room, an offense is incurred by the monks lying in all the rooms.
85:
The manner in which an offense is incurred by a monk sleeping in a certain place is as follows: In brief, for a monk sleeping in a monastery that is only half-roofed (aḍḍhakuṭṭaka), if pigeons and the like sleep on beams, rafters, etc., an offense is indeed incurred. If they sleep within the eaves outside the enclosure, there is no offense. In a row of rooms with a continuous roof, whether circular or square, even if it is a monastery with a hundred rooms, if one enters through a single common door and can enter all rooms because the room precincts are not separately partitioned by walls, then if an unordained person lies down in even one room, an offense is incurred by the monks lying in all the rooms. If the rooms have porches (pamukha) and the porch is covered from above, a person sleeping on the porch does not cause an offense to the monks sleeping in the rooms. However, if the roof is connected to the roof of the room itself, a person sleeping there causes an offense to all the monks. Why? Because it is all covered and all enclosed. For the enclosure of the room is indeed the enclosure of that porch.

In large palaces with one, two, three, or four wings, if it is possible to wander everywhere after entering and washing one's feet at a single spot, one is not exempt from the sahaseyya offense in those palaces. If the precincts are partitioned and made separate in various places, an offense is incurred only in the place with the same precinct. If a wall is built in the middle of a plaster-roofed pavilion (maṇḍapa) with two doors, and an unordained person sleeps on one side entered by one door while a monk sleeps on the other side, there is no offense. If there is a hole in the wall just large enough for monitor lizards and the like to enter, and monitor lizards sleep on one side, there is no offense. This is because a house is not called a single precinct merely because of a hole. If a door is installed by cutting through the middle of the wall, an offense is incurred because it becomes a single precinct. Even if they sleep after closing that door with a door-leaf, an offense is still incurred. A house is not called having separate precincts merely by closing a door; a door does not become 'not a door.' For a door-leaf is made for the purpose of using it as one pleases by closing and opening, not for the purpose of cutting off usage. If that door is then closed with bricks, it is no longer a door and remains in the previous state of having separate precincts. In a cetiya house with a long porch, if one door is inside and one is outside, an unordained person [sleeping] between the two doors causes an offense to a monk sleeping inside the cetiya house because it is a single precinct.

The summary here is: whether the monastery is small or large, whether it is connected or not connected to another, whether it is long, circular, or square...
86:
Whether it is circular or square, single-storied or multi-storied, in whatever monastery has a single precinct, an offense of Sahaseyya (sleeping together) occurs in all places. Regarding this Sahaseyya, an offense of Pācittiya is committed in a monastery that is fully roofed and fully walled with any kind of covering. One should know that there are eight Pācittiya offenses: (1) fully roofed and fully walled, (2) mostly roofed and mostly walled, (3) fully roofed and mostly walled, (4) fully roofed and half walled, (5) mostly roofed and half walled, (6) fully walled and mostly roofed, (7) fully walled and half roofed, and (8) mostly walled and half roofed.

One should know that there are five Dukkaṭa offenses: (1) half roofed and half walled, (2) fully roofed and slightly walled, (3) mostly roofed and slightly walled, (4) fully walled and slightly roofed, and (5) mostly walled and slightly roofed. There is no offense in a monastery that is: fully roofed and not walled at all; fully walled and not roofed at all; mostly not roofed and mostly not walled; half roofed and slightly walled; half walled and slightly roofed; and slightly roofed and slightly walled.

The same decision applies to a monk sleeping with a woman (mātugāma). The distinction here is: for a monk sleeping with an unordained person (anupasampanna), the offense occurs on the fourth day; for a monk sleeping with a woman, it occurs on the first day. If one sleeps with female yakkhas or female petas who have visible forms, or with a female animal that can be an object for sexual intercourse, it is a Dukkaṭa offense. For other female yakkhas, petas, and animals, there is no offense.

## Thus ends the Discussion on the Decision regarding Sleeping Together in the Pālimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-saṅgaha.
## 17. Mañcapīṭhādi-saṅghika-senāsanesu paṭipajjitabba-vinicchaya-kathā
## (Discussion on the Decision on How to Proceed Regarding Communal Beds, Benches, etc.)

"Spreading bedding in a communal monastery and then departing" means spreading bedding in a communal monastery and then leaving the monastery because of a desire to stay elsewhere. In such a departure, this is the decision:

According to the words: "If a monk spreads bedding or has it spread in a communal monastery, and when departing, neither removes it nor has it removed, and goes away without asking permission, it is a Pācittiya," a monk who spreads bedding himself or has another spread it, and then crosses the boundary of a fenced monastery or the precinct of an unfenced monastery without putting it away or having it put away, and without asking permission, commits a Pācittiya offense.

In that context, bedding (seyyā) is of ten kinds: a mattress (bhisi), a ground cloth, a coverlet, a floor covering, a mat, a leather piece, a sitting cloth (nisīdana), a rug, a grass mat, and a leaf mat. Among these ten, a mattress (bhisi) is one spread on a bed or a bench. A ground cloth (cimilikā) is a covering made to protect the surface of a plastered floor; they spread this ground cloth below and a mat on top of it. A coverlet (uttarattharaṇa) is a rug spread on top of a bed or bench. A floor covering (bhūmattharaṇa) is an ornate mat or similar covering spread on the ground. A mat (taṭṭikā) is a covering made of palm leaves or fibers. A leather piece (cammakhaṇḍa) is the skin of animals such as lions, tigers, and leopards...
87:
Because of this word, if a monk spreads bedding himself or has it spread by another in a communal dwelling (Saṅghika vihāra), and then departs beyond the enclosure of a fenced monastery or the precinct of an unfenced monastery without putting it away or having it put away, etc., he commits a Pācittiya offense.

In that context, 'bedding' (seyyā) is of ten kinds: a mattress, a coarse cloth rug, a coverlet, a floor mat, a woven mat, a piece of hide, a sitting cloth, a bolster-spread, a grass mat, and a leaf mat. Among these ten, a 'mattress' (bhisī) is either a mattress for a couch or a mattress for a stool. A 'coarse cloth rug' (cimilika) is a covering made to protect the color of a floor that has been finished with plaster and so on; they spread this coarse cloth rug below and spread a reed mat on top of it. A 'coverlet' (uttarattharaṇa) is a spread to be laid on top of couches and stools. A 'floor mat' (bhūmattharaṇa) is an ornamental spread such as a reed mat to be laid on the ground. A 'woven mat' (taṭṭikā) is a mat made of palm leaves or bark fibers. A 'piece of hide' (cammakhaṇḍa) is any skin such as the hide of a lion, tiger, leopard, or other animals. In the commentaries, it is observed that there is no prohibition against using hides in a dwelling; therefore, the prohibition should be understood only regarding the carrying of lion skins, tiger skins, and so on when traveling. A 'sitting cloth' (nisīdana) should be understood as one with a border. Regarding 'bolster-spread' (paccattharaṇa), only the mantle (pāvāra) and the rug (kojava) are mentioned. A 'grass mat' (tiṇasanthāra) is a spread made of any kind of grass. This same method applies to a 'leaf mat' (paṇṇasanthāra).

Thus, a monk who departs after spreading these ten kinds of bedding in a communal dwelling, or having them spread, must do so after giving notice. When giving notice, if a monk is present, notice must be given to the monk. If no monk is present, to a novice; if no novice, to a monastery attendant (ārāmika); if no monastery attendant, to the donor who built and offered the dwelling, or to anyone in that donor's family. If none of these people are present, he should place a couch upon four stones, stack the remaining couches and stools upon that couch, pile the ten kinds of bedding such as mattresses on top, store away the woodenware and earthenware, close the doors and windows, fulfill the duties of a departing monk, and then depart.

If the dwelling leaks, and if grass or tiles have been brought for roofing, he should roof it if he is able. If he is unable to roof it, he should place the couches, stools, and so on in a place that does not leak and then depart. If the entire dwelling leaks, a monk who is able should store them in the house of lay devotees in the village. If those donors say, 'Venerable sir, communal property is a heavy responsibility; we fear fire and other hazards,' and do not accept them, it is proper to place a couch on stones even in the open air, place the remaining spreads according to the method mentioned before, cover them with grass and leaves, and then depart. This is because even if only a portion of those couches, stools, and spreads remains, it will be of great benefit to other monks who come to that dwelling; therefore, it is proper to cover them and depart. A monk who departs after storing them should remove the couch, stool, and door-panels, gather them together, and hang them on a rack before leaving. An arriving guest monk should also put those couches and stools back in place and then depart. He must do this himself. A monk who spreads bedding from inside a wall to the outside of the wall and stays there must, upon departing, store it back in the place from which it was taken. If one brings it down from an upper floor...
88:
...thinking, 'It will be of benefit to the monks who come to this monastery.' A monk who departs after putting things away should remove the couch, stool, and door-panels, gather them together, and hang them on the robe-pole before leaving. A monk who comes and stays later should also put the couch and stool back in place, and when he departs, he must do the same. A monk who spreads bedding from inside a wall to the outside of the wall and stays there must, upon departing, store it back in the place from which it was taken. This same method applies to a monk who brings items down from an upper floor and stays on the lower floor. When one spreads a couch or stool in night-quarters or day-quarters and goes outside, they must be placed back in the place from which they were taken.

Regarding dwellings, there is this decision on whether notice must be given or not: for a long hall or a leaf-roofed hall situated on the ground, or a dwelling built on wooden posts where termites are likely to rise, a monk departing from such a dwelling must depart only after giving notice. Indeed, if such a place is not looked after for even a few days, termite mounds will form. However, for a dwelling built on a stone slab or on stone pillars, or a mountain cave, or a plastered dwelling where there is no fear of termites, it is proper for a monk departing from there to go either after giving notice or without giving notice; however, giving notice is the proper duty (vatta). If termites are rising from one side even in such a dwelling, he must depart only after giving notice. If a guest monk stays by following a monk who has already taken possession of a communal dwelling, without taking a dwelling for himself separately, as long as he does not take possession, that dwelling remains the responsibility (palibodha) of the first monk. When that guest monk takes possession of the dwelling and stays there by his own authority, from then on it is the responsibility of the guest monk alone. If both divide and take possession, it is the responsibility of both.

In the Mahāpaccariya, it is said: If two or three monks spread bedding together, all must give notice when departing. Among them, if the one who departs first goes with the thought, 'The one remaining behind will look after it,' it is proper; however, the one remaining behind is not released from the offense by the thought of the one who left. If many monks have one monk spread the bedding, all must give notice when departing, or they must send one monk to give notice. If couches, stools, and so on are brought from another place and used while staying in a different place, they must be returned to that very place upon departing. If a more senior monk arrives while one is staying with items brought from elsewhere, he does not...
89: That senior monk should not be prevented. One should say, "Venerable sir, I brought this bed and bench from another residence; please keep it in its original place." If that senior monk agrees, saying, "Very well, I will do so," the other monk may go. For a monk who brings it to another place and uses it as communal property (saṅghika), if it is lost, worn out, or stolen by thieves, he is not liable to pay compensation. However, for a monk who uses it as personal property (puggalika), he is liable to pay compensation. If the bed and bench belonging to another monk is lost, whether used as communal or personal property, he must pay compensation. If one spreads out bedding inside a monastery with the intention of returning, thinking, "I will return today and tend to it," and while traveling to the other side of a river or to another village, at the place where the thought to continue the journey arises, he sends someone to inform the monastery, or if he is unable to return due to obstacles such as flooding, danger from kings, or danger from thieves, there is no offense for such a monk. If one spreads out bedding—or has it spread out—in the precincts of a monastery, such as in an assembly hall, a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree, and departs without putting it away, without having it put away, or without informing anyone, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). The reason is that if a monk spreads out the aforementioned ten types of bedding in a secure place like an inner room and leaves, both the bedding and the monastery building may be destroyed by termites and become a termite mound; therefore, it was declared a Pācittiya offense. However, for a monk who spreads it out in an external assembly hall and so on, only the bedding might be destroyed because the place is not secure, but the monastery building will not be destroyed; therefore, it was declared a Dukkaṭa offense in this case. As for a bed or bench, since termites cannot eat them immediately, it is said to be a Dukkaṭa offense for a monk who spreads them in a monastery and leaves. For a monk who spreads them in the monastery precincts—in an assembly hall, a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree—and departs, it is also only a Dukkaṭa offense. "Whatever monk spreads out—or has spread out—a communal bed, bench, mattress, or stool in the open air, and departing, neither puts it away nor has it put away, or goes without informing [anyone], it is a Pācittiya offense" (Pācittiya 109). According to these words, for a monk who spreads out—or has spread out—these four communal items such as a bed and bench in the open air and goes without putting them away and so on, even if he thinks "I will return today," he commits a Pācittiya offense once he passes the distance of a stone's throw of a man of average strength. Here, a "kocca" (stool) is an object made of bark, usīra-grass, muñja-grass, or pabbaja-grass, constructed in the shape of a drum, wide at the top and bottom and narrow in the middle, and bound together. It is said that they also decorate the middle of that stool with lion or tiger skin; there is no "unallowable skin" in this context. Since monastery bedding is allowable even if made of gold, such monastery bedding is of great value.
90: "Monks, I allow you to keep monastery bedding for the eight months marked as non-rainy, in a pavilion or at the foot of a tree where crows or hawks do not drop excrement" (Pācittiya 110). According to these words, it is allowable to keep [monastery bedding] in a leaf-pavilion, a plank-pavilion, or at the foot of a tree during the eight months—the four months of winter and the four months of summer—which are not designated as the rainy season. However, it should not be kept at the foot of a tree where crows, hawks, or other birds live and have built nests as their permanent dwelling. Because of the words "for eight months," in regions where it does not rain during the rainy season, it is still not allowable to keep them for those four months. Because of the words "marked as non-rainy," in places where it rains during the winter, it is not allowable to keep them in the open air even during the winter. In the summer, however, the clouds disappear in all places and the sky is clear; at such a time, it is allowable to keep a bed or bench in the open air for some necessary business. A monk who lives in the open air (an abbhokāsika) should also know the duties. If he has a personal bed, he should sleep only on that bed. A monk taking a communal bed should take one woven with rattan or bark; if such a bed is not available, an old bed should be taken; if an old bed is not available, a newly woven bed or one covered with leather should be taken. After taking it, he should not spread it out and lie down in the open air or at the foot of a tree at an improper time without even making a robe-tent, saying, "I am an excellent tree-foot dweller, I am an excellent open-air dweller." If a tent made of a fourfold robe cannot protect against getting wet, and there is rain for seven days and so on, it is allowable [to keep the bed there] because it follows the condition of the monk's body [getting wet]. Because of the perfection of virtue of monks living in leaf-huts in the forest, people with faithful hearts donate new beds and benches, saying, "Please use these as communal property." Monks who depart after staying there should send them to fellow monks (sabhāga) in a nearby monastery before going; if there are no fellow monks, they should be kept in a place where they will not get wet from rain before going; if there is no place where they will not get wet, they should be hung on a tree before going. Having taken a broom at the Cetiya courtyard and swept or washed any place such as the dining hall courtyard, the Uposatha hall courtyard, a daytime resting place within the precinct, or the fire room, it should be placed back only on the broom-rack. The same rule applies to a monk who takes a broom from one of the places like the Uposatha hall and sweeps the remaining areas.
91:
A monk who, while sweeping the path for alms-round, wishes to go, should place the broom in a rest house (sālā) if there is one along the way. If there is no rest house, he should observe that no rain clouds are rising, and if he knows, "It will not rain until I return from the village," he may leave it anywhere and, upon returning, must place it back in its original position. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya: "If he leaves it in the open while knowing it is about to rain, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." If a broom is already kept in various places for sweeping, it is proper to return it to those same places after sweeping. A monk sweeping the rest house (sālā) should know the duties. In those duties, it is as follows: starting from the center, the sand should be leveled towards the place where feet are set; rubbish should be picked up by hand and discarded outside.

If one causes an unordained person (a layperson or a novice) to spread out communal lodging (saṅghika senāsana) of the four types mentioned above in the open, at the foot of a tree, or in a pavilion (maṇḍapa), the responsibility (palibodha) lies with the one who caused it to be spread. If he causes an ordained monk to spread it, the responsibility lies with the one who spread it. In this matter, there is this decision (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 111): A senior monk (thera), having finished his meal in the dining hall, commands a junior monk (dahara), "Go and set up a bed and stool (mañcapīṭha) in a pleasant daytime spot." If that junior monk does so and remains there, and the senior monk, after wandering as he pleases, arrives at that place and places his bag or his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) there, from that moment, the responsibility lies with the senior monk. If, after sitting, he leaves by himself and neither puts it away nor has someone else put it away, and goes beyond a stone's throw (leḍḍupāta), he commits an offense of expiation (pācittiya). However, if the senior monk does not place his bag or upper robe there but, while walking in the cloister, says to the junior monk, "You may go," the junior monk should inform him, "Venerable sir, here the bed and stool are set up." If the senior monk knows the duty, he should say, "You go, I will take care of it." If he is an ignorant senior monk who has not learned the duties, and merely threatens the junior monk, saying, "Go, do not stand here; I will not let you sit or lie down," the junior monk should ask permission, saying, "Venerable sir, may you rest in comfort," pay respects, and leave. After that junior monk has left, the responsibility lies only with the senior monk; it should be understood that the offense is incurred by that senior monk as in the previous method.

Alternatively, if at the very moment of being commanded, the junior monk says, "I have some duties to perform, such as washing my belongings," but the senior monk says, "Go after setting it up," and then leaves the dining hall for another place, by the lifting of his foot...
92:
...he should be made to undergo the offense. If he goes to that very place and sits down, the offense is incurred as in the previous method if he exceeds a stone's throw. However, if the senior monk commands a novice (sāmaṇera), even if the novice is sitting there after setting up the bed and stool, the senior monk who goes elsewhere from the dining hall should be made to undergo the offense upon lifting his foot. If he goes and sits there, he should be made to undergo the offense upon exceeding a stone's throw when he leaves again. But if the senior monk, while commanding, says, "Set up the bed and stool and sit right there," he is allowed to go and come as he pleases. As for the senior monk himself, if he leaves without putting things back to their normal state, he commits a pācittiya offense upon exceeding a stone's throw. Those who sit after setting up beds and stools at occasional assemblies should, when leaving, tell the park-keepers (ārāmika), "Put these away." For those who leave without saying so, an offense is incurred upon exceeding a stone's throw.

When there is a great Dhamma preaching (mahādhammassavana), beds and stools are brought from the Uposatha hall (uposathāgāra) and the dining hall to be set up; the responsibility lies only with the resident monks (āvāsika). If visiting monks (āgantuka) take them, saying, "This belongs to our preceptor (upajjhāya), this belongs to our teacher (ācariya)," from that moment, the responsibility lies with those monks. When leaving, an offense is incurred by those who exceed a stone's throw without putting things back to their normal state. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, it is said: "As long as others do not sit, the burden lies with those who set them up; when others come and sit, the burden lies with those who are sitting. If they leave without removing them or having them removed, they commit a dukkaṭa offense. Why? Because they were set up without being commanded." When a Dhamma seat (dhammāsana) is set up, as long as the announcer (ussāraka) or the Dhamma preacher (dhammakathika) has not arrived, the responsibility lies with those who set it up. When that preacher arrives and sits, the responsibility lies with him. If the Dhamma preaching lasts the whole day and night, and one announcer or preacher gets up and another sits down, the burden lies with whoever comes and sits. The one getting up should leave after saying, "This seat is your responsibility." Even if the first person who was sitting gets up and leaves before the other person arrives, if the other person arrives and sits while the first person is still within the precincts (upacāra), the one who got up and left should not be made to undergo the offense. However, if the first person who was sitting gets up from the seat and exceeds a stone's throw before the next person arrives, he should be made to undergo the offense. "In all cases, upon exceeding a stone's throw, a dukkaṭa is incurred at the first step, and a pācittiya at the second step"—this method is stated in the Mahāpaccariya.
93:
If a monk spreads out or causes to be spread out in the open any communal property (saṅghika) other than the aforementioned lodgings—such as a coarse mat, a coverlet, a ground mat, a mat, a piece of skin, a foot-wiper, or a foot-washing board—and when departing, neither removes it nor causes it to be removed, or goes away without informing [another], he commits a Dukkaṭa offence. For one who goes away after leaving in the open a bowl-stand, a bowl-lid, a foot-washing shard, a palmyra fan, a leaf fan, any wooden utensil, or even a water ladle or a water conch, there is a Dukkaṭa offence. After boiling dye in the open, everything such as the dye-pot, the dye-ladle, and the dye-trough should be stored in the fire-hall (aggisālā). If there is no fire-hall, it should be placed in a rain-proof rock-shelter. If such a place is also absent, it is allowable to go after placing it in a spot where looking monks can see it. Even for lodgings like beds and chairs belonging to another individual, it is only a Dukkaṭa offence. However, in this regard, it is stated in the Mahāpaccarī and other commentaries: 'In the property of one with whom intimacy (vissāsa) is not established, there is a Dukkaṭa offence. In the property of one with whom intimacy is established, it is like one's own personal property.' In one's own personal property, there is no offence. If a monk, novice, or monastery attendant (ārāmika) is a conscientious person (lajjī) and regards [the property] as his own concern, there is no offence even for one who goes away without informing such a person. If one who is drying [items] in the sun goes away thinking 'I will remove them when I return,' there is no offence for him.

## Thus, in the Pālimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha,
## The Discussion on the Decision regarding the Conduct towards Communal Lodgings such as Beds and Chairs is finished.
## 18. Discussion on the Decision regarding the Period-limited (Kālika)

Regarding the phrase 'The Kālikas are four,' here the four Kālikas should be known as: Yāvakālika, Yāmakālika, Sattāhakālika, and Yāvajီvika. Among those four, any edible food (khādanīya) or staple food (bhojanīya) received in the morning and to be consumed until the time known as noon is called Yāvakālika because it is to be consumed for that duration. The eight kinds of drinks along with the suitable (anuloma) drinks [to be consumed] until the night...
94: ...until the end of the night known as the last watch; because it has a time for consumption [up to that point], it is called 'watch-limited' (yāmakālika). Because the five kinds of medicines such as ghee are received and may be stored for seven days, having a time-period of seven days, it is called 'seven-day-limited' (sattāhakālika). Excluding water, all other received items that are carried for life and consumed when there is a reason are called 'lifelong-limited' (yāvajīvika). Among those four time-limited allowables, in the 'morning-limited' (yāvakālika), 'staple food' (bhojanīya) refers to: cooked rice, barley-meal, flour-cake, fish, and meat. Excluding the five staple foods, the watch-limited, the seven-day-limited, and the lifelong-limited, the remainder is called 'edible food' (khādanīya). Here, regarding edibles made of pre-harvest crops (pubbaṇṇa) and post-harvest crops (aparaṇṇa) such as twisted cakes and sweets, there is no need for further explanation. Items that have the nature of material food (āmisa), such as various wild roots, are also considered edibles. They are: root-edibles, tuber-edibles, bulb-edibles, sprout-edibles, stem-edibles, bark-edibles, leaf-edibles, flower-edibles, fruit-edibles, seed-edibles, powder-edibles, and resin-edibles; all these also fall under the category of edibles. To distinguish those that have the nature of material food (āmisa) among those edibles, this is merely an illustration: among root-edibles, the roots of plants with leaves used in curries, such as Mūlaka, Khāraka, Cuccu, Tambaka, Taṇḍuleyyaka, Vatthuleyyaka, Vajakali, and Jajjhari roots, etc., are edibles with the nature of material food. Here, in the case of the Vajakali root, the mature part is usually cut and discarded; that mature part is lifelong-limited (yāvajīvika). Other roots should also be understood in this same way. It is said that the mature parts of Mūlaka, Khāraka, and Jajjhari roots are also edibles with the nature of material food. As for the roots mentioned in the Pāḷi: 'Monks, I allow medicinal roots: turmeric, ginger, orris root, white orris root, ativisa, black hellebore, usīra-grass, nut-grass, or whatever other medicinal roots there are that do not serve the purpose of edible food (khādanīya) among edibles, nor serve the purpose of staple food (bhojanīya) among staple foods'—these are lifelong-limited (yāvajīvika). If these roots are counted by methods such as the 'five minor roots' and 'five major roots,' there is no end to the counting. The characteristic of these roots is simply that they do not fulfill the function of edible or staple food. Therefore, if any root serves the purpose of edible or staple food as a natural food for people in various regions, that root is morning-limited (yāvakālika). Any other root should be known as lifelong-limited (yāvajīvika).
95:
It should be understood. Indeed, even if much is said, one should remain fixed on this characteristic. When names are mentioned, those who do not know the various names will only become confused; therefore, without giving much weight to the names, only the characteristic is shown. Just as the decision regarding roots is understood, so too shall we show the characteristic in the case of tubers and so on; the decision should be understood by means of that characteristic. The eight types of roots such as turmeric mentioned in the Pali—their stems, bark, flowers, fruits, and so on—are all medicinal and are called life-long (yāvajīvika).

In the category of edible tubers (kanda), there are two types: long tubers (such as lotus stalks, kiṃsuka roots, etc.) and round tubers (such as lotus root-bulbs, kaseruka tubers, etc.), which are also called knots or root-heads. Among these edible tubers, the old and mature parts, the outer skin/bark, and the fine rootlets of all tubers are life-long (yāvajīvika). However, the young and easily edible tubers such as the young sālakalyāṇī tuber, young kiṃsuka tuber, ambāṭaka tuber, ketaka tuber, kanyin tuber, the tubers of paduma and puṇḍarīka lotuses (known as lotus stalks and lotus roots), piṇḍālu, māsālu, and so on, as well as the khīravallī tuber, āluva tuber, siggu (drumstick) tuber, young palm tuber, the tubers of blue lotus, red lotus, kumuda, and sogandhika, banana tubers, bamboo tubers, kaseruka tubers, and so on—those that serve as food or snacks for people in various regions as their natural diet—are temporary (yāvakālika). The khīravallī tuber is life-long (yāvajīvika) if unwashed (not boiled or processed), but temporary (yāvakālika) if washed (boiled or processed). Tubers such as khīrakākoli, jīvaka, usabhaka, garlic, and so on are only life-long (yāvajīvika). These tubers are included in the collection of root medicines in the Pali text as: 'Whatever other roots there are that are medicinal.'

In the category of edible sprouts (muḷāla), the paduma sprout and puṇḍarīka sprout are just like the roots. Sprouts such as eraka and kandula, which serve as food or snacks for people in various regions as their natural diet, are temporary (yāvakālika). However, the sprouts of turmeric, ginger, takkhāna, sugarcane, ketaka, palm, dhannun, min, coconut, areca nut trees, and so on are life-long (yāvajīvika). All these sprouts are also included in the collection of root medicines in the Pali text as: 'Whatever other roots there are that are medicinal.'

In the category of edible shoots/tops (matthaka), the shoots known as kaḷīra of palm, dhannun, min, ketaka, coconut, areca nut, date palm, rattan, eraka, and banana; bamboo shoots, reed shoots...
96:
...sugarcane shoots, radish shoots, mustard shoots, asparagus shoots, the shoots of the seven types of grain, and so on—the shoots of trees, creepers, etc., that serve as food or snacks for people in various regions as their natural diet—are temporary (yāvakālika). The shoots of turmeric, ginger, vacā, makaci, and garlic, as well as the mature nodes cut and fallen from the shoots of palm, dhannun, minbo, and coconut, are life-long (yāvajīvika).

In the category of edible stems (khandha), the underground stem of sālakalyāṇī, sugarcane stems, the stalks/stems of blue lotus, red lotus, kumuda, and sogandhika lotuses, and so on—the stems that serve as food or snacks for people in various regions as their natural diet—are temporary (yāvakālika). The leaf-stalks of blue, white, and red lotus species, all stalks of the paduma lotus species, karavinda stalks, and all other remaining stems are life-long (yāvajīvika).

In the category of edible bark (taca), only sugarcane bark is temporary (yāvakālika), and that sugarcane bark must be juicy. All other remaining barks are life-long (yāvajīvika). These three—shoots, stems, and bark—should be understood as being included under astringent medicines (kasāvabhesajja) in the Pali. For it was said:
'Monks, I allow astringent medicines: astringent of neem, astringent of kuṭaja, astringent of paṭola, astringent of phaggava, astringent of nattamāla, or whatever other astringent medicines there are that do not serve the purpose of food in snacks, nor serve the purpose of food in meals.'
In this Pali passage, the inclusion of these (shoots, stems, and bark) is also accomplished. It should be understood that the aforementioned astringents are all allowable (kappiya).

In the category of edible leaves (pattakhādanīya), the leaves of plants such as radish, khāraka, caccutambaka, spinach (taṇḍuleyyaka), pappunnāga, vatthuleyyaka, vajakali, jajjhari, sellu (thanat), siggu (drumstick), kāsamadda, ummācīna, mung bean, black gram, cowpea, and other beans (excluding the large bean), agnimantha, sunisannaka, white varaṇa, nāḷikā, and the ground-salt plant (bhūmiyam-jātaloṇī); and other such leaves that serve as food or snacks for people in various regions as their natural diet, are strictly temporary (yāvakālika)...
97:
Furthermore, the leaf of the loṇi plant, which has leaves about the size of a fingernail and climbs on trees and bushes, is yāvajīvika. The inhabitants of the island of Ceylon say that the brahmi leaf is also yāvakālika. Mango sprouts are yāvakālika, while asoka sprouts are yāvajīvika. In the Pali: "Monks, I allow medicinal leaves: neem leaves, kuṭaja leaves, paṭola leaves, basil leaves, cotton leaves, and whatever other medicinal leaves there are. These leaves do not serve the purpose of hard food among hard foods, nor the purpose of soft food among soft foods" (Mahāvagga, 263)—other such leaves are also yāvajīvika. Not only the leaves, but the flowers and fruits of these plants are also yāvajīvika. Among the yāvajīvika leaves, there are dog-strangling vine leaves, phaukphari leaves, kinpuppa leaves, betel leaves, lotus leaves, and so on, which are infinite in number.

Among edible flowers, radish flowers, hin-ko flowers, hin-gala flowers, red hin-chi flowers, kin-peik flowers, hin-kha-pan-tu flowers, pea-creeper flowers, lablab bean flowers, hog-plum flowers, the young flowers of coconut, palm, and screw-pine, white varana flowers, drumstick (moringa) flowers, and the flowers of blue, white, and red lotuses that are the size of an earring-stud, as well as flame-of-the-forest flowers, elephant-trunk flowers, and moe-swe flowers, etc., which are consumed as regular food by people in various regions as hard or soft food, are yāvakālika. However, the flowers of asoka, chayar, su-yit, punnāga, campaka, jasmine, Arabian jasmine, mahā-hle-ga, thin-khwe, night-jasmine, and kyat-yone, etc., are yāvajīvika. These flowers are infinite in number. In the Pali, it should be understood that these flowers are included under medicinal astringents (kasāva-bhesajja).

Among edible fruits, the fruits of jackfruit, wild jackfruit, palm, coconut, mango, rose apple, rambutan, tamarind, citron, wood apple, gourd, pumpkin, cucumber, persimmon, wild cucumber, eggplant, seeded banana, seedless banana, and thit-mai-zi, etc., which are consumed as regular food by people in various regions as hard or soft food, are all yāvakālika. It is impossible to show the limit of these by name. In the Pali: "Monks, medicinal fruits such as bilaṅga, long pepper, black pepper, yellow myrobalan, beleric myrobalan, emblic myrobalan, goṭṭha fruit, and whatever other medicinal fruits..." as stated...
98:
Furthermore, "there are other medicinal fruits that do not serve the purpose of hard food among hard foods, nor the purpose of soft food among soft foods" (Mahāvagga, 263); such fruits are yāvajīvika. Among these fruits, the unripe fruits of acchiva, bimba, varaṇa, ketaka, kāsmari, etc., as well as nutmeg (jātiphala), kaṭukaphala, cardamom (eḷā), and takkola, cannot be fully enumerated by name.

Among edible seeds, the young seeds of wild jackfruit, jackfruit, hway, sal, thin-baung, screw-pine, and persimmon, as well as tamarind seeds, kyi seeds, and the lotus seeds of various lotus species, etc., are yāvakālika because they are widely used as regular food for the purpose of hard or soft food by people in various regions. The seeds of thit-mai-zi, punnāga, yellow myrobalan, etc., as well as red mustard and mustard seeds, are yāvajīvika. It should be understood that these seeds are included in the Pali under medicinal fruits (phala-bhesajja).

Among edible flours, first, the flour of the seven types of grain and grain-like seeds such as kyit-lan, as well as jackfruit flour, wild jackfruit flour, hway flour, sal flour, boiled palm flour, and yu-ywan flour, etc., are yāvakālika because they are widely used as regular food for the purpose of hard or soft food by people in various regions. Unboiled palm flour, yu-ywan flour, and wild taca flour, etc., are yāvajīvika. It should be understood that these flours are included in the Pali under medicinal astringents (kasāva) and medicinal roots and fruits (mūla-phala).

Among edible resins, only sugarcane resin (juice) is sattāhakālika (seven-day medicine). Regarding the remaining resins: "Monks, I allow medicinal resins: hiṅgu (asafoetida), hiṅgu-resin, hiṅgu-stems/leaves resin, hiṅgu-sprout resin, hiṅgu-leaf resin, hiṅgu-mixed resin, lac, and whatever other medicinal resins there are" (Mahāvagga, 263)—the resins mentioned in this Pali are yāvajīvika. The resins included by the word "other" in that Pali, such as mango resin and mahā-hle-ga resin, etc., cannot be fully enumerated by name. Thus, in this context of medicinal roots and so forth, whatever is yāvakālika is collectively included here under the term "remaining edibles" (avasesa-khādanīya).
99:
Regarding the yāmakālika (drinks allowed from noon until dawn), the eight kinds of drinks are: mango juice (ambapāna), rose-apple juice (jambupāna), seeded banana juice (cocapāna), seedless banana juice (mocapāna), madhuka juice (madhukapāna), grape juice (muddikapāna), water-lily root juice (sālūkapāna), and phārusaka juice (phārusakapāna). These eight are the drinks. Among these eight drinks, mango juice is that which is made from either raw or ripe mangoes. In making that mango juice with raw mangoes, one should cut young mangoes, place them in water, cook them by the heat of the sun, filter them, and then mix them with honey, sugar, camphor, and so on, which have been received on that same day. Juice prepared in this way is allowable only in the morning. However, if one receives juice prepared by unordained persons (anupasampanna) and it is accepted in the morning, it is allowable even if consumed with food in the morning. After noon, it is allowable to be consumed without food until dawn. This same principle applies to all drinks.

Rose-apple juice is juice made from rose-apples. Seeded banana juice is juice made from bananas with seeds. Seedless banana juice is juice made from bananas without seeds. Madhuka juice is juice made from the natural juice of madhuka flowers. That juice is allowable only when mixed with water; it is not allowable if pure. Grape juice is juice made by crushing grapes in water, similar to mango juice. Water-lily root juice is juice made by crushing the roots of red water-lilies, blue water-lilies, and so on. Phārusaka juice is juice made from phārusaka fruits, similar to mango juice. These eight drinks are allowable whether they are cold or cooked by the sun; they are not allowable if cooked by fire.

Other juices from small fruits such as rattan fruit, tamarind, citron, wood-apple, koshamba, and karamanda are similar to the eight drinks. Although these juices are not explicitly mentioned in the Pali, they are allowable because they conform to what is allowable (anuloma). Because it was said, "Bhikkhus, I allow all fruit juices except grain juice," there is no other fruit juice that is unallowable, except for grain juice and its equivalents; all are yāmakālika. In that statement, grain juice and its equivalents refer to the juice of the seven kinds of grains, the juice of the nine large fruits—namely, palmyra, coconut, jackfruit, breadfruit, gourd, pumpkin, bitter cucumber, cucumber, and melon—and the juice of all other crops and equivalent grains. Since these juices are yāvakālika (allowable only until noon), they are not allowable after noon. Because it was said, "Bhikkhus, I allow all leaf juices except the juice of cooked vegetables," the juice made by crushing yāvakālika leaves in cold water or juice cooked by the sun is allowable, excluding the juice of cooked vegetables. Because it was said, "Bhikkhus, I allow all flower juices except madhuka flower juice," all flower juices are allowable, excluding madhuka flower juice.
100:
Sattāhakālika (seven-day medicine) refers to ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses; these five are medicines. Among these five, ghee (sappi) means ghee from cows, goats, buffaloes, or any animal whose meat is allowable. Fresh butter (navanīta) is the butter from those same animals. Oil (tela) refers to sesame oil, mustard oil, madhuka oil, castor oil, and animal fat. Honey (madhu) is the honey produced by small bees. Molasses (phāṇita) is the syrup produced from sugarcane. As for yāvajīvika (lifetime medicine), it should be understood in the same way as mentioned below in the yāvakālika section regarding edible roots and so forth.

Among these four types of kālika, yāvakālika received at dawn may be stored even a hundred times and consumed as long as the noon hour has not passed. Yāmakālika may be consumed for one full day and night (24 hours), sattāhakālika for seven days, and the other, yāvajīvika, may be consumed for life if there is a reason. However, for any yāvakālika or yāmakālika that has been kept past one night, a monk who takes it with the intention to swallow commits a dukkaṭa offense at the moment of receiving it. When swallowing, he commits a pācittiya offense for every swallow due to the factor of storage (sannidhi). If a bowl is washed improperly, such that a mark appears when rubbed with a finger, or if oil has entered the crevices of a knotted bowl and leaks out when dried in the sun, or if oil becomes visible when hot gruel is placed in it—a monk who eats from such a bowl the next day commits a pācittiya offense. Therefore, after washing the bowl, one should pour clear water into it again and rub it with a finger to ensure it is free of oil. If there is oil in the water or if a finger mark appears on the bowl, it is considered improperly washed. However, on a bowl that has the color of oil, if a finger mark appears, it is considered negligible (not an offense). If monks give food to novices without expectation, and the novices store it and give it back, it is all allowable. Indeed, if one receives it oneself and does not give it away, it is not allowable on the second day. For swallowing even a single grain of such stored rice, a pācittiya offense is committed. Among unallowable meats, eating human meat results in a pācittiya along with a thullaccaya offense. For the remaining nine types of forbidden meat, a pācittiya along with a dukkaṭa offense is committed.

One who swallows yāmakālika when there is a reason commits a pācittiya offense. One who swallows it for the sake of nutriment commits a pācittiya along with a dukkaṭa offense. If one who has finished their meal (pavārita) swallows food that has not been made leftover (anatirittakata), they commit two pācittiya offenses for ordinary food; for human meat, two pācittiyas along with a thullaccaya; for the remaining unallowable meats, two pācittiyas along with a dukkaṭa. Regarding yāmakālika...
101:
If a monk who is pavārita (one who has finished his meal and refused further food) swallows food without it being made atiritta (allowable leftovers), he commits two Pācittiya offenses for ordinary food such as alms-food. For human flesh, he commits two offenses: a Thullaccaya and a Pācittiya. For the remaining nine types of forbidden flesh, he commits two offenses: a Dukkaṭa and a Pācittiya. If there is a reason, for one who swallows a yāmakālika (afternoon tonic) with a mouth containing food residue (sāmisa), there are two Pācittiya offenses; for one who swallows with a mouth free of food residue (nirāmisa), there is only one Pācittiya offense. For one who swallows for the sake of nourishment, a Dukkaṭa offense is added in both cases of the alternatives. If he swallows at the wrong time (after noon), for ordinary food, he commits two Pācittiya offenses due to storage (sannidhi) and eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana). For forbidden flesh, Thullaccaya and Dukkaṭa offenses are added. For yāmakālika, there is no offense due to the wrong time. Because it was not made atiritta, there is no offense for all alternatives in the wrong time. For one who accepts sattāhakālika (seven-day tonic) and yāvajīvika (lifelong medicine) for the sake of nourishment, a Dukkaṭa offense is first committed due to the act of receiving. At the time of swallowing, if it is free of food residue, a Dukkaṭa is committed for every swallow. If it was received mixed with food, only a Pācittiya is committed according to the object, such as alms-food.

Regarding sattāhakālika such as ghee, this is the decision: If ghee is received in the morning, it may be consumed on that day in the morning either mixed with food or pure. From the afternoon onwards, it must be consumed pure for seven days. If seven days have passed, if it is kept in one vessel, one Nissaggiya offense is committed; if kept in many vessels, Nissaggiya offenses are committed according to the number of vessels. If received in the afternoon, only the pure form is allowable. Whether in the morning or evening, if it is made into uggahitaka (invalidated acceptance) and kept, it is not allowable to swallow; it should only be used for anointing, etc. Even after seven days, there is no offense because it is not to be swallowed. If a layperson or a novice makes ghee from butter received in the morning and offers it, it is allowable even with food in the morning. If he makes it himself, it is allowable only if pure for seven days. Ghee made by anyone from butter received in the afternoon is allowable only if pure for seven days. If made from butter whose acceptance has been invalidated, the decision should be understood according to the method of pure ghee mentioned before. Ghee made by a layperson or a novice from milk or curd received in the morning is allowable even with food on that day in the morning. If he makes it himself, it is allowable only if pure on that day in the morning. For one who boils butter, it is not 'cooking for oneself' (sāmaṃpāka). However, it is not allowable to mix food with that self-boiled ghee, and it is also not allowable from the afternoon onwards. Even after seven days, there is no offense because it was received with its substance. Ghee made from milk or curd received in the afternoon should only be used for anointing, etc. The same applies to ghee made from milk or curd whose acceptance was invalidated in the morning. In both cases, there is no offense even after seven days.
102:
The same method should be understood for the ghee of forbidden animals (such as elephants, horses, etc.). There is this distinction: where a Nissaggiya is incurred for ghee mentioned in the Pāḷi, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred for this ghee of forbidden animals. In the Andhaka Commentary, a statement resembling a reason is made to forbid human ghee and human butter. Such a prohibition is inappropriate because they are permitted in all other commentaries. The decision regarding human ghee and butter will also appear later.

Butter mentioned in the Pāḷi, if received in the morning, is allowable even with food on that day in the morning. From the afternoon onwards, it is allowable only if pure. If seven days have passed, if kept in various vessels, Nissaggiya offenses are incurred according to the number of vessels; even if in a single vessel, if kept as separate lumps without being mixed, Nissaggiya offenses are incurred according to the number of lumps. Butter received in the afternoon should be understood according to the method stated for ghee.

In this butter, there may be small lumps of curd and drops of whey. Therefore, half of the elders said it is allowable only after washing and straining. However, Mahāsīva Thera said, 'From the time the Blessed One permitted it, they ate it just as it was taken out from the whey.' Therefore, a monk consuming butter should wash and strain it, removing curd, whey, flies, ants, etc., before consuming. A monk who wishes to cook it into ghee and consume it may cook it even without washing. The curd or whey contained in that butter will be consumed (evaporated) when cooked. The intention here is that this does not count as 'receiving with its substance' (savatthukapaṭiggahita). Because it is cooked with food residue, monks who are scrupulous (kukkuccaka) have doubts about that ghee.

Now, regarding butter whose acceptance has been invalidated, butter made from milk or curd received in the morning, butter made from milk or curd received in the afternoon, butter made from milk or curd whose acceptance has been invalidated, and butter from forbidden animals like elephants and horses—the entire method of offense or non-offense, and whether it is allowable for consumption or not, should be taken exactly as the method stated for ghee.

For monks who enter the village for oil-alms, people pour ghee, butter, cooked oil, and raw oil into that same oil-container (alms-bowl). In that oil, there may be drops of whey and curd, grains of rice, broken rice, flies, etc. If it is cooked by the heat of the sun, strained, and taken, it becomes a seven-day tonic (sattāhakālika) medicine. It is also allowable to cook it with medicines that have been received and use it as oil for nasal treatment. If, during a period of continuous rain, a conscientious novice melts it over a fire so that the fallen rice grains etc. do not get cooked, strains it, cooks it again, and offers it, it is allowable for seven days just as in the previous method.

Among various oils, sesame oil, if received in the morning, is allowable even with food in the morning. From the afternoon onwards, it is allowable only if pure.
103:
Upon the lapse of seven days, it should be known that a Nissaggiya offense is incurred according to the number of containers of that oil. Oil received after the meal (in the afternoon) is allowable for seven days only when it is free from food (nirāmisa). Oil that has been stored after its formal acceptance has been invalidated (uggahitaka) is not allowable for swallowing; it should only be used for purposes such as anointing the head. Even if seven days have passed, there is no offense.

Oil made from sesame seeds received before the meal (in the morning) is allowable even with food (sāmisa) during the morning. From the time after the meal onwards, it is not fit for swallowing; it should only be used for purposes such as anointing the head. Even if seven days have passed, there is no offense. Oil made from sesame seeds received after the meal is not fit for swallowing because it was received along with the substance (sesame). Even if seven days have passed, there is no offense; it should be used for purposes such as anointing the head. The same method should be understood for oil made from sesame seeds whose formal acceptance was invalidated, whether in the morning or the evening.

If oil is made from sesame seeds received in the morning by roasting them, or by steaming sesame powder, or by mixing it with hot water, and if it is prepared by a novice (sāmaṇera), it is allowable even with food in the morning. However, if one prepares it oneself, since it originates from a 'time-limited' (yāvakālika) substance, it is allowable in the morning only when free from food; it is not allowable with food because it is 'cooked by oneself' (sāmaṃpāka). Because it was received along with the substance, both types are unfit for swallowing from the time after the meal onwards; they should only be used for purposes such as anointing the head. Even if seven days have passed, there is no offense. If the hot water is only a small amount, just enough for sprinkling, it is considered negligible (abbohārika) and does not count as 'cooking by oneself'. In the case of mustard oil and others, if they are received without the substance, the judgment is the same as that stated for sesame oil without the substance.

If oil can be made from the powder of mustard seeds and others received in the morning by drying them in the sun, that oil is allowable even with food in the morning. From the time after the meal onwards, it is allowable only when free from food. If seven days have passed, a Nissaggiya offense is incurred. Since oil is made by steaming mustard seed powder or madhuca powder, or by roasting castor seeds, if such oil is prepared by novices, it is allowable even with food in the morning. Since the substances are 'life-long' (yāvajīvika), there is no fault in receiving them along with the substance. If one prepares it oneself, it should be used for seven days only in a manner that is free from food. If it is made from substances whose formal acceptance was invalidated, it is not fit for swallowing but is allowable for external use. Even if seven days have passed, there is no offense.

Oil made from mustard seeds, madhuca seeds, or castor seeds received for the purpose of making oil is allowable for seven days (if made on the day of reception). If made on the second day, it is allowable for six days; if made on the third day, for five days; if made on the fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day, it is allowable only on that specific day. If it remains until dawn, a Nissaggiya offense is incurred. If made on the eighth day, it is not fit for swallowing, but since it is not a Nissaggiya, (it is allowable for external use).
104:
It is allowable for external use. Even if one does not make oil, if mustard seeds and others received for the purpose of making oil are kept for more than seven days, only a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. There are other oils not directly mentioned in the Pali, such as coconut oil, neem oil, trumpet flower oil (kosamba), etc.; for a monk who keeps these oils for more than seven days after receiving them, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. This is the distinction regarding these oils. For the rest, by considering whether the substances are 'time-limited' (yāvakālika) or 'life-long' (yāvajīvika), all the procedures regarding cooking by oneself, receiving with the substance, receiving in the morning or at the wrong time, and invalidation of formal acceptance should be understood according to the method already stated.

Animal fat (vasā-tela) refers to the fat of the five types allowed: "Monks, I allow five kinds of fat: bear fat, fish fat, porpoise fat, pig fat, and donkey fat." Here, by the word "bear fat," the fat of all animals whose meat is unallowable is permitted, excluding human fat. By the mention of fish, porpoises are also included, but they are mentioned separately because they are fierce fish. By the inclusion of fish and others, the fat of all animals whose meat is allowable is also permitted here. Among meats, ten kinds—human, elephant, horse, dog, snake, lion, tiger, leopard, bear, and hyena—are unallowable; among fats, however, only human fat is unallowable. Among substances like milk, there is nothing that is unallowable. Animal fat prepared by laypeople or novices, if received in the morning, is allowable with meat in the morning; from the time after the meal onwards, it is allowable for seven days only when pure and free from meat. If there is a small amount of meat, sinew, bone, or blood resembling fine dust in that fat, it should be regarded as negligible (abbohārika). If one receives the fat and prepares it oneself, if it is received, cooked, and strained in the morning, it should be used for seven days in a manner free from meat. Intending this use free from meat, it was said: "Oil that is received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time, may be used as oil."

In that case too, the negligible remains negligible. However, in the afternoon (wrong time), it is not allowable to either receive or prepare it. For it has been said:

"Monks, if it is received at the wrong time, cooked at the wrong time, and mixed at the wrong time, and if one should consume it, there is an offense of three dukkaṭas. Monks, if it is received at the proper time but cooked at the wrong time and mixed at the wrong time, and if one should consume it, there is an offense of two dukkaṭas. Monks, if it is received at the proper time and cooked at the proper time but mixed at the wrong time, and if one should consume it, there is an offense of one dukkaṭa. Monks, if it is received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time, and if one should consume it, there is no offense."
105:
The disciples asked the Venerable Upatissatthera, "Venerable Sir, are the substances produced by cooking clarified butter, butter, and liquid fat together allowable or not?" The Elder replied, "Friends, they are not allowable." It is said that the Elder was scrupulous regarding these substances cooked together, just as one would be regarding the dregs of cooked oil. Then they asked him further, "Venerable Sir, there may be curd globules or drops of buttermilk in the butter; is this allowable?" "Friends, this too is not allowable," he replied. Then they said to him, "Venerable Sir, substances cooked and mixed together become potent and can suppress diseases, can they not?" "Friends, that is good," the Elder acknowledged. However, the Venerable Mahāsummatthera said, "The liquid fat of animals whose meat is allowable is permitted when consumed with food (sāmisa); the rest (the liquid fat of animals whose meat is not allowable) is permitted when consumed without food (nirāmisa)." But the Venerable Mahāpadumatthera rejected this decision, asking, "What is this? Do not monks with wind ailments drink gruel after adding bear's fat, pig's fat, and so on into a gruel made from the decoction of five roots? Does that gruel not become potent and suppress the disease?" Having said this, he stated, "It is allowable."

Honey (madhu) is that which is made by honey-bees, small bees, and large bees. If that honey is received in the morning, it is allowable to be consumed with food in the morning; from noon onwards, it is allowable for seven days only when consumed without food. If seven days are exceeded, it is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense. If large-bee honey, which is like resin, is divided into portions and kept, or if other honey is kept in separate vessels, Nissaggiya Pācittiya offenses are incurred according to the number of items. If it is made into a single portion or kept in a single vessel, only one Nissaggiya Pācittiya is incurred. Honey taken by oneself (without being offered) should be understood in the same manner as mentioned; it may be used for anointing sores and so on. If a honeycomb or beeswax is pure and not smeared with honey, it is lifelong (yāvajīvika); if it is smeared with honey, it follows the rule of honey. There are winged honey-wasps called cīrika, long-winged wasps called tumbaḷa, and large black carpenter bees with bone-like wings; in their nests, there is honey like resin, which is lifelong (yāvajīvika).

Molasses (phāṇita) refers to all sugarcane products without pulp, whether uncooked or cooked without pulp, derived from sugarcane juice. If that molasses is received in the morning, it is allowable to be consumed with food in the morning; from noon onwards, it is allowable for seven days only when consumed without food. If seven days are exceeded, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred according to the number of items. If many lumps are powdered and put into a single vessel so that they form a solid mass, only one Nissaggiya Pācittiya is incurred. Molasses taken by oneself should be understood in the same manner as mentioned; it may be used for fumigating the house and so on.
106:
If molasses is made from unstrained sugarcane juice received in the morning and is prepared by a layperson or a novice, it is allowable to be consumed with food. If it is prepared by oneself (the monk), it is allowable only when consumed without food. From noon onwards, however, because it was received with the sugarcane pulp, it must not be swallowed; even if seven days pass, there is no offense. Molasses made from unstrained sugarcane juice received in the afternoon is also not to be swallowed, and there is no offense even after seven days. This same rule applies to molasses made after receiving sugarcane stalks. If molasses is made from strained sugarcane juice received in the morning and is prepared by a layperson or a novice, it is allowable with food in the morning; from noon onwards, it is allowable for seven days only without food. If prepared by oneself, it is allowable in the morning only without food. Molasses made from strained sugarcane juice received in the afternoon is allowable for seven days only without food. Preparation from juice taken by oneself (not offered) follows the same rule as mentioned. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is said, "Molasses made from burnt sugarcane or crushed sugarcane is allowable only in the morning." However, in the Mahāpaccariya, the question is raised, "Is molasses cooked with the pulp in this way allowable or not?" and it is stated, "There is no such thing as sugarcane molasses being unallowable in the afternoon." That statement is very appropriate. Molasses made from Madhuka flowers with cold water is allowable with food in the morning; from noon onwards, it is allowable for seven days only without food. After seven days, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred according to the number of items. Molasses made from Madhuka flowers with milk added is yāvakālika (temporary). Sugar crystals (khaṇḍasakkharā) are allowable because they are prepared by removing and cleaning the milk scum.

Madhuka flowers, whether fresh or dry, are allowable in the morning. If they are roasted and pounded, whether mixed with sesame etc. or unmixed, they are allowable. However, if those Madhuka flowers are taken and mixed to make liquor, they are not allowable from the moment the fermentation starter is added. The molasses of all yāvakālika fruits such as bananas, dates, mangoes, breadfruits, and tamarinds is only yāvakālika. Molasses made from ripe chilies is yāvajīvika (lifelong). Regarding the five medicines such as clarified butter which are allowable for seven days as mentioned, because they are permitted under the name of 'medicine' (bhesajja) by the Buddha saying, "Monks, I allow five medicines," whether they perform a medicinal function or not, and even if they are capable of serving as nutriment, they may be consumed as desired on the day they are received in the morning. From noon onwards, if there is a reason, they should be consumed for seven days as mentioned. If seven days are exceeded, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred according to the Bhesajja training rule. Even if it is only the size of a mustard seed, or even if it is just a single lick with the tongue after taking it with a finger, it must be forfeited and the offense confessed. If that medicine is received back after being forfeited, it must not be swallowed, nor used for bodily application...
107: They should be used in the manner already mentioned. They must not be smeared on the body or on a sore on the body. Robes, walking sticks, sandals, foot-rests, potsherds, couches, stools, and so forth, which have been smeared with those medicines past seven days, must also not be used. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya: "The parts of doors and window-shutters that are grasped by the hand must also not be smeared." However, it is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā: "Doors and window-shutters may be smeared by mixing the dye (or syrup) with [the expired] butter, oil, etc." It is allowable to use them for lamps or for black pigment (ink). Another monk, however, may use it for bodily application, but it must not be swallowed. Based on the statement, "There is no offense if one undertakes it within seven days" (Pārājika 625), if one undertakes butter, oil, or ghee within seven days as head-oil or massage-oil, honey for smearing a sore, or molasses for smearing the monastery, there is no offense, and it does not become a Nissaggiya. If one wishes to pour oil that has been undertaken into a vessel containing oil that has not been undertaken: if the hole in the vessel is small and the oil, as it enters, is overwhelmed by the old oil, it must be undertaken again. If the mouth of the vessel is wide and a large amount of oil enters quickly and overwhelms the old oil, there is no need to undertake it again. This is because that old oil simply follows the status of the oil that was undertaken. In this way, the pouring of non-undertaken oil into a vessel containing undertaken oil should also be understood. If one gives medicine past seven days to a novice after relinquishing it, it is allowable to use that medicine when given back by the novice as his own property. If that novice, whether after preparing it or without preparing it, gives it to the monk for use as nasal treatment, he should take it and perform the nasal treatment. If the novice is ignorant and does not know how to give it, another monk should ask, "Novice, do you have any oil?" If he replies, "Yes, Bhante, I have," the monk should say, "Bring it, we shall make medicine for the Elder." Speaking in this way is also allowable. If the property of two monks is accepted by one monk and has not yet been divided, there is no offense for both even after seven days. However, it is not allowable to use it. If the monk who accepted it says to the other monk, "Friend, it is allowable to use this oil for seven days," and that monk does not use it, who incurs an offense? No one. Why? Because the monk who accepted it has relinquished it, and the other monk has not yet accepted it. Among these four Kālikas, only these two—Yāvakālika and Yāmakālika—are subject to being "stored indoors" (antovuṭṭha) and "stored up" (sannidhi). As for Sattāhakālika and Yāvajīvika, it is allowable to keep them in an unallowable hut (akappiyakuṭi), and storage...
108:
...does not occur. Yāvakālika, however, brings the other three Kālikas—Yāmakālika and so forth—whose flavors are mixed with it, into its own nature. Yāmakālika also brings the other two—Sattāhakālika and so forth—into its own nature. Sattāhakālika also brings Yāvajīvika mixed with it into its own nature. Therefore, the other three Kālikas mixed in flavor with Yāvakālika accepted on that day are allowable only during the pre-noon period of that day. The other two Kālikas mixed with Yāmakālika accepted on that day are allowable until dawn. Yāvajīvika mixed with Sattāhakālika accepted on that day, whether the Yāvajīvika was accepted on that day or previously, is allowable for seven days. If mixed with Sattāhakālika that has been accepted for two days, it is allowable for six days; if mixed with that accepted for three days, five days... and if mixed with Sattāhakālika accepted for seven days, it should be understood as allowable only for that day. In this context, offenses should be understood according to the training rules on eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana), storage (sannidhi), and medicines (bhesajja) due to exceeding the noon, dawn, and seven-day limits.

If the four Kālikas, even if accepted together, do not have their flavors mixed, they are allowable for use according to their respective time limits. If mango juice or similar drinks are accepted together with a whole coconut without even removing the husk, it is allowable to use that drink even at the wrong time after removing the coconut. If a lump of butter is placed on top of cold milk rice and offered, it is allowable to remove the butter that is not mixed with the milk rice and use it for seven days. The same rule applies to hard honey, molasses, and so forth. If alms-food is offered decorated with nutmeg, mace, and so forth, these should be removed, washed, and may be used for life. The same rule applies to fresh ginger and so forth put into congee, or licorice and so forth put into oil and so forth. Thus, whatever Kālika has its flavor unmixed, even if accepted together, it is allowable to use it according to its respective time limit after washing it until it is pure or after scraping it. If the flavor is mixed and blended, it is not allowable.

## Thus ends the Discussion on the Determination of the Kālikas
## in the Compendium of the Vinaya-Determinations Exempt from the Pali (Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha).
109:
## 19. Kappiyabhūmivinicchayakathā
Regarding the matika term "Kappiyā catubhūmiyo," according to the words from the Mahāvagga Pāḷi, "Monks, I allow four types of allowable grounds (kappiyabhūmi): ussāvanantikā, gonisādikā, gahapati, and sammuti," these four types of allowable grounds should be understood.

Among those four, the ussāvanantikā-kuṭi should first be established in this way: For a monastery built by burying the base of walls or on top of pillars, the stones supporting the pillars underneath are considered as part of the ground itself. Many monks should surround the first pillar to be set or the first wall-base to be laid, and while uttering the words, "We make an allowable hut (kappiyakuṭi), we make an allowable hut," as laypeople lift and set the pillar, the monks should set the pillar or the wall-base either by touching it or by lifting it themselves.

In the Kurundī and Mahāpaccarī Commentaries, however, it is stated that it should be set while saying, "Kappiyakuṭi, kappiyakuṭi." In the Andhaka Commentary, it is said, "I designate this allowable hut for the Saṅgha."
