Even if those specific words are not said, there is no fault if it is done according to the method stated in the Commentaries. The general characteristic in this matter of ussāvanantikā is that "it is proper for the setting of the pillar and the conclusion of the spoken words to be simultaneous." If the pillar is set before the words are finished, or if the words are finished before the pillar is set, the allowable hut is not properly made. For this very reason, it is stated in the Mahāpaccarī, "It should be said by many monks surrounding it; among those monks, the conclusion of the words of at least one monk and the setting of the pillar will surely occur simultaneously."

In huts made of bricks, stones, or clay, whether a foundation is laid below or not, from the point where they wish the wall to rise, they should take the very first brick, stone, or lump of clay and establish the allowable hut according to the method already mentioned. Bricks and such are not proper below the first bricks laid in the wall, but pillars rise upwards, therefore they are proper. In the Andhaka Commentary, it is stated, "When made with pillars, four pillars at the four corners should be designated; in a hut made of bricks and such, two or three bricks at the four corners should be designated." However, even if it is not done in that way, there is no fault; only what is stated in the Commentaries is the standard.

There are two types of gonisādikā: ārāma-gonisādikā and vihāra-gonisādikā. Among these two, where neither the monastery grounds (ārāma) nor the dwellings (senāsana) are enclosed, this is called ārāma-gonisādikā. Where the dwellings...
110:
...all or some of the dwellings are enclosed, but the monastery grounds (ārāma) are not enclosed, this is called vihāra-gonisādikā. Thus, in both cases, the unenclosed state of the monastery grounds is the standard. It is stated in the Kurundī and Mahāpaccarī that "even if the monastery grounds are half-enclosed or mostly enclosed, they are still called enclosed." In this case, it is proper to obtain an allowable hut (kappiyakuṭi).

Gahapati refers to when laypeople, having built a dwelling, request, "We donate this as an allowable hut; please use it." Such a dwelling is called gahapati. Even if they say, "We donate this to make an allowable hut," it is also proper. In the Andhaka Commentary, it is stated, "Excluding the monk, if the receiving, storing, and keeping inside from the hands of the other four types of co-religionists (sahadhammika) or any devas or humans are their own property, it is proper for the monk. Therefore, their houses or the allowable huts donated by them are called gahapati." Furthermore, it is stated, "Excluding the dwellings of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, a nunnery, the house of monastery attendants (ārāmika), the house of titthiyas (heretics), or even the mansions of devas, nagas, or brahmas can be an allowable hut." This is well-said. This is because a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha or to a monk cannot be called a gahapati-kuṭi.

Sammuti refers to a dwelling designated by proclaiming it through a formal act consisting of a motion and a proclamation (ñattidutiya-kammavācā). And in this way, monks, it should be designated. A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should designate the dwelling named so-and-so as an allowable ground (kappiyabhūmi). This is the motion.

Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. The Saṅgha designates the dwelling named so-and-so as an allowable ground. If the designation of the dwelling named so-and-so as an allowable ground is pleasing to the venerable ones, let them be silent. If it is not pleasing to anyone, he should speak.

The dwelling named so-and-so has been designated by the Saṅgha as an allowable ground. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus I record it."

Even if it is done by making it known through a formal act of announcement (apalokana-kamma) without reciting the kammavācā, it is still considered designated (sammata).
111:
(Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā, 295) All the āmisa (edible food) present in these four types of kappiyabhūmi (allowable grounds) mentioned above does not fall under the category of antovuttha (stored indoors). The kappiyakuṭis (allowable huts) were permitted for monks and nuns for the purpose of being free from the offenses of antovuttha and antopakka (cooked indoors). However, āmisa—whether belonging to the Saṅgha, an individual, or a monk or nun—that is kept for even one night in a house on akappiyabhūmi (unallowable ground) where it is possible to sleep together, is called antovuttha. Āmisa cooked in such a place is also called antopakka. It is not allowable to consume such āmisa. However, sattāhakālika (seven-day medicine) and yāvajīvika (life-long medicine) are allowable.

The decision in this matter is as follows: If a novice brings āmisa such as rice belonging to a monk, keeps it in a kappiyakuṭi, and then cooks and offers it the next day, it is not antovuttha. In such cooking, if any item like ghee kept in an akappiyakuṭi is added and offered, it is called mukhasannidhi (stored in the mouth/personal possession). In the Mahāpaccarī, however, it is stated as "it becomes antovuttha." In both cases, the difference is merely in name. If a monk cooks and eats ghee kept in an akappiyakuṭi together with yāvajīvika leaves, it is allowable if it is not mixed with āmisa within seven days. If it is eaten mixed with āmisa, it becomes both antovuttha and sāmaṃpakka (self-cooked). In this manner, all types of mixing should be understood. It is not allowable for a monk to cook any āmisa himself. Even if basil leaves, fresh ginger, or salt are added to hot gruel, it is not allowable to stir that gruel. However, it is allowable to stir it with the intention of "I will cool the gruel." If one receives alms-food with raw rice on top, it is not allowable to cover it. If laypeople cover it and offer it, it is allowable. It is allowable to cover it with the intention "so that the food does not get cold." In the case of milk, buttermilk, and the like, it is allowable to add fuel to the fire once they have boiled, because re-cooking is permitted.

When do these kappiyakuṭis lose their status (become ruined)? First, the ussāvanantika huts are made by burying them above the pillars or at the base of the walls. Such a hut is said to lose its status when all the pillars and all the wall bases are removed. However, if the pillars or wall bases are replaced, it remains established in that place as long as it stands. Even if all the pillars are replaced, it does not yet lose its status. In a hut made of bricks and the like, it is said to lose its status when the bricks, stones, or lumps of clay placed for the wall above the brickwork are destroyed. As for the bricks with which it was determined (adhiṭṭhāna), even if those bricks are removed, if it still stands on other bricks, it does not yet lose its status.
112:
The kappiyabhūmi known as gonisādika (ox-lying ground) loses its status when it is enclosed by walls and the like. It is then allowable to re-establish a kappiyakuṭi (allowable hut) in that monastery. However, if the walls and such are broken in various places and cows enter through those gaps, it becomes a kappiyakuṭi again. As for the other two types of huts, if the entire roof is destroyed, leaving only the rafters, they lose their status. If even one pakkhapāsaka-ring (rafter-ring) remains above the rafters, it preserves the status (of kappiyabhūmi).

In a place where these four types of kappiyabhūmi do not exist, what should be done? It should be given to an anupasampanna (unordained person) to make it their property, and then consumed. Regarding such consumption, there is this story: It is said that Karavikatiissa Thera, a leader among those who knew the Vinaya, went to the presence of Mahāsīva Thera. Seeing a jar of ghee by the light of a lamp, he asked, "Venerable Sir, what is this?" The Thera replied, "Friend, this jar of ghee was brought from the village to be eaten with ghee on days when the food is coarse." Then Tissa Thera said to him, "Venerable Sir, it is not allowable." The Thera had it placed in the front of the house the next day. Tissa Thera came again another day, saw the jar, and after asking as before, said, "Venerable Sir, it is not allowable to keep it in a place sufficient for sleeping together." The Thera had it taken outside and placed there the next day, and thieves took it away. He said to Tissa Thera, who arrived another day, "Friend, because you said 'it is not allowable,' that jar was placed outside and has been taken by thieves." Then Tissa Thera said to him, "Venerable Sir, should it not have been given to an anupasampanna? For if it is given to an anupasampanna and made their property, it is allowable to consume it."

## Thus ends the Discussion on the Decision of Kappiyabhūmi
## in the Pālimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-saṅgaha.
## 20. Discussion on the Decision of Receiving (Paṭiggahena)
Receiving snacks and the like (paṭiggahena) means the receiving of any snack or food that is to be swallowed. Regarding such receiving, there is this decision: Receiving is valid only when it is endowed with five factors: it must be only as much as a man of average strength can lift, it must be within a forearm's length (hatthapāsa), the act of offering (abhihāra) must be evident, whether a deity or...
113:
Whether it be a human or an animal, if they give by means of the body, or by means of something connected to the body, or by releasing (dropping) it, and the monk receives it with his body or with something connected to his body; in this way, being endowed with the five factors, the formal acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa) is valid.

In that formal acceptance, the forearm's length (hatthapāsa) should be understood according to the positions of those standing, sitting, or lying down: if the monk is sitting, it is measured from the back edge of the seat; if standing, from the edge of the heels; if lying down, from the back edge of whichever side he is lying on. Excluding the donor's extended hand (for giving), whether the donor is sitting, standing, or lying down, the distance of two and a half cubits measured from the nearest part of the donor's body is called the forearm's length (hatthapāsa).

If one of the two, the donor or the recipient, is in the air and the other is on the ground, the forearm's length should be measured from the head of the one on the ground to the nearest part of the body of the one in the air, excluding the extended hand (for giving or receiving). If one is in a well and the other is on the bank of the well, or if one is in a tree and the other is on the ground, the forearm's length should be measured in the same manner as mentioned. If, while staying within such a forearm's length, a bird gives a flower or a fruit holding it with its beak, or an elephant gives it holding it with its trunk, the formal acceptance is valid. If a monk sitting on the back of an elephant that is seven and a half cubits high receives what is given by that elephant with its trunk, it is certainly allowable. If one gives with any part of the body such as the hands, or even with a toe at the very least, it is called 'given by the body.' The same method applies to formal acceptance. Indeed, if one receives with any part of the body, it is called 'received by the body.' If nasal medicine is given and a sick monk receives it with the nostrils or with the mouth, in this case, the attention (ābhoga) or the intention to receive is the measure.

If one gives with any utensil such as a ladle, it is called 'given by something connected to the body.' The same method applies to formal acceptance. If one receives with a bowl, a cup, or similar objects connected to the body, it is called 'received by something connected to the body.' Releasing (dropping) an object from the body or from something connected to the body so that it falls onto the monk's body or onto something connected to his body while he is within the forearm's length is also called 'given by the effort of releasing.' If a person carries many pots of rice and curry on their head and comes to the monks and stands there saying, 'Please take,' the act of presentation (abhihāra) is not yet evident. Therefore, it should not be accepted. If they incline even slightly, the monk should extend his hand and receive even a part of the pot. By this much, all those pots are formally accepted. After such formal acceptance, it is allowable to have them set down or opened and to take whatever one wishes. In the case of a single vessel like a rice-basket, there is no need for further explanation.
114:
If a person carrying many pots of rice and curry on their head comes to the monks and says while standing, 'Please take,' the act of presentation (abhihāra) is not yet evident; therefore, it should not be accepted. If they incline even slightly, the monk should extend his hand and receive even a part of the bottom-most pot. By this much, all the pots are formally accepted. From that point on, it is allowable to have them set down or opened and to take whatever one wishes. In the case of a single vessel like a rice-basket and such, there is no need for further explanation.

Even a person carrying rice with a shoulder pole (kāja), if they incline the pole and give, it is allowable. If there is a bamboo pole of thirty cubits with a pot of molasses tied to one end and a pot of ghee tied to the other end, if that pot is formally accepted, all are considered formally accepted. If one says, 'Please take the juice,' referring to sugarcane juice that is still flowing from the sugarcane press, it should not be accepted because the act of presentation (abhihāra) is not evident. However, if one removes the dregs, scoops it up with the hand, and gives it, it is allowable. Suppose many bowls are placed on a bed, a stool, a mat, a trough, or a plank. If the donor is within the reach (hatthapāsa) of a monk standing in a certain place, and that monk, with the intention of formal acceptance, stands, sits, or lies down while touching the bed or such with a finger, then everything given into those bowls is formally accepted. If he intends to formally accept and climbs onto the bed or such and sits, it is also allowable.

On the ground, if the bowls are placed touching one another, and the monk sits touching whichever bowl with a finger or a needle, then whatever is given into those respective bowls is formally accepted. The statement that formal acceptance is not valid for a bowl placed on a certain large mat or carpet should be understood as referring to exceeding the forearm's length (hatthapāsa). If it is within the forearm's length, formal acceptance is valid in any place except for those 'grown in that place' (tatthajāta). Regarding things 'grown in that place,' such as a lotus leaf or a Butea monosperma (palāsa) leaf, it is not valid. This is because they do not count as being connected to the body. Just as with things 'grown in that place,' formal acceptance is not valid on a bed or such tied to a tree stump, or on an immovable plank or a stone slab. This is because they also fall into the category of things 'grown in that place.' Formal acceptance is not valid on small leaves like tamarind leaves spread on the ground. This is because those leaves are not capable of supporting the weight (of the offering). However, it is valid on large leaves like lotus leaves. If a person standing beyond the forearm's length gives with a long-handled ladle, they should be told, 'Come closer and give.' If, without hearing or without heeding those words, they simply pour it into the bowl, it must be formally accepted again. The same method applies when someone stands at a distance and throws a lump of rice as an offering.
115:
If, while taking the bowl out of the bowl-bag, there are particles of dye powder on the bowl, it should be washed if water is available. If there is no water, the dye powder should be wiped off, and after having it formally offered, one should go for alms. If dust falls into the bowl of a monk wandering for alms, the food should be taken after having it formally offered. For a monk who takes it without having it formally offered, there is a Vinaya dukkaṭa offense. However, for one who wipes away that dust, has it formally offered again, and then eats, there is no offense. If, despite saying "Please give it after it has been formally offered," they offer the alms food either because they did not hear or out of disrespect, there is no Vinaya dukkaṭa offense. One should have it formally offered again and take other alms food. If a strong wind causes dust to fall from here and there, and it is not possible to take the alms food, it is allowable to take it by making a mental resolution with a pure mind, "I will give this to an unordained person (anupasampanna)."

After wandering for alms in this way, having gone to the monastery or the refectory and given that food to an unordained person, it is allowable to eat it after receiving it back as a gift from that person or through the intimacy of trust (vissāsa). If, during the alms round, someone gives a monk a bowl with dust on it, that monk should be told, "Receive this bowl formally and then either collect alms or eat." He should act accordingly. If dust is floating on top, one should pour off the sour gruel (kañjika) and eat the rest. If it has entered inside, it must be formally offered. If no unordained person is present, one should take it to where an unordained person is, without letting go of it from the hand, and have it formally offered. It is allowable to eat dry food after removing the dust that fell on it. If the dust is very fine, it should be removed along with the top layer of food, or it should be eaten after being formally offered. If drops of water splashing from the vessels of those stirring congee (yāgu) or soup (sūpa) placed in front fall into the bowl, the bowl must be formally offered.

If drops from the ladles of those bringing and giving food with a ladle fall into the bowl first, they are considered "well-fallen"; because they were brought [for the purpose of giving], there is no fault. Even if soot or ash falls from a small vessel while pouring food with it, there is no fault because it was brought [for giving]. If food being given to a nearby monk jumps from his bowl and falls into another monk's bowl, it is considered "well-fallen." This is because it has already been formally offered. If, while splitting branches of a jajjhari tree etc. to give to a monk, drops from the branch fall into another monk's bowl, that bowl must be formally offered. Regarding the monk over whose bowl they are splitting [the branch], if [drops] fall into his bowl, there is no fault because they were brought with the intention to give. When they give a bowl filled with milk rice (pāyāsa), if one is unable to hold it from the bottom because it is hot, it is allowable to hold it by the rim.
116:
If even in that way [holding by the rim] one is unable, it should be held with a bowl-stand (ādhāraka). If a monk sitting in the refectory holding his bowl falls asleep and does not know that [food] is being brought or given, it is not formally offered. However, if he sits with attention (mindfulness), it is allowable. Even if that monk lets go of the bowl-stand with his hand and supports it with his foot while sleeping, it is still allowable. But for a monk who is awake to receive it by treading on the bowl-stand with his foot, it is a disrespectful reception; therefore, it should not be done.

Some teachers say, "Receiving with a bowl-stand in this way is called receiving with something connected to what is connected to the body (kāyapaṭibaddha-paṭibaddha); therefore, it is not allowable." That is merely a statement; in terms of meaning, all this is indeed connected to the body. This method is also shown in [the section on] bodily contact (kāyasaṃsaggā). It is allowable for a monk to personally take and eat food that falls while being given to him.

In this regard, there is this scriptural passage:
"Monks, I allow you to personally take and eat what falls while being given. Monks, that object has been relinquished by the donors" (Cūḷavagga, 273).

This scriptural passage also has a meaning that must be inferred (neyyattha). Therefore, the intention here should be understood thus: if, while being given, it slips from the donor's hand and falls on clean ground, or on a lotus leaf, or on cloth, a mat, a rug, etc., it is allowable to personally take and eat that food. However, if it falls on ground with dust, one should eat it after wiping away the dust, or washing it, or having it formally offered [again]. If it rolls and reaches the presence of another monk, it is allowable to have that monk bring it. If he says to that monk, "You yourself eat it," it is allowable for that monk to eat it; however, without being urged, he should not take it. In the Kurundī, it is said, "Even if not urged, it is allowable to take it with the thought, 'I will give it to the other monk.'"

Why is it not allowable for another monk to pick up that fallen food? Because the Blessed One did not allow it. By saying "Take it personally and eat," the Blessed One allowed the monk to whom it was being given when it fell to take and use it even if it had not been formally offered. By the words "Monks, that object has been relinquished by the donors," the state of it being another's property is shown here; therefore, it is not allowable for another monk to personally take and eat it. However, it is allowable by the urging of the intended monk—this is said to be the intention here. And because this...
117:
Because things that have not been formally accepted are permitted, food or snacks that have been covered with something and kept without being touched by hand as they were placed may be consumed even on the second day. There is no offense due to the reason of sannidhi (storing up). However, it should be consumed only after being formally accepted. It is permitted to take and consume it by oneself only on the day it was offered; if it exceeds that day, it is not permitted—this is the intended meaning here.

Now, the abbhohārika (negligible) method is stated. When monks eat almsfood, their teeth wear down, their nails wear down, and the color of the alms-bowl wears down; all such wearing down is abbhohārika. When splitting sugarcane and the like with a small knife, if rust appears, that rust is called 'newly arisen'; it must be formally accepted before eating. If the knife is washed and used for splitting, and no rust appears but only the smell of iron is present, that smell is abbhohārika. The same rule applies when splitting with a knife that is always carried. This is because that knife is not carried for the purpose of consumption. When grinding or pounding medicinal roots and the like, the grindstone, the muller, the mortar, and the pestle wear down. If a carried knife is heated and put into buttermilk or milk for medicinal purposes, and a blue-green tint (nīlikā) appears, the decision is the same as mentioned for the knife. However, monks should not put it into raw buttermilk and the like themselves; if they do, they are not free from the fault of 'self-cooking' (sāmaṃpākata). When it is raining, if dirty water from the body or the robes of a monk wandering for alms falls into the alms-bowl, it must be formally accepted. The same rule applies if it falls while eating under a tree and the like. However, if it rains for seven days and the water is pure, or if it falls from the open sky, it is allowable.

A monk giving rice to a sāmaṇera (novice) should give it without touching the rice already in the novice's bowl, or he should formally accept the novice's bowl. For a monk who touches the rice in a bowl that has not yet been formally accepted and then takes rice back into his own bowl, it becomes uggahitaka (invalidated offering). If, with the intention to give, he says, 'Novice, bring the bowl, take the rice,' and the novice refuses saying, 'It is enough,' or even if he says again, 'I have relinquished this for you,' and the novice says, 'I have no need for this,' even if he relinquishes it a hundred times, as long as it remains in his own hand, it remains formally accepted. However, if he says 'Take it' without any lingering concern for the bowl placed on a stand, it must be formally accepted again. If he places the bowl on a stand with lingering concern and tells the novice, 'Take a cake or rice from here,' and the novice washes his hands and takes it even a hundred times without touching the rice in his own bowl, it is not necessary to formally accept it again. If he touches the rice in his own bowl and takes from that bowl, it becomes mixed with the novice's rice and must be formally accepted again. Some teachers say that if the rice being taken breaks and falls into that monk's bowl, it must be formally accepted again. This statement should be understood in the context where it is specified as 'Take one handful of rice, take one cake, take this much portion of this palm-sugar ball.' If he says 'Take a cake or rice from the bowl' without such specification, then whatever cake or rice is in the novice's bowl...
118:
If the sāmaṇera puts the rice into his own bowl, it is not necessary to formally accept it again. If he touches the rice in his own bowl and then takes from it, it becomes mixed with the novice's property and must be formally accepted again. Some teachers say, 'Even while being taken, if it breaks and falls there, it must be formally accepted again.' This should be understood only in the case where it is specified as 'Take one handful of rice, take one cake, take this much portion of this molasses ball.' Here, however, there is no such specification; therefore, whatever falls into the novice's bowl alone loses its formal acceptance. As for what is in the hand, as long as the novice does not stop saying 'It is enough' or the monk does not prevent him, it still belongs to the monk; therefore, it does not lose its formal acceptance.

If one wishes to put rice for someone into a pot where rice gruel (yāgu) is being cooked, whether for oneself or for other monks, one should say, 'Novice, place your hand over the pot,' and put it into that novice's hand. The rice that falls from the novice's hand into the pot does not make the pot akappiya (unallowable) on the next day because it has been relinquished by the novice. If it is put in without doing this, the pot must be used only after making it free from food remnants (āmisa), just as one washes an alms-bowl.

When donors leave after placing a pot of rice gruel, and a young novice is unable to formally accept that pot, the monk should bring his alms-bowl near. If the novice places the neck of the pot on the rim of the bowl and tilts it, the rice gruel that reaches the bowl is considered formally accepted. Or, if the monk places his hand on the ground and the novice rolls it and places it on the monk's hand, it is allowable. The same method applies to baskets of cakes, baskets of rice, loads of sugarcane, and the like. If two or three novices give a load that is suitable for formal acceptance, or if one strong novice lifts it and two or three monks receive it, it is allowable. If a jar of oil or a jar of molasses is hung on the leg of a bed (mañca) or a chair (pīṭha), the monk is allowed to sit on that bed or chair, and it does not become uggahitaka (invalidated offering).

If two jars of oil are hung on a wall peg (nāgadantaka) or a hook, and the upper one has been formally accepted while the lower one has not, it is allowable to take the upper one. If the lower one has been formally accepted and the upper one has not, for a monk who takes the upper one and then the lower one, the upper one becomes uggahitaka. If there is an unaccepted oil dish under the bed, and a monk sweeping touches it with the broom, it does not become uggahitaka. If he takes an unaccepted one intending to take an accepted one, and puts it back upon realizing it, it does not become uggahitaka. If he realizes it only after taking it outside, he should not leave it outside but should carry it and put it back in the same place; there is no fault.
119:
If it was opened previously, it should not be closed. It should be left exactly as it was before. If it was placed outside, it should not be touched again.

The growth of mold on offered oil and the like, or the turning of ginger and the like into powder, is considered to arise from that oil and ginger themselves. There is no need to have that mold or powder offered again. A novice (sāmaṇera) who has climbed a palmyra or coconut tree and lowers a bunch of fruit with a rope, saying "Take it" while still remaining above, should not be accepted from. If another person standing on the ground takes the rope loop and lifts it up to give it, it is allowable.

If a large branch with fruit is made allowable (kappiya) and then accepted, the fruits are also considered accepted. It is allowable to consume them as one pleases. If someone standing inside a fence cuts sugarcane or a wood-apple and gives it, it is allowable if it is within a forearm's length (hatthapāsa). It is allowable for one who takes what has fallen out due to striking the fence posts. No fault is shown in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) regarding what falls out due to being struck. However, we consider that "it is as if it fell by itself from the place where it was struck." This is appropriate even if it falls further away, like goods that roll outside from a customs house (suṅka-ghāta). Suppose they give it by passing it over a fence or a wall. If the wall is not thick or wide, and the hatthapāsa of those standing inside and outside the wall reaches, it is allowable. Even if it reaches up to a hundred cubits high, it is allowable to take it.

A monk (bhikkhu) carries a sick novice on his shoulder. While traveling, the novice sees various fruits, picks them, and gives them while still sitting on the shoulder; this is allowable. If another person carries a monk and gives to the monk sitting on the shoulder, it is also allowable. A monk carries a branch with fruit for the sake of shade; if the thought to eat those fruits arises, it is allowable to eat them after having them offered. If a branch is made allowable and accepted for the purpose of driving away flies, and if the desire to eat arises, the initial acceptance is sufficient, and there is no fault for the one who eats. A monk travels after placing items worthy of acceptance on a layperson's vehicle. If the vehicle gets stuck in the mud and a young novice takes the wheel and lifts it, it is allowable; it is not called "taken" (uggahita). If placed on a boat and one rows the boat with an oar or pulls it by hand, it is allowable. The same method applies to a raft. It is allowable to place items in a large jar or a basin, have a non-ordained person (anupasampanna) hold it, and then cross by holding that person's arm. Even if such a jar is not available, it is allowable to have a non-ordained person hold the items and then cross by holding that person's arm.
120:
Lay devotees (upāsakas) give travel provisions of rice to traveling monks. If the novices (sāmaṇeras) take the monks' rice and are unable to take their own rice, the monks carry the novices' rice. When the rice carried by the novices is exhausted, they cook rice gruel (yāgu) with the remaining rice [carried by the monks], arrange all the monks' bowls in order, and pour the gruel. A wise novice takes his own bowl and gives it to the elder (thera), gives the elder's bowl to the second elder, and thus exchanges all the bowls. By doing so, all the monks eat what belongs to the novice, and it is allowable.

If the novice is not wise and starts to drink the gruel in his own bowl himself, it is also allowable for the elders to request and drink it, saying, "Friend, give your gruel to me." If done this way, all the monks eat only the gruel that is the property of the novice; they do not incur a fault due to the reason of "taken" (uggahita) or "storing up" (sannidhi). In this matter, no distinction is seen between monks who carry oil etc. for their parents, or branches etc. for the sake of cool shade, and these monks who eat by exchanging bowls with the novice. Therefore, the underlying reason should be investigated.

If a novice wishes to cook rice but is unable to wash and rinse the rice, the monk may accept the rice and the pot, wash and rinse the rice, and place the pot on the stove. He should not light the fire. When it is cooked, he should open it and check if it is done. If it is not yet well-cooked, it is not allowable to close it for the purpose of cooking; however, it is allowable to close it to prevent dust or ash from falling in. When it is cooked, it is allowable to take it down and eat it; there is no need for a second offering. If the novice is capable of cooking but has no free time as he wishes to go somewhere, the monk should accept the pot with rice and water, place it on the stove, and say, "Light the fire and then go." After that, it is allowable to do everything according to the previous method. If a monk places a clean pot to cook gruel and heats the water, it is allowable. If the novice throws the rice into the hot water, from that point on, the monk should not attend to the fire. It is allowable to accept and drink the cooked gruel. While a novice is cooking gruel, if a monk with restless hands (hatthakukkucca) playfully touches the pot, touches the lid, or breaks and strikes the rising foam, it is not allowable for that monk alone to drink that gruel; it is called "improperly handled" (durupaciṇṇa). If he takes a ladle or a spoon...
121:
If one stirs [the pot] using a ladle or a blowpipe without lifting it, it is not allowable for anyone. It is both self-cooked and improperly handled. If one lifts it, the formal acceptance is also broken.

113. A monk, having wandered for alms, has placed his bowl on a bowl-stand. In that situation, if another frivolous monk, while playing, touches the bowl or touches the bowl-lid, the alms-food obtained from that bowl is not allowable for that [frivolous] monk alone. If he lifts and places the bowl [elsewhere], it is not allowable for anyone. If one shakes the fruits of a tree by holding a branch or a vine, the fruit obtained from that branch or vine is not allowable for that person alone, and he incurs an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) due to improper handling. "However, it is allowable to lean against a fruiting tree or to lift a bowl caught in that tree; it does not constitute improper handling," so it is stated in the Mahāpaccariya commentary. Seeing mangoes or yellow myrobalan etc., fallen in the forest, it is allowable to bring and give them, thinking, "I will give these to the novice." Even upon seeing lion's leftovers (sīhavighāsa) etc., it is allowable to bring and give them, whether having formally accepted them or not, thinking, "I will give these to the novice." If, however, one is able to purify the thought [of ownership], it is allowable even to eat what is received from those novices; the fault does not apply either on account of accepting raw meat or on account of the breaking of formal acceptance. For a monk who is traveling while carrying oil etc., for the sake of his parents, if an illness arises on the way, it is allowable for him to take and consume whatever item he desires from that oil etc. If it was already formally accepted at the beginning, there is no need for formal acceptance again. If he brings and gives rice for the sake of his parents, and those parents prepare gruel (yāgu) etc., from that very rice and give it to the monk, it is allowable. There is no fault on account of storing up (sannidhi) or on account of the breaking of formal acceptance.

14. If a monk heats water while keeping it covered, it is allowable to use it without formal acceptance until it is exhausted. If, however, ash falls into this boiling water pot, it must be formally accepted. For a monk cooking oil by holding a vessel with long tongs, if ash falls in, he should cook it without letting go with his hand, and after taking it down, it must be formally accepted. If charcoal or firewood have been formally accepted and kept, the original formal acceptance is sufficient. If a monk is eating sugarcane and a novice says, "Please give some to me too," and the novice takes it after being told, "Cut and take from this [sugarcane] I am eating," there is no need for formal acceptance again for the remaining sugarcane. The same method applies to one eating a lump of jaggery. Indeed, the portion remaining after being cut and taken from the specified place remains as that which has not been relinquished from formal acceptance. When a monk is distributing jaggery, if he formally accepts it and makes portions, and monks or novices come and take each portion in a single grasp, the portion remaining after being taken is considered as already formally accepted. If
122:
If a frivolous novice repeatedly takes [portions] and puts them back, the portion remaining after being taken by that novice is considered as not formally accepted.

A monk, having formally accepted a medicinal cigar (dhūmavaṭṭi), inhales the smoke; even if the mouth and throat become as if smeared with red arsenic (manosilā), it is allowable to consume 'morning-period' (yāvakālika) food; there is no fault in the mixing of 'morning-period' food with 'life-long' (yāvajīvika) medicine. For a monk baking a bowl or boiling dye, if smoke enters through the ear-holes or nostrils, or if he smells a flower or a fruit due to illness, it is allowable because it is considered negligible (abbohārika). If a food-burp reaches the palate and goes back inside, it is allowable as it is not within the scope [of an offence]; however, for a monk who swallows a food-burp that has reached the mouth during the 'wrong time' (vikāla), it is an offence. If the taste of food particles stuck between the teeth enters [the throat], it is indeed an offence. If the food particle is subtle and the taste is not apparent, it falls under the category of negligible (abbohārika). Near noon, in a place where there is no water, after eating, one should cough and spit out two or three lumps of phlegm, and then go to a place with water to wash the mouth. If sprouts emerge from ginger etc., that have been formally accepted and kept, there is no need for formal acceptance again. If there is no salt, it is allowable to use sea water for the purpose of salt. Salt water that has been formally accepted and kept remains allowable if it turns into salt, or if salt turns into water, or if liquid turns into jaggery, or if jaggery turns into liquid; the original formal acceptance is sufficient.

Hailstones (himakaraka) are of the same nature as water. If one clears water using a clearing nut (kataka) that is carried [as a personal item], that water is abbohārika and is allowable to be used with food. Water cleared with wood-apples (kapittha) etc., which are of the nature of food, is allowable only in the morning. If water is abundant in ponds etc., it is allowable. If, however, [food particles] are stuck on the mouth or hands, it is not allowable; it must be formally accepted before use. In the plowed areas of fields, if water is abundant, it must be formally accepted. If that water flows and enters ravines etc., and fills a river, it is allowable. Places like the Kakudha pond have water covered with flowers fallen from trees. If the taste of the flowers is not apparent, there is no need for formal acceptance. If the water is little and the taste is apparent, it must be formally accepted. The same method applies to water covered with dark leaves in mountain ravines etc.

If flowers with pollen or flowers with sap in their stems are placed in a drinking water jar, it must be formally accepted, or the flowers must be formally accepted before being put in. If trumpet flowers (pāṭali) and jasmine (mallikā) are put in and only the scent remains, that water is negligible (abbohārika).
123:
On the second day also, it is allowable together with almsfood. If a novice takes drinking water and pours the remainder back into the same water pot from which a monk had set aside flower-scented water, it should be formally received [again] and consumed. In ponds with lotuses and such, it is allowable to take water by pushing aside the pollen covering the water with a pot. Regarding a tooth-stick that has been made allowable and formally received, if one wishes to drink its juice, the initial formal reception is sufficient. However, a tooth-stick that has not been formally received must be formally received. Even if the juice enters [the throat] of a monk who is unaware, it is still an offense. This is because this training rule is acittaka (not depending on intention).

Among the elements (mahābhūta) produced in the body, what is allowable and what is not? First, milk is allowable. Whether it is the milk of an animal whose flesh is allowable or the milk of an animal whose flesh is not allowable, there is no offense for a monk who drinks it. Tears, saliva, snot, urine, feces, phlegm, tooth-tartar, eye-wax, ear-wax, and salt produced on the body—all these are allowable. If saliva and so on from this body fall from their place into the bowl or onto the hand, they must all be formally received. As long as they are attached to the body, they are considered already received. If sweat runs down the fingers of a monk eating hot milk-rice and stays in the food, or if it falls from the hand or the rim of the bowl into the bowl while on almsround, there is no need for formal reception in such cases. Regarding bones well-burnt by fire, there is no such thing as an unallowable bone. However, unburnt bone is not allowable. Even human bone, if well-burnt and powdered, is allowable to be added to electuaries. The four great foul things (mahāvikaṭa) are allowable to be taken and consumed by oneself if no lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) is present. In this context, a difficult person or an incapable lay attendant is also counted as being in the category of 'not present'. If there is no ash, one should burn dry wood to obtain ash. If there is no dry wood, it is allowable even to cut green wood from a tree to make it. These four great foul things are called kālodissa (referring to a specific time). They are allowable only at the moment of a snake bite.

## Thus, in the Pālimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha,
## The Discussion on the Decision Regarding Formal Reception is finished.
## 21. Pavāraṇāvinicchayakathā
Refusal-pavāraṇā means the rejection of food brought forward by a donor while one is eating any of the five kinds of staple food. This pavāraṇā does not occur merely by rejection, but only when it is endowed with five factors.
124:
In that pavāraṇā (refusal of food), there are these five factors: eating, the food, standing within the donor's hatthapāsa, the offering, and the rejection of what is offered.

Among those five, eating (asana) means the meal is not yet finished; it means the person is currently eating. Food (bhojana) means food sufficient for pavāraṇā; it means any of the five staple foods, such as cooked rice, which is to be rejected. Standing within the donor's hatthapāsa means standing within a distance of two and a half cubits while holding food sufficient for pavāraṇā. Offering (abhihāra) means the donor standing within the hatthapāsa makes an offering with the body. Rejection of what is offered means rejecting the food thus offered either by body or by speech. Thus, pavāraṇā occurs by means of these five factors. This has also been said:

"Upāli, pavāraṇā is known by five modes: eating is known, food is known, standing within the hatthapāsa, offering, and rejection is known."

## In this regard, there is this decision.

Among the terms beginning with asana, first, that which one eats and that food which is offered by one standing within the hatthapāsa and is rejected, should be understood as any one of these five: cooked rice (odana), gruel (kummāsa), parched corn flour (sattu), fish (maccha), or meat (maṃsa).

Among those five, cooked rice (odana) is that produced from the grains of the seven kinds of cereals: sāli rice, vīhi rice, barley (yava), wheat (godhuma), millet (kaṅgu), varaka, and kudrūsaka. Among those seven, sāli refers to all types of sāli rice, including at least nīvāra rice. Vīhi refers to all types of vīhi rice. There is no distinction between barley and wheat. Kaṅgu refers to all types of millet, distinguished as white, red, and black. Varaka refers to all types of white varaka, including at least varakacoraka. Kudrūsaka refers to all types of grass-grains, including black kudrūsaka and varieties like sāmāka grass-grain.

Among these, nīvāra, varaka, and coraka are also called grain-substitutes (dhanyānuloma). Whether they are grains or grain-substitutes, if one takes the grains of these seven kinds and cooks them with the intention 'I will cook rice,' or 'I will cook rice-gruel (yāgu),' or 'I will cook one of the sour gruels, milk-rice, etc.,' if, while eating it hot or cold, a distinct portion (limit) is visible at each place where it is taken, it falls under the category of cooked rice (odana) and produces pavāraṇā. If a distinct portion is not visible, it falls under the category of rice-gruel (yāgu) and does not produce pavāraṇā.
125:
Whether it be milk-rice mixed with leaves, fruits, and shoots, or sour gruel, if it is very hot just after being removed from the stove and can be drunk by tilting the bowl, it does not cause pavāraṇā if no distinct boundary (mark) is visible at the place where it is held by the hand. However, if it becomes thick and shows a boundary when it cools down after the steam has gone, it causes pavāraṇā again; the previous thin state does not protect (prevent it). If one adds curd, buttermilk, etc., and many leaves, fruits, and shoots, and even a handful of rice is added, it causes pavāraṇā if a boundary is evident at the time of eating. In an invitation without gruel, they say, "We will offer gruel," and pour water, rice-scum, milk, etc., into the rice and offer it, saying, "Please take the gruel." Even if that gruel is thin, it certainly causes pavāraṇā. If it is offered after being cooked in boiling water, etc., it falls under the category of gruel. Even when it falls under the category of gruel, if fish or meat is added to that gruel or any other soup, and if even a piece of fish or meat or a tendon as small as a mustard seed is evident, it causes pavāraṇā. However, pure liquid gruel (rasa-yāgu) does not cause it.

Setting aside the aforementioned types of rice, rice made from other things such as bamboo seeds, or rice made from tubers, roots, or fruits, does not cause pavāraṇā; if this is so for such rice, what need is there to mention thick gruel? However, if fish or meat is added to this bamboo rice, etc., it causes pavāraṇā. In the Mahāpaccari Commentary, it is said, "Rice made for the purpose of pupphi (parched rice) also causes pavāraṇā." Rice made for the purpose of pupphi refers to rice that has been boiled (steamed) by putting it into boiling water for the sake of pupphi snacks. If those rice grains are dried in the sun and eaten, it is allowable; they fall neither into the category of sattu (flour-lumps) nor into the category of rice. Rice made again from those grains certainly causes pavāraṇā. If those grains are cooked in ghee, oil, etc., or made into cakes, they do not cause pavāraṇā. Neither flattened rice (puthuka) nor flour-lumps or rice made from those grains cause pavāraṇā.

Kummāsa refers to kummāsa made from barley. However, kummāsa made from other beans, such as green gram, does not cause pavāraṇā.

Sattu refers to sattu made from sālī rice, paddy, or barley. Millet, maize, and kudrūsaka, etc., are also roasted, lightly pounded to remove the husks, and then pounded again thoroughly to make powder. Even if that powder is moist and forms a single mass, it still falls under the category of sattu. The rice of paddy that has been well-roasted is pounded and offered; that powder also falls under the category of sattu. However, rice from paddy that is only moderately roasted, or rice from hollow paddy, or roasted rice grains themselves, do not cause pavāraṇā.
126:
The powder of those rice grains causes pavāraṇā. The bran of well-roasted paddy also causes pavāraṇā. However, the bran of paddy that is only moderately roasted or sun-dried does not cause pavāraṇā. Parched rice (lāja), or rice and flour-lumps made from such parched rice, do not cause pavāraṇā. Roasted flour or any kind of pure snack does not cause pavāraṇā. However, a snack filled with fish or meat, or a flour-ball (sattu-modaka) made with molasses, causes pavāraṇā. Fish and meat are clearly [causes of pavāraṇā].

This is the distinction: If two pieces of fish or two pieces of meat, which are only the size of a grain of rice from gruel, are offered in a single vessel or in various vessels to a monk who is drinking gruel, and if that monk, not yet having eaten those pieces of fish or meat, refuses any other food that is sufficient to cause pavāraṇā, it does not cause pavāraṇā. If he has eaten one of them and one remains in his hand or bowl, and he then refuses other food, it causes pavāraṇā. If he has eaten both and there is not even a mustard-seed-sized remnant in his mouth, it does not cause pavāraṇā even if he refuses other food. If he refuses allowable meat (kappiya-maṃsa) while eating allowable meat, it causes pavāraṇā. If he refuses unallowable meat (akappiya-maṃsa) while eating allowable meat, it does not cause pavāraṇā. Why? Because it is not a valid object (avatthu) for pavāraṇā.

The reason is that pavāraṇā occurs only for one who refuses food that is allowable for a monk to eat. Whether he refuses this unallowable meat knowing it is unallowable, or refuses it without knowing, it is still considered refusing something that stands in the position of being refused; therefore, it does not cause pavāraṇā. However, if a monk who is eating unallowable meat refuses allowable meat, it causes pavāraṇā. Why? Because it is a valid object (vatthu) for pavāraṇā. The reason is that the object refused by that monk is a valid object for pavāraṇā. Although the food being eaten stands in the position of being refused, it does not lose its nature as meat while being eaten; therefore, it causes pavāraṇā. If he refuses unallowable meat while eating unallowable meat, it does not cause pavāraṇā, just as in the previous case. If he refuses any of the five types of allowable food while eating either allowable or unallowable meat, it causes pavāraṇā.

If he refuses unallowable food obtained through wrong livelihood (anesanā), which is censured by the Blessed One—such as that arising from corrupting families, practicing medicine, proclaiming superhuman states, or consenting to gold and silver—it does not cause pavāraṇā. If he refuses allowable food while eating either allowable or unallowable food, it causes pavāraṇā. If he refuses unallowable food, it does not cause pavāraṇā; the reason should be understood in all cases by the method already stated.

Thus, regarding the terms such as "asana" (eating), the monk who eats a certain food and refuses another food brought within arm's reach (hatthapāsa) incurs pavāraṇā. Having spoken of that pavāraṇā, this decision (vinicchaya) is now given for the purpose of knowing how it is incurred. In the phrase "asanaṃ bhojanaṃ," first, if a monk has swallowed (is swallowing) even a single mouthful of rice...
127:
If that monk has any one of the five types of food in any of these three places—the bowl, the mouth, or the hand—and refuses another of the five types of food, pavāraṇā (refusal of further food) is incurred. If there is no food in any of those places and only the smell of food is apparent, even if he refuses, pavāraṇā is not incurred. If there is no food in the mouth or hand, but it is only in the bowl, yet he does not wish to eat in that place but wishes to enter the monastery to eat, or wishes to give it to another, and refuses food in the meantime, pavāraṇā is not incurred. Why? Because the state of being in the process of eating has been interrupted. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya: "For a monk who, wishing to go and eat at another place, swallows the food in his mouth and takes the rest with him, and refuses other food on the way, pavāraṇā is not incurred." As it is with the bowl, so it should be understood with the hand. Even if there is food in the mouth, if he does not wish to swallow it and refuses other food at that moment, pavāraṇā is not incurred. This is because the characteristic stated in one instance should be understood in all cases. Furthermore, this method is also shown in the Kurundiya. It is stated there: "If one has swallowed the food in the mouth, and wishes to give the food in the hand to a consumer of leftovers, or wishes to give the food in the bowl to a monk, and refuses at that moment, pavāraṇā is not incurred."

Regarding the phrase "standing within a forearm's length (hatthapāsa)": if the monk is sitting, it is measured from the back edge of the seat; if he is standing, from the back of the heels; if he is lying down, from the back edge of the side on which he is lying. Excluding the extended hand of the donor who is sitting, standing, or lying down, the distance of two and a half cubits measured from the nearest part of the donor's body is to be known as the "hatthapāsa." Only when one refuses an offering brought while standing within that hatthapāsa does pavāraṇā occur; not beyond that.

"Brings (abhiharati)" means standing within the hatthapāsa and presenting the food closely so that it can be received. However, even if a monk is sitting nearby, if he merely says "Take the food" without lifting or moving the bowl that is placed in his hand, on his lap, or on a bowl-rest, and the other refuses, pavāraṇā is not incurred. The same rule applies if a food basket is brought and placed on the ground in front and one says "Take it." Only when one refuses while the donor says "Take it" while slightly lifting or tilting the basket does pavāraṇā occur. If an Elder sitting in the Elder's seat sends a bowl to a junior (dahara) monk sitting far away and says "Take rice from here," but the person who took the bowl stands silently and the junior monk refuses saying "Enough for me," pavāraṇā is not incurred. Why? Because the Elder is far away.
128:
Because the messenger is far away and does not [formally] offer the food, pavāraṇā is not incurred. However, if the monk who has taken the food and arrived says, "Take this food," pavāraṇā is incurred for the one who refuses it. In the case of serving food, if a donor serves a monk while holding a rice basket in one hand and a ladle in the other, and if another person comes and says, "I will hold the basket, you give the rice," and merely holds the basket while the server himself is still supporting it, that food is considered "brought" (abhihaṭa). Therefore, pavāraṇā is incurred for the monk who refuses the food being held with the intention to give. If the server only touches the basket with his hand and the other person is the one actually supporting it, pavāraṇā is not incurred for the one who refuses the food held with the intention to give. However, it does occur in the case of food scooped up with the ladle. This is because the act of bringing with the ladle is indeed the server's act of bringing. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya: "Even if both support it equally, the one who refuses still incurs pavāraṇā." If, while food is being offered to a nearby monk, another monk covers his bowl with his hand, pavāraṇā is not incurred. Why? Because he refused what was being brought for another.

Regarding the phrase "refusal is evident (paṭikkhepo paññāyati)": pavāraṇā is not incurred for one who refuses by words alone when the food has not yet been brought. However, it should be understood that pavāraṇā is incurred for one who refuses food that has been brought by body, in any manner, whether by body or by speech. Therein, refusal by body means moving a finger, a hand, a fly-whisk, or the corner of the robe; or making a sign with the eyebrows, or looking as if angry. Refusal by speech means saying "Enough," "I do not accept," "Do not pour," or "Go away." Thus, if one refuses in any manner by body or by speech, pavāraṇā is incurred.

If a monk, fearing that pavāraṇā will occur while food is being brought, moves his hand away and says to the person repeatedly pouring rice into the bowl, "Pour! Pour! Press it down and fill it up!", how would it be? Mahāsuma Thera said, "Because it is said for the purpose of not having it poured, pavāraṇā is incurred." However, Mahāpaduma Thera said, "Could there ever be pavāraṇā for one who says 'Pour, fill it up'?" and thus stated, "pavāraṇā is not incurred."

When another monk sees a monk bringing food and says, "What is it, friend? Will you take anything more from this? I shall give you something," Mahāsuma Thera said, "Because this is said so that the other will not come [again], pavāraṇā is incurred." Mahāpaduma Thera said, "Could there ever be pavāraṇā for one who says 'Will you take more?'" and thus stated, "pavāraṇā is not incurred."
129:
Mahāpaduma Thera, however, said, "Is there any pavāraṇā for someone who says 'Will you take?'" and stated, "It does not constitute pavāraṇā."

If someone brings broth with meat and says, "Take the broth," there is no pavāraṇā for one who hears this and refuses. If it is said, "Fish broth" or "Meat broth," pavāraṇā occurs for the one who refuses. Even if it is said, "Take this [food]," it indeed occurs. If meat is separated and one says, "Take the meat broth," and if there is even a piece of meat as small as a mustard seed in that broth, pavāraṇā occurs for the one who refuses it. However, if it is strained so that no meat pieces remain, Abhaya Thera said, "It is allowable [not to count as pavāraṇā]."

Regarding the case where the Mahāthera said to someone asking with meat broth, "Wait a moment," and then said, "Friend, bring the tray," how does it stand? First, Mahāsumma Thera said, "The movement of the one who brought it has ceased; therefore, pavāraṇā is incurred." Mahāpaduma Thera, however, said, "Where is this person going? What kind of going is his going? Indeed, would there be pavāraṇā for someone who is still taking [food]?" and stated, "Pavāraṇā is not incurred."

Meat is cooked mixed with bamboo shoots, jackfruit, and so on. If one takes that meat and says, "Take the bamboo shoot curry," or "Take the jackfruit dish," even if said this way, pavāraṇā is not incurred. Why? Because it is spoken by the name of an object that does not qualify for pavāraṇā. If, however, they say, "Fish curry" or "Meat curry," or if they say, "Take this [food]," pavāraṇā is incurred. This is because it is a meat mixture (māṃsakarambaka). Even if one who wishes to give that meat mixture says, "Take the mixture (karambaka)," it is allowable and pavāraṇā is not incurred. But if it is called "meat mixture" or "this," pavāraṇā is incurred. This method is the same for all mixtures of fish and meat.

In the Mahāpaccari, it is stated: "If a monk who is eating at an invitation refuses meat that is brought, thinking, 'This is meat specifically prepared for me (udissakata),' he indeed becomes pavārita." The discussion regarding mixtures is well-stated in the Kurundī. It is said there: A monk on alms round brings gruel mixed with rice and says, "Take the gruel"; pavāraṇā is not incurred. If it is said, "Take the rice," pavāraṇā is incurred. Why? Because the object with which he was asked exists. The meaning here is: If one says, "Take that which is mixed with gruel," and in that mixture, if the gruel is more or equal in quantity, pavāraṇā is not incurred. If the gruel is less and the rice is more, pavāraṇā is incurred. Since this statement is mentioned in all commentaries, it cannot be rejected, though the reason for it is difficult to see. If one says, "Take that which is mixed with rice," whether the rice is more, equal, or less...
130:
...it indeed constitutes pavāraṇā. When one says, "Take the mixture," without specifying rice or gruel, if the rice is more or equal in quantity, it constitutes pavāraṇā; if it is less, it does not. This should not be equated with mixed meat (karambaka). For a mixture (karambaka) can be mixed with meat or not mixed with meat. Therefore, when "mixture" is said, there is no pavāraṇā. But this case is specifically rice-mixed. In this case, pavāraṇā occurs according to the method already mentioned. In rice with much broth, if one separates the broth; in rice with much milk, the milk; and in milk-rice with much ghee, the ghee, and gives it saying, "Take [this]," there is no pavāraṇā for the monk who refuses that gift.

A monk who becomes pavārita while walking is allowed to eat only while walking. If he reaches mud or water and stands, he must have the food made "leftover" (atirikta) [by another monk to continue eating]. If there is a river full of water in the middle of the journey, he should eat while walking around the bushes on the riverbank. If there is a boat or a bridge, he should eat while walking to and fro even after boarding them; the posture of walking must not be interrupted. A monk who becomes pavārita while sitting in a vehicle, on the back of an elephant or horse, or even [metaphorically] on the moon or sun disk, must eat only while sitting as long as those vehicles are moving, until noon. A monk who becomes pavārita while standing must eat only while standing; one who becomes pavārita while sitting must eat only while sitting. If he wishes to eat by changing those respective postures, he must have the food made "leftover" (atirikta). A monk who becomes pavārita while squatting must eat only while squatting. A straw stool or some kind of seat should be placed under him. A monk who becomes pavārita while sitting on a stool is allowed to eat while turning to the four directions without moving the seat. A monk who becomes pavārita while sitting on a couch (mañca) is not allowed to move from here to there. However, if they carry him along with the couch to another place, it is allowable. A monk who becomes pavārita while lying down must eat only while lying down. When turning on his side, he must not exceed the place of the side on which he was lying.

What should a monk who has become pavārita do? If he eats by changing the posture in which he became pavārita to another posture, he must have the food made "leftover" (atirikta) before eating. If he chews or eats any hard food or soft food categorized as "temporary" (yāvakālika) that is not made "leftover" (anatirikta), he incurs a pācittiya offense for every swallow.

In that context, "not made leftover" (anatirikta) means not leftover, not remaining. Because that food is not made through the seven Vinaya procedures such as being made allowable (kappiya-kata), or because it is not in excess for one who is ill, it is stated in the Padabhājana as follows:
131:
'Anati-ritta' (not formally made allowable) is that which is made in an unallowable way, made without being formally received, made without being uttered, made outside the hatthapāsa (forearm's length), made by one who has not yet eaten, made by one who has finished eating and refused further food but has risen from the seat, or made without saying 'All this is enough,' and is not the leftover of a sick person. This is called anati-ritta (Pācittiya Pāḷi, 239).

Among those terms, 'akappiya-kata' (made in an unallowable way) refers to fruits, tubers, or roots in the bowl that have not been made allowable by the five types of samaṇa-kappiya (making allowable for recluses), as well as unallowable meat or unallowable food. Even if such unallowable food is made ati-ritta (formally made allowable) by saying 'All this is enough,' it should be understood only as 'akappiya-kata.' 'Appaṭiggahita-kata' (made without being received) refers to making food ati-ritta as per the previous method without the monk having formally received it. 'Anuccārita-kata' (made without being uttered) refers to the monk who comes to make the food allowable but does not slightly lift or tilt the bowl. 'Ahatthapāse kata' (made outside the hatthapāsa) refers to making it while standing outside the hatthapāsa of the monk who comes to make it allowable. 'Abhuttāvinā kata' (made by one who has not eaten) refers to the monk who makes it ati-ritta by saying 'All this is enough' before he has eaten enough food to constitute pavāraṇā (refusal of further food). 'Made by one who has finished eating and refused further food but has risen from the seat' is clear in its meaning. 'Made without saying "All this is enough"' means not uttering these words. Thus, food that is not made ati-ritta through these seven Vinaya procedures and food that is not the leftover of a sick person—both are to be understood as 'anati-ritta.'

Ati-ritta (formally made allowable/leftover), however, should be understood by the opposite method of anati-ritta. Therefore, it is stated in the Padabhājana: 'Ati-ritta is that which is made in an allowable way, made after being formally received, made by lifting the bowl, made within the hatthapāsa, made after having eaten, made by one who has finished eating and refused further food without rising from the seat, made by saying "All this is enough," and is the leftover of a sick person. This is called ati-ritta' (Pācittiya Pāḷi, 239).

Furthermore, 'made after having eaten' here should be understood as being made even after eating a single grain of rice or a piece of meat from the bowl of a fellow monk sitting nearby. Regarding the phrase 'without rising from the seat'...
132:
To avoid confusion, this decision should be understood: Suppose two monks are eating early in the morning and have refused further food (pavārita). One of those monks must remain in his original seat. The other monk, having brought either a regular meal (niccabhatta) or food distributed by tickets (salākabhatta), pours half of the food into the bowl of the monk who is waiting, washes his hands, and then has the remaining food made allowable (kappiya) by that monk before eating it. Why? Because the food sticking to his hand is unallowable. However, if the monk who sat first takes the food from the other's bowl with his own hand, there is no need to wash the hands. If, while a monk is eating food made allowable in this way, some curry or snacks are poured into his bowl, the monk who first made it allowable cannot do so again. Another monk who has not yet done so must do it. Also, the newly added food that has not been made allowable must be made so. 'The one who has not yet done so' means another monk, or the monk who did not do it first, must do it. 'The thing that has not yet been made allowable' means even the monk who first made it allowable must make the newly added, unmade food allowable. However, it cannot be done again in the first vessel. If it were done in that vessel, it would be done along with the food already made allowable. Therefore, the meaning is that it is proper to do it in another vessel. Food made in this way is proper for that monk to eat along with the food made allowable first.

When making food allowable, it should be done not only in a bowl but also in a cup or a basket, placed in front, in a tilted vessel. If a hundred monks have refused further food (pavārita), that food is proper for all of them to eat; it is also proper for those who have not refused further food. However, it is not proper for the monk who made it allowable. If a monk who has refused further food enters for alms and is seated at an auspicious invitation where he must eat, he must have the food made ati-ritta before eating. If there is no other monk there, he should send the bowl to the dining hall or the monastery to have it made so. The monk making it allowable, however, must not do so while the food is in the hands of an unordained person (anupasampanna). If there is an unskilled monk in the dining hall, he should go himself, have it made allowable, and then bring it back to eat.

Regarding 'gilānātiritta' (leftover of a sick person), it does not only mean the actual leftovers of a sick person; rather, any food brought for a sick person with the thought, 'He will eat it today or whenever he wishes,' all such food should be understood as gilānātiritta. For a monk who consumes yāmakālika, sattāhakālika, or yāvajīvika as nutriment without the ati-ritta procedure, a dukkaṭa offence is incurred for every swallow. If yāmakālika and others are mixed with solid food (āmisa), a pācittiya offence is incurred for the monk who receives and carries it, whether for the sake of nutriment or as a medicinal support for the sick. There is no offence for a monk who consumes yāmakālika and others not mixed with solid food when there is a reason. Thus ends the Discussion on the Decision of Pavāraṇā in the Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha.

## 22. Pabbajjā-vinicchaya-kathā

In this term 'Pabbajjā' (Ordination), the meaning should be understood as follows: A monk who ordains a clansman who desires monkhood should exclude those persons prohibited in the Pāḷi text with words such as, 'Monks, one afflicted by the five diseases should not be ordained,' and ordain only those worthy of monkhood. In that Pāḷi text, this is the decision: leprosy (kuṭṭha), boils (gaṇḍa), eczema (kilāsa), consumption (soso), and epilepsy (apamāra).
133:
For a monk who consumes any yāmakālika, sattāhakālika, or yāvajīvika item that has not undergone the atiritta-vinaya procedure for the purpose of nutriment, there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every swallow. However, if yāmakālika and such are mixed with food (āmisa), there is only an offence of expiation (pācittiya) for the monk who, having accepted it, swallows it whether for the purpose of nutriment or for a purpose other than nutriment (as a medicinal requisite for the sick). But for yāmakālika and such that are not mixed with food, there is no offence for a monk who consumes them when there is a valid reason.

## In the Pālimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-saṅgaha,
## the Decision on the Invitation (Pavāraṇāvinicchaya-kathā) is thus concluded.
## 22. Decision on Ordination (Pabbajjāvinicchaya-kathā)

Regarding the term 'Pabbajjā' (Ordination): A monk who ordains a clansman seeking ordination should exclude those persons prohibited in the Pali Canon by such statements as, 'Monks, one afflicted with the five diseases should not be ordained' (Mahāvagga 89), and should only ordain a person who is free from the faults of ordination (pabbajjā-dosa). In that Pali text, this is the decision: One afflicted with these five diseases—leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, and epilepsy—should not be ordained. If one ordains such a person, one falls into an offence of wrong-doing because the Blessed One said, 'Whoever should ordain [such a person], there is an offence of wrong-doing.'

Among those five diseases, 'kuṭṭha' (leprosy) refers to red leprosy, black leprosy, or any variety such as eczema, ringworm, or scabs; all these are said to be types of leprosy. Even if that leprosy is only the size of a fingernail, if it is in a spreading stage, the person should not be ordained. However, if a fingernail-sized patch of leprosy is in a non-spreading stage and is in a place normally covered by the undergarment or robe, it is allowable to ordain him. In the Kurundī, it is stated: 'If it is on the face, or on the backs of the hands or feet, even if it is in a non-spreading stage and is smaller than a fingernail, it is certainly not allowable.' Even when ordaining after having the person treated, he should be ordained only when the skin has returned to its natural color; it is not allowable to ordain one whose body is covered with powder like the back of a monitor lizard.

'Gaṇḍa' (boils) refers to a fatty cyst or any other boil. If any boil, even the size of a jujube seed, is in a spreading stage, the person should not be ordained. However, if it is the size of a jujube seed in a non-spreading stage and is in a covered place, it is allowable; if it is in an uncovered place like the face, even if it is in a non-spreading stage, it is not allowable. Even when ordaining after treatment, the person should be ordained only after making the skin of the body natural. Boils called uṇṇigaṇḍā...
134:
...hang down from various parts of the body like cow teats or like the tips of the forefingers. These pendulous boils (warts) are also classified as boils (gaṇḍa); if they are present, it is not allowable to ordain the person. In childhood, there are 'milk-spots' (khīrapīḷakā, measles), and in youth, there are 'rough spots' (kharapīḷakā, acne) on the face; these disappear in old age. These acne spots are not counted as boils (gaṇḍa). Even if these are present, it is allowable to ordain the person. There are also other spots on the body called kharapīḷakā (warts), and others called padumakaṇṇikā (lotus-seed spots/freckles). Others called sāsapabījakā (mustard-seed spots) are only the size of mustard seeds but spread over the whole body. All these are varieties of leprosy (kuṭṭha). If these are present, the person should not be ordained.

'Kilāsa' (eczema) is a type of leprosy that neither breaks nor oozes, and has the color of a white lotus petal. Because of this disease, the body becomes mottled like that of a cow. Regarding this leprosy, the decision should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. 'Sosa' (consumption) refers to the disease of wasting (tuberculosis). If that disease is present, the person should not be ordained. 'Apamāra' (epilepsy) refers to madness caused by bile or madness caused by spirits (yakkhas). Among these two, one possessed by a spirit with a past grudge is difficult to cure. Even if there is only a slight degree of epilepsy, the person should not be ordained.

'Monks, a royal servant (rājabhaṭa) should not be ordained; whoever should ordain one, there is an offence of wrong-doing' (Mahāvagga 90). According to this statement, a royal servant should also not be ordained. In this context, whether he is a minister, a high official, a royal attendant, or someone who has or has not attained a certain rank, anyone who receives food and wages (salary) from the king is counted as a royal servant (rājabhaṭa). Such a person should not be ordained. However, it is allowable to ordain the sons, grandsons, or brothers of that royal servant who do not receive food and wages from the king. If a person has returned the permanent allowance or the monthly or yearly allowance received from the king back to the king, or if he has had his son or brother accept that position in his place and has informed the king, 'I am no longer Your Majesty's servant,' or if he has completed the task for which the wages were taken, or if he has been permitted by the king saying, 'Go and ordain,' it is allowable to ordain that person.

A 'flag-bound thief' (dhajabandha cora) should also not be ordained. This is because it was said, 'Monks, a flag-bound thief should not be ordained; whoever should ordain one, there is an offence of wrong-doing' (Mahāvagga 91). In that text, he is called a 'flag-bound thief' because he wanders as if a flag were tied to him; it means he is someone well-known in the world like Mūladeva and others. Therefore, any thief who wanders about destroying villages, plundering travelers, or breaking into houses in the city, etc.
135:
If it is well-known that "such and such a person did this or that deed," that person should not be ordained. However, a prince who, desiring the kingship, commits acts such as destroying villages and so on, should be ordained. This is because kings are usually pleased when such a prince is ordained; if, however, the kings are not pleased, he should not be ordained. If a thief who was previously well-known among the public later abandons his thieving ways and undertakes the five precepts, and if the people are aware of this, he should be ordained. Small-time thieves such as mango thieves, or even housebreakers and the like, who commit theft secretly and are not later identified as "this person did this deed," may also be ordained.

However, a thief who has broken out of jail should not be ordained, as it is said: "Monks, a thief who has broken out of jail should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" (Mahāvagga 92). In that context, 'kāra' refers to a prison. Here, whether it be binding with shackles, binding with iron chains, binding with ropes, confinement to a village, confinement to a market town, confinement to a city, being under guard, confinement to a district, or confinement to an island—whoever escapes while the guards are not looking by breaking, cutting, loosening, or opening any of these bonds is reckoned as a 'jailbreaker' (kārabhedaka). Therefore, such a jailbreaker should not be ordained even if he has broken his island-confinement and reached another island. One who is not a thief but was bound by royal officials because he did not perform manual labor, with the thought "thus he will work for us without running away," may be ordained even if he breaks his bond and escapes. One who has taken a lease on a village, market town, or port, etc., and is imprisoned for failing to fulfill the payment, should not be ordained if he escapes and comes [to the Saṅgha]. One who earns a living through farming and the like, but is bound by someone due to slanderous reports that "this man has found a hidden treasure," should not be ordained in that same place; however, if he escapes and goes elsewhere, he may be ordained in the place he reaches.

Based on the words, "Monks, a proclaimed thief should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" (Mahāvagga 93), a proclaimed thief (likhitaka) should not be ordained. In that context, a 'proclaimed thief' refers to anyone who, after committing theft or another serious royal offense, has fled, and the king...
136:
...has caused a proclamation to be written on palm leaves or in books, stating: "Wherever such a person is seen, he is to be caught and killed there," or "His hands and feet, etc., are to be cut off," or "He is to be made to pay such and such a fine." This person is called a proclaimed thief (likhitaka). He should not be ordained.

A person who has been flogged as a punishment should also not be ordained. This is because of the words: "Monks, one who has been flogged as a punishment should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" (Mahāvagga 94). In this context, one who is beaten for not following orders or for not obeying prohibitions is not called 'one punished' (kata-daṇḍakamma). Only the person who, having taken and consumed something through a lease or other means, is unable to pay it back and is beaten with canes while being told, "Let this beating be your punishment," is called 'one who has been flogged as a punishment' (kasāhato kata-daṇḍakammo). Whether he was beaten with canes or with one of the short-jointed sticks, etc., he should not be ordained as long as the wounds are fresh; he should be ordained only after the wounds have returned to their normal state (healed).
