If he was released after being struck with knees, elbows, coconuts, stones, and so on, and if lumps and swellings are visible on his body, he should not be ordained; he should be ordained only when those lumps have subsided and he has become comfortable.

A person who has been branded as a punishment should not be ordained. This is because of the words: "Monks, one who has been branded as a punishment should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" (Mahāvagga 95). Here too, the status of being 'one punished' should be understood in the same way as the previous method. For one whose forehead, thighs, etc., have been branded with a hot iron, if he is a free man, he should not be ordained as long as the wounds are fresh. Even if his wounds are healed and the skin is uniform, if the brand is not visible, or if it is in a concealed place covered by the upper robe when the three circles (of the robes) are properly worn, it is allowable to ordain him. If it is in an unconcealed place, it is not allowable.

Based on the words, "Monks, a debtor should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" (Mahāvagga 96), a debtor should also not be ordained. In that context, a 'debtor' (iṇāyika) refers to one who has a debt taken by his parents or grandparents, or a debt taken by himself, or one who has to carry that debt because he was pawned by his parents to obtain some property. If relatives other than parents pawn a person to take something, that person is not called a debtor. This is because those relatives do not have the right to pawn him. Therefore, it is allowable to ordain such a person, but not the others. If the parents or relatives of that person say, "We will pay it; please ordain this person," and take the debt as their own responsibility, or if another person, seeing that person's perfection in virtue and conduct, says, "Please ordain this person; I will pay the debt," [then it is allowable].
137:
Whether a person has borrowed money himself, or has been pawned by his parents to obtain some wealth, such a person is one who carries the debt of others and is called a 'debtor' (iṇāyika). However, if relatives other than the parents pawn him to take something, he is not called a debtor. This is because those relatives have no authority to pawn him. Therefore, it is proper to ordain such a person; but it is not proper to ordain other types of debtors.

If the relatives, such as the parents of that person, say, "We will pay; please ordain him," and take the debt as their own responsibility, or if another person, seeing his accomplishment in conduct and virtue, says, "Please ordain him; I will pay the debt," then it is proper to ordain him. If there is no such person to pay, the monk should inform a supporter (dāyaka) of that kind, saying, "This being, who possesses special merit (sahetuko satto), is unable to ordain due to the encumbrance of debt." If that supporter takes responsibility, he should be ordained. If he himself possesses allowable property (kappiya-bhaṇḍa), he should be ordained with the intention, "I will pay the debt with this property."

If the relatives and others do not take responsibility, and he himself has no property, it is not proper to ordain him with the thought, "After ordaining, I will pay the debt by going on almsround." If one ordains him, one commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa). Even if he runs away, he must be brought back and given to the creditor. If he is not given back, the entire debt falls upon the neck (responsibility) of the monk. If one ordains him without knowing, there is no offense; however, if he is seen, he must be brought and shown to the creditors. If he is not seen, the responsibility does not fall upon the monk's neck.

If a debtor goes to another place and, even when questioned, says, "I do not owe anything to anyone," and thus receives ordination, and the creditor comes to that place while searching for him, and the young monk flees upon seeing the creditor, the creditor might approach the Elder and say, "Venerable sir, who ordained this young monk? He has fled after taking this much of my wealth." In that case, the Elder should say, "Lay follower, I ordained him because he said, 'I am free of debt.' What can I do now? Just look at my bowl and robes." Saying this is the appropriate conduct in that situation. If the person has fled, the responsibility does not fall on the Elder's neck.

If the creditor sees him in the presence of the Elder and says, "This is my debtor," the Elder should say, "You yourself should know your debtor." Even in saying this, the responsibility does not fall on his neck. If the creditor says, "He has become a monk now; where can he go?" the Elder should also say, "You yourself should know." Even so, if the person flees, the responsibility does not fall on the Elder.

If, however, the Elder says, "Where will this young monk go now? Let him stay right here," and then the person flees, the responsibility falls on the Elder's neck. If that young monk is one who possesses special merit and is accomplished in his duties, the Elder should say, "This young monk is such a person."
138:
If that young monk is accomplished in his duties, the Elder should say, "This young monk is such a person." If the creditor says, "Very well," and releases him, and the Elder takes responsibility to pay that debt, it is excellent; there is no offense. If the creditor says, "Give me half," it should be given. If later the monk becomes one who greatly pleases the teacher, even if the creditor says, "Give the whole debt," it should indeed be given. If that person is skilled in the study of the Pāḷi and Commentaries and is of great service to the monks, the debt should be paid even by seeking it through the duty of alms-gathering.

A slave also should not be ordained, because of the word: "Monks, a slave should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa)" (Mahāvagga 97). In that context, there are four kinds of slaves: one born in the house (antojāta), one bought with wealth (dhanakkīta), one brought as a captive (karamarānīta), and one who has gone into slavery of his own accord (sāmaṃ dāsabyaṃ upagata). Among these four, one who is the son of a female household slave and is a slave by birth is called 'born in the house' (antojāta). One who is bought by giving wealth, whether it be a son from parents or a slave from masters, and is designated as a slave, is called 'bought with wealth' (dhanakkīta). Both of these types of slaves should not be ordained. If one wishes to ordain them, they must be made non-slaves according to the customs of the respective regions before being ordained.

What is called a 'captive slave' (karamarānīta) refers to those who are captured and brought from another country, either by destroying that country or by enticement, who were previously free people. Or, within the country itself, the king orders a certain village that has committed a crime, saying, "Plunder it," and people are brought from there; in that case, all the men are slaves and all the women are female slaves. Such a captive slave should not be ordained if he is living with those who brought him, or is confined in a prison, or is guarded by men. However, if he has fled and gone elsewhere, he may be ordained in the place he reaches. If the king, being pleased, says, "Release the captive slaves," or if they are released from bondage by a general amnesty, they may indeed be ordained.

One who has 'gone into slavery of his own accord' (sāmaṃ dāsabyaṃ upagata) is one who, for the sake of livelihood or for the sake of protection, has entered into slavery himself, saying, "I am your slave." This is like the royal elephant-keepers, horse-keepers, cattle-keepers, buffalo-keepers, and so on. Such a slave should not be ordained. The sons of the king's concubines and harem women are like the sons of ministers; they too should not be ordained. Free women who are unrestrained may wander together with the harem women; it is proper to ordain the sons of those women. If they themselves are registered as "king's slaves," it is not proper. The slaves of groups of royal attendants and others should also not be ordained without their permission.
139:
In monasteries, kings often donate attendants known as monastery-slaves (ārāmika-dāsa). It is not proper to ordain them [without being freed]; it is only proper to ordain them after they have been made free (bhujissa). However, in the Mahāpaccarī, it is stated: "Domestic slaves or purchased slaves are brought and given to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha as monastery attendants; they are like those who have been freed by having fermented rice-water poured over their heads. It is proper to ordain them." But in the Kurundī, it is stated: "They are given using the allowable term 'We give a monastery attendant.' No matter what term is used, they should not be ordained [as they are not freed]." Poor people who become monastery attendants (kappiyakāraka) thinking, "We will live depending on the Saṅgha," may be ordained. If both parents of a person are slaves, or if only the mother is a slave and the father is not, it is not proper to ordain him. If, however, the mother is not a slave but only the father is, it is proper to ordain him. Relatives or supporters of a monk may donate a slave saying, "Please ordain this person; he will perform services (veyyāvacca) for you," or if a monk has his own slave, he should only be ordained after being made free. If owners donate a slave saying, "Please ordain this person; if he is happy [in the monkhood], he is no longer a slave. If he disrobes, he shall be our slave again," such a person is called a temporary slave (tāvakālika); it is stated in the Kurundī that it is not proper to ordain him. If he is an ownerless slave (nissāmika-dāsa), he should also only be ordained after being made free. If one ordains or confers higher ordination unknowingly and finds out later, one should only act to make him free.

To clarify this meaning, they tell this story: It is said that a certain high-born slave woman fled from Anurādhapura with a man and, while living in the Rohaṇa region, gave birth to a son. When that son was ordained and became a fully ordained monk, he was conscientious and scrupulous regarding the Vinaya. Then one day, he asked his mother, "Lay devotee, do you have no brother or sister? I see no relatives at all." She replied, "Dear son, I was a high-born slave in Anurādhapura; I fled with your father and live here." The virtuous monk, feeling a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) thinking, "My ordination is not pure," asked his mother for the name and clan of that family. He went to Anurādhapura and stood at the door of that family's house. Even when told, "Please pass on, Bhante," he did not move but remained standing. They came out and asked, "Why, Bhante?" He asked, "Do you have a runaway slave woman of such-and-such a name?" They replied, "We do, Bhante." He said, "I am her son. If you give me permission, I shall obtain the state of a monk. You are my masters." They were delighted and said, "Bhante, may your monkhood be pure," and having made him free, they supported him with the four requisites and had him reside in the Mahāvihāra monastery. While residing there depending on that family, the Elder attained the fruit of Arahantship. Thus it should be understood.
140:
(Those people) had him reside in the Mahāvihāra monastery and supported him with the four requisites. While residing there depending on that family, the Elder attained the fruit of Arahantship.

"Monks, one with a hand cut off should not be ordained. One with a foot cut off, one with both hands and feet cut off, one with an ear cut off, one with a nose cut off, one with both ear and nose cut off, one with a finger cut off, one with a thumb or big toe cut off, one with a severed tendon, one with webbed fingers, a hunchback, a dwarf, one with a goitre, one branded with a mark, one who has been scourged, one who is a branded criminal, one with elephantiasis, one with a bad disease, one who disgraces the assembly (extremely ugly), one-eyed, one with a crooked limb, a person with a club-foot, a paralytic, one with ruined posture, one disabled by old age, one who is blind, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is blind and mute, one who is blind and deaf, one who is mute and deaf, one who is blind, mute, and deaf should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain such a person, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" (Mahāvagga 119). Because of these words, those with hands cut off and so forth should not be ordained.

Among those, "one with a hand cut off" refers to a person whose one or both hands are cut off at the palm, the wrist, the elbow, or anywhere else. "One with a foot cut off" refers to a person whose one or both feet are cut off at the toes, the ankles, the shins, or anywhere else. "One with hands and feet cut off" refers to a person whose two, three, or all four limbs are cut off as described. "One with an ear cut off" refers to a person whose one or both ears are cut off at the base or the ear-flap. However, if a person's ear-lobe is cut but can be reattached, one should reattach the ear and then ordain him. "One with a nose cut off" refers to a person whose nose is cut off at the bridge (like a goat's foot), the tip, one nostril, or anywhere else. If a person's nose can be reattached, one should make him well and then ordain him. "One with both ear and nose cut off" should be understood as having both cut. "One with a finger cut off" refers to a person whose one or many fingers are cut off such that no trace of the nail is visible. If even a thread-like trace of the nail is visible, it is proper to ordain him. "One with a thumb or big toe cut off" refers to a person whose one or many of the four thumbs and big toes are cut off in the same manner as described for fingers. "One with a severed tendon" refers to a person whose major tendons called kaṇḍara are severed either at the front or the back. If even one of those is severed, such that he walks on his toes or on his heels and cannot plant his foot firmly on the ground, [he should not be ordained].
141:
One whose fingers are joined together like the wings of a bat is called a phaṇahatthaka. If one wishes to ordain such a person, one should cut and remove the skin between the fingers, treat the wound until it is healed, and only then grant ordination. One who has six fingers, if one wishes to ordain him, the extra finger should be cut off, the wound healed, and then ordination may be granted.

One who is hunchbacked because the chest, back, or sides are protruding is called a khujja. However, if the limbs are only slightly crooked, it is permissible to grant ordination. Only the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) has a body as straight as a Brahmā; among other beings, there is almost no one who is not somewhat 'hunched'.

A vāmana (dwarf) is one who is short in the shanks, short in the waist, or short in both. For one short in the shanks, the lower body from the waist down is short, while the upper body is full. For one short in the waist, the upper body from the waist up is short, while the lower body is full. For one short in both, both parts of the body are short. Because they are so short, they have bodies that are rounded like a ghost and resemble a large-bellied pot. These three types of vāmana should not be granted ordination.

One who has a lump in the throat like a pumpkin is called a galagaṇḍī. This is merely an example; if there is a tumor or lump anywhere on the body, ordination should not be granted. This decision should be understood according to the method stated in the Mahāvagga Pali: 'Monks, one afflicted with the five diseases should not be granted ordination.' The discussion regarding those branded with hot iron, those lashed with whips, and those with inscribed marks has already been mentioned below.

One who has swollen feet (elephantiasis) is called a sīpadī. If the feet are large, lumpy, rough, and hard, ordination should not be granted. However, if they have not yet become hard, and it is possible to reduce the swelling by wrapping them in coarse cloth, placing them in a pit of warm water, or filling it with warm water or warm sand until the veins become visible and the shanks become like oil tubes, then after such treatment, ordination may be granted. If the swelling recurs, the same procedure must be followed even when granting higher ordination (upasampadā).

One who is constantly suffering from a disease such as hemorrhoids, fistula, bile disorders, phlegm disorders, cough, or consumption, or who has an incurable, loathsome, and disagreeable disease, is called a pāparogī (one with a foul disease). Such a person should not be granted ordination.

One who spoils the assembly by his own deformity is called a parisadūsaka. This includes one who is excessively tall, such that the heads of others only reach his navel; or one who is excessively short, like the form of a ghost with both parts of the body short; or one who is excessively dark, like a burnt stump in a field...
142:
...like a burnt stump in a field; or one who is excessively pale, like the color of copper rubbed with curd or buttermilk; or one who is excessively thin, with little flesh and blood, appearing as only skin and bones; or one who is excessively obese, with much flesh and a large belly, resembling a ghost; or one with an excessively large head, as if carrying a basket on the head; or one with a head excessively small and disproportionate to the body; or one with a head like a cluster of palmyra fruits; or one with a pointed head that tapers upwards; or one with a tube-shaped head like a large bamboo joint; or one with a head tilted to any of the four sides; or one with a scarred head, or a foul head; or one with hair growing in patches like crops in a field eaten by insects; or one with a hairless head; or one with coarse, thick hair like palmyra fibers; or one with naturally white hair; or one with hair that is always red as if on fire; or one with whorls of hair on the head that turn upwards like the hair-whorls on a cow's body; or one whose eyebrows are joined with the hair of the head, making the forehead appear as if bound by a net.

Also, one whose eyebrows are joined together; or one with no eyebrows; or one with eyebrows like a monkey's; or one with excessively large eyes; or one with excessively small eyes; or one with eyes like holes made by striking buffalo hide with the tip of a chisel; or one with uneven eyes, one large and one small; or one with uneven eye sockets, one low and one high; or one who is squint-eyed; or one with deep-set eyes like bubbles in a deep well; or one with protruding eyes like a crab's; or one with ears like an elephant's with large ear-flaps; or one with ears like a mouse's; or one with small ears like a bat's; or one with no ear-flaps, having only ear-holes; or one with unpierced ears (if he is of the Yonaka race, he is not a 'spoiler of the assembly,' for not piercing the ears is natural for them); or one with a chronic ear infection that always has a foul discharge.
143:
One who has an abscess in the ear with pus constantly discharging, or one with ears like the tip of a cattle-feed tube (short-eared), or one with excessively squinted eyes should not be ordained. However, one with honey-colored eyes is allowed to be ordained. One without eyelashes, or one with constantly tearing eyes, or one with cataracts or a pterygium, or one with eyes affected by conjunctivitis should not be ordained.

One with an excessively large nose, or an excessively small nose, or a flat nose, or a crooked nose that leans to one side instead of being straight in the middle, or one with a nose so long it can be licked by the tongue like a parrot's beak, or one with a constantly runny nose should not be ordained. One with a large mouth (where only the mouth-mark is large like a frog's, but the mouth itself is very small like a gourd), or one with a cleft mouth, or a distorted mouth, or one with thick lips like the rim of a pot, or one with thin lips stretched like a drumhead that are unable to cover the teeth, or one with a large lower lip, or a thin upper lip, or a thin lower lip, or a large upper lip, or a split lip, or one with drooling lips, or one with inflamed lips, or one with lips like a conch shell—white on the outside and very red on the inside—or one with foul breath should not be ordained.

One with large teeth like the teeth of a harrow, or one with protruding teeth either above or below should not be ordained. However, if they can be covered by the lips and are only noticeable when speaking but not when silent, it is permissible to ordain him. One with decayed teeth, or no teeth, or excessively small teeth should not be ordained. If there are fine teeth like a squirrel's teeth between the gaps, it is permissible to ordain him.

One with a large jaw like an ox's jaw, or a long jaw, or a flat jaw that is very short as if recessed inward, or a cleft jaw, or a crooked jaw, or one who is beardless and has a face like a bhikkhunī should not be ordained. One with a long neck like a crane's neck, or a short neck as if recessed inward, or a cleft neck, or one with drooping shoulders, or one with no hands, or only one hand, or excessively short hands, or excessively long hands, or a deformed chest, or a deformed back, or one with scabies, or an itch, or ringworm, or one whose skin flakes off like a monitor lizard's should not be ordained. All these are mentioned with reference to physical disfigurement.
144:
This has been explained in detail. The decision here should be understood according to the method mentioned regarding the five diseases.

There are those with sagging buttocks, or large buttocks, or those with protruding buttock muscles like a tripod, or those with large thighs, or enlarged testicles (hydrocele), or large knees, or knocking knees, or long calves, or calves like sticks, or those who are bow-legged, or those whose calves knock together, or those with sagging calf muscles. The latter is of two types: those with large calf muscles that either sag downwards or rise upwards. There are also those with large calves, or fleshy calves, or large feet, or large heels, or a long instep, or those whose calf muscle starts from the middle of the foot, or those with crooked feet. The latter is of two types: those with feet turned either inwards or outwards. There are also those with knobby finger joints like ginger, or those with "blind" nails—having rotten nails of a black color. All these are called those who spoil the assembly (parisadūsaka). Such a person who spoils the assembly should not be ordained.

"Kāṇa" refers to one who cannot see, whether due to loss of visual clarity or having clarity destroyed by cataracts and so forth, being unable to see with both eyes or one eye. Such a person should not be ordained. In the Mahāpaccari, however, one blind in one eye is called "kāṇa," while one blind in both eyes is included under the term "andha" (blind). In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, one blind from birth is called "andha." Therefore, both terms are suitable by way of figurative usage. "Kuṇī" refers to one with crooked hands, crooked feet, or crooked fingers; it means anyone in whom some crookedness of the hands and so forth is evident. "Khañja" (lame) refers to one with bent knees, or a broken calf, or a club-footed person who walks on the middle of the instep because the middle of the sole is contracted, or a club-footed person who walks on the tip of the instep because the tip of the sole is contracted, or one who limps by walking only on the tips of the feet, or one who limps by walking on the heels, or one who limps by walking on the outer edge of the foot, or one who limps by walking on the inner edge of the foot, or one who walks on the entire instep because of a break above the ankles. All these are simply "khañja" and should not be ordained.

"Pakkhahata" (paralyzed) refers to one who cannot properly use one hand, or one foot, or one side of the body. "Chinniriyāpatha" (one whose postures are cut off) refers to a pīṭhasappī (one who moves by means of a stool). "Jarādubbala" (weak from old age) refers to...
145:
One who is weak due to old age and is unable to perform even his own tasks such as dyeing robes should not be ordained. If, however, despite being old, he is strong and able to look after himself, he may be ordained. The 'blind' (andha) refers to one who is blind from birth. The 'mute' (mūga) is one who cannot speak; even if he can speak but cannot recite the Refuges (saraṇagamana) completely, such a stammerer (mammana) should not be ordained. However, a stammerer who can recite the Refuges completely may be ordained. The 'deaf' (badhira) is one who cannot hear any sound at all. If he can hear a loud sound, he may be ordained. The blind, the mute, and others are mentioned as those who should not be ordained because of their dual defects. For those whom the 'going forth' (pabbajjā) is forbidden, the higher ordination (upasampadā) is also forbidden. If the Saṅgha ordains them, they all become properly ordained; however, the officiating Saṅgha, the teachers (ācariya), and the preceptors (upajjhāya) are not free from an offense (āpatti).

These eleven types of persons—the paṇḍaka, the hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka), the one who lives by stealth (theyyasaṃvāsaka), the one who went over to another sect (titthiyapakkantaka), the animal (tiracchāna), the matricide (mātughātaka), the patricide (pitughātaka), the killer of an Arahant (arahantaghātaka), the one who shed the Buddha's blood (lohituppādaka), the schismatic (saṅghabhedaka), and the defiler of a nun (bhikkhunīdūsaka)—are unfit for the Dispensation according to the words: "Monks, a paṇḍaka, if not ordained, should not be ordained; if ordained, he should be expelled" (Mahāvagga 109), etc. For them, neither the 'going forth' nor the higher ordination is valid; therefore, they should not be given the 'going forth' or the higher ordination. One who ordains them knowingly commits a dukkaṭa offense. Even if they were ordained unknowingly, they must be expelled by stripping them of their marks (liṅganāsanā) once they are discovered.

Among those eleven, there are five types of paṇḍaka: the āsittapaṇḍaka, the usūyapaṇḍaka, the opakkamikapaṇḍaka, the pakkhapaṇḍaka, and the napuṃsakapaṇḍaka. Among these five, the āsittapaṇḍaka is one whose lustful fever is calmed only after taking the male organ of another into his mouth and being showered with semen. The usūyapaṇḍaka is one whose lustful fever is calmed by the envy that arises from watching others engage in sexual intercourse. The opakkamikapaṇḍaka is one whose testicles have been removed by surgical effort. Some, due to the result of unwholesome kamma, become a paṇḍaka during the dark fortnight, but their fever is calmed during the bright fortnight; such a person is called a pakkhapaṇḍaka. One who is born without sexual organs from the moment of conception is a napuṃsakapaṇḍaka. Among these five...
146:
The 'going forth' is not forbidden for the āsittapaṇḍaka and the usūyapaṇḍaka, but it is forbidden for the other three. "Among those three, for the pakkhapaṇḍaka, the 'going forth' is forbidden only during the fortnight when he is a paṇḍaka," as stated in the Kurundī.

A hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka) (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā 116) is so called because they possess both sexual characteristics due to kamma that produces female characteristics and kamma that produces male characteristics. There are two types: the female hermaphrodite (itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka) and the male hermaphrodite (purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka). Between the two, for the female hermaphrodite, the female characteristics are apparent while the male characteristics are hidden. For the male hermaphrodite, the male characteristics are apparent while the female characteristics are hidden. When a female hermaphrodite acts as a male towards women, the female characteristics become hidden and the male characteristics become apparent. When a male hermaphrodite takes on the female state towards men, the male characteristics become hidden and the female characteristics become apparent. The female hermaphrodite can both conceive a fetus herself and cause others to conceive. The male hermaphrodite, however, cannot conceive himself but can cause others to conceive. This is the difference between them. For both types of hermaphrodites, there is neither the 'going forth' nor the higher ordination.

The one who lives by stealth (theyyasaṃvāsaka) is of three types: the thief of the marks (liṅgatthenaka), the thief of communion (saṃvāsatthenaka), and the thief of both (ubhayatthenaka). Among these three, one who ordains himself, goes to a monastery, but does not count his years of seniority (vassa), does not accept salutations according to seniority, does not take a seat by seniority, and does not appear at the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremonies, is called a liṅgatthenaka because he has stolen only the marks (the appearance of a monk). One who has been ordained as a novice (sāmaṇera) by monks but goes to another place and lies, saying, "I have ten years or twenty years of seniority," and thus counts years of seniority, accepts salutations according to seniority, takes a seat by seniority, and appears at the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies, is called a saṃvāsatthenaka because he has stolen only the communion. Indeed, in this context, all monastic activities such as counting years of seniority should be understood as 'communion' (saṃvāsa). The same rule applies to one who, having given up the training, thinks, "No one will know me," and behaves in this manner again. One who ordains himself, goes to a monastery, counts years of seniority, accepts salutations according to seniority, takes a seat by seniority, and appears at the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies, is [a thief of both] the marks...
147: Because he steals both the mark of a monk and the communion (saṃvāsa), he is called an ubhayatthenaka (a thief of both). These three types of theyyasaṃvāsaka persons, if not yet ordained as a novice, should not be given the higher ordination; if already ordained, they should be expelled. Even if they request the going forth (pabbajjā) again, it should not be granted.## To avoid confusion in this matter, this miscellaneous decision should be understood:## "Due to danger from kings, famine, wilderness, disease, or enemies, or for the sake of obtaining robes, whoever takes up the mark [of a monk] in this Dispensation; as long as he does not accept the communion (such as receiving homage) while his mind is pure, for that long he is not called a theyyasaṃvāsaka."## The detailed explanation is as follows: In this Dispensation, a king is angry with a certain person. That person, thinking, "In this way, I shall be safe," takes up the mark of a monk by himself and flees. Seeing him, people inform the king. The king, thinking, "If he has gone forth, nothing should be done to him," lets go of his anger toward that person. If that person, thinking, "The danger from the king has subsided for me," returns and takes up the lay life without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, he should be given the going forth. However, if he feels spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "I have gained my life by depending on the Dispensation; now I shall go forth," and comes in that same mark but does not accept the duties of a guest monk, and whether questioned by the monks or not, reveals his true situation and requests the going forth, he should be given the going forth after removing that mark. But if he accepts the duties, displays the behavior of one who has gone forth, and follows all the procedures such as the counting of years (seniority) mentioned previously, he should not be given the going forth.## In this Dispensation, if a certain person, unable to survive during a famine, takes up the mark by himself and eats the food offered to various sects, and when the famine has passed, returns and takes up the lay life without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, everything is the same as the previous case.## Another person wishes to cross a great wilderness, and a caravan of traders is traveling with monks. He, thinking, "In this way (by taking the mark of a monk), the caravan will take me along," takes up the mark by himself, crosses the wilderness with the traders, reaches safety, and returns and takes up the lay life without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha; everything is the same as the previous case.
148: Another person, unable to survive when the danger of disease arises, takes up the mark (of a monk) by himself and eats the food of all sects. When the danger of disease has subsided, he returns and takes up the lay life without approaching the midst of the Saṅgha. All this is the same as the previous case.## Another person has an enemy who is angry and wandering about wishing to kill him. That person, thinking, "In this way (by going forth), I shall be safe," takes up the mark by himself and flees. The enemy, searching for him and asking, "Where is he?", hears that "He has gone forth and fled." Thinking, "If he has become a monk, nothing can be done to him anymore," the enemy dispels his anger toward him. That person, saying, "The danger from the enemy has subsided for me," returns and takes up the lay life without approaching the midst of the Saṅgha. All this is also the same as the previous case.## Another person goes to his relatives' house, renounces the training, and becomes a layman. Later, he thinks, "These robes will be ruined here. If I take these robes and go to the monastery, they will catch me as a thief on the way. It would be better if I go wearing them on my body." Thinking thus, he goes to the monastery wearing the robes for the purpose of carrying them. Seeing him coming from afar, the novices and junior monks go out to meet him and perform the major and minor duties. He does not accept those duties and clearly explains his true situation. If the monks, saying, "Now we will not let you go," wish to forcefully ordain him, he should be given the going forth again after removing the ochre-dyed clothes. But if he thinks, "These monks do not know that I have returned to the lower life (disrobed)," and professes to be a monk, practicing all the procedures such as the counting of vassa mentioned before, he should not be given the going forth.## Another senior novice goes to his relatives' house and disrobes. Being overwhelmed by work, he later thinks, "Now I will become a novice again; the elder will not know that I have disrobed." Taking those same bowls and robes, he goes to the monastery. He does not inform the monks of the matter and professes to be a novice. This person is indeed a theyyasaṃvāsaka (one who lives in communion by theft) and cannot obtain the monkhood. Even if at the time of taking the mark he thought, "I will not tell anyone," but upon reaching the monastery he did inform them, he is still a theyyasaṃvāsaka from the very moment of taking the mark. Furthermore, if at the time of taking the mark he had the thought, "I will tell them," but upon reaching the monastery and being asked, "Friend, where did you go?", he thinks, "Now these monks do not know me," and remains silent, he is also a theyyasaṃvāsaka. If at the time of taking the mark (he intended to tell)...
149:
If one deceives and does not inform, thinking "I will not inform," then along with the laying down of the burden, this person is also one who lives in communion by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka). However, if at the time of taking the appearance, he has the intention "I will inform," and upon reaching the monastery he does inform, he can receive ordination again.

Another case: a young novice or an elder but ignorant novice. As in the previous method, he leaves the monkhood but does not wish to perform tasks such as herding or guarding cattle at home. His relatives make him wear those same saffron robes, place a bowl or a dish in his hand, and drive him out of the house, saying, "Go, just be a recluse." He goes to the monastery. The monks do not know that "this person has left the monkhood and has returned to ordain by himself," nor does he himself know that "one who ordains in this way is called one who lives in communion by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka)." If they grant him higher ordination (upasampadā) when he reaches the age of twenty, he is properly ordained. If, before receiving higher ordination, he hears the Vinaya decision and realizes that "one who ordains in this way is called a theyyasaṃvāsaka," he must inform the monks, saying, "I have done this." If he informs them, he can receive ordination again. However, if he remains silent, thinking "Now no one can know about me," he becomes a theyyasaṃvāsaka at the very moment he lays down the burden (of honesty).

If a monk renounces the training but does not remove the marks (robes), whether he commits an act of immorality or not, and subsequently follows the procedures such as counting the number of years (vassa) as mentioned before, he becomes a theyyasaṃvāsaka. One who has not renounced the training and, while remaining in his own marks, engages in sexual intercourse and then follows the procedures such as counting the number of years, does not become a theyyasaṃvāsaka; he only receives the status of ordination (pabbajjā). In the Andhaka Commentary, however, it is said, "This person is a theyyasaṃvāsaka," but that statement should not be accepted.

A monk, while still having the desire for the saffron robes, wears white lay clothes and engages in sexual intercourse, and then wears the saffron robes again and follows the procedures such as counting the number of years; this person also does not become a theyyasaṃvāsaka, he only receives the status of ordination. If, however, he lays down the burden of the saffron robes, wears white lay clothes, engages in sexual intercourse, and then wears the saffron robes again and follows the procedures such as counting the number of years, he becomes a theyyasaṃvāsaka. A novice, while remaining in his own marks, even if he commits acts unbecoming of a recluse such as sexual intercourse, does not become a theyyasaṃvāsaka. Even if he has the desire for the saffron robes, removes them, engages in sexual intercourse, and then wears the saffron robes again, he still does not become a theyyasaṃvāsaka. If, however, he lays down the burden of the saffron robes and, whether naked or wearing white lay clothes...
150:
...or by engaging in sexual intercourse, etc., and then wears the saffron robes while not being a recluse, he becomes one who lives in communion by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka).

If, desiring the state of a layman, he wears the saffron robe by tucking it up (as a loincloth) or wears it in any other manner as laypeople do, for the purpose of testing, "Does the lay appearance look good on me or not?", he still preserves his monkhood during that time. But after accepting that "it looks good," if he then delights in the lay appearance, he becomes a theyyasaṃvāsaka. The same rule applies to wearing white clothes for testing and accepting. However, if he wears white clothes over the saffron robes he is already wearing and tests or accepts it, he still preserves his monkhood.

The same rule applies to a bhikkhunī. If that bhikkhunī, desiring the state of a laywoman, removes her saffron robes and wears them as laypeople do for the purpose of testing, "Does the lay appearance look good on me?", she still preserves her state as a bhikkhunī. However, if she accepts that "it looks good," she no longer preserves it. The same rule applies to wearing white clothes for testing and accepting. But if she wears white clothes over the saffron robes she is already wearing, whether she tests or accepts it, she still preserves her state as a bhikkhunī.

## 22. Theyyasaṃvāsakavinicchayakathā

If someone who ordained late in life does not count the years (vassa), does not abide by the order of the Pali texts, and goes to one side to present his bowl for alms-food and snacks taken with a ladle from large pots, etc., and goes away like a hawk taking a piece of meat, that person is not a theyyasaṃvāsaka. However, if he takes them while counting the years of a monk (falsely), he becomes a theyyasaṃvāsaka. If he, being only a novice, counts and takes according to a fraudulent sequence of novice years, he is not a theyyasaṃvāsaka. If a monk counts and takes according to a fraudulent sequence of monk years, he should be punished according to the value of the goods (bhaṇḍaggha).

'Titthiyapakkantaka' means one who has gone over to or entered among the followers of other sects; such a person should not be ordained again. The decision in this matter is as follows: If a person who is ordained as a monk intends, "I will become a member of another sect," and goes to the dwelling of those sectarians while still in his own monk's marks, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) with every step. At the mere moment he takes the marks of those sectarians, he becomes a titthiyapakkantaka. Anyone who, of his own accord, wears garments of kusa grass, etc., with the intent "I will become a member of another sect," also becomes a titthiyapakkantaka. If a monk, while naked and bathing, looks at himself and thinks, "My state as an Ājīvaka looks good; I will become an Ājīvaka," and without taking his saffron robes, remains naked...
151:
If one goes to the monastery of the Ājīvakas, for every step, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If, while on the way, shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) arise in that monk, he is released from the offenses after confessing the dukkaṭa offenses. Even if he goes to the monastery of those heretics, whether he is admonished by them or by his own volition, if he sees that "the monkhood of these heretics is extremely painful" and returns, he is indeed released from the offense. However, if he asks, "What practice is supreme in your religion?" and is told, "Plucking out hair and beard, etc., is supreme," and he has even a single hair plucked, or if he undertakes practices such as striving while squatting, or if he wears peacock feathers, etc., or takes on the appearance of those heretics, or admits that "this monkhood is supreme," then he is not released from the offense and becomes a titthiyapakkantaka (one who has gone over to a heretical sect).

If, for the sake of testing, "Does the heretical monkhood suit me or not?" he wears garments made of kusa grass, etc., or ties his hair in a topknot, or takes up a carrying pole, as long as he does not accept their view, he is considered to be guarding his monkhood. At the moment he accepts it, he becomes a titthiyapakkantaka. A monk whose robes have been stolen does not become a titthiyapakkantaka even if he wears garments of kusa grass, etc., or takes on the appearance of a heretic due to fear of the king, etc., because he does not hold their view. It is stated in the Kurundī commentary: "This term titthiyapakkantaka is spoken in relation to an ordained monk (upasampanna); therefore, even if a novice (sāmaṇera) goes to a heretical monastery in his own appearance, he can still receive novice ordination and higher ordination again." The previously mentioned "one who lives in communion by stealth" (theyyasaṃvāsaka) is spoken in relation to one who is not ordained (anupasampanna). Therefore, a person who is a monk does not become a non-monk even if he counts fraudulent years of seniority. One who has the effort to maintain the appearance of a monk, even if he counts years of seniority after committing a pārājika offense, does not become a theyyasaṃvāsaka.

An animal (tiracchāna) means a nāga, or any of the garuḍas (supaṇṇa) who take the form of youths, or ultimately any non-human being (amanussa) including Sakka, the king of devas; all are to be understood as "animals" in this context. Such a being should not be given higher ordination or novice ordination; if already ordained, he must be expelled.

Regarding those who kill their mother (mātughātaka), etc., if a person, being human himself, intentionally deprives of life his own biological mother who is a human woman, he is a mātughātaka who has committed an ānantariya karma. For him, novice ordination and higher ordination are forbidden. If a person kills a woman who is a human but not his biological mother, such as a foster mother or an aunt, or if he kills his biological mother who is not a human woman...
152:
...mother is killed, the novice ordination of that person is not forbidden, and he does not become one who has committed an ānantariya karma. If a person who is himself an animal kills his mother who is a human woman, he also does not become one who has committed an ānantariya karma; however, because he is an animal, his novice ordination is rejected. The same principle applies to a parricide (pitughātaka). Even if he is the son of a prostitute and does not know "This is my father," if he kills the man from whose semen he was conceived, he is designated as a pitughātaka and incurs the ānantariya karma.

A killer of an Arahant (arahantaghātaka) is also to be understood only in terms of a human Arahant. If one intentionally deprives of life a human being who is an Arahant, even if it is a child or a young girl who is a non-ordained Arahant, he is indeed an arahantaghātaka, incurs the ānantariya karma, and his novice ordination is forbidden. However, by killing a non-human Arahant or any other noble person (ariya) who is a human but not an Arahant, one does not become an ānantariya offender, and his novice ordination is not forbidden, though the karma is very powerful. If an animal kills a human Arahant, it does not become an ānantariya offender, but the karma is heavy; this is the decision here.

One who, like Devadatta, with a corrupt and murderous mind, causes blood even as much as what a small fly might drink to be shed from the living body of the Tathāgata, is called a shedder of the Buddha's blood (lohituppādaka). For him, novice ordination and higher ordination are forbidden. However, one who, like Jīvaka, for the sake of curing a disease, makes an incision with a knife, removes putrid flesh and blood, and makes the Buddha comfortable, produces much merit.

One who, like Devadatta, making the teaching non-Dhamma and non-Vinaya, causes a schism in the Saṅgha by means of any of the four formal acts, is called a schismatic (saṅghabhedaka). For him, novice ordination and higher ordination are forbidden.

One who violates a nun (bhikkhunī) of good character in any of the three ways (passages), is called a violator of a nun (bhikkhunīdūsaka). For him, novice ordination and higher ordination are forbidden. One who causes the destruction of virtue through physical contact does not have his novice or higher ordination forbidden. One who forcibly makes a nun wear white clothes and violates her even against her will is indeed a bhikkhunīdūsaka. However, one who forcibly makes her wear white clothes and violates her when she is willing is not a bhikkhunīdūsaka. Why? Because at the moment she accepts the status of a layperson, she is no longer a nun. For one who has once fallen from virtue...
153:
A person who later defiles [someone], or a person who behaves wrongly towards a sikkhamānā or a sāmaṇerī, is not called a bhikkhunī-dūsaka (defiler of a nun); such a person can still receive both pabbajjā (novicehood) and upasampadā (higher ordination). Thus, these eleven types of abhabba-puggala (excluded persons) should be understood.

For a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty, only higher ordination is prohibited; novicehood is not prohibited. Therefore, higher ordination should be conferred upon a person who has completed twenty years of age, starting from the time of conception. Even a person who is twenty years old including the period in the mother's womb is counted as a person who has completed twenty years. This is in accordance with what the Blessed One said: "Monks, whatever first thought arises in the mother's womb, whatever first consciousness appears, starting from that [rebirth-linking consciousness], it is called his birth. Monks, I allow the conferring of higher ordination on one who is twenty years old including the period in the womb."

In that Pali text, a person who has lived in the mother's womb for twelve months and is born on the full moon day of Assayuja (Mahāpavāraṇā) should be given higher ordination on the first waning day after the full moon of Assayuja of his nineteenth year. In this way, the decrease and increase of years should be understood. Ancient teachers, however, confer higher ordination on a sāmaṇera who is nineteen years old on the first waning day after the full moon of Sāvaṇa (Nikkhamanīya). Why? In one year, there are six uposatha days consisting of fourteen days; thus, within twenty years, four months are decreased. Kings add an intercalary month every three years; thus, within eighteen years, six months are increased. If the four months decreased due to the uposatha are removed from those six increased months, two months remain. Taking those two months into account and having no doubt that twenty years are complete, they confer higher ordination on the first waning day after the full moon of Sāvaṇa.

In this context, the phrase "one who is nineteen years old" is said in reference to a person who will complete twenty years after performing the pavāraṇā. Therefore, a person who lived in the mother's womb for twelve months is one who is twenty-one years old. One who lived for seven months is twenty years and seven months old. A person born at six months does not survive. There is no offense for one who confers higher ordination on a person who has not yet reached twenty years of age under the mistaken impression that "he has completed twenty years"; however, that person does not actually become a bhikkhu. If, after ten years, that person confers higher ordination on another, and if the quorum of the Saṅgha is complete even without counting him, then that [newly ordained] person is properly ordained.
154:
As long as that person does not know, there is no obstacle to heaven or to liberation (magga-phala) for him; however, when he comes to know, he must receive higher ordination again.

Thus, even if one is free from these disqualifications for monkhood, according to the words, "Monks, a son who does not have the permission of his parents should not be ordained," one who does not have parental permission should not be ordained. In that Pali text, the word "parents" refers to the biological mother and father. If both are alive, permission must be requested from both. If the father or the mother has died, permission must be requested from the one who is still alive; even parents who have themselves become monastics must be asked for permission. When asking for permission, one should go in person or send someone else. Or that person himself should be sent, saying, "Go, come back after asking your parents for permission." If he says, "I have received permission," he should be ordained out of trust. If a father has himself become a monk and wishes to ordain his son, let him ordain him after asking the mother for permission. Or if a mother wishes to ordain her daughter, let her ordain her only after asking the father for permission. If a father has fled because he has no desire for his wife and children, and the mother gives the son to the monks saying, "Please ordain this boy," and when asked "Where is his father?" she says, "He has fled to play as he pleases," it is proper to ordain that boy. If a mother has fled with some man and the father says, "Please ordain him," the same method applies here. If a father is away in another place and the mother gives permission to ordain the son, and when asked "Where is his father?" she says, "What does it have to do with your father? I know [about it]," it is proper to ordain him; so it is stated in the Kurundī commentary.

If the parents are dead and the boy has grown up with a stepmother or others, when that boy is being ordained, relatives might quarrel or criticize; therefore, for the sake of cutting off disputes, he should be ordained after asking for permission. However, there is no offense for a monk who ordains him without asking. Those who take and raise a child from a young age are called parents; the same method applies to them. 

A son might live depending on himself and not on his parents. Even if that son is a king, he should be ordained only after asking for permission. If one disrobes after being ordained with parental permission, even if he disrobes and ordains a hundred times, permission must be requested repeatedly every time he comes back to ordain. If they say, "This person does not do our work even when he disrobes and returns home, and he does not fulfill your duties (vatta) when he is a monk; for this person..." [the text breaks off].
155:
If it is said, 'There is no need for further asking; ordain this person whenever he comes,' and he has been thus relinquished, it is proper to ordain him without asking again.

Even if a person was given in childhood with the words, 'This boy is given to you; ordain him when you wish,' it is proper to ordain him when he comes without asking again. However, if permission was granted in childhood saying, 'Venerable, please ordain this boy,' but later when he reaches adulthood they do not grant permission, he should not be ordained without asking. If a person, having quarreled with his parents, comes saying, 'Ordain me,' and when told, 'Come back after asking permission,' he says, 'I will not go; if you do not ordain me, I will burn down the monastery, or I will strike you with a weapon, or I will cause harm to your relatives or supporters by destroying their groves, etc., or I will die by jumping from a tree, or I will enter among thieves, or I will go to another region,' then it is proper to ordain him for his own protection. If his parents come and ask, 'Why did you ordain our son?' they should be told the reason: 'We ordained him for his protection; you know your son's nature.' If someone climbs a tree saying, 'I will jump,' and lets go of his hands and feet, it is certainly proper to ordain him (without asking).

If a person goes to another region and requests ordination, if he comes after asking permission, he should be ordained. If he comes without asking, a junior monk should be sent to ask permission before ordaining him. If it is very far, it is proper to ordain him and then send him with other monks to show him to the parents. In the Kurundī Commentary, it is said: 'If it is far and the path is through a great forest, it is proper to ordain him with the intention, "I will go and ask later."' If parents have many sons and say, 'Venerable, ordain whichever of these boys you wish,' then after examining the boys, the one desired should be ordained. If permission is given by an entire family or village saying, 'Venerable, ordain whoever you wish in this family or village,' then the one desired should be ordained.

Thus, when ordaining one who is free from the defects of ordination and has parental permission, if he has unshaven hair and there are other monks within the same boundary (sīmā), one must ask permission for the shaving of the hair (bhaṇḍukamma) for the purpose of hair-cutting. In the Vinaya, this is the procedure for asking: Having assembled the monks within the boundary and bringing the candidate there, one should say once, twice, or thrice: 'Venerables, I request the shaving of this boy's hair from the Saṅgha.' In this request, it is also proper to say, 'I request the shaving of this boy's hair,' or 'I request the making of this boy into a recluse,' or 'This person wishes to be a recluse,' or 'This boy wishes to go forth.' If it is a common residence and it is known that ten, twenty, or thirty monks reside there, one should go to the place where those monks are standing or sitting and ask in the same manner as before.
156:
If there are other monks within the same boundary (sīmā), one must ask permission for the shaving of the hair (bhaṇḍukamma) for the purpose of hair-cutting. Herein, this is the procedure for asking (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā 98): Having assembled the monks included within the boundary and bringing the candidate for ordination to that assembly, one should say once, twice, or thrice: 'Venerables, I request the shaving of this boy's hair from the Saṅgha.'

In this request, it is proper to say, 'I request the shaving of this boy's hair,' or 'I request the making of this boy into a recluse,' or 'This boy wishes to be a recluse,' or 'This boy wishes to go forth.' If it is a common residence and it is known that ten, twenty, or thirty monks reside there, one should go to the place where those monks are standing or sitting and ask in the same manner as before. Even without bringing the candidate, it is proper to send junior monks or novices to ask, saying: 'Venerable, there is a candidate for ordination; we request the shaving of his hair,' and so forth. If some monks have entered dwellings or thickets and are sleeping or practicing the Dhamma of a recluse, and those asking do not find them despite searching and thus think, 'We have asked all the monks,' then since ordination (pabbajjā) is a light act (lahukakamma), such an ordination is a valid ordination, and there is no offense for the one ordaining.

If it is a large monastery where many thousands of monks reside, it is difficult to assemble all the monks, let alone ask them individually in order; in that case, one should ordain him by standing in a sectional boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) or by going to a river, the ocean, etc. For one who is newly shaven, or has recently disrobed, or is a member of another sect such as the Nigaṇṭhas, or has hair two finger-breadths long or less, there is no need for hair-cutting; therefore, it is proper to ordain such a person even without asking for the shaving of the hair. However, if one has hair longer than two finger-breadths, even if he wears only a single topknot, he should be ordained only after asking for the shaving of the hair.

When ordaining after thus asking, one should ordain only a person who is fully equipped with a bowl and robes (pattacīvara). If he does not have them, it is proper to ordain him with a borrowed bowl and robes, or by taking them through intimacy in a common residence. If he comes bringing an unbaked bowl and cloth intended for robes, it is proper to give him untouched alms-food (anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapāta) while he resides in the monastery until the bowl is baked and the robes are made; it is proper for him to eat from dishes. In the morning...
157:
It is allowable to give a portion of alms-food equal to a novice's (sāmaṇera) share. However, accepting a lodging (senāsana) is not allowable; but alms-food by ticket (salākabhatta), designated food (uddesabhatta), invited food (nimantana), and so forth, are allowable. Even in the afternoon, it is allowable to give a portion of medicine such as oil, rice, honey, and molasses, equal to a novice's share. If he is sick, it is allowable to provide medical treatment for him; it is allowable to perform all acts of nursing and care just as one would for a novice.

However, it is not allowable to grant higher ordination (upasampadā) to a candidate with a borrowed bowl and robes. It was said: "Monks, one should not grant higher ordination with a borrowed bowl and robes. Whoever should grant it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." Therefore, one should grant higher ordination only to one who has a complete set of bowl and robes. If he does not have them, and if the teachers and preceptors (upajjhāya) wish to give them, or if other monks, being free from attachment, relinquish them, then a bowl and robes suitable for formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) should be given. An offense is incurred only by the one who grants higher ordination with a borrowed bowl or robes; however, the formal act (kamma) is not invalidated.

When ordaining a novice (pabbajjā) who has a complete set of bowl and robes, if the preceptor has the opportunity, he should perform the ordination himself. If he is busy with teaching, reciting, or questioning and does not have the opportunity, a junior monk should be told, "Ordain this person." Even if not told, if a junior monk ordains him on behalf of the preceptor, it is allowable. If there is no junior monk, even a novice should be told, "Take this person to the khaṇḍasīmā (small ordination hall), ordain him, dress him in saffron-dyed robes (kāsāya), and return." However, the Refuges (saraṇagamana) must be given by the monk himself. Only in this way is it considered that the person was ordained by a monk. For no one other than a monk is permitted to ordain a man; and no one other than a bhikkhunī is permitted to ordain a woman. However, a novice (sāmaṇera) or a female novice (sāmaṇerī) may, by command, give the saffron-dyed robes; as for the shaving of the hair, it is well done regardless of who performs it.

If the candidate is a noble son (kulaputta) who is worthy (of the Path and Fruit), possesses the necessary supporting conditions (hetu), and is well-known and illustrious, the preceptor should make time and ordain him personally. He should not be dismissed with the words, "Take a handful of clay, bathe, and then come back." For those who wish to ordain, there is initially strong enthusiasm, but later, upon seeing the saffron-dyed robes and the razor for shaving, they may become frightened and flee from that very place. Therefore, the preceptor should personally take him to the bathing place and, if he is not too young, tell him, "Take a bath." As for the hair, the preceptor himself should take fine clay...
158:
...and wash the hair. If it is a young boy, the preceptor should personally go down into the water and bathe him by rubbing him with cow dung and fine clay. Even if the boy has scabies or boils, just as a mother is not repulsed by her son, the preceptor, without being repulsed, should bathe him by thoroughly and repeatedly rubbing him starting from the hands, feet, and head. Why? Because through such assistance, noble sons develop strong affection and deep respect for their teachers and preceptors, as well as for the Dispensation (Sāsana), and they become firm in their nature. They dispel any arising dissatisfaction (anabhirati) and reach the status of an Elder (thera). They become those who recognize and reciprocate gratitude.

While bathing him in this way, or while shaving his hair and beard, one should not say, "You are well-known and illustrious; now, depending on you, we shall not suffer for the four requisites." Other talk that does not lead out of saṃsāra (aniyyānika-kathā) should also not be spoken. Instead, one should say to him, "Friend, reflect well; establish mindfulness," and teach him the meditation on the five skin-ending parts (tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna). When teaching it, one should make it clear how it is impure, loathsome, and repulsive by way of color, shape, smell, location, and basis, and how it is soulless and not a living being.

If that person has previously cultivated the formations (saṅkhāra) and practiced meditation, he is like a ripe boil waiting to be pricked by a thorn, or like a mature lotus waiting for the sun to rise. Then, as soon as he begins to attend to the meditation subject, his knowledge proceeds, crushing the mountain of defilements (kilesa) just as Indra's thunderbolt crushes mountains. He attains Arahantship at the very end of the shaving (khuragge). All those who have attained Arahantship at the end of shaving did so by hearing such instruction and depending on the method given by a teacher who is a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitta), and not without such dependence. Therefore, such talk should be spoken to him from the very beginning.

After the hair has been shaved, the head and body should be rubbed with turmeric powder or scented powder to remove the lay smell, and he should be made to receive the saffron-dyed robes (kāsāya) three times, twice, or once. Furthermore, if the teacher or preceptor personally robes him without placing them in his hands, it is allowable. If he commands another junior monk, a novice, or a lay follower, saying, "Friend, take these saffron-dyed robes and robe this person," or if he commands the candidate himself, "Take these and robe yourself," all of that is allowable. All of it is considered as being given by that monk himself. As for the robe that is worn...
159:
If one has donned or wrapped oneself [in a robe] without being commanded, that robe must be removed and given again. For a monk, only a saffron-dyed cloth (kāsāya) given by his own hand or by his command is allowable; that which is not given is not allowable. Even if it is his own property [it is only allowable if given]; it goes without saying if it belongs to the preceptor (upajjhāya).

Having made him wear the saffron-dyed cloths thus given, and having made him place the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) over one shoulder, he should be made to pay homage at the feet of the monks assembled there. Then, for the purpose of taking the refuges, he should be made to sit in a crouching position (ukkuṭika), with hands raised in salutation (añjali), and told, "Speak thus," or "Repeat what I say."

Then the preceptor or the teacher (ācariya) should administer the refuges starting with "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi" only in the sequence as taught in the Pāḷi; they should not be given out of sequence. If one gives them out of sequence by even a single word or a single syllable, or if one gives only "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ" three times and then gives the other refuges three times each, the refuges are not [properly] given.

While the Upasampadā (higher ordination) which was permitted after abolishing this ordination by taking the refuges is valid through the phonetic purity of one side (the teacher), the making of a novice (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā) is valid only through the phonetic purity of both [teacher and pupil]; it is not valid through the purity of only one. Therefore, in the Upasampadā, if the teacher performs the act (kamma) avoiding faults in the motion (ñatti) and faults in the formal reading (kammavācā), it is well performed. In the case of making a novice, however, these three refuges must be recited by both the teacher and the pupil without failing in the perfection of the places (ṭhāna) and means (karaṇa) of articulation of the consonants such as the letter 'Bu' and the letter 'Dha'. If the teacher can recite but the pupil cannot, or if the pupil can recite but the teacher cannot, or if both cannot, it is not valid. It is valid only if both can recite. When giving these refuges, they may be given either by connecting them into one, ending with the nasal (anunāsika/niggahīta) as in "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi," or by breaking them to end with the 'ma' consonant as in "Buddhaṃ ma saraṇaṃ ma gacchāmi."

In the Andhaka Commentary, it is said that after announcing the name, one should say, "Venerable Sir, I, Buddharakkhita, go to the Buddha for refuge as long as life lasts." That statement is not found in any other commentary, nor is it mentioned in the Pāḷi. Since it is merely the preference of those teachers, it should not be accepted. The refuge of one who does not speak thus is not broken. By this much, one is established in the status of a novice.

If this novice is capable of recitation and is of a wise nature, then the training rules (sikkhāpada) should be recited to him in that very place. In what way? Just as they were laid down by the Blessed One. For it was said:
160:
“Monks, I allow ten training rules for novices, and I allow novices to train in them. (They are:) refraining from killing living beings, refraining from taking what is not given, refraining from unchaste conduct, refraining from false speech, refraining from fermented and distilled liquors that cause heedlessness, refraining from eating at the wrong time, refraining from dancing, singing, music, and watching shows, refraining from wearing garlands, using perfumes, and beautifying with ointments, refraining from high and large beds, and refraining from accepting gold and silver.”

In the Andhaka Commentary, however, it is stated that the training rules should be given in the same manner as the refuges, such as: “Venerable sir, I undertake the training rule of refraining from killing living beings for as long as I live.” This statement is found neither in the Pali nor in the other commentaries; therefore, the training rules should be pointed out exactly as they appear in the Pali. Indeed, the going forth (pabbajjā) is accomplished solely by the taking of the refuges; the training rules are to be known merely for the purpose of fulfilling the training. Therefore, for one who is unable to learn them in the manner coming from the Pali, it is proper to explain them by way of their meaning in any language.

For as long as one does not yet know the training rules that must be practiced, and is not yet skilled in such matters as wearing the double robe, the bowl, and the robes, or in standing and sitting, etc., or in the procedures for drinking congee and eating food, etc., for that long, he should not be sent to the dining hall, the place for distributing lots, or any other such place. He should only be made to stay in the vicinity [of the teacher]. He should be treated like an untrained child. Everything that is allowable and unallowable should be explained to him. He should be disciplined in the minor duties (abhisamācārika) such as dressing and robing. 

Regarding that novice—
“Monks, I allow a novice endowed with ten factors to be expelled. (They are:) he kills living beings, he takes what is not given, he is unchaste, he is a liar, he is a drinker of liquor, he speaks in dispraise of the Buddha, he speaks in dispraise of the Dhamma, he speaks in dispraise of the Saṅgha, he holds wrong views, or he is a violator of bhikkhunīs.”
One who avoids these ten factors of expulsion mentioned here and fulfills the minor duties should train well in the ten kinds of virtue (sīla).
161:
If a novice (sāmaṇera) performs even one of the ten acts leading to expulsion (nāsananga), such as killing a living being, that novice should be expelled by the destruction of his marks (liṅga-nāsana). Indeed, among the three types of expulsion, it is the destruction of the marks that is intended here. The various offenses that occur for monks regarding killing and so forth do not occur for novices in the same way.

In fact, if a novice kills even a bedbug or an ant, or breaks even a bedbug's egg, he reaches the state of being expelled. At that very moment, his refuges (saraṇagamana), his taking of a preceptor (upajjhāya-gahaṇa), and his taking of lodgings (senāsana-ggahaṇa) cease. He no longer receives the Sangha's gains; only the mere appearance of a novice remains. If that novice is a habitual offender and does not abide by future restraint, he should be driven out. If, however, he quickly feels remorse, thinking, "I have done wrong," and wishes to abide by future restraint, there is no need for the destruction of his marks; the refuges should be given to him while he is still wearing his robes as before, and a preceptor should also be given.

The training rules (sikkhāpada) are fulfilled by the refuges alone. The refuges of novices are similar to the formal act of ordination (upasampadā-kammavācā) for monks. Therefore, just as the fourfold purifying virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla) is for monks, the ten precepts are considered undertaken by this refuge. Even so, for the sake of firmness and to establish him in future restraint, they should be given again. If the refuges were taken again during the first part of the rainy season, he receives the vassa-residence allowance in the latter part. If they were taken in the latter part, the gains should be given after informing the Sangha.

In the case of taking what is not given (adinnādāna), even with an object as small as a blade of grass; in the case of unchastity (abrahmacariya), by misconduct in any of the three paths; in the case of false speech (musāvāda), if one speaks falsely even with the intent of joking, one is no longer a recluse and falls into the state of being expelled. Regarding the drinking of intoxicants (majjapāna), however, for a monk, if he drinks an intoxicant starting from the seed stage even without knowing, he commits a pācittiya offense. A novice reaches the breach of virtue only if he drinks knowing it to be an intoxicant, not if he drinks without knowing. As for the remaining five training rules, even if they are broken, he should not be expelled; only punishment (daṇḍakamma) should be carried out. Whether the training rules are given again or not, it is valid. However, they should indeed be given for the purpose of establishing him in future restraint by pressing him with punishment.

## Regarding the speaking of dispraise

If one speaks dispraise of the Buddha by opposing his qualities such as "Arahaṃ Sammāsambuddho," or dispraise of the Dhamma by opposing its qualities such as "Svākkhāto," or dispraise of the Sangha by opposing its qualities such as "Suppaṭipanno," thus insulting and blaming the Triple Gem, the teachers and preceptors should restrain him by showing the danger of such dispraise, saying, "Do not speak thus." If, even after three times...
162:
...being told three times, he does not stop, he should be expelled by the destruction of his marks, which is like destruction by thorns (kaṇṭaka-nāsana)—so it is stated in the Kurundī. However, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated: "If, when so addressed, he relinquishes that view (the dispraising speech), he should be made to undergo punishment (daṇḍakamma) and be made to confess his fault. If he does not relinquish it but remains firmly holding to it, he should be expelled by the destruction of his marks (liṅga-nāsana)." This statement is appropriate. Indeed, among the three types of expulsion, it is this destruction of the marks that is intended here. This same method applies to one with wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). If a novice who holds either the view of eternalism (sassata) or annihilationism (uccheda) relinquishes it when admonished by teachers and so forth, he should be made to undergo punishment and confess his fault; if he does not relinquish it, he should be expelled.

In this context, a violator of a nun (bhikkhunī-dūsaka) is certainly included under the term "one who is unchaste" (abrahmacārī). However, a novice who has committed unchastity (with a layperson) and wishes to abide by future restraint may be given the refuges and then ordained as a monk. A violator of a nun, even if he wishes to abide by future restraint, cannot even obtain the state of a novice (pabbajjā), let alone full ordination (upasampadā). To show this meaning, this tenth factor, "bhikkhunī-dūsaka," is stated separately.

"Monks, I allow punishment (daṇḍakamma) to be carried out against a novice who possesses five factors: he strives for the non-gain of monks, he strives for the harm of monks, he strives for the non-residence of monks, he reviles and threatens monks, and he causes dissension among monks." According to this statement, these five factors, along with the last five training rules starting from eating at the wrong time (vikāla-bhojana), constitute the ten grounds for punishment (daṇḍakamma-vatthu). If it is asked, "What kind of punishment should be carried out here?"—according to the statement, "Monks, I allow a restriction to be made in the place where he dwells or where he frequents," a restriction should be made in the lodging where he dwells or enters, saying, "Do not enter here." By both these words, one's own precinct (pariveṇa) and the lodging assigned to one according to seniority (vassaggena patta-senāsana) are meant. Therefore, a restriction should not be made for the entire monastery (saṅghārāma); a monk who does so commits a dukkaṭa offense. For it was said: "Monks, a restriction should not be made for the entire monastery. Whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

Also, a restriction should not be made regarding food taken through the mouth; a monk who does so commits a dukkaṭa offense. For it was said: "Monks, a restriction should not be made regarding food taken through the mouth. Whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." Therefore, for a monk who says, "Do not eat or drink today," or for a monk who, intending to restrict food, puts away the novice's bowl and robes inside, there is a dukkaṭa offense in all such efforts. For a novice of improper conduct who is difficult to admonish, after carrying out punishment, one may show him the gruel, the meal, or the bowl and robes...
163:
... "It is proper to say, 'If you perform this much penalty, you shall receive this alms-food, bowl, or robe.' The Blessed One spoke only of the penalty of prohibition. However, the Elders who recited the Dhamma said that carrying water, wood, sand, etc., should also be done according to the offense. Therefore, that penalty should also be carried out. Such a penalty should be given out of compassion, thinking, 'He will desist, he will refrain,' and not with an evil intention such as, 'He will be ruined, he will disrobe.' It is not proper to make one lie on hot stones, or place stones, bricks, etc., on the head, or put one into water, saying, 'I am imposing a penalty.'

A penalty should not be imposed without informing the preceptor (upajjhāya). Because of the word, 'Monks, a prohibition should not be imposed without informing the preceptor; whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),' one should not impose a penalty without informing the preceptor. In this matter, if the preceptor does not impose a penalty even after being told three times, 'Your novice (sāmaṇera) has such an offense; please impose a penalty on this novice,' then it is proper to do it oneself. If the preceptor says from the beginning, 'If there is a fault in my novices, you may impose a penalty,' then it is also proper to do so. Just as it is proper to impose a penalty on novices, so it is proper for co-residents (saddhivihārika) and pupils (antevāsika). However, one should not lure away another's followers (parisa). Because of the word, 'Monks, another's followers should not be lured away; whoever should lure them away, there is an offense of wrong-doing,' one who lures them away commits an offense of wrong-doing. Therefore, it is not proper to take away another's followers, whether they be novices or ordained monks, or even a monk of poor virtue, by supporting them with the thought, 'I will give you a bowl, I will give you a robe,' in order to make them serve oneself. However, it is proper to speak of the disadvantage, saying, 'One who lives depending on a person of poor virtue is like one who comes to bathe but gets smeared with excrement.' If that person, realizing it himself, requests a preceptor or dependence (nissaya), it is proper to give it.

## Thus, in the Palimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-sangaha,
## The Discussion on the Decision regarding Ordination (Pabbajjā-vinicchaya-kathā) is finished.
164:
## 23. Discussion on the Decision regarding Dependence (Nissaya-vinicchaya-kathā)
