In this term 'nissaya' (dependence): Who should give this dependence? Who should not give it? To whom should it be given? To whom should it not be given? How is it taken? How does it subside? Who should live in dependence? And who should not live in dependence? Among those questions, regarding 'Who should give it? Who should not give it?', it should first be understood thus: Because of the word, 'Monks, I allow a competent and capable monk of ten years or more than ten years to ordain others and to give dependence,' the monk who is competent (byatta), capable (paṭibala), and has ten years or more than ten years of seniority (vassa) for ordaining others, he should give it; another monk should not give it. If he gives it, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Here, by the word 'byatta' (competent), one who is learned and capable of attending to followers should be understood. One who attends to followers must, at the very least, have mastered and memorized the two Vibhangas to train the followers in the Vinaya Piṭaka without confusion. If he cannot master them alone, he must be proficient in reciting them together with three other monks. He must also learn the major and minor formal acts (kamma) and the duties in the Khandhakas. To train the followers in the analysis of mind and matter (Abhidhamma), if he is a reciter of the Middle Length Discourses (Majjhima-bhāṇaka), he must learn the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka. A reciter of the Long Discourses (Dīgha-bhāṇaka) must learn the Mahāvagga of the Suttas. A reciter of the Connected Discourses (Saṃyutta-bhāṇaka) must learn the first three books (Sagāthā-vagga, Nidāna-vagga, Khandha-vagga) or the Mahāvagga. A reciter of the Numerical Discourses (Aṅguttara-bhāṇaka) must learn half of the Nikāya, either the lower or upper part. For one who is unable, it is also proper to learn starting from the Tika-nipāta. In the Mahāpaccari, however, it is said, 'One who wishes to learn one Nipāta should learn the Catukka-nipāta or the Pañcaka-nipāta.' A reciter of the Birth Stories (Jātaka-bhāṇaka) must learn the Jātaka together with its commentary; anything less than that is not proper. It is said in the Mahāpaccari, 'It is also proper to learn the Dhammapada together with the stories.' Although it is said that collecting from various texts to the extent of the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka is proper, it is rejected in the Kurundī Commentary, saying 'It is not proper.' In other commentaries, there is no such investigation. It is not stated that anything in the Abhidhamma must be learned. However, for one who has mastered the Vinaya Piṭaka and Abhidhamma Piṭaka together with their commentaries, but does not have the specific texts mentioned in the Suttanta, he is not allowed to attend to followers. But one who has learned the required amount of texts from both the Suttanta and the Vinaya is indeed a learned person who attends to followers; he is a prominent teacher (disāpāmokkha) who can go wherever he wishes and is allowed to attend to followers. Such a person is intended by the term 'byatta' (competent) in this context. One who is capable of attending to the sick, or to a co-resident or a pupil, is intended by the term 'paṭibala' (capable) in this context.
165:
One who is able to perform nursing and other duties for a sick resident pupil or a co-resident pupil is intended here as 'competent' (paṭibala).

"Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence (nissaya), and should not be attended by a novice." This was spoken. (What are the five?) He is not endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekha), he is not endowed with the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, he is not endowed with the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training, he is not endowed with the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training, and he is not endowed with the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training. Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice.

Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice. (What are the five?) He himself is not endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training, and he does not encourage others to undertake the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training. He himself is not endowed with the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, and he does not encourage others to undertake the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training. He himself is not endowed with the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training, and he does not encourage others to undertake the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training. He himself is not endowed with the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training, and he does not encourage others to undertake the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training. He himself is not endowed with the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training, and he does not encourage others to undertake the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training. Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice.

Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice. (What are the five?) He is faithless, he lacks shame, he lacks fear of wrongdoing, he is lazy, and he is unmindful. Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors...
166:
...should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice.

Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice. What are the five? They are: being deficient in virtue regarding higher virtue (adhisīla), being deficient in conduct regarding behavior (ajjhācāra), being deficient in view regarding higher view (atidiṭṭhi), being of little learning, and being of weak wisdom. Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice.

Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice. What are the five? They are: being unable to nurse a sick resident pupil or a co-resident pupil himself, or to have them nursed by others; being unable to dispel dissatisfaction (anabhirata) that has arisen himself, or to have it dispelled by others; being unable to dispel remorse (kukkucca) that has arisen according to the Dhamma; not knowing an offense (āpatti); and not knowing the emergence from an offense (vuṭṭhāna). Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice.

Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice. What are the five? They are: being unable to train a resident pupil or a co-resident pupil in the training of higher conduct (ābhisamācārika); being unable to guide them in the training of the beginning of the holy life (ādibrahmacariya); being unable to guide them in Abhidhamma; being unable to guide them in Abhivinaya; and being unable to refute a wrong view that has arisen according to the Dhamma. Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice.

Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors should not give ordination, should not give dependence, and should not be attended by a novice...
167:
A novice should be attended to. [If a monk] does not know an offense, does not know what is not an offense, does not know a light offense, does not know a heavy offense, and both Pātimokkhas have not been well-handed to him in detail, nor well-analyzed, nor well-recited, nor well-ascertained in terms of the rules (Sutta) and the explanations (Anubyañjana). Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should not ordain [others], should not give dependence (nissaya), and should not be attended to by a novice.

"Monks, a monk endowed with five other factors should not ordain, should not give dependence, and should not be attended to by a novice. He does not know an offense, does not know what is not an offense, does not know a light offense, does not know a heavy offense, and has less than ten years of seniority (vassa). Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should not ordain, should not give dependence, and should not be attended to by a novice," and so forth (as stated in the Mahāvagga). This statement was made to explain in detail the characteristics of a preceptor (upajjhāya) and a teacher (ācariya), which were briefly stated as: "Monks, I allow a competent, capable monk with ten years of seniority or more than ten years of seniority to ordain and to give dependence."

In that [Commentary], some [factors] are prohibited on the grounds of unsuitability, and some on the grounds of being factors of an offense. This is true. In the three groups of five (pañcaka) beginning with "not being endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekha-sīlakkhandha)," "not being oneself one beyond training," and "lacking faith," the prohibition is made on the grounds of unsuitability, not on the grounds of being factors of an offense. For if a person who is not endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training, etc., and is unable to establish others in those aggregates of virtue, and is possessed of faults such as lack of faith, leads a group, that group will only decline in virtues like morality and will not grow. Therefore, the statement "he should not ordain," etc., was made because of unsuitability, not because of being a factor of an offense. Indeed, the Blessed One did not allow the status of preceptor or teacher only to those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). If he had allowed it only to them, he would not have said, "If dissatisfaction arises in the preceptor," and so forth. Because the group of a khīṇāsava does not decline in virtues like morality, it was said, "Monks, a monk endowed with five factors should ordain," and so forth.
168:
In the phrases such as "one who has failed in virtue regarding the higher virtue" (adhisīle sīlavipanno), a monk who has fallen into a Pārājika or a Saṅghādisesa offense is called "failed in virtue regarding the higher virtue." One who has fallen into the remaining five groups of offenses (pañcāpattikkhandha) is called "failed in conduct regarding behavior" (ajjhācāre ācāravipanno). One who, having abandoned right view, is endowed with extremist wrong views (antaggāhikā diṭṭhi) is called "failed in view regarding the higher view" (atidiṭṭhiyā diṭṭhivipanno). One who is devoid of the learning (suta) that should be desired for one leading a group is called "of little learning" (appassuto). One who does not know what should be known by him, such as offenses, is called "of poor wisdom" (duppañño). In this group of five, the first three terms are spoken of on the grounds of unsuitability, and the last two on the grounds of being factors of an offense.

"He does not know an offense" (āpattiṃ na jānāti) means when it is said, "I have done such and such an act," he does not know, "This person has fallen into such and such an offense." "He does not know the emergence" (vuṭṭhānaṃ na jānāti) means he does not know that "from an offense requiring emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī) or an offense requiring confession (desanāgāminī), emergence occurs in such and such a way." In this group of five, the first two terms are spoken of on the grounds of unsuitability, and the last three on the grounds of being factors of an offense.

"In the training regarding higher good conduct" (ābhisamācārikāya sikkhāya) means he is not capable of training [others] in the duties found in the Khandhakas. "In the body of the fundamental holy life" (ādibrahmacariyakāya) means he is not capable of training [others] in the Sekha rules (the training rules in the Vibhaṅga). "In the Abhidhamma" means he is not capable of training [others] in the delimitation of mind and matter (nāmarūpa-pariccheda). "In the Abhivinaya" means he is not capable of training [others] in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. "Not capable of training" (vinetuṃ na paṭibhalo) means in all these cases he is unable to teach. "To dissuade according to the Dhamma" (dhammato vivecetum) means to make [someone] relinquish [doubt] through a reason consistent with the Dhamma. In this group of five, there is an offense in all terms.

In the group of five beginning with "he does not know an offense," "in detail" (vitthārena) means together with both Vibhaṅgas (Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī). "Not well-handed" (na svāgatāni) means not well-mastered by heart. "Well-analyzed" (suvibhattāni) means well-distinguished, being free from the faults of mispronouncing words or confusing the order of words. "Well-recited" (suppavattīni) means proficient or mastered by heart and well-ascertained. "According to the Sutta" (suttaso) means well-ascertained by way of the Suttas (texts) to be brought from the Khandhakas and Parivāra. "According to the explanation" (anubyañjanaso) means well-ascertained through the completeness of syllables and words, being unbroken and with non-inverted syllables. By this, the Commentary is illustrated. For this decision comes from the Commentary. In this group of five also, there is an offense in all terms. The same method applies to the group of five ending with "less than ten years of seniority" (ūnadasavassa). Thus, the first three groups of five, three terms from the fourth, and two terms from the fifth—all these four groups of five are spoken of on the grounds of unsuitability. In the fourth group of five...
169:
In the fourth group of five (pañcaka), there are two items; in the fifth group of five, there are three items; and the three groups of five—the sixth, seventh, and eighth—are also mentioned. Thus, all four groups of five are stated in terms of the factors of the offense. However, in the bright side (sukkapakkha), as the reverse of the aforementioned dark side (kaṇhapakkha), eight groups of five appear, beginning with: "Monks, a monk endowed with five factors should perform the ordination ceremony, should give dependence (nissaya), and should be served by a novice; he is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekha)," and so on. In that bright side, there is no offense in any of the eight groups of five.

Regarding the question of to whom it should be given and to whom it should not be given: it should be given to one who is conscientious (lajjī). It should not be given to another. This is because of the word: "Monks, dependence should not be given to the shameless (alajjī); for him who gives it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." Even a monk living in dependence must not live in dependence on a shameless person. For it has been said: "Monks, one should not live in dependence on the shameless; for him who lives so, there is an offense of wrong-doing." Here, the word "alajjīnaṃ" uses the genitive case in the sense of the accusative, meaning one should not live in dependence on shameless individuals.

Therefore, a monk who has arrived at a new place, even if told, "Come, monk, take dependence," should take dependence only after investigating the conscientiousness of the dependence-giver for four or five days. This is because it has been said: "Monks, I allow you to wait for four or five days to know the compatibility of the monks." If, having heard from monks that "the Elder is conscientious," he wishes to take it on the very day of arrival, but the Elder says, "Wait a while, you will know while living here," and gives dependence after investigating his conduct for a few days, it is proper. However, a monk who goes to a place specifically to take dependence should take it on the very day he arrives; there is no exemption even for a single day. If the teacher is not available during the first watch and, not finding an opportunity, he sleeps thinking, "I will take it at dawn," and does not realize the sun has risen, there is no offense. But if he sleeps without the intention of "I will take it" and the sun rises, there is an offense of wrong-doing. A monk who goes to a place he has never been before and wishes to leave after staying for two or three days may stay without taking dependence. If he has the intention to stay, thinking "I will stay for seven days," then he must take dependence. If the Elder says, "What is the use of dependence for one staying only seven days?" then from the time of refusal, he is exempt from the offense.
170:
Because of the word: "Monks, I allow a monk who is traveling on a long journey and cannot find a dependence-giver to live without dependence," a monk on a long journey, if he does not find a dependence-giver traveling with him, is permitted to travel and live for many days without obtaining or taking dependence. If he enters a monastery where he has previously lived after taking dependence, he must take dependence even if staying for only one night. If he stays for a few days while resting mid-journey or searching for a caravan of travelers, there is no offense. During the Rains Retreat (vassa), however, he must reside permanently and must take dependence. For a monk traveling by boat, if the Rains Retreat arrives and he does not find a dependence-giver, there is no offense. If he falls ill mid-journey, it is proper for him to stay without taking dependence if he cannot find a dependence-giver.

A monk attending to the sick is also allowed to stay without taking dependence if requested by the sick monk. For it has been said: "Monks, I allow a sick monk who cannot find a dependence-giver to live without dependence. Monks, I allow a monk attending to the sick, who cannot find a dependence-giver and is requested (by the sick monk), to live without dependence" (Mahāvagga, 121). If, however, the sick monk is told "Request me" but does not request out of pride, the attendant should go (to seek dependence).

Because of the word: "Monks, I allow a forest-dwelling monk who is reflecting on a comfortable dwelling and cannot find a dependence-giver to live without dependence, thinking, 'When a suitable dependence-giver arrives, I will live in dependence on him,'" a monk who reflects on such a comfortable dwelling—where there is comfort by way of attaining serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā)—may live without dependence if he cannot find one. This privilege is not obtained by a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī), a Non-returner (Anāgāmī), or an Arahant. Nor is it obtained by one who has already achieved strong concentration or insight. As for the foolish worldlings (bālaputhujjana) who have abandoned meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), there is no need to mention them. This privilege is obtained by one whose serenity or insight is still tender (taruṇa). The support through invitation (pavāraṇā) is also allowed only for such a person. Therefore, even if this person goes after inviting the teachers, he may live without taking dependence until the full moon of Āsāḷhī, intending: "When a suitable dependence-giver arrives, I will live in dependence on him." If the teacher does not arrive in the month of Āsāḷhī, he must go to a place where dependence can be obtained.
171:
In the phrase “How is [a preceptor] taken?”, the meaning should be understood thus: First, one taking a preceptor in the presence of the preceptor should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet, sit in a squatting position, raise his hands in salutation, and say three times: “Venerable sir, please be my preceptor (Upajjhāyo me, bhante, hohi).” When the student (saddhivihārika) has spoken thus, if the preceptor makes it known by body, by speech, or by both body and speech, using such words as “Very well (Sāhu),” “It is a light burden (Lahu),” “It is appropriate (Opāyika),” “It is fit (Patirūpa),” or “Strive with grace (Pāsādikena sampādehi),” then the preceptor has been taken. In this regard, the taking of a preceptor consists solely of making one of these five phrases heard by speech or making the meaning known by body. Some teachers, however, say this with reference to the student’s acceptance of “Very well,” but that is not the standard. The preceptor is taken merely by the request and the granting; in this case, the [student's] acceptance is not a factor. 

The student (saddhivihārika) should not merely think, “I have taken a preceptor with this phrase,” but should also recognize this: “From this day forward, the Elder is my responsibility, and I am also the Elder’s responsibility.” For it has been said: 
“Monks, the preceptor will set up a mind towards the student as towards a son; the student will set up a mind towards the preceptor as towards a father. Thus, when they live with mutual respect, deference, and a common mode of living, they will arrive at growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma-Vinaya.”

This same decision applies to the taking of dependence (nissaya) in the presence of a teacher (ācariya). The distinction here is that the monk taking dependence in the presence of a teacher should squat and say three times: “Venerable sir, be my teacher; I will live in dependence on you (Ācariyo me, bhante, hohi, āyasmato nissāya vacchāmi).” The rest is exactly as previously described.

In the question “How is dependence settled (ceased)?”, first, the cessation of dependence from a preceptor should be known by five ways, and from a teacher who gives dependence by six ways. For it has been said: 
“Monks, there are these five cessations of dependence from a preceptor: the preceptor has departed, or has disrobed, or has died, or has gone over to another sect; the fifth is the order [of dismissal]. These, monks, are the five cessations of dependence from a preceptor.”
172:
'Monks, there are these six ways in which dependence on a teacher ceases: the teacher has departed, or has disrobed, or has died, or has joined another sect; dismissal is the fifth; or he has reunited with his preceptor. Monks, these are the six ways in which dependence on a teacher ceases.'

In this matter, the judgment is as follows: 'Pakkanto' (departed) means having gone to another region. When he has gone thus, if there is another teacher in the monastery who can provide dependence—one from whom dependence was previously taken or one with whom there is shared communion and use of requisites—dependence should be taken from him; one is not allowed to remain without dependence even for a single day. If no such person exists, but there is another virtuous (lajjī) and amiable (pesala) monk, then upon knowing his amiable nature, dependence should be requested on that very day. If he grants it, that is good.

If he asks, 'Will your preceptor return soon?' and the preceptor had said so, one should reply, 'Yes, venerable sir.' If he then says, 'In that case, wait until the preceptor arrives,' it is proper to wait. Otherwise, if one does not naturally know the monk's amiable nature, one should observe that monk's compatibility for four or five days, ask for permission, and then take dependence.

If there is no one in the monastery to provide dependence and the preceptor departed saying, 'I will return in a few days, do not be anxious,' one is allowed to remain without dependence until his return. Furthermore, if the people there cause the preceptor to stay five or ten days beyond the appointed time, the teacher should send word to the monastery saying, 'Let the young monks not be anxious; I will return on such-and-such a day.' In this case too, one is allowed to remain without dependence. Or, if while returning, there is an obstacle on the way such as a flood in the river or danger from robbers, and the young monks hear that the Elder is waiting for the water to recede or is seeking a companion, they are allowed to remain without dependence until his return. However, if the preceptor sends word saying, 'I will stay right here,' then they are no longer allowed to remain without dependence. They must go to a place where dependence can be obtained. In cases of disrobing, death, or joining another sect, one is not allowed to remain without dependence even for a single day; one must go to a place where dependence can be obtained.
173:
Command (āṇatti) means dismissal from dependence (nissaya). Therefore, whether by the method found in the Pāḷi, such as: 'I dismiss you,' or 'Do not enter this monastery,' or 'Take away your bowl and robes,' or 'You are not to serve me anymore'; or by the method outside the Pāḷi, such as: 'Do not ask me for permission to enter the village,' and so on—a pupil who has been dismissed from dependence by the teacher of dependence must apologize to the preceptor (upajjhāya). If he is not forgiven at first, he should perform a penalty (daṇḍakamma) and apologize personally three times. If he is still not forgiven, he should apologize by taking along the great elders (mahattheras) of that monastery. If he is still not forgiven, he should apologize by taking along monks from neighboring monasteries. If, despite doing so, he is still not forgiven, he should go elsewhere and live in the presence of monks who are peers of the preceptor. He should live there thinking, 'Perhaps he will forgive me upon knowing that I am living in the presence of his peers.' If he is still not forgiven even while living there, he should continue to stay in that place. If it is not possible to stay there due to faults such as famine, he should return to that very monastery and live after taking dependence (nissaya) in the presence of another teacher. This is the decision regarding dismissal (āṇatti).

Regarding the cessation of dependence (nissaya-paṭippassaddhi) from a teacher, in the phrase 'the teacher has departed,' some teachers depart after asking permission, while some depart without asking. The same applies to the pupil. Among them, if a pupil asks the teacher, 'Venerable Sir, I wish to go to such a place for some business,' and the teacher asks, 'When will you go?' and he says, 'I will go in the evening or after rising at night,' and the teacher consents, saying, 'Good,' the dependence ceases at that very moment. However, if when he says, 'Venerable Sir, I wish to go to such a place,' the teacher says, 'You shall know after wandering for alms in such a village,' and the pupil consents, saying, 'Good,' and goes from there, it is a proper departure. If he does not go, the dependence does not cease. Furthermore, if when he says, 'I am going,' the teacher says, 'Do not go yet; we shall know after consulting at night,' and he goes after consulting, it is a proper departure. If he does not go, the dependence does not cease. For a pupil who departs without asking the teacher, the dependence ceases upon crossing the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā); it does not cease for one who returns from within the precinct boundary. If the teacher asks the pupil, 'Friend, I will go to such a place,' and the pupil...
174:
...when asked "When?", the teacher says, "I will go in the evening or during the night," and the student consents, saying "Very well," the dependence lapses at that very moment. However, if the teacher says, "I will go tomorrow after wandering for alms," and the student consents, saying "Very well," the dependence does not lapse for the whole day, but lapses only on the following day. If the teacher says, "I will know whether I go or not after wandering for alms in such-and-such a village," and then does not go, the dependence does not lapse. Furthermore, if the teacher says, "I will go," and the student says, "Do not go yet; you shall know after consulting at night," and the teacher does not go even after consulting, the dependence does not lapse.

If both the teacher and the student go outside the boundary for some business, and if the teacher, having developed the intention to travel further, goes without asking but returns within the distance of two stone-throws (leḍḍupāta), the dependence does not lapse. If he returns after exceeding the distance of two stone-throws, it lapses. If the teacher and preceptor stay in another monastery after exceeding the distance of two stone-throws, the dependence lapses. If the teacher disrobes, passes away, or joins another faction (pakkha-saṅkanta), the dependence lapses at that very moment.

In the case of dismissal (āṇatti), if the teacher dismisses the student with the desire to release him from dependence, but the student still has attachment (ālaya), thinking, "Even though the teacher dismisses me, he is still soft-hearted," the dependence does not lapse. Even if the teacher has attachment but the student has no attachment and lays down the burden (dhura-nikkhepa), thinking, "I will no longer stay depending on this teacher," the dependence still does not lapse. If both have attachment, it certainly does not lapse; the dependence lapses only when both lay down the burden. The dismissed student must perform a penalty and apologize three times. If he is not forgiven, he should proceed according to the method mentioned regarding the preceptor.

It is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for a teacher to dismiss an antevāsika student or a saddhivihārika student who fulfills the duties toward the teacher and preceptor as prescribed and who is endowed with the five factors such as extreme affection. It is also an offense of wrongdoing for a teacher not to dismiss a student other than that (one who does not fulfill duties). This was spoken by the Blessed One:

"Monks, one who conducts himself properly should not be dismissed. Whoever should dismiss him, there is an offense of wrongdoing. And monks, one who does not conduct himself properly should not be kept without being dismissed. Whoever should not dismiss him, there is an offense of wrongdoing."
175:
“Monks, a teacher who does not dismiss a pupil (antevāsika) endowed with five qualities is at fault; one who dismisses him is not at fault. (Those five qualities are:) there is no excessive love for the teacher, no excessive devotion, no excessive shame, no excessive respect, and no excessive cultivation (of loving-kindness). Monks, a teacher who does not dismiss a pupil endowed with these five qualities is at fault; one who dismisses him is not at fault.” (Mahāvagga 81).

“Monks, a preceptor (upajjhāya) who does not dismiss a co-resident (saddhivihārika) endowed with five qualities is at fault; one who dismisses him is not at fault. (Those five qualities are:) there is no excessive love for the preceptor, no excessive devotion, no excessive shame, no excessive respect, and no excessive cultivation (of loving-kindness). Monks, a preceptor who does not dismiss a co-resident endowed with these five qualities is at fault; one who dismisses him is not at fault,” and so forth (Mahāvagga 68).

In that text (Mahāvagga Commentary 68), 'no excessive love' means there is no excessive worldly love (gehassita-pema) for the preceptor. 'No excessive cultivation' means there is no excessive cultivation of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā).

In the phrase 'coming together (samodhāna) with the preceptor' (Mahāvagga Commentary 83), the meeting should be understood by way of seeing and hearing. For if a co-resident living in dependence on a teacher sees the preceptor paying homage to a shrine in the same monastery, or wandering for alms in the same village, the dependence (nissaya) is re-established. If the preceptor sees him, but the co-resident does not see the preceptor, it is not re-established. If he sees the preceptor traveling on a road or going through the air, but because of the distance he only knows 'it is a monk' and does not know 'it is my preceptor,' it is not re-established. If he knows, it is re-established. If the preceptor lives on the upper floor of a mansion and the co-resident lives below, and the co-resident departs after drinking congee without seeing him, or departs after eating in a place in the sitting hall without seeing the preceptor sitting there, or in the Dhamma-hearing hall...
176:
...even if the preceptor is sitting there, if he departs after hearing the Dhamma without seeing him, the dependence is not re-established. Thus should meeting by way of seeing be understood. As for meeting by way of hearing: if he hears the voice of the preceptor who is preaching the Dhamma or giving a blessing (anumodanā) either in the monastery or in a house, and recognizes it as 'This is the voice of my preceptor,' the dependence is re-established. If he does not recognize it, it is not re-established. This is the decision regarding coming together (samodhāna).

Regarding 'Who should live in dependence, and who should not live in dependence?': because of the word, 'Monks, I allow a competent and capable monk to live in dependence for five years, and an incompetent one for as long as he lives' (Mahāvagga 103), an incompetent monk must live in dependence for his whole life. If that monk does not find a teacher more senior than himself, even if he has sixty or seventy years of seniority since his higher ordination, he must sit in the crouching position (ukkutika) before a competent monk who is junior to him, raise his hands in salutation (añjali), and say three times: 'Venerable sir, be my teacher; I will live in dependence on the venerable one.' Thus he must take dependence. Even when asking permission to enter a village, he should sit in the crouching position, raise his hands in salutation, and say: 'Teacher, I ask permission to enter the village.' This is the method for all requests for permission.

A monk who is competent and has five years since higher ordination is allowed to live without dependence. Therefore, a monk who is to be released from dependence (nissaya-muccanaka) must, at the minimum limit of five years since higher ordination, have mastered and memorized the two Mātikās (Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī). He should learn four recital sections (bhāṇavāra) from the Suttas for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma on the full-moon and new-moon days. He should learn one course of discourse similar to the Andhakavinda Sutta, Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, or Ambaṭṭha Sutta for the purpose of preaching to the gathered assemblies. He should learn the three types of blessings (anumodanā) for the purpose of giving thanks at Sangha-meals, auspicious, and inauspicious occasions. He should learn the decisions on formal acts (kammākamma-vinicchaya) to know about Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so on. He should learn one meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) ending in Arahatship, either by way of serenity (samādhi) or insight (vipassanā), for the purpose of performing the duties of a recluse. This much should be learned. By this much, that monk becomes a learned one (bahussuta) of the four directions, and is allowed to live by his own authority in any place.

Regarding the statement: 'Monks, a monk endowed with five qualities may live without dependence.' Those five qualities are: 'Monks, here in this teaching, a monk is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekha), the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.' Monks, a monk endowed with these five qualities is allowed to live without dependence.
177:
Monks, a monk endowed with five factors should not live without a teacher (without taking dependence). (What are the five?) He is not endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (an Arahant), he is not endowed with the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, he is not endowed with the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training, he is not endowed with the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training, and he is not endowed with the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training. Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should not live without a teacher.

Monks, a monk endowed with another five factors should also not live without a teacher. (What are the five?) He is without faith, he is without shame, he is without fear of wrongdoing, he is lazy, and he is unmindful. Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should not live without a teacher.

Monks, a monk endowed with another five factors should also not live without a teacher. (What are the five?) He is deficient in virtue regarding the higher virtue (adhisīla), he is deficient in conduct regarding proper behavior (ajjhācāra), he is deficient in view regarding excessive views (atidiṭṭhi), he is of little learning, and he is of poor wisdom. Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should not live without a teacher.

Monks, a monk endowed with another five factors should also not live without a teacher. (What are the five?) He does not know what is an offense, he does not know what is not an offense, he does not know what is a light offense, he does not know what is a heavy offense, and both of his Pātimokkhas are not well-transmitted to him in detail, not well-analyzed, not well-recited, and not well-decided according to the rules and the accessory features. Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should not live without a teacher.

Monks, a monk endowed with another five factors should also not live without a teacher. (What are the five?) He does not know what is an offense, he does not know what is not an offense, he does not know what is a light offense, he does not know what is a heavy offense, and he has less than five years of standing (vassa). Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should not live without a teacher (thus He said).
178:
In this Pali text also, it should be understood that the prohibition is made by way of unsuitability and by way of the factors of offense, just as in the previous method.

Permission should not be given to pupils (antevāsika) and disciples (saddhivihārika) who do not know the Vinaya rules, who are unskilled in the Vinaya rules, and who wish to travel to other regions. If they give permission, the teachers (ācariya) and preceptors (upajjhāya) incur an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). If those pupils go without permission, they also incur an offense of wrongdoing. For it has been said:

"Monks, in this Dispensation, many monks who are ignorant, unskilled, and wishing to travel to other regions ask permission from their teachers and preceptors. Monks, those pupils should be asked by the teachers and preceptors: 'Where will you go? With whom will you go?' Monks, if those ignorant and unskilled monks should name other ignorant and unskilled monks (as companions), monks, the teachers and preceptors should not give permission. If they should give permission, they incur an offense of wrongdoing. Monks, if those ignorant and unskilled monks should go without the permission of their teachers and preceptors, they incur an offense of wrongdoing."

## Thus, in the Pālimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-saṅgaha,
## The Discussion on the Decision regarding Dependence (Nissaya-vinicchaya-kathā) is finished.
## 24. Discussion on the Decision regarding Boundaries (Sīmā-vinicchaya-kathā)

In this term "Sīmā" (boundary), there are two kinds: the bound boundary (baddha-sīmā) and the unbound boundary (abaddha-sīmā). Among them, a boundary that is designated by connecting sign to sign (nimitta), being endowed with the three kinds of perfection (sampatti) and avoiding the eleven kinds of defective boundaries (vipatti-sīmā), is called a bound boundary. The boundaries are called defective boundaries because it is said that the formal acts (kamma) fail due to the boundary in these eleven ways: a boundary that is too small, one that is too large, one with broken signs, one with shadow signs, one without signs, one designated while standing outside the boundary, one designated in a river, one designated in the sea, one designated in a natural lake (jātassara), one designated by overlapping one boundary with another, and one designated by covering one boundary with another.

Among those defective boundaries, a boundary that is too small is one where twenty-one monks are unable to sit. A boundary that is too large is one that is designated exceeding three yojanas even by a hair's breadth.
179: A broken boundary mark (khaṇḍanimittā) refers to a boundary with disconnected marks. If one proclaims the mark in the east, then successively in the south, west, and north, and then once more proclaims the previously proclaimed mark in the east to close it, it becomes an unbroken boundary (akhaṇḍanimittā). However, if one brings it around successively and proclaims the mark in the north and stops there, it is a broken boundary. Another type of broken boundary is one consecrated by making a single mark in the middle of things that do not qualify as marks, such as a tree with bark-core (such as palms or coconuts), a stump, a mound of earth, or a mound of sand. A shadow-mark boundary (chāyānimittā) is one consecrated by making any shadow, such as a mountain shadow, the mark. A markless boundary (animittā) is one consecrated without proclaiming any marks at all. A boundary consecrated while standing outside (bahisīme ṭhitasammatā) is one consecrated by a person standing outside the marks after they have been proclaimed. A boundary consecrated in a river, sea, or natural lake (jātassara) is one consecrated in those places. Even if so consecrated, it is considered unconsecrated because of the word: 'Monks, the entire river is not a boundary, the entire sea is not a boundary, the entire natural lake is not a boundary.' A boundary consecrated by mixing boundaries (sīmāya sīmaṃ sambhindantena) is one consecrated by mixing one's own boundary with the boundary of others. For example, if to the east of an old monastery, there are two trees, a mango (amba) and a rose-apple (jambu), with branches intertwined; the rose-apple is to the west of the mango. The monastery boundary was established by including the rose-apple inside and proclaiming the mango as the mark. Later, monks building a new monastery to the east of that monastery establish a boundary by including the mango inside and proclaiming the rose-apple as the mark; thus the boundaries are mixed. Therefore, if the boundary of the first-established monastery has not yet been consecrated, a boundary precinct (sīmā-upacāra) should be left. If it has been consecrated, an inter-boundary space (sīmantarikā) of about a cubit (hattha) from the final edge should be left. In the Kurundī, it is said: 'Even about a span (vidatthi) is allowable.' In the Mahāpaccari, it is said: 'Even about four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) is allowable.' A single tree can also serve as a mark for two boundaries. However, as that tree grows, it causes boundary confusion (sīmasaṅkara), so it should not be done. A boundary consecrated by overlapping boundaries (sīmāya sīmaṃ ajjhottharantena) is one consecrated by overlapping one's own boundary onto the boundary of others. If one consecrates one's own boundary by including the whole or a part of a boundary already established by others, it is called overlapping a boundary. It is allowable to consecrate a boundary for monks even inside, overlapping the boundary of bhikkhunīs. For bhikkhunīs also, in the boundary of monks...
180:
This method is the same. This is because those [bhikkhunīs] do not serve as quorum-fillers (gaṇapūraka) in the legal acts of the others [monks], nor do they make the formal act (kammavācā) schismatic (vagga). Thus, a boundary should be consecrated by avoiding these eleven defective boundaries (vipattisīmā).

A boundary endowed with the three successes (sampatti) is one endowed with the success of marks (nimittasampatti), the success of the assembly (parisampatti), and the success of the formal act (kammavācāsampatti). Among these, success of marks means a boundary consecrated by properly proclaiming the marks available in each direction from among the eight types of marks mentioned: mountain-mark (pabbata), stone-mark (pāsāṇa), forest-mark (vana), tree-mark (rukkha), path-mark (magga), anthill-mark (vammika), river-mark (nadī), and water-mark (udaka), in this manner: 'What is the mark in the east?' 'A mountain, venerable sir.' 'This mountain is the mark.'

Regarding the proclamation of marks, this is the decision (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā 138): The Vinaya-holder (vinayadhara) should ask, 'What is the mark in the east?' The answer should be, 'A mountain, venerable sir.' In proclaiming this mark, whether an ordained person or an unordained person (layperson or novice) proclaims it, it is allowable. Then the Vinaya-holder should proclaim the mark thus: 'This mountain is the mark.' However, it is not allowable to proclaim it as: 'We make this mountain the mark,' 'We will make it,' 'The mark has been made,' 'Let it be the mark,' 'It is,' or 'It will be.' The same method applies to stones and so on. When asking 'What is the mark?' in the east, the south-east, the south, the south-west, the west, the north-west, the north, and the north-east, if the answer is 'Water, venerable sir,' one should proclaim, 'This water is the mark.' Here, without stopping at the north-east, one should proclaim the first-proclaimed mark again: 'What is the mark in the east? A mountain, venerable sir. This mountain is the mark,' and only then stop. Only in this way are the marks connected to one another, and even though the marks are proclaimed only once each, they are considered proclaimed. In the Andhaka Commentary (Andhakaṭṭhakathā), however, it is said: 'One who is binding the boundary circle should proclaim the mark three times.'

Now, mountains and so on that qualify as marks should be understood: A mountain is of three types: a pure earth mountain, a pure stone mountain, and a mixture of both. All three types of mountains are allowable as marks, but a mound of sand is not. Other mountains, if smaller than the size of an elephant (seven cubits and a span), are not allowable; from the size of an elephant up to the size of Mount Sineru, they are allowable. If there are four mountains in the four directions, or three mountains in three directions...
181:
(The markers) exist. It is permissible to designate (a boundary) with four or three mountain markers. However, it is not permissible to designate it with two markers or one marker. This same principle applies to other markers such as stone markers. Therefore, one who establishes a mountain marker must ask, "Is it continuous or not continuous?" If it is continuous, it should not be used. This is because even if one proclaims it in four or eight directions, it amounts to proclaiming only a single marker.

Therefore, if a mountain stands surrounding a monastery in a circular fashion, one should proclaim it as a marker in one direction, and for the other directions, one should place that mountain on the outside and proclaim other markers that are on the inside. If one wishes to include one-third or one-half of the mountain within the Sīmā, one should not proclaim the mountain as the marker; instead, for whatever area one wishes to include inside, one should proclaim one of the markers such as a tree or an anthill growing on that very mountain beyond that area. If one wishes to include an entire mountain measuring one or two leagues within the Sīmā, one should proclaim markers such as trees or anthills located on the ground outside the mountain.

Regarding stone markers, an iron ball also falls under the category of stone. Therefore, any kind of stone is permissible. In terms of size, however, a stone the size of an elephant is categorized as a mountain, and thus it is not permissible. A stone the size of a large ox or a large buffalo is permissible. At the minimum limit, a stone the size of a ball of molasses weighing thirty-two palas is permissible. A stone smaller than that is not permissible. A brick, even if large, is not permissible. A pile of stones not suitable for use as a marker is also not permissible, let alone a pile of earth or sand.

Whether it is a flat rock level with the ground and resembling a threshing floor, or a stone rising from the ground like a stump, if it is of the prescribed size, it is permissible. A flat rock, even if very large, still falls under the category of stone. Therefore, if one wishes to include a portion of a large flat rock within the Sīmā, one should not proclaim that flat rock as the marker, but should instead proclaim another stone situated upon that flat rock. If a monastery is built upon a flat rock, or if a flat rock pierces through the middle of a monastery, such a flat rock is not permissible as a marker. For if one proclaims it as a marker, the monastery would be above the marker. Since a marker must necessarily be outside the Sīmā, the monastery would also end up being outside the Sīmā. A flat rock that stands surrounding a monastery, having been proclaimed as a marker in one place, should not be proclaimed again in another place.
182:
Regarding forest markers, a grass forest or a forest of trees with bark-cores such as palms and coconuts is not permissible. However, a forest of heartwood trees such as Teak and Sal, or a forest of trees mixed with heartwood trees, is permissible. Such a forest is permissible even if it consists of at least four or five trees; if fewer than that, it is not permissible. At the maximum, it is permissible even if it spans a hundred leagues. If a monastery is built in the middle of a forest, the forest should not be proclaimed as a marker. Monks who wish to include a portion of the forest within the Sīmā should not proclaim the forest as a marker, but should instead proclaim the trees, stones, etc., within that forest as markers. A forest that stands surrounding a monastery, having been proclaimed as a marker in one place, should not be proclaimed again in another place.

Regarding tree markers, trees with bark-cores such as palms and coconuts are not permissible. A living heartwood tree is permissible if it is at least eight finger-breadths in height and has a girth about the size of a stylus. If smaller than that, it is not permissible. At the maximum, even a tree as large as the well-established Suppatiṭṭhita Banyan tree, which is twelve leagues wide, is permissible. A tree raised from a seed in a bamboo tube, a reed tube, or a small cup is not permissible even if it reaches the prescribed size. However, if it is removed from that nursery pot and planted in the ground even for a moment, and a basin is made and watered, it is permissible to proclaim it as a marker. The emergence of new roots and branches (while in the bamboo tube, etc.) is not a valid factor. However, in the case of a tree planted by cutting the trunk, it is only suitable if such new roots and branches emerge. A person proclaiming the marker is permitted to say "tree," or "Teak tree," or "Sal tree." A large tree similar to the continuous, well-established Suppatiṭṭhita Banyan tree, having been proclaimed as a marker in one place, should not be proclaimed again in another place.

Regarding road markers, forest paths, field paths, river paths, and tank paths are not permissible. Only a footpath or a cart-road is permissible. A road that goes through and connects two or three villages (is permissible). A road that branches off from a footpath or cart-road and then returns to the same cart-road, and footpaths or cart-roads that are no longer used by people, are not permissible. Only roads that are constantly used by pedestrian caravans or cart caravans are permissible. If two roads branch out and later merge into one like the pole of a cart, they should be proclaimed as a marker only once, either at the point of branching or at the point of merging; they should not be proclaimed again. This is because such a road marker is a continuous marker. If four roads surrounding a monastery go in four directions, having proclaimed one in the middle, it is not permissible to proclaim another. This is because it is a continuous marker. However, a road that passes through the corner of a monastery is permissible to be proclaimed on the other side. A road that passes through the middle of a monastery should not be proclaimed as a marker. For if it is proclaimed, it would be as if the monastery is above the marker. If the inner wheel track of a cart-road is made the marker, the road is outside the Sīmā. If the outer wheel track is made the marker, the outer wheel track is outside the Sīmā...
183:
(The outer track of the cart) is outside the boundary; the remaining inner track falls within the boundary. One who designates a road as a boundary mark (nimitta) is allowed to designate it by any of the ten names such as "magga, pantha, patha, pajja," etc. It is not permissible to designate a road that surrounds a monastery in the form of a moat as a boundary mark in one place and then again in another place.

Regarding an anthill as a boundary mark, at the minimum, an anthill that has arisen on that very day, eight finger-breadths high and about the size of an ox horn, is permissible; anything smaller is not. At the maximum, an anthill as large as Mount Himavanta is also permissible. However, a single continuous large anthill that surrounds the monastery should not be designated as a boundary mark in one place and then again in another.

Regarding a river as a boundary mark: if, during the reign of righteous kings, it rains once every fortnight, every ten days, or every five days, but the flow of water ceases as soon as the clouds disappear, such a flow does not count as a river. A river is one where the flow does not cease throughout the four months of the rainy season during such a good rainy period. Whether at a crossing point or not, if a bhikkhunī crosses it while covering the three circles (of the body) according to the Sekhiya rules and without lifting her inner robe, and her inner robe gets wet even by one or two finger-breadths, that river can serve as a boundary mark for monks establishing a sīmā. This same type of river should be considered for a bhikkhunī crossing to the other side, for performing Saṅgha activities such as the Uposatha, and for establishing a boundary that spans both sides of the river. Like a road, a river that flows around a monastery in the shape of a cart-pole or a moat should not be designated as a boundary mark in one place and then again in another. The same rule applies to four rivers that flow through the four directions of the monastery and intersect. If they are distinct, unmixed rivers, all four may be designated as boundary marks. If the flow of a river is blocked by planting tree trunks like a fence and using creepers, straw, etc., but the water still overflows the barrier and continues to flow, it is permissible to use it as a boundary mark. If a bridge is constructed in such a way that the water cannot flow, it is not permissible to designate it as a river-mark at that non-flowing spot. At the flowing spot, it is a river-mark; at the non-flowing spot, it is permissible to designate it as a water-mark (udakanimitta). A river that does not flow due to lack of water during a drought or in the summer is also permissible (as a boundary mark). When a canal is diverted from a large river, even if it resembles a small river and flows constantly, sustaining three types of crops, it is not permissible to designate it as a boundary mark (because it is man-made). However, if a canal originally diverted from a large river eventually breaks through and flows naturally along that path over a long period, becoming a river inhabited by crocodiles, turtles, etc., and navigable by boats, then it is permissible to designate that river as a boundary mark.
184:
In designating a water-mark (udakanimitta), it is not permissible to fill a boat or jars, etc., with water in a waterless place and proclaim it as a water-mark; only water situated on the ground is permissible. That water must be still water situated in a pit, a pond, a reservoir, a natural lake, a salt-pit, the ocean, etc. Unstable water in a flowing river, a pipe, or a canal is not permissible. In the Andhaka Commentary, it is said, "Water that must be drawn from deep pits and such should not be made a boundary mark." This statement is poorly said and is merely their own opinion (attanomati). At the minimum, whether it be water in a hole dug by a pig or in a pond where village children play, or even water drawn with jars and filled into a pit dug in the ground at that very moment—if it remains until the end of the formal act (kammavācā), it is permissible, whether it be little or much. To mark the boundary in that place, one should make a pile of stones, sand, or earth, or set up a stone pillar or a wooden post. It is permissible for a monk to do this or have it done. However, this is not permissible in the case of a boundary for gains (lābhasīmā). Since a boundary of common communion (samānasaṃvāsakasīmā) does not oppress anyone but merely facilitates the Vinaya acts of the monks, it is permissible in this boundary (to set up boundary markers, etc.).

It is permissible to establish a boundary using these eight kinds of boundary marks, either of one kind or mixed with one another. A boundary thus established and bound cannot be formed with only one or two marks. Starting from three, it can be bound by even a hundred of the aforementioned marks. If established with three marks, the boundary has the shape of a triangle. If with four, it may be square, or shaped like a cross, a half-moon, or a drum (mudiṅga), etc. With more marks, it can have various shapes. A boundary established by proclaiming the marks in this manner should be known as "a boundary endowed with the perfection of marks" (nimittasampatti).

## Endowed with the Perfection of the Assembly (Parisāsampatti)
Being endowed with the perfection of the assembly means that at least four monks must assemble, and all monks present within that village territory—excluding those within an existing established boundary (baddhasīmā), a river, the ocean, or a natural lake—must either be within arm's reach (hatthapāsa) or have their consent (chanda) conveyed.

## Endowed with the Perfection of the Formal Act (Kammavācāsampatti)
Being endowed with the perfection of the formal act means:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. As many marks as have been proclaimed all around, if the Saṅgha is ready, the Saṅgha should establish a boundary of common communion and a single Uposatha by these marks. This is the motion (ñatti).
Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. As many marks as have been proclaimed all around, the Saṅgha establishes a boundary by these marks."
185:
If the agreement of the sīmā for common affiliation and a single Uposatha by these markers pleases the venerable ones, let them be silent. If it does not please anyone, he should speak. The Sangha has agreed upon the sīmā for common affiliation and a single Uposatha with these markers. It pleases the Sangha, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this agreement. By this pure ñattidutiya kammavācā (motion and second proclamation) thus spoken, the boundary is agreed upon. At the conclusion of the kammavācā, the area within the markers becomes the sīmā, and the markers are outside the sīmā.

Once the sīmā is thus bound, for the sake of the comfort of not being separated from the three robes (ticīvara) and for the sake of firmness, the agreement of non-separation (avippavāsa) should be made. That agreement of non-separation should be performed as follows: "Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. If it is suitable for the Sangha, the Sangha should agree upon that sīmā for common affiliation and a single Uposatha, which has been agreed upon by the Sangha, as a boundary of non-separation from the three robes, excluding the village and its precincts. This is the motion.

Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. The Sangha agrees upon that sīmā for common affiliation and a single Uposatha, which has been agreed upon by the Sangha, as a boundary of non-separation from the three robes, excluding the village and its precincts. If the agreement of this sīmā as a boundary of non-separation from the three robes, excluding the village and its precincts, pleases the venerable ones, let them be silent. If it does not please anyone, he should speak.

The Sangha has agreed upon that sīmā as a boundary of non-separation from the three robes, excluding the village and its precincts. It pleases the Sangha, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this matter."

In this context, market towns and cities are also to be included under the term 'village' (gāma). The 'precincts of a village' (gāmūpacāra) refers to the fence if the village is enclosed, or the surrounding area if it is not. In these villages and village precincts, a monk who has determined his three robes (ticīvara) cannot obtain the privilege of non-separation from the robes. This is because this avippavāsa sīmā is stated as "excluding the village and its precincts," and thus it does not spread over (overlap) the village and its precincts, but only overlaps the samānasaṃvāsa sīmā. Here, the samānasaṃvāsa sīmā exists by its own nature. The avippavāsa sīmā exists only where the samānasaṃvāsa sīmā is. For that avippavāsa sīmā, there is no need to separately proclaim the markers (nimittha). If a village exists in that place at the time of agreeing upon the avippavāsa sīmā, that sīmā does not overlap the village. If a village is established later after the sīmā has been agreed upon, that village falls within the sīmā. Just like a village established later, an area that flourishes later behind an initially established house or village also falls within the sīmā. Thus, whether it is a house or a village that enters first, it falls within the sīmā.
186:
The avippavāsa sīmā does not overlap the village precincts; it only overlaps the samānasaṃvāsa sīmā. Here, the samānasaṃvāsa sīmā exists by its own nature, while the avippavāsa sīmā exists only where the samānasaṃvāsa sīmā is. For that avippavāsa sīmā, there is no separate proclamation of markers. If a village exists there at the time of the agreement of non-separation, the sīmā does not overlap it. However, if a village is settled after the sīmā has been agreed upon, it is counted as being within the sīmā. Just as with a later settlement, an area that expands later after an initial settlement is also counted as being within the sīmā. If houses were built at the time of the boundary agreement and there was the intention (ālaya) "we shall move in," but people have not yet entered, or if they have abandoned houses in an old village and gone elsewhere, it is no longer a village, and the sīmā can overlap it. If even a single family has entered or remains without leaving, it is still a village, and the sīmā cannot overlap it. This is the summary here.

In detail (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā 138): A monk wishing to bind a sīmā should ask monks from neighboring monasteries about the limits of their boundaries. He should leave aside the interval between boundaries (sīmantarika) for monasteries with bound boundaries, and the precincts (upacāra) for monasteries without bound boundaries. At a time when traveling monks are not moving about, if he wishes to bind a sīmā in a village territory, he should send word to the monks in the monasteries with bound boundaries there, saying, "We shall bind a sīmā today; do not leave the limits of your own sīmā." Monks in monasteries without bound boundaries should be assembled together, and the consent (chanda) of those entitled to give it should be brought. Mahāsummatthera said: "If one wishes to include other village territories as well, the monks living in those villages must also come; the consent of those who do not come must be brought." Mahāpadumatthera, however, said: "Different village territories are like separately bound boundaries; consent and purity (pārisuddhi) do not come from there. However, monks within the markers must come." He further said: "At the time of agreeing upon the samānasaṃvāsa sīmā, coming or not coming is permissible. But at the time of agreeing upon the avippavāsa sīmā, monks within the markers must come, and the consent of those who do not come must be brought."

When the monks have thus assembled and the consent of those entitled to give it has been brought, attendants (ārāmika) and novices (sāmaṇera) should be stationed at roads, river crossings, village gates, etc., to quickly bring visiting monks into the hatthapāsa (forearm's reach) or to keep them outside the boundary. After signaling with the sound of a drum or conch shell and proclaiming the markers, the sīmā is bound with the kammavācā beginning with "Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs." Only at the conclusion of the kammavācā are the markers placed outside, and the sīmā reaches down through the substance of the earth to the water's edge. This is how monks wishing to agree upon a samānasaṃvāsa sīmā first bind a khaṇḍasīmā (small boundary) so that they can easily perform Sangha acts such as novice ordination and higher ordination (upasampadā). Monks binding that khaṇḍasīmā should know the duty (vatta). How? If it is bound in a monastery where all buildings such as the Bodhi tree, stupa, and refectory have been built, it should not be bound in a place where many people assemble, but in a quiet place at the edge of the monastery. If it is bound in a monastery not yet built, the locations for the Bodhi tree, stupa, etc., should be marked, and it should be placed in a quiet spot at the edge of the monastery among the structures that will eventually stand. Thus it is.
187:
After signaling with a large drum or a conch shell and proclaiming the markers (nimitta), the boundary (sīmā) is established with the kammavācā beginning with 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.' Only at the conclusion of the kammavācā, having excluded the markers, does the boundary extend downwards to the water-bearing level of the earth.

Those wishing to consecrate this boundary of common communion (samānasamvāsaka-sīmā) should first establish a small boundary (khaṇḍa-sīmā) to facilitate Saṅgha acts such as going forth (pabbajjā) and higher ordination (upasampadā). Those establishing that khaṇḍa-sīmā must know the proper conduct. If establishing it in a monastery already built with all structures like the Bodhi tree, cetiya, and refectory, it should not be established in the center where many people gather, but in a secluded spot at the edge of the monastery. For those establishing it in a monastery not yet built, they should mark the locations for all structures like the Bodhi tree and cetiya, and establish it in a secluded spot at the edge of the monastery site. At its minimum limit, if it can accommodate 21 bhikkhus, it is valid; if fewer, it is not valid. It is valid even if it accommodates more than a thousand bhikkhus. Those establishing that boundary should place stones as markers around the boundary precinct (sīmā-māḷaka). Monks standing within a khaṇḍa-sīmā must not establish a mahā-sīmā (great boundary), nor should those in a mahā-sīmā establish a khaṇḍa-sīmā. One must stand within the khaṇḍa-sīmā itself to establish a khaṇḍa-sīmā.

The procedure for establishing it is as follows: Proclaiming the markers all around as 'This stone is a marker,' the boundary is consecrated with the kammavācā. Then, to strengthen it, the kammavācā for non-separation (avippavāsa) should be performed. By doing so, those who come saying 'We will uproot the boundary' will not be able to do so. After consecrating the boundary, stones for the inter-boundary space (sīmantarikā) should be placed outside the boundary. The inter-boundary space is valid at a minimum of one cubit (ratana). The Kurundī Commentary states, 'Even one span (vidatthi) is valid.' The Mahāpaccari Commentary states, 'Even four finger-breadths (aṅgula) is valid.' If the monastery is large, two, three, or even more khaṇḍa-sīmās should be established.

After thus consecrating the khaṇḍa-sīmā, when the mahā-sīmā is to be consecrated, one should leave the khaṇḍa-sīmā, stand in the mahā-sīmā, and proclaim the inter-boundary stones while moving around in order. Then, after proclaiming the remaining markers, the samānasamvāsaka-sīmā is consecrated with the kammavācā without leaving the hatthapāsa (forearm's length). To strengthen that boundary, the avippavāsa kammavācā should also be performed. By doing so, those who come saying 'We will uproot the boundary' will not be able to do so. If...
188:
After proclaiming the markers of the khaṇḍa-sīmā, then the markers of the inter-boundary space (sīmantarikā), one proclaims the markers of the mahā-sīmā. Having proclaimed the markers in these three places, it is permissible to first establish whichever boundary is desired. Nevertheless, it should be established starting from the khaṇḍa-sīmā according to the method already mentioned. When boundaries are established in this way, monks standing in a khaṇḍa-sīmā do not invalidate the acts of those performing a Saṅgha act in the mahā-sīmā, nor do those in the mahā-sīmā invalidate the acts of those in the khaṇḍa-sīmā. However, those standing in the inter-boundary space do not invalidate the acts of those in either boundary. For those performing acts while standing in the village territory (gāmakhetta), those standing in the inter-boundary space do invalidate their acts. This is because the inter-boundary space is connected to the village territory.

A boundary is not said to be established only when it is established on the ground; indeed, it is truly established even when established on a rock surface, in a hut, in a cave, in a mansion, or on a mountain top. Among these, when establishing it on a rock surface, one should not make a marker by carving a line or digging a small hole on the rock; rather, stones suitable for markers should be placed and proclaimed. At the conclusion of the kammavācā, the boundary descends and is established down to the water-bearing level of the earth. Since marker stones do not remain in their original places, a line should be carved around them, or stones should be bored into the four corners, or letters should be carved saying, 'This is the limit of the boundary.' Some malicious people might set fire, saying 'We will burn the boundary,' but only the stones burn; the boundary cannot be burned.

In a hut as well, without proclaiming the walls, the boundary should be consecrated by placing stone markers, encompassing a space for twenty-one monks within. The boundary exists only within the walls. If there is no space for twenty-one monks within the walls, the marker stones should be placed at the front entrance and consecrated. If even this is insufficient, markers should be placed outside at the drip-line (nibbodakapatanaṭṭhāna) and consecrated. When consecrated in this way, the entire hut is within the boundary.

In a cave with four walls, those establishing the boundary should proclaim only the stones without proclaiming the walls. If there is no space inside, markers should be placed at the entrance. In this way, the boundary exists both inside and outside the cave.
189:
In an upper mansion (pāsāda) as well, the boundary (sīmā) should be consecrated by placing stones inside without proclaiming the wall as a marker (nimitta). If there is not enough space inside, it should be consecrated by placing stones on the porch. A boundary consecrated in this way exists only in the upper mansion and does not extend downwards. However, if the wall on the lower floor of a mansion built upon many pillars and beams is within the markers and rises to be continuous with the beams, the boundary also extends downwards. A boundary established on the upper floor of a single-pillar mansion extends downwards if there is space for twenty-one monks at the top of the pillar. If the boundary is established by placing stones on the eaves or projections extending from the mansion wall, the mansion wall is within the boundary. Whether it extends to the lower part of that mansion should be understood according to the method already stated.

Those marking the boundary in a lower mansion should also not proclaim the wall or wooden pillars as markers; however, it is permissible to mark stone pillars attached to the wall. A boundary marked in this way exists only within the outer pillars of the lower mansion. If the wall of the lower mansion is connected to the upper floor, the boundary also rises to the upper mansion. If the markers are placed at the drip-line outside the mansion, the entire mansion is situated within the boundary.

If the plateau on a mountain top is suitable as a space for twenty-one monks, the boundary should be established there as if on a stone slab; the boundary extends down to the base of the mountain within that same limit. On a mountain shaped like the base of a palmyra tree, a boundary established at the top also extends downwards. If a mountain is shaped like a canopy and has space for twenty-one monks at the top but not at the bottom, a boundary established at the top of that mountain does not extend downwards. Similarly, whether it is shaped like a mudinga-drum or a paṇava-drum, if there is no space of boundary-size at the bottom or in the middle, a boundary established at the top does not extend downwards. If two mountain peaks are situated close together and neither peak has enough space for a boundary at the top, the space between those peaks should be built up or filled to make them continuous, and then the boundary should be consecrated at the top. If there is a mountain shaped like a snake's hood and a boundary is established because there is enough space at the top, the boundary does not extend down if there is a hollow cavern underneath. However, if there is a stone cavity of boundary-size in the middle, it does extend down, and that stone is situated within the boundary. Furthermore, if the summit of the lower cave of that mountain reaches the tip and stands there, the boundary extends; it is a boundary both below and above. If there is a cave from the outside to the inside of the base of the mountain, outside the boundary markers consecrated above, the boundary does not extend to the outside. Furthermore, if there is a cave from the inside to the outside of the base of the mountain, within the boundary markers consecrated above, the boundary does not extend to the inner cave. Furthermore, if the boundary limit at the top is narrow and the cave below is large, the boundary exists only at the top, exceeding the boundary limit, and does not extend downwards. If the cave is...
190:
...and stays there, the boundary descends; it is a boundary both below and above. If there is a cave extending from outside to inside the limit of the boundary consecrated above, the boundary does not descend to the outside. Furthermore, if there is a cave extending from inside to outside the limit of the boundary consecrated above, the boundary does not descend into the inner cave. Moreover, if the boundary limit above is small and the cave below is large, extending beyond the boundary limit, the boundary exists only above and does not descend below. If the cave is small, being of the minimum boundary size, and the boundary above is large and covers that cave, the boundary descends. If the cave is very small and does not meet the boundary size, the boundary exists only above and does not descend below. If half of it breaks and falls away, even if it is of boundary size, the half that fell outside is not the boundary. As for the part that did not fall, if it is of boundary size, it is indeed the boundary.

A khaṇḍasīmā (small boundary) may have a low foundation; if that foundation is filled to make it high, it remains a boundary. Even if a house is built within the boundary, it is situated within the boundary. Even if a pond is dug within the boundary, it remains a boundary. If a flood overflows and covers the boundary circle, it is proper to perform the (Saṅgha) act by constructing a platform in the boundary courtyard (sīmā-māḷaka). If there is a river flowing like a tunnel beneath the boundary and a monk with psychic powers sits in that river: if that river existed first and the boundary was consecrated later, it does not invalidate the act. If the boundary was consecrated first and the river came later, it can invalidate the act; a monk standing on the ground below also certainly invalidates the act.

If there is a banyan tree in the boundary courtyard, and its branches or the aerial roots originating from it touch the ground of the Mahāsīmā (great boundary) or the trees growing there, the act should be performed after clearing the Mahāsīmā, or those branches and aerial roots should be cut so they stay outside. Monks who have climbed onto branches that do not touch (the ground) should be brought within the hatthapāsa (reach). Similarly, if a branch or aerial root of a tree growing in the Mahāsīmā rests on the boundary courtyard in the manner described, the act should be performed after clearing the boundary in the same manner, or those branches and aerial roots should be cut so they stay outside the boundary. If, while an act is being performed in the courtyard, any monk enters the courtyard and sits on a branch in the air, and his feet reach the ground, or his worn or covered robe touches the ground, it is not proper to perform the act. However, it is proper to perform the act after making him lift his feet and his worn or covered robes.
191:
This aforementioned characteristic should also be understood in the method described for the previous Khaṇḍasīmā. This is the distinction: in that Khaṇḍasīmā, it is not proper to perform the formal act by having [the foot or robe] lifted; one must be brought within the hatthapāsa (forearm's length). If a mountain rises from within the boundary, a monk standing on that mountain must be brought within the hatthapāsa. This same method applies even if one enters the inside of the mountain by psychic power. Indeed, a boundary that is being established does not extend to an area without limit. However, it should be understood that once a boundary is established, whatever object arises in any place and is connected to it is considered part of the boundary.

One establishing a Mahāsīmā (great boundary) with an extent of three yojanas should stand in the center and establish it so that it is one and a half yojanas in each of the four directions. If, standing in the center, one makes it three yojanas in each direction, it becomes six yojanas, which is not proper. When establishing a square or triangular boundary, it should be established so that it is three yojanas from corner to corner. If even a hair's breadth exceeds three yojanas at any edge, an offense is committed, and the boundary is not valid.

According to the words, "Bhikkhus, a boundary spanning across a river should not be established; for one who establishes it, there is an offense of dukkaṭa," a boundary spanning across a river should not be established. However, in a river where there is a permanent boat or a permanent bridge at the direct crossing point, it is proper to establish such a boundary spanning across the river.
