For it was said, "Bhikkhus, I allow the establishing of such a boundary spanning across a river where there is a permanent boat or a permanent bridge." If it is not at the direct crossing point but is slightly upstream or downstream, it is also proper. The Elder Karavika Tissa, however, said, "It is proper even if it is within the distance of a gāvuta."

A monk establishing this boundary spanning across a river should stand on one bank and proclaim the marker (nimitta) at the upper riverbank. From there, encompassing himself as much as the desired limit, he should proclaim the marker at the lower riverbank at the end of that limit. Then, he should proclaim the marker on the opposite bank directly facing the [first] marker. From there, by the power of the desired limit, he should proclaim markers up to the riverbank directly facing the first proclaimed marker upstream, bring it back, and connect it with the first proclaimed marker. Then, having brought the monks standing within all the markers into the hatthapāsa...
192:
...the boundary should be established with the kammavācā. Monks who are in the river and do not come [to the act] do not invalidate the formal act. At the conclusion of the establishment, excluding the river, both the opposite bank and this bank within the markers become a single boundary. The river, however, is not counted as part of the baddhasīmā (bound boundary); it is simply a separate nadīsīmā (river boundary).

If there is an island in the river and one wishes to include that island within the boundary, one should, following the previous method, proclaim the markers on the bank where one is standing and then proclaim markers at the near and far edges of the island. Then, one should proclaim a marker on the opposite bank directly facing the marker on this bank of the river, and from there, following the previous method, proclaim markers up to the point directly facing the first proclaimed marker upstream. Then, one should proclaim markers at the far and near edges of the island, bring them back, and connect them with the first proclaimed marker. Then, having brought all the monks on both banks and the island into the hatthapāsa, the boundary should be established with the kammavācā. Monks who are in the river and do not come do not invalidate the formal act. At the conclusion of the establishment, excluding the river, the two banks and the island within the markers become a single boundary. The river, however, is just a nadīsīmā.

If the island is longer than the extent of the vihārasīmā (monastery boundary) either upstream or downstream, one should proclaim a marker at the near edge of the island directly facing the marker of the vihārasīmā extent. From there, encompassing the tip of the island, one should again proclaim a marker at the far edge directly facing the marker at the near edge of the island. After that, following the previous method, starting from the facing marker on the opposite bank, one should proclaim the markers on the opposite bank and the markers at the far and near edges of the island and connect them with the first proclaimed marker. A boundary established by proclaiming in this way has the shape of a mountain (pabbata-saṇṭhāna). If the island is longer than the extent of the vihārasīmā in both directions, upstream and downstream, one should encompass both tips of the island and proclaim the markers, following the previous method, to complete the connection of markers. A boundary established by proclaiming in this way has the shape of a mudiṅga drum (mudiṅga-saṇṭhāna). If the island is small and within the extent of the vihārasīmā, the markers should be proclaimed on the island according to the very first method. A boundary established by proclaiming in this way has the shape of a paṇava drum (paṇava-saṇṭhāna). Thus far, the binding of a boundary should be understood.

When does a boundary established in this way cease to be a boundary? It ceases to be a boundary when the Saṅgha abolishes the boundary. How is it to be abolished?
193:
"Monks, a monk who designates a boundary should first designate the samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā (boundary of common communion), and afterwards, the avippavāsa-sīmā (boundary of non-separation from the three robes) should be designated. Monks, a monk who abolishes a boundary should first abolish the avippavāsa-sīmā, and afterwards, the samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā should be abolished." According to these words, it should be understood that the avippavāsa-sīmā is to be abolished first, and the samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā is to be abolished afterwards.

How is it abolished? A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha thus:

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. That avippavāsa-sīmā which was designated by the Saṅgha as one not to be separated from the three robes—if the Saṅgha is ready, the Saṅgha should abolish that avippavāsa-sīmā. This is the motion.

Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. That avippavāsa-sīmā which was designated by the Saṅgha as one not to be separated from the three robes—the Saṅgha is abolishing that avippavāsa-sīmā. Whichever venerable one approves of the abolition of this avippavāsa-sīmā, let him be silent. Whichever does not approve, let him speak.

The Saṅgha has abolished that avippavāsa-sīmā. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I understand it." (Thus he should inform).

In this way, the avippavāsa-sīmā is first abolished.

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. That boundary which was designated by the Saṅgha as a samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha (common communion and single Uposatha), if the Saṅgha is ready, the Saṅgha should abolish that samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha boundary. This is the motion.

Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. That boundary which was designated by the Saṅgha as a samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha—the Saṅgha is abolishing that samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha boundary. Whichever venerable one approves of the abolition of this samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha boundary, let him be silent. Whichever does not approve, let him speak."
194:
"The Saṅgha has abolished that samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha boundary. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I understand it." (Mahāvagga, 146) — In this way, the boundary is abolished.

A monk who abolishes a boundary should know the proper conduct. This is the conduct (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā, 144): Standing in a khaṇḍasīmā (partial boundary), one should not abolish an avippavāsa-sīmā; likewise, standing in an avippavāsa-sīmā, one should not abolish a khaṇḍasīmā. A monk standing in a khaṇḍasīmā should only abolish a khaṇḍasīmā; likewise, one standing in another boundary should only abolish that other boundary. Boundaries are abolished for two reasons: either to make a small boundary large for the expansion of the monastery, or to make a large boundary small to provide space for other monks' dwellings. In such abolition, if they know both the khaṇḍasīmā and the avippavāsa-sīmā, they will be able to both abolish and establish them. Even if they know the khaṇḍasīmā but not the avippavāsa-sīmā, they will still be able to abolish and establish them. Monks who do not know the khaṇḍasīmā but know only the avippavāsa-sīmā might be able to abolish them by standing in places free from doubt, such as the courtyard of a cetiya, the courtyard of a Bodhi tree, or an Uposatha hall, but they will certainly not be able to re-establish them. If they were to establish them, they would cause an overlapping of boundaries (sīmāsambheda), making a monastery boundary a non-monastery boundary; therefore, they should not be abolished. Those monks who know neither of the two will be able to neither abolish nor establish them. A boundary becomes a non-boundary either through a kammavācā (formal act) or through the disappearance of the Dispensation (Sāsana). Monks who do not know the boundary cannot perform the kammavācā; therefore, it should not be abolished. Only after knowing it well should it be abolished and established. This is the decision regarding the baddha-sīmā (bound boundary).

Abaddha-sīmā (unbound boundaries) are of three types: gāmasīmā (village boundary), sattabbhantarayasīmā (seven-inter-space boundary), and udakukkhepasīmā (water-splash boundary). Among these three, whatever is the extent of a village's land is called a gāmasīmā. By taking the village, the city and the town are also included (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā, 147). In those cities and villages, whatever area the village-headmen receive taxes from, whether that area is small or large, it is counted only as a gāmasīmā. The same method applies to city boundaries and town boundaries. Even within a single village land, if the king demarcates a certain area saying, "Let this be a separate village (visuṃgāma)," and gives it to someone, that area also becomes a visuṃgāma-sīmā. Therefore, that visuṃgāma-sīmā and other boundaries...
195: The boundaries of natural villages, towns, and market towns are just like fixed boundaries (baddha-sīmā); however, they do not provide protection from the offense of being separated from the three robes (ticīvara-vippavāsa). In a forest where there is no village, a boundary extending seven abbhantaras all around is called a sattabbhantara-sīmā. Here, a forest without a village is found in forest tracts such as the Viñjhāṭavī, or in the middle of the ocean, or on small islands in the ocean where fishermen do not go. 'Seven abbhantaras all around' means seven abbhantaras in every direction from the monks standing in the middle; diametrically, it is fourteen abbhantaras. In this context, one abbhantara is twenty-eight cubits (hattha) in length. This boundary expands according to the size of the assembly; therefore, the measurement of the abbhantara should be made starting from the edge of the assembly all around. If two groups of the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha separately, another abbhantara should be left between the two seven-abbhantara boundaries for the sake of an outskirt (upacāra). 'Monks, every river is not a baddha-sīmā, every ocean is not a baddha-sīmā, every natural lake is not a baddha-sīmā'—having thus rejected the status of fixed boundaries for rivers and so on, it was further said: 'Monks, in a river, in the ocean, or in a natural lake, the area defined by the splash of water all around a man of average strength is where they are of common communion and have a single Uposatha.' This is called a water-splash boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā). In that statement, a river has the characteristics already mentioned in the signs of a river; the ocean is also well-known. A hole (pool) that is not made by anyone digging, but is self-formed and remains filled with water coming from all around, and where water remains during the rainy season as described for a river, is called a natural lake (jātassara). Even a hole dug by water breaking out from a river or the ocean attains this characteristic; this too is simply a jātassara. In these rivers and so on, the area defined by the splash of water all around a man of average strength is called a water-splash boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā). How should the water-splash be performed? Just as gamblers throw a wooden ball, so a man of average strength should take water or sand in his hand and throw it with all his strength. The place where the water or sand thus thrown falls is called one water-splash. A monk standing outside the reach of that water-splash invalidates the formal act (kamma). As far as the assembly expands, so far the boundary expands; the water-splash from the edge of the assembly is the measure. This udakukkhepa-sīmā, in these rivers and so on...
196: ...is obtained only within these rivers and so on, not outside. Therefore, in a river or a natural lake, the area that the water overflows for the four months of the natural rainy season, and in the ocean, the area where the natural waves descend and stay—from that point onwards is the allowable ground (kappiya-bhūmi). Standing on that ground, it is proper to perform formal acts such as the Uposatha. Even in times of drought or in the summer when rivers and natural lakes are dry, that overflow area remains the allowable ground. However, if people dig a well or cultivate a field in a dried-up natural lake, that place becomes village territory (gāmakhetta). The water-splash boundary does not extend outside the area called the allowable ground; it only extends within. Therefore, within those rivers and so on, the limit of the water-splash should be determined all around starting from the edge of the assembly; this is the summary here. This is the detailed explanation: If a river is not very long and the Saṅgha sits everywhere from the source to the mouth, there is no need for the water-splash boundary; the entire river is sufficient for those monks. The statement made by Mahāsumatthera, 'In a river flowing for one yojana, one should abandon the upper half-yojana and perform the formal act in the lower half-yojana,' was rejected by Mahāpadumatthera. For the Blessed One said, 'The inner robe of a bhikkhunī who crosses at any place while covering the three circles gets wet'—this was stated as the measure of a river, not a yojana or a half-yojana. Therefore, by the power of this Pali text, it is proper to perform Saṅgha acts starting from the source of a river that has the characteristics previously mentioned. If, however, many monks perform formal acts separately in this river, all of them should leave another water-splash between their own and others' water-splash limits for the sake of a boundary interval (sīmantarika); it is said that more than that is proper, but less is not. The same method applies to natural lakes and the ocean. When monks go to perform a formal act in a river, if the river water is full to the brim, they should wear a water-cloth (udakasāṭika) and perform the act only within the river. If they are unable to do so, they may also perform it while staying on a boat. However, it is not proper to perform it on a moving boat. Why? Because the boundary is only the extent of the water-splash. A boat passes that boundary very quickly; in such a case, the motion (ñatti) would be in one boundary and the proclamation (anusāvanā) would be in another. Therefore, having stopped the boat with an oar or...
197:
A Sangha act should be performed by suspending from a rock or by tying to a tree growing within the river. It is permissible for monks standing on a platform (scaffolding) constructed within the river or on a tree growing within the river to perform the act.

If a branch of the tree or an aerial root extending from it rests upon a monastery boundary (vihāra-sīmā) or a village boundary (gāma-sīmā) outside the riverbank, the act should be performed only after clearing the boundary or cutting the branch. It is not permissible to perform the act by tying a boat to a branch or an aerial root of a tree growing outside the riverbank that has entered into the river; those performing the act must either clear the boundary or cut the branch to remove its connection to the bank. It is absolutely not permissible to perform the act with a boat tied to a stake driven into the riverbank.

When a bridge is built across a river, if both the bridge and the bridge pillars (supports) are located only within the river, it is permissible for monks standing on that bridge to perform the act. If the bridge or the bridge pillars rest upon the bank, it is not permissible; it should be performed only after clearing the boundary. Alternatively, if the bridge pillars are within the river and the bridge itself exists in the open space above both banks, it is permissible.

If there is a stone slab or a small island within the river, the area that is submerged by water throughout the four months of the normal rainy season, as previously mentioned, is reckoned as the river itself. An area submerged by a torrent during a period of excessive rain should not be taken as such. This is because such an area is reckoned only as a village boundary (gāma-sīmā).

When those who draw a canal from a river create a dam in the river, if that water flows either over the dam or by breaking through it, it is permissible to perform the act in all such places where the water flows. If the current is cut off by a dam or by a stone embankment and the water no longer flows, it is not permissible to perform the act in that place where the water does not flow. It is also not permissible to perform it on the dam itself. If some part of the dam is submerged by water like the aforementioned stone slab or island, it is permissible there. This is because that place is reckoned as the river itself.

When a lake is created by destroying a river, if the water comes and fills the lake because a levee is built below, it is not permissible to perform the act in this lake. However, it is permissible in the place where the water flows above. Below the lake, it is permissible starting from the place where the excess water discharged descends into the riverbed and flows.

In the winter and summer seasons when it does not rain, it is also permissible in a dry river; however, it is not permissible in a canal drawn from a river. If that canal breaks over time and becomes a riverbed, reaching the state of a river, it is permissible. If some river overflows and flows covering a village or town boundary (nigama-sīmā), it is indeed a river; it is permissible to perform the act there. If it overflows a monastery boundary (vihāra-sīmā), it is reckoned only as a monastery boundary.
198:
In the ocean as well, it is not permissible for monks performing a Sangha act to do so in a place where rising water or normal waves come with force and submerge it. However, in a place where normal waves subside and remain steady, that area is called the 'inner ocean' starting from the edge of the water; the act should be performed by those standing there. If the force of the waves is troublesome, it should be performed while standing in a boat or on a platform. The decision regarding these boats and so on should be understood in the same manner as mentioned for the river. If there is a stone slab in the ocean and waves sometimes come and submerge that stone slab and sometimes do not, it is not permissible to perform the act on that stone slab. This is because that stone slab is reckoned only as a village boundary (gāma-sīmā). If, however, it is always submerged by normal water whether waves come or not, it is permissible.

If there is an island or a mountain, and if that island is in a remote place where fishermen do not go, it is reckoned only as a forest boundary (arañña-sīmā). Within the limit of a round-trip journey that those fishermen can make in a day, however, it is reckoned as a village boundary; in that place, it is not permissible to perform the act without clearing the village boundary. If the ocean overflows and stays upon a village boundary or a town boundary (nigama-sīmā), it is indeed the ocean; it is permissible to perform the act in that ocean. If it overflows a monastery boundary, it is reckoned only as a monastery boundary.

Monks performing a Sangha act in a natural lake (jātassara) should not perform the act in a lake that dries up and has no water for drinking or for washing hands and feet as soon as the rain stops in the rainy season as mentioned before; this lake is not called a jātassara, but is reckoned only as village land (gāma-khetta). However, if water remains in the rainy season as mentioned, this lake alone is called a jātassara. In whatever part of that lake water remains throughout the four months of the rainy season, it is permissible to perform the act in that jātassara lake. If the water is deep, it is permissible for monks standing on a platform that has been constructed, or on a platform tied to a tree growing within the lake. The decision regarding stone slabs and islands within this jātassara lake is the same as mentioned for the river.

A jātassara lake that is sufficient for performing the act during a time of normal rainfall is permissible for performing a Sangha act even if it dries up and becomes waterless during a time of drought or in the summer and winter seasons. The statement mentioned in the Andhaka Commentary, 'Every jātassara lake that is dry and waterless belongs only to the village land (gāma-khetta),' should not be accepted. If, however, they dig a hole or a pond etc. for the sake of water in this jātassara lake, that place is not a jātassara and is reckoned as a village boundary. The same rule applies even when gourds, cucumbers, etc., are planted. If they fill that jātassara lake with earth and make it dry land...
199:
If an embankment is built on one side, making that natural lake into a large reservoir, the entire lake becomes an artificial lake (ajātassara) and is classified as a village boundary (gāmasīmā). A salt lake (loṇī) is also classified as a natural lake (jātassara). It is permissible to perform Sangha acts in a place where there is water throughout the four months of the rainy season. This is the decision regarding unbound boundaries (abaddhasīmā).

## In the Pālimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha,
## the discussion on the decision regarding boundaries is concluded.
## 25. Discussion on the Decision Regarding Uposatha and Pavāraṇā

In this matter of Uposatha and Pavāraṇā (according to the Nidānavatthanā of the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-aṭṭhakathā), there are three kinds of Uposatha based on the day: the fourteenth-day Uposatha (cātuddasī), the fifteenth-day Uposatha (pannarasī), and the harmony Uposatha (sāmaggi-uposatha). Among these Uposathas, in the three seasons of winter (hemanta), summer (gimha), and the rainy season (vassāna), by performing two on the third and seventh fortnights (pakkha) of each season, there are six fourteenth-day Uposathas. The remaining days are fifteenth-day Uposathas. Thus, there are twenty-four Uposathas in a year. This is the regular practice. When there is a suitable reason, it is also permissible to perform the Uposatha on another fourteenth day.

For monks who have completed the first rains-retreat (purimavassa), the full moon day of the first Kattika month (Pubbakattika) is the Pavāraṇā day. If those same monks postpone the Pavāraṇā because of harassment by quarrelsome people, then either the fourteenth day of the waning moon of the Kattika month or the full moon day of the second Kattika month (Pacchimakattika) becomes the Pavāraṇā day. For monks who have completed the second rains-retreat (pacchimavassa), the full moon day of the second Kattika month is the Pavāraṇā day. These three are the Pavāraṇā days. This is also the regular practice. When there is a suitable reason, it is also permissible to perform Pavāraṇā on the fourteenth days preceding the two Kattika full moon days.

However, when a divided Saṅgha is reunited according to the method mentioned in the Kosambakakkhandhaka, and the Saṅgha performs the act of communal harmony (saṅghasāmaggi) to settle that legal issue (adhikaraṇa), the Uposatha should be performed at that very moment. Because of the statement, "The Pātimokkha should be recited," any day other than the fourteenth or fifteenth can be called an Uposatha day. For monks who have completed the rains-retreat, this very day within the month of Kattika is called the Harmony Pavāraṇā day (sāmaggi-pavāraṇā). Thus, the Uposatha should be performed on these three types of days. When performing it, if it is the fourteenth-day Uposatha, one should say, "Today is the fourteenth-day Uposatha." If it is the harmony Uposatha,
